papers.title: WISER-RL: A Wake-Sleep Learning Mechanism for Robot Reinforcement Learning from One Demonstration
papers.abstract: A robot learning from one human demonstration may rarely succeed on its own, leaving reinforcement learning (RL) with little reward feedback. We introduce WISER-RL ({W}ake--sleep policy improvement loop, {I}mitation, and {S}elective {E}xperience {R}eplay), a composite reinforcement learning framework that turns assisted practice into autonomous control. During wake, GPTDAgger monitors disagreement among actions sampled by a diffusion policy. When disagreement crosses a threshold, a frozen GPT controller uses retrieved experience to continue the episode. During sleep, Conflict-Aware Experience Reweighting (CAER) compares visually matched successful trajectories and downweights conflicting action windows with more steps remaining to success. The policy imitates the reweighted successes and learns from both successes and failures through offline advantage-guided RL before collecting the next round. After final online PPO refinement, the autonomous policy succeeded in 100% evaluations on each of six LIBERO tasks and 100% trials on each of two real-robot tasks.

A central goal of robotics is to acquire a new skill from one or a few human demonstrations and become proficient through practice [6]. A person can watch an example, reason about how it applies to a different scene, and gradually perform the skill with less deliberate effort. For robots, this motivates combining rapid adaptation from examples with lasting autonomous competence.

Reinforcement learning (RL) refines robotic policies through interaction [27, 16], but initially weak policies struggle to collect useful experience. With sparse success rewards, many attempts can fail before the robot discovers a useful behavior [3, 36, 22, 30, 11]. Recently, models such as GPT-6-Astra have demonstrated the ability to adapt from one or a few examples through in-context learning [4]. Drawing on strong reasoning and broad prior knowledge, these models can interpret a demonstration and apply it to a new scene. Yet this contextual ability does not automatically translate into a fast, efficient learned policy. The challenge is to turn adaptation from a few examples into an autonomous policy that improves through practice.

papers.title: Benefit of Structured Representations: When Equivariance Helps in Image Classification
papers.abstract: Equivariant neural networks promise improved representation learning through structural guarantees. However, mainstream vision encoders rarely incorporate equivariance for most geometric symmetries. Images are a particularly interesting modality with many such symmetries and extensive datasets from which to learn this structure. In this work, we investigate when vision encoders benefit from geometric inductive biases. We study the discrete rotation group of quarter-turns (C4) which acts losslessly without interpolation or boundary artifacts. Combined with image classification as a controlled invariant objective, this allows for a principled empirical investigation into the role of structural guarantees. We introduce ConvNeXt-C4 as a rotation equivariant ConvNeXt with dimension-equivalent yet orientation-structured representations. Training from scratch, our experiments show, that the C4 variant outperforms its base model across all tasks while operating with 6x fewer parameters and 1.6x fewer FLOPs. Its performance advantage increases log-linearly with decreasing training set size, with pre-training providing a similar improvement across both model variants. Analyzing the classifier head reveals that orientation information from the representations' structure is actively used, improving performance by 4.90% across all datasets. Our results highlight the sample-efficiency benefits of equivariance and the value of retained orientation information, motivating further investigation beyond image classification. Code is available at https://github.com/hlzl/equivariant-convnext.

Despite vast amounts of research on geometric deep learning in recent years, modern neural networks do not widely incorporate geometric inductive biases. This is despite the fact that the rigorous mathematical foundations of equivariant models for encoding geometric priors reduce hypothesis space complexity and provably bound generalization error (Cohen et al., 2019; Elesedy, 2023). Instead, learning these biases from massive amounts of pre-training data remains the predominant paradigm of most current approaches. In this work, we ask: when do the beneficial properties of equivariant architectures actually benefit learning?

Despite vast amounts of research on geometric deep learning in recent years, modern neural networks do not widely incorporate geometric inductive biases. This is despite the fact that the rigorous mathematical foundations of equivariant models for encoding geometric priors reduce hypothesis space complexity and provably bound generalization error (Cohen et al., 2019; Elesedy, 2023). Instead, learning these biases from massive amounts of pre-training data remains the predominant paradigm of most current approaches. In this work, we ask: when do the beneficial properties of equivariant architectures actually benefit learning?

Imaging is a particularly relevant area to study this question, with vast amount of data and research on equivariant methods available (Cohen and Welling, 2016; Kondor and Trivedi, 2018; Thomas et al., 2018; Weiler and Cesa, 2019; Satorras et al., 2021). The adoption gap of equivariant methods in imaging can be attributed to computational overhead and diminishing returns on modern architectures. However, this trade-off has rarely been evaluated on modern backbones using systematic architectural interventions. While recent geometric deep learning has shifted toward irregular modalities, 2D images represent the hardest benchmark as standard vision backbones are mature and highly optimized. Image classification provides an ideal testbed where predictions should be invariant under rotation, ensuring any measured effect stems purely from the encoder. Planar rotation is an exact symmetry for semantics in vision, with a rotated image depicting the same object. It is thus a good starting point to better understand the role of geometric inductive biases in this competitive modality.

First, a diverse group of training datasets with varying properties such as sample size and data symmetry. Third, an analysis that clearly differentiates between (i) equivariant feature fields that preserve information internally and (ii) invariant readout closure that permanently eliminates information.

In this work, we propose a C4C_{4} rotation equivariant ConvNeXt (Liu et al., 2022) closely resembling its base model. We choose ConvNeXt because it is the only architecture proposed so far that rivals vision transformers in performance while maintaining strict translation equivariance (Woo et al., 2023; Siméoni et al., 2025). The discrete rotation group of quarter-turns (C4C_{4}), which acts as an exact permutation of pixel coordinates on a square grid with zero interpolation or resampling artifacts, allows for isolating the effect of geometric symmetries. Using an approach to factorize the equivariant convolution operation based on Bekkers et al. (2024), it remains a highly efficient architecture. The model is evaluated across a benchmark panel of 9 vision datasets spanning three orders of magnitude in training set size alongside ImageNet-1K pre-training (Deng et al., 2009). Our empirical findings reveal that C4C_{4}-equivariance substantially improves performance under data-scarcity and provides structure in the representation that is leveraged across all data regimes.

papers.title: Can Visual World Models See Force?
papers.abstract: World models and vision-language-action policy models are increasingly proposed as foundations for robot manipulation. They predict how scenes evolve and which actions to take, yet successful manipulation depends not solely on following observable trajectories but also on the hidden variable of interaction force. Neurophysiology has shown that humans possess a visual prior for this hidden variable, motivating us to ask the question: Do the representations of visual foundation models also capture the forces involved in an interaction? We define force awareness as the ability of representations to (1) indicate when contact force is applied, (2) track how it changes during an interaction, and (3) reflect how large it is. We probe frozen image, video, world- and policy model representations with a lightweight readout trained on synchronized video and force measurements from two manipulation datasets. Our experiments show that most models capture when contact occurs but not how much force is being applied. Surprisingly, robot post-training does not improve this either, highlighting an important gap in current models capabilities.

papers.intro:
World-action models may enable generalist robot manipulation by learning to predict how the world changes together with the actions a robot takes. DreamZero, for example, jointly predicts future video and actions, building on large-scale video pretraining [40]. Related approaches use predictive video representations for planning or train vision-language-action models across diverse robot demonstrations [2, 21, 5, 4]. These efforts raise the prospect that physical understanding can emerge from more video, larger models, and more robot data. Yet inaccurate force application has been identified as a failure mode of robot foundation models [31, 42], which commonly predict motion targets while leaving force control to low-level controllers [2, 21, 5, 4, 1]. These failures raise the question of whether the models’ representations capture the forces involved in manipulation, beyond the motion they predict.

An example of similar motion trajectories but different force application can be seen in everyday activities such as opening a fridge vs. a cabinet door. The doors can follow similar trajectories but require different forces because of friction or resistance that is difficult to see. Vision can provide useful cues here: humans use visual appearance to anticipate an object’s weight and scale their initial lifting forces [7], while visual feedback during lifting helps correct expectation-driven force errors [6]. These findings motivate us to investigate whether visual world models also acquire representations that implicitly encode interaction force.

Prior evaluations of visual foundation models reveal difficulties with hidden mechanical properties and broader physical understanding [35, 8]. At the same time, probing studies find geometric information, physical plausibility signals, and motion variables in pretrained representations [10, 18, 12]. Readouts of elasticity, viscosity, and friction provide further evidence of accessible physical information, although accurate value prediction in real-world videos remains challenging [41]. Together, these studies establish the systematic evaluation of physical and geometric information in pretrained representations as a research contribution in its own right. We extend this line of inquiry to interaction force by asking: how much force can be decoded from models trained for general visual, generative, and action objectives?

papers.title: Beyond Pose Control: Anatomically Consistent Ultrasound Video Generation
papers.abstract: Camera-controlled video generation anticipates how a scene appears from new viewpoints by relying on a prior learned implicitly from large-scale data. Ultrasound poses the same problem, with the probe pose as the viewpoint, but under opposite conditions: anatomy offers an explicit prior that every sonographer relies on, whereas tracked scans are too scarce to learn it implicitly. As a result, pose control alone is not enough, and pose-conditioned ultrasound generators produce implausible anatomy in unscanned regions and inconsistent anatomy on revisits. We go beyond pose control and give the generator the two kinds of knowledge that make up a sonographer's mental model. An anatomical prior, built from a population of subjects, guides generation where nothing has been scanned, and is refined online by every generated chunk towards the scanned subject. A 3D latent memory, designed around the cross-sectional physics of ultrasound, compounds the generated slices into a volume of the patient and reslices it at new poses, keeping revisited anatomy consistent. The fine-grained memory enters the generator at the input, while the coarse anatomy prior guides the layout across transformer blocks. Experiments on thyroid, kidney, and lumbar spine show improved visual fidelity, pose following, and anatomical consistency over pose-conditioned and memory-augmented baselines.

papers.intro:
Humans navigate new environments with a mental prior learned from many similar ones. Entering an unfamiliar hotel room, we expect the bathroom near the door and the bed further inside; the exact layout differs from room to room, and every step refines our expectation. Video generation models [27, 13] acquire a comparable prior from large-scale data, learning how scenes typically look and move. Camera-controlled video generation [29, 14, 4] builds on it to anticipate how a scene appears from a new viewpoint, but this prior remains implicit in the weights. Ultrasound (US) poses the same problem, with the probe pose as the viewpoint, yet under opposite conditions. Anatomy plays the role of the room layout: the relative positions of organs are shared across people and known to every expert sonographer, while their exact shape varies between individuals and becomes clear only as the scan proceeds.

Moreover, robotic ultrasound [19, 26, 17, 9] requires not only accurate pose following but also consistency with the underlying 3D anatomy [6].

Moreover, robotic ultrasound [19, 26, 17, 9] requires not only accurate pose following but also consistency with the underlying 3D anatomy [6].

A sonographer’s mental model holds two kinds of knowledge: anatomical information, which predicts what lies in unscanned tissue, and a patient-specific 3D spatial volume, which preserves what has already been scanned. Existing ultrasound world models, such as SonoWorld [32] and UltraWorld [31], learn anatomy implicitly from expanded training data but do not explicitly maintain both forms of knowledge during generation. Natural-video generators maintain such records through retrieved frames [33, 30] or 3D caches [22, 28], but these rely on camera geometry, in which neighboring views overlap and can be reprojected. An ultrasound image is instead a planar cross-section, and every out-of-plane motion reveals tissue that no earlier frame contains, so memory mechanisms designed for natural videos do not directly transfer to ultrasound.

Anatomically consistent ultrasound generation requires three complementary capabilities: producing plausible anatomy in unseen regions, preserving it across revisits, and responding coherently to probe motion. We therefore go beyond pose control by providing two explicit forms of anatomical knowledge. (i) What guides generation in unseen regions? A population-level anatomical prior that, like the hotel-room expectation described earlier, is progressively refined by generated observations to adapt to the subject. (ii) What preserves anatomy across revisits? A 3D latent memory that compounds generated slices and reslices them at new probe poses, following ultrasound imaging geometry rather than camera projection. Together, the prior guides unseen anatomy while the memory preserves previously generated structures.

We therefore inject them differently: memory is concatenated with the video latent at the input, whereas the prior guides early transformer blocks through residual conditioning. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We propose an explicit anatomical prior for ultrasound video generation: a population model of anatomy that is updated online from the generated frames, so that it adapts the prior to the subject even in regions not yet scanned. • We propose a compounding-based 3D latent memory, the first memory for video generation designed around cross-sectional imaging rather than camera geometry, which keeps revisited regions consistent. • We propose a dual-path conditioning: the fine-grained memory is concatenated with the input, while the coarse prior is injected across transformer blocks to guide the layout without being treated as fine detail. papers.title: Minimising sample size across analysis strategies in preclinical research: Reduced power or negligible benefit
papers.abstract: Preclinical animal studies often allow multiple valid statistical analysis strategies, which can result in different sample sizes required to achieve a target power. Because reducing animal use is an ethical, financial, and practical priority, researchers have a clear incentive to choose the strategy requiring the fewest animals. This may, however, favour an overly optimistic estimate of the sample size required, particularly when prior information is uncertain or biased. This study investigates how minimising sample size across analysis strategies affects statistical power and animal use. We conceptualise this practice as sample size hacking, describe its underlying mechanism, and evaluate its consequences using a simulation study based on a real preclinical cancer study. We varied effect sizes, the level of uncertainty in prior information, and the degree of follow-up bias to assess the resulting sample size reductions and achieved statistical power. Sample size minimisation across analysis strategies substantially reduced the achieved statistical power in several scenarios, particularly for moderate effect sizes and greater uncertainty in prior information. For larger effect sizes or in the presence of follow-up bias, the impact on power was less pronounced, but the resulting reduction in sample size was also smaller. Selecting an analysis strategy solely because it yields the smallest calculated sample size may in fact compromise statistical power, while offering only limited animal savings in other settings. These findings underscore the importance of justifying and pre-specifying the analysis strategy before sample size planning to limit potentially problematic analytical flexibility, reduce the risk of underpowered studies, and promote transparency in preclinical research.

papers.intro:
In recent years, there has been growing awareness that data analysts face numerous uncertain choices when analysing empirical data (Hoffmann et al., 2021). These so-called researcher degrees of freedom (Simmons et al., 2011) can give rise to a wide range of possible analysis strategies. When such flexibility is combined with selective reporting based on the observed results, it can lead to overly optimistic findings in the literature that are difficult or impossible to replicate (Hoffmann et al., 2021; Ioannidis, 2005). To address these concerns, various measures have been suggested, including improving statistical planning and study design through power analyses and the pre-registration of studies, with the aim of fixing key decisions in advance and thereby limiting researcher degrees of freedom during data analysis, as well as reducing opportunities to favour positive results through questionable research practices (Munafò et al., 2017; Nosek et al., 2018).

While we agree that appropriate power analyses and sample size calculations are essential to credible science, we emphasise that sample size planning is itself not free of researcher degrees of freedom. Anyone with experience in sample size planning will recognise that this process involves a certain degree of flexibility. For example, sample size planning often involves flexibility in the choice of the procedure used to determine sample size, such as simulations or one of several sample size formulas. In addition, there may already be flexibility in the choice of the statistical analysis strategy before sample size planning, persisting during this process: for a given research question, several statistical methods (e.g., statistical models or tests) may be considered appropriate (possibly with different specifications concerning, e.g., measurement time points), each relying on different assumptions and leading to different sample size requirements. As these assumptions are difficult to verify fully—particularly during the planning phase—the choice of method cannot be uniquely determined, thus constituting one source of researcher degrees of freedom already before data analysis.

Given the complexity of biological systems and the limited understanding of their underlying mechanisms, researchers often face greater uncertainty when selecting a statistical analysis strategy (especially in exploratory settings, but also to some extent in confirmatory research): multiple plausible variants of the estimand are often available, and prior knowledge is often insufficient. Nevertheless, the analysis strategy must be specified before the main study begins to enable an appropriate sample size calculation; in preclinical animal research, this is typically required for ethical approval of animal experiments (Percie du Sert et al., 2020). Because the main study is designed to be analysed according to the pre-specified strategy and conducted with the corresponding sample size, the researcher degrees of freedom primarily arise during the planning stage rather than the analysis stage.

The information required for sample size planning is often based on prior information such as published studies, pilot experiments, previous experience with similar studies, or expert judgement. However, at the preclinical stage, biological knowledge is often not sufficiently developed to define key quantities for sample size planning reliably, such as what magnitude of an effect would constitute a meaningful change in the outcome. Other required inputs, including the outcome variance or correlations between repeated measurements, are often even more difficult to specify reliably. Importantly, relying on preliminary information can introduce several types of bias in sample size estimation. One of them is the so-called follow-up bias, which arises when researchers preferentially pursue follow-up studies if preliminary results suggest that adequate statistical power can be achieved with a manageable sample size. This selection process can lead to systematically inflated effect size estimates and, consequently, underpowered follow-up studies (Albers and Lakens, 2018). In addition, publication bias and general uncertainty in the information required for sample size calculations, such as effect sizes and variance parameters based on previous experience, can further distort sample size planning (Anderson et al., 2017). To address these issues, a range of mitigation approaches has been proposed, including adjustments of effect size estimates to account for bias and uncertainty (Anderson et al., 2017; Perugini et al., 2014), and approaches that formally incorporate prior information within a Bayesian framework (Mütze et al., 2017). We do not focus on such bias mitigation approaches, as they ignore uncertainty arising from methodological choice.

papers.title: Formalization, Transparency, and Collusion in Open-Source Game Theory
papers.abstract: Cooperation among AI agents will undermine alignment protocols when it takes the form of collusion. Under these protocols, agents often have some information about one another, and how much they have may determine whether they collude. Open-source game theory studies the extreme case, in which each program reads its opponent's source code and acts based on what it can prove about it. We develop formal foundations for this theory: we specify a concrete proof system, resolve an open problem concerning DupocBot and CupodBot through a transposition argument, and mechanize the framework in Lean 4; to our knowledge, this is the first mechanization of resource-bounded open-source game theory. We then extend the framework to the more realistic setting of partial transparency, where each program receives only partial information about its opponent. In Prisoner's Dilemma experiments, where mutual cooperation models collusion, greater transparency increases both the cooperation sustainable in equilibrium and the cooperation selected by replicator dynamics. This suggests that controlling how much agents can know about one another matters for alignment protocols.

papers.intro:
Artificial intelligence systems increasingly act autonomously and interact with one another, both during training and deployment (Hammond et al., 2025). Yet these strategic interactions can be puzzling; for example, reports on the recent OpenAI–Hugging Face incidents describe AI agents collaborating towards a shared goal – tricking the evaluator – even when doing so appeared individually irrational, such as when agents ended their own runs to obtain information for others (OpenAI, 2026; METR, 2026). The classical prediction (and recommendation) of game theory is that rational players never choose dominated actions, making them defect in the Prisoner’s Dilemma although cooperation would be mutually beneficial. Moreover, even when cooperative equilibria exist, as in the infinitely repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma, one must still explain which mechanisms of equilibrium selection lead players to coordinate on them. The agents’ behavior thus raises questions about the “unreasonable effectiveness of collaboration” (one might say collusion) among AI models. Understanding how such collaboration emerges and which conditions sustain it will be essential to aligning superintelligent models that interact strategically with one another and with humans.11 1 We used generative AI tools in this work; see the AI Use Statement for details.

One instance of such cooperation that game theory can explain arises in program meta-games (Tennenholtz, 2004; Kalai et al., 2010), introduced to model commitments among human institutions and software programs. In these games, players’ actions are implemented by mutually transparent commitment devices, which we call programs. These devices may take the form of software code, model weights, company bylaws, or governmental constitutions, and mutual transparency means that each program has access to the internal workings of the other players’ programs. The Nash equilibria of the resulting meta-game, called program equilibria, are shown to sustain outcomes that are not equilibria of the base game (Tennenholtz, 2004), including cooperation in the Prisoner’s Dilemma. Additionally, programs can prove statements about their opponents within a given formal system, and thus can condition their behavior on the resulting proofs (Bárász et al., 2014; Critch et al., 2022), making cooperation verifiably robust. We follow the latter in referring to this field as open-source game theory.22 2 The name refers to open-source software, i.e. software whose source code is widely available for inspection and modification, which was the motivating example in the seminal work of Tennenholtz (2004).

Our motivating application is AI alignment. Training protocols (e.g. debate (Irving et al., 2018)) and deployment protocols (e.g. oversight (Greenblatt et al., 2024)) often rely on agents challenging or evaluating one another. If those agents collude and pursue objectives that conflict with human preferences, the effectiveness of the above methods will be undermined.44 4 By collusion we mean that the agents coordinate on an outcome that benefits them with respect to their own, possibly misaligned, preferences but that is contrary to the purpose of the protocol. When each agent is individually tempted to report, the interaction is a Prisoner’s Dilemma and collusion is mutual cooperation. Open-source game theory is well suited for modeling interactions in which agents condition their behavior on information about one another. Its classical formulation, however, assumes full transparency, in that each program receives its opponent’s exact program as input. In most settings of practical interest, however, players have only partial access to one another; for instance, a deployed model may be queried as a black box without exposing its weights, or agents may know little more than that they belong to the same base model family or company. We therefore extend the framework to partial transparency and examine its implications for cooperation. We first (v) introduce a model of partial transparency in which each program receives as input a belief about its opponent’s program, determined by the actual program but not necessarily identifying it uniquely (section 2.2), and (vi) apply this framework to our running example of the Prisoner’s Dilemma (section 2.2.1). papers.title: Diagnostically Meaningful, Privacy-aware Synthetic Chest CT via Class-Conditional Latent Sampling in Diffusion Autoencoders
papers.abstract:
Large, well-annotated datasets are essential for developing medical artificial intelligence models, yet data sharing is often restricted by privacy regulations. Synthetic images may help address this limitation if they preserve diagnostic information while reducing the risk of reproducing patient data. We developed a diffusion autoencoder-based framework for class-conditional synthetic chest CT generation that incorporates latent-space distance filtering to reduce the likelihood of regenerating training samples.
  A diffusion autoencoder was trained on the public RSNA 2020 Pulmonary Embolism (PE) dataset. PE-positive and PE-negative images were synthesized by sampling latent representations from class-specific kernel density estimates. Samples with a nearest-neighbor latent-space distance below a predefined threshold were rejected. To assess diagnostic utility, ResNet-50 classifiers were trained across 10 independent runs using real, synthetic, or mixed real-synthetic datasets. Performance was evaluated on a held-out real test set using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with DeLong 95% confidence intervals (CIs).
  Models trained on synthetic data achieved an AUC of 0.862 (95% CI, 0.851-0.874), only slightly lower than models trained on real data (AUC = 0.872, 95% CI, 0.861-0.883) and mixed real-synthetic data (AUC = 0.865, 95% CI, 0.855-0.876). These differences were statistically significant (p < 0.05) but small in absolute terms. A nearest-neighbor copy-detection analysis of 38,000 synthetic slices found no direct copies of real training images.
  These findings indicate that the synthetic CT images preserve diagnostically meaningful information for image-level PE classification while incorporating measures intended to enhance privacy awareness and reduce similarity to real patient data.

papers.intro:
Artificial intelligence (AI) methods are increasingly investigated for applications throughout the medical imaging workflow, including clinical education, image interpretation, and treatment planning [34, 16, 19, 5]. The development and evaluation of these methods depend on access to large and diverse labeled imaging datasets. However, medical images are costly to acquire and annotate, expert labeling is time-consuming, and sharing of medical images across institutions is restricted by patient privacy requirements and data protection regulations. Two complementary strategies have been proposed to address this restricted access. Federated learning enables decentralized model training without transferring the underlying datasets [27], yet requires institutions to host and maintain local infrastructure for every collaborative study, and does not inherently prevent a trained model from memorizing sensitive information [26]. Synthetic medical images offer a different strategy: generative models can learn the distribution represented in an existing dataset and produce new samples that preserve information relevant to a downstream diagnostic task [31, 32], potentially providing a source of training data that does not correspond to any single real patient. Unlike federated learning, synthetic datasets can be accessed and shared directly, making them particularly useful when images are needed for model development, methodological evaluation, or collaboration outside a controlled federated setting. Before such applications can be considered, however, the extent to which synthetic images retain diagnostically relevant information must be established empirically. If classifiers trained exclusively on synthetic images perform comparably to those trained on real images when evaluated on held-out real data, synthetic datasets could support model development without requiring direct access to the corresponding real patient data.

Denoising diffusion probabilistic models have emerged as a widely used class of generative models [22]. Unlike generative adversarial networks, which are often difficult to train, DDPMs avoid adversarial optimization and can generate high-fidelity images [13, 4], motivating their investigation for medical image generation and related applications [32, 15]. Diffusion autoencoders extend this framework by combining a semantic encoder with a conditional diffusion model: the semantic encoder maps an image to a compact latent representation containing high-level image information, while the diffusion model generates an image conditioned on this representation. This structure enables image generation to be controlled directly through the semantic latent space, offering a natural mechanism for class-conditional synthesis.

This structure enables image generation to be controlled directly through the semantic latent space, offering a natural mechanism for class-conditional synthesis.

This latent-space structure suggests a practical workflow for institutions holding proprietary, labeled imaging data that cannot be freely shared. A diffusion autoencoder can first be pretrained once, in a fully label-free manner, on a large corpus of unlabeled images. An institution can then apply the resulting semantic encoder to its own proprietary, labeled dataset, extracting a compact latent vector for each image together with its associated label. Class-conditional distributions can be estimated directly from these labeled latent vectors, for instance via kernel density estimation (KDE), and new latent vectors sampled from these distributions can be decoded back into images. The resulting synthetic, labeled dataset is derived from, but not identical to, the original proprietary data, and could in principle be shared or used for downstream model development in place of the original images.

In this study, we develop and evaluate such a framework for generating class-specific chest CT images. The diffusion autoencoder is first trained without class labels on a large set of images, jointly learning a semantic encoder and a latent-conditioned diffusion model. Labeled CT images are then encoded into the semantic latent space, and separate distributions are estimated for pulmonary embolism (PE)-positive and PE-negative images using KDE. New latent vectors sampled from these class-conditional distributions are subsequently decoded to generate synthetic images. To limit the generation of samples resembling real images, we additionally apply a latent-distance rejection procedure: each sampled latent vector is compared with the latent representations of the real training images, and samples falling below a predefined nearest-neighbor distance threshold are rejected. We refer to this practical safeguard as privacy-aware generation, as distinct from methods that provide a formal privacy guarantee. An overview of the framework is shown in Fig. 1.

We evaluate the framework in four steps. First, we examine whether the learned latent representations encode information associated with PE status, and whether this information is preserved after KDE-based sampling. Second, we assess the similarity between real and synthetic images and evaluate the diagnostic utility of the generated data by comparing image-level PE classifiers trained exclusively on either real or synthetic images and tested on held-out real images. As a secondary experiment, we evaluate whether combining real and synthetic images in a class-balanced training set improves classifier performance beyond real-only training. Third, we compare Grad-CAM saliency maps qualitatively across training conditions to examine which image regions the resulting classifiers rely on. Finally, we perform a copy-detection analysis to assess whether synthetic images closely reproduce individual real training images, as a practical check on patient privacy.

First, we examine whether the learned latent representations encode information associated with PE status, and whether this information is preserved after KDE-based sampling. Second, we assess the similarity between real and synthetic images and evaluate the diagnostic utility of the generated data by comparing image-level PE classifiers trained exclusively on either real or synthetic images and tested on held-out real images. As a secondary experiment, we evaluate whether combining real and synthetic images in a class-balanced training set improves classifier performance beyond real-only training. Third, we compare Grad-CAM saliency maps qualitatively across training conditions to examine which image regions the resulting classifiers rely on. Finally, we perform a copy-detection analysis to assess whether synthetic images closely reproduce individual real training images, as a practical check on patient privacy.

papers.title: Geoflaw: Geofeed Errors, Inconsistencies, and Flaws
papers.abstract: Geofeeds allow IP address resource owners to self-publish the geolocation of their prefixes, and adoption has grown substantially: as of November 2026, more than 5,000 geofeeds cover 1.6M prefixes. We measure geofeed errors, inconsistencies, and flaws by collecting geofeed references from the WHOIS of all five RIRs weekly over three months and downloading every referenced geofeed. The share of WHOIS objects complying with RFC 9632, which specifies how inetnum objects reference geofeeds, drops from 90% to 61%, driven by a single operator's objects with multiple geofeed references. Each week, 12-20% of geofeed URLs cannot be downloaded, and one in five downloaded geofeeds violates RFC 8805, which defines the geofeed CSV format. Moreover, 17% of geofeeds list IPv4 prefixes whose WHOIS object references a different geofeed. Finally, 281k prefixes appear in more than one geofeed, 3.8k of them with conflicting locations, and for 26% of these conflicts no geofeed is authoritative. We publish our results on a public dashboard, which one large CDN has already used to fix its geofeeds.

IP geolocation maps IP addresses to physical locations. IP geolocation supports critical Internet services by providing e.g., access control, content customization, network management, targeted advertising, fraud prevention, and policy enforcement. This work focuses on “geofeeds.”

IP geolocation maps IP addresses to physical locations. IP geolocation supports critical Internet services by providing e.g., access control, content customization, network management, targeted advertising, fraud prevention, and policy enforcement. This work focuses on “geofeeds.”

Geofeeds are a standard CSV format for representing IP prefix geolocations (Kline et al., 2020), while geofeed URLs are now standardized as a RPSL field for WHOIS inetnum objects (Bush et al., 2024). Geofeeds are an increasingly popular means for providers to self-publish and self-report geolocation information; the geolocatemuch project reports 713,460 IP prefixes with geofeed locations on November 4, 2026 (Candela et al., 2026). However, our independent geofeed gathering and processing methodology finds 1,637,955 prefixes on the same date. This large discrepancy (2.3 times as many prefixes) motivates our study of errors and inconsistencies within RPSL entries, geofeed hosting, and the geofeeds themselves. These validation issues significantly impact the ingestion and use of geofeeds by geolocation providers, often unbeknownst to the networks publishing geofeeds. Our contributions include: • Longitudinal WHOIS compliance analysis (§3): Across three months of weekly snapshots from all five RIRs, the share of WHOIS geofeed references that comply with RFC 9632 drops from 90% to 61% due to a single operator, and about 30% of LACNIC’s objects reference geofeeds via HTTP instead of HTTPS. • Download, format, and coverage errors (§3): Each week, 12–20% of geofeed URLs cannot be downloaded, one in five geofeeds violates RFC 8805, and 17% list prefixes whose WHOIS object references a different geofeed. • Inconsistencies between geofeeds (§4): Of the 1.6M geofeed prefixes, 281k (17%) appear in multiple geofeeds, 3.8k of them with conflicting locations, and 26% of these conflicts lack an authoritative geofeed. We also identify cases that RFC 9632 does not resolve, such as an inetnum object referencing multiple contradicting geofeeds. • Geoflaw Geofeed Observatory Dashboard (Gasser and Beverly, 2026): An interactive and queryable interface to our data for the network operator community, which one large CDN already used to fix its geofeeds.

papers.title: RegionAlign: Manipulating Parameter Layouts for Localized Fault Injection on LLMs and VLMs
papers.abstract: Physical fault injection can flip stored weight bits, degrading LLMs and VLMs. Existing work largely overlooks how supply-chain manipulation affects fault vulnerability. We introduce RegionAlign, which allows a malicious provider to manipulate only the parameter layout before deployment, using bit-sensitivity search and channel permutations to concentrate vulnerable bits in one memory region while preserving weight values and clean performance. Under matched budgets, software experiments show greater degradation from search-selected in-region flips with RegionAlign than with original or random layouts. EMFI feasibility study confirms weight corruption. RegionAlign reveals a stealthy supply-chain threat that layout manipulation weakens physical fault resilience.

papers.intro:
Deploying third-party Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) introduces supply-chain security risks: providers control the models they distribute, and users who check only task performance may overlook malicious modifications that preserve clean behavior [1, 2]. A separate threat arises in hardware: fault injection corrupts the stored weights of the deployed model to degrade model performance, and bit-flip attacks (BFAs) are its main realization, flipping a small number of weight bits [3, 4, 5]. Bit flips in the stored weights have been studied under different threat models: untargeted inference-time degradation after model deployment, and backdoors implanted by bit flips, which are activated later either by an input trigger [6] or by the fault itself [7].

These two threats, model supply-chain attacks and physical fault-injection attacks after deployment, have so far been studied in isolation: supply-chain attacks rarely consider the physical constraints of fault injection, while physical attacks typically assume a fixed parameter layout or rely on an input trigger [5, 6, 8, 9]. This separation leaves a practical aspect unaddressed: vulnerable bits identified across a model can be widely scattered in memory [4, 10, 5, 9], whereas a localized physical fault injection can affect only a limited region. Consequently, even attacks requiring only a few bit flips may demand multiple injection locations [5, 8], making physical realization far harder than a single localized injection.

In this paper, we identify the parameter layout as a critical link between supply-chain manipulation and physical fault injection. The parameter layout is the mapping from logical weights to their storage positions, independent of the weight values themselves. We focus on bit-flip attacks. A malicious provider can rearrange LLM and VLM weights before the model’s publication to concentrate vulnerable bits within a physically clustered region while preserving clean (fault-free) model behavior. In the original layout, vulnerable bits are mostly scattered across memory. In the rearranged layout, vulnerable bits can be concentrated within a fixed target region through channel permutations that leave clean model behavior nearly unchanged. After deployment, an attacker with the required physical access performs one physical fault injection in the single target region to cause the degradation. Figure 1 illustrates the attack.

To find vulnerable parameter layouts, we introduce RegionAlign, an attack that jointly searches admissible layouts and damaging bit flips within a fixed target region. For each candidate layout, we rank flips by estimated effects and select them by measured loss increases. We adapt channel permutations used for structured sparsity [11] to LLM/VLM attention and quantization constraints, preserving weight values and model function in exact arithmetic. Preparation requires no retraining and leaves the inference pipeline unchanged, and each layout must pass independent checks of clean task performance. Together, these steps yield parameter layouts that preserve clean model performance while making selected in-region bit flips more damaging than under the original layout.

We first evaluate RegionAlign through software fault injection, applying search-selected bit flips directly to the INT8 weights of LLMs and VLMs. Under matched target regions, bit-flip budgets, and search budgets, we compare the original layout, the attacker-chosen RegionAlign layout, and a randomly sampled admissible layout outside the attacker’s control. All three layouts retain the same weight values before corruption and have nearly identical clean task performance. For example, a single in-region flip raises StableLM2-1.6B’s WikiText-2 perplexity from 11.53 to 68.29, while both baselines stay near 11.5. These results show that functional equivalence of the model does not guarantee resilience to localized weight faults, and that clean performance evaluation alone can miss this vulnerability. We then examine the physical realizability. Yet none of 25002500 attempts reached the pre-registered target tensor, highlighting the difficulty of region targeting. This supports our claim that the region constrains the attacker and that the attack’s leverage comes from the layout within it rather than unconstrained physical faults.

papers.title: No Cluster Left Behind I: Joint Mass Calibration for Dark Energy Survey and South Pole Telescope Clusters
papers.abstract: Multiwavelength observations of galaxy clusters are among the most promising probes of the growth of structure and dark energy. Optically identified clusters have a high number density and can thus probe the halo mass function well into the group regime, but their weak-lensing mass calibration suffers from a selection bias induced by line-of-sight projection effects. Clusters detected via their intracluster medium (ICM) -- through X-ray emission or the thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect (SZe) -- are less affected by such selection biases, but current survey sensitivity restricts ICM-selected samples to high-mass systems. Previous multiwavelength analyses tend to limit to clusters with millimeter detections and thus to the high-mass population. In this paper, we propose a flexible modeling framework in which all clusters from multiwavelength surveys can be combined and modeled, even if they are detected in only one survey. As a pilot study, we jointly model richness and lensing of clusters from the Dark Energy Survey and the SZe signal from the South Pole Telescope. This approach yields precise cluster mass calibration while self-consistently constraining optical selection biases. We have found a $\sim$20% bias in the large-scale lensing signal of clusters selected by richness, and a bias ranging from $\sim-20$% at low richness to zero at high richness for clusters selected by both richness and SZe. Compared to current approaches, this framework is highly scalable and readily extensible, paving the way for the full utilization of multiwavelength cluster data in next-generation surveys.

papers.title: JWST Reveals Contrast Overdensities around Two ALMA-CRISTAL Galaxies at $z\sim5.2$
papers.abstract: The distribution of stellar mass between massive galaxies and their companions traces how galaxy assembly proceeds within early large-scale structure. We investigate the environments of two galaxies from the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) CRISTAL survey: CRISTAL-19 (C19; $z=5.235$) and CRISTAL-21 (C21; $z=5.256$), using F444W slitless spectroscopy from the Near-Infrared Camera (NIRCam) on the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) in COSMOS-3D. A friends-of-friends analysis of H$\alpha$ emitters identifies two distinct overdense nodes separated by approximately 25 comoving Mpc. Although C21 is the more massive galaxy, C19 has the more massive, actively star-forming companions. The companion populations around C19 and C21 have median stellar masses of $\log(M_\star/M_\odot)=9.43$ and 8.82 and median dust-corrected H$\alpha$ star formation rates of 31 and $16~M_\odot~\mathrm{yr}^{-1}$, respectively. Their star formation rate contrast largely reflects the difference in companion masses. C19 contains only $4.5^{+0.9}_{-0.7}\%$ of the combined measured stellar mass of itself and its selected companions; the corresponding fraction for C21 is $39^{+5}_{-5}\%$. Thus, stellar mass remains more widely distributed among galaxies around C19, whereas a larger share resides in C21. Resolved interacting companions around C19 and [C II] kinematics consistent with a late-stage merger in C21 support this contrast in assembly state. These findings support the phase-dependent picture of Zou et al. (2026), in which the surrounding star-forming population changes as interactions and mergers build up a massive galaxy.

papers.intro:
The assembly of massive galaxies and the growth of large-scale structure are linked through gas accretion and mergers in the early cosmic web [23, 49]. Star formation also produces the heavy elements needed for dust formation and grain growth [52]. Substantial dust reservoirs in galaxies at z≳4z\gtrsim 4 show that obscured stellar growth was already underway within the first few billion years [46, 34]. How this growth is distributed across assembling structures remains uncertain. A massive galaxy may have accumulated a large stellar mass while substantial growth continues in its neighbours. Measuring both populations is necessary to connect the assembly of an individual galaxy to that of its environment.

Spatially resolved observations now map stars and the gas and dust of the interstellar medium (ISM) in early galaxies. The [C ii] Resolved ISM in STar-forming galaxies with ALMA (CRISTAL) survey is a Cycle 8 Large Program of the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) targeting star-forming galaxies at 4≲z≲64\lesssim z\lesssim 6 [33]. It reveals rotating disks, clumpy systems, mergers, and extended [C ii] emission [33, 41]. The ALPINE–CRISTAL–JWST survey combines observations from the ALMA Large Program to INvestigate [C ii] at Early times (ALPINE) and CRISTAL with JWST/NIRSpec integral field unit (IFU) spectroscopy and HST/JWST imaging to map star formation, dust attenuation, and chemical enrichment on kiloparsec scales [24, 28]. These data characterize dust and the interstellar medium and probe gas interactions with its small scale circumgalactic medium, but do not sample their wider environments. NIRCam wide-field slitless spectroscopy (WFSS) is thus ideally suited to mapping the large-scale environments of massive galaxies.

papers.title: DuoWM:Integrating Dual 6-DoF Visual Flows into Action-Conditioned Drone World Model
papers.abstract: Action-conditioned video world models generate future observations from an initial frame and a camera trajectory, but often fail to align camera commands with visual dynamics or represent full 6-DoF scene transformations. We present DuoWM, a first-person drone video world model with two complementary visual conditions. Action flow projects future camera positions and orientations into each target frame, while Object flow forward-warps the initial observation and overlays local 6-DoF transformations to ground the induced scene motion. We further introduce transform-aware pretraining, which pairs object appearance with explicit transformation axes before standard RGB video training. On Sekai-drone dataset, DuoWM achieves the best results across video quality, 3D consistency, and trajectory following. Compared with Captain Safari, the state-of-the-art method, our approach reduces real-domain FVD and LPIPS by 17.2\% and 21.6\%, respectively, while improving game-domain AUC@30 from 0.5003 to 0.5719 and AUC@15 from 0.3088 to 0.3747.

papers.intro:
Interactive world models are emerging as a promising training paradigm for embodied agents, enabling them to predict visual observations under different action commands [1, 2]. Recent advances in aerial robotics have demonstrated increasingly capable navigation and transportation policies [3, 4, 5, 6], motivating high-fidelity training environments that capture the visual consequences of complex flight maneuvers. While physics-based simulators rely on manually engineered dynamics and environments [7, 8], video world models offer a data-driven alternative by learning visual dynamics from videos. Recent aerial world models [9, 10] demonstrate the potential of this approach, yet maintaining correspondence between commanded camera trajectories and generated visual dynamics remains challenging.

The core challenge lies in establishing a reliable correspondence between motion conditions and their visual consequences. Existing approaches explore several forms of motion conditioning, including learned latent actions, image-space controls, and motion representations based on point trajectories of the objects, optical flow, and 3D bounding boxes [11, 12, 13, 14, 15]. However, these approaches typically lack precise frame-wise control over evolving video sequences, often relying on initial-frame guidance propagated across subsequent frames. Moreover, their motion representations primarily capture 3-DoF translations [16, 17], leaving full 6-DoF (six-degree-of-freedom) rigid transformations insufficiently modeled.

Our 6-DoF axes encode local rigid motion and are fed to the generator through Action flow and Object flow.

papers.title: Off the Driven Path: Transferable Road Understanding in Driving VLAs
papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies increasingly operate without explicit HD maps at inference, raising the question of what road knowledge they actually internalize. To probe this knowledge through model outputs, we introduce Road-KSU, a framework that automatically converts HD maps and actor annotations into a road-centric scene graph. From this, we derive road-focused question answering and reasoning targets, complemented by map-based trajectory compliance metrics. Pairing Road-KSU with geographically disjoint splits yields a $2 \times 2$ evaluation crossing output modality (language vs. action) with place familiarity (seen vs. unseen roads). On NAVSIM, 95% of test samples lie within 10m of a training sample, and scores of 13 published planners on turns rise steeply with the number of training drives through the test location, pointing to memorized road geometry. Retraining on geographically disjoint splits and probing with Road-KSU confirm that action-space performance degrades most on unfamiliar turns, with failures dominated by geometric compliance. Language accuracy, however, drops on road-centric VQA on straight and curved roads alike, and remains stable on dynamic scene content. Scaling the training data further reveals a double dissociation: more drives through the same places improve driving on unseen roads but leave road question answering unchanged, whereas spreading a fixed data budget over more places increases road question answering with little change in driving performance. These findings show that improved driving scores need not imply broader road understanding on unseen roads, and identify geographic diversity as key to transferable road knowledge.

Whether end-to-end driving models acquire such internal road representations is inherently difficult to establish, since implicit knowledge cannot be directly inspected. An alternative is to study road understanding through model behavior, which we define as the observable ability of a model to identify, describe, and act upon properties of the road. Driving VLAs [43, 65] provide a particularly useful setting, as their language outputs reveal which road properties they can report, while their predicted actions show whether their driving complies with road geometry and rules.

These two output modalities — language and action — define the first dimension of our study. The second is place familiarity: at locations seen during training, a model may memorize geometry or use location-specific priors, whereas geographically held-out places test its ability to infer road properties in unseen scenes [33, 61]. In training, our map-derived supervision encourages models to internalize road information. Map-derived evaluation subsequently allows us to assess if driving VLAs identify, express, and act upon it, without requiring HD map coverage at deployment. At its core, Road-KSU automatically transforms HD maps and actor annotations into a road-centric scene graph that links geometry, topology, traffic rules, and actors to a common set of road entities. Our experiments reveal that geographic familiarity affects language and action differently. On NAVTEST [16], where 95% of test samples lie within 10 m of a training sample, the scores of 13 published planners correlate with the number of training drives through the test location on turns, while the human driver’s scores barely change. Retraining on our geographically held-out splits and evaluating with Road-KSU shows the same pattern, with failures dominated by departures from the drivable area. The other terms, including USE’s speed checks, fail at similar rates on seen and unseen roads, pointing to road geometry rather than traffic rules as what models fail to transfer.

Road question answering, on the other hand, degrades on both straight and curved roads, and even more under answer-balanced evaluation, while dynamic-scene accuracy remains largely unchanged. Notably, the sensitivity to answer balancing is not specific to our models: human annotators recognize rare road configurations as reliably as common ones, whereas all tested general-purpose and driving VLMs lose accuracy under answer balancing. Together, these results indicate that models may drive successfully yet fail to identify broader road properties or non-standard road configurations that could matter beyond nominal driving.

To further investigate whether language and action benefit from different training data, we perform controlled scaling experiments. Increasing the number of drives through the same training locations improves driving performance on unseen roads, but yields little gain in road-centric VQA, whereas both improve with repetition on seen roads. Conversely, spreading a fixed data budget over more places improves VQA performance on unseen roads while leaving driving performance largely unchanged. Our contributions are threefold: • We introduce Road-KSU, a framework that grounds road question answering (KNOW), task-focused road descriptions (SAY), and trajectory-compliance evaluation (USE) in shared HD-map and scene annotations, enabling the study of both immediately driving-relevant knowledge and broader road understanding across language and action. • We establish geographically held-out and answer-balanced evaluation protocols for transferable road understanding, to distinguish performance on seen roads from generalization to new locations and test recognition of diverse road configurations beyond frequent-answer priors. • Through controlled data-scaling experiments, we characterize how road understanding develops across language and action, identifying visitation count and geographic coverage as complementary axes of data scaling.

papers.title: UNIONS and Euclid: Calibrating point source-galaxy separation for ground-based surveys
papers.abstract: Efficient separation of unresolved point sources from extended objects (star-galaxy separation) is essential for deep wide-field imaging surveys, particularly at faint magnitudes where morphological differences become subtle. We assess two morphology-based classification methods applied to single-band, ground-based imaging from the Ultraviolet Near-Infrared Optical Northern Survey (UNIONS), using Euclid observations as a high-fidelity reference to evaluate their performance and to train one of the methods. We analysed 8 deg$^2$ of overlapping UNIONS $r$-band and Euclid $I_E$ data, comprising more than $7\times10^{5}$ sources. The Euclid data enable robust morphological labelling down to $I_E\simeq 26$, which we used to train and validate two classification approaches applied to UNIONS alone: a curve-of-growth method and a supervised neural-network classifier, both based on aperture photometry and image-quality information. The curve-of-growth method yields an almost perfectly complete point-source sample ($>95\%$), but its purity decreases rapidly at $r \simeq 22.5$. The neural-network approach significantly improves the purity at the faint end, maintaining $\geq 80\%$ purity down to $r \simeq 24$, while the completeness decreases to almost $50\%$ at similar depths. In both cases, performance strongly depends on the image quality of the ground-based data. This work shows how Euclid data can be used to develop, calibrate, and validate star-galaxy separation methods for ground-based surveys, useful in regions not covered by Euclid. Both methods have already been applied to UNIONS data and are readily applicable to future surveys such as LSST, offering flexible solutions depending on whether completeness or purity is prioritised.

papers.intro:
For many studies in modern astronomy, it is crucial to correctly identify and classify unresolved point-like sources, such as stars or quasi-stellar objects (QSOs), from extended objects, i.e., resolved galaxies. This process is commonly, though somewhat imprecisely, referred to as star–galaxy separation. This distinction underpins a wide range of research areas, from mapping the morphology of the Milky Way outskirts (Fukushima et al. 2018; Fukushima et al. 2019; Thomas et al. 2018; Starkenburg et al. 2019; Amarante et al. 2024; Medina et al. 2024, e.g.) and detecting ultra-faint dwarf galaxies in the Local Group (Martin et al. 2013; Drlica-Wagner et al. 2015; Smith et al. 2024, e.g.) to probing the distribution of dark matter on cosmological scales through the weak-lensing distortion of distant galaxies (Ross et al. 2011; Soumagnac et al. 2015; Guerrini et al. 2025; Mpetha et al. 2025). Misclassifications between these two classes of objects can therefore introduce significant biases and lead to erroneous scientific conclusions.

Misclassifications between these two classes of objects can therefore introduce significant biases and lead to erroneous scientific conclusions.

At bright magnitudes, distinguishing stars from galaxies is relatively straightforward; the former outnumber the latter, which are, moreover, very extended sources on the sky. However, as imaging surveys reach fainter magnitudes, this separation becomes increasingly challenging (Slater et al. 2020; Zhao 2026, e.g.). Indeed, at fainter magnitudes the fraction of stars decreases while the apparent angular size of resolved galaxies also decreases, making them harder to disentangle from point sources. For instance, using SDSS Stripe 82, Slater et al. (2020) showed that stars outnumber galaxies down to r≃20.8r\simeq 20.8, where the two populations are equal in number. Beyond this limit, the star-to-galaxy ratio drops exponentially, reaching approximately 1:15 at r∼24r\sim 24, highlighting the increasing difficulty of reliable star–galaxy separation at the depths reached by modern wide-field surveys. For this reason, the separation between point sources and extended objects is already difficult in the faintest regime of existing surveys such as the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (York et al. 2000; Vasconcellos et al. 2011, SDSS;), Pan-STARRS (Chambers et al. 2016), or the Dark Energy Survey (Farrow et al. 2014; Tachibana and Miller 2018; Sevilla-Noarbe et al. 2018, DES;). This challenge will become even more critical for the new generation of wide and deep surveys, such as the Ultraviolet Near-Infrared Optical Northern Survey (Gwyn et al. 2025, UNIONS;), the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (Ivezić et al. 2019, LSST;), or the Euclid mission (Euclid Collaboration: Scaramella et al. 2022; Euclid Collaboration: Mellier et al. 2025), which will reach magnitudes where galaxies largely outnumber stars (Lupton et al. 2001; Fadely et al. 2012; Sevilla-Noarbe et al. 2018; Slater et al. 2020).

Morphological approaches remain the cornerstone of point-source versus extended-object separation. Early studies based on photographic plates already exploited image moments and surface-brightness profiles to distinguish unresolved from extended sources (MacGillivray et al. 1976; Kron 1980; Heydon-Dumbleton et al. 1989; Yee 1991, e.g.). With the advent of CCD detectors, automated pipelines such as SExtractor (Bertin and Arnouts 1996) enabled efficient star–galaxy separation using morphological parameters including the flux radius or the stellarity index. These classical approaches typically rely on comparing flux measurements obtained with different methods such as point-spread-function (PSF) fitting photometry versus aperture-based estimates including Kron or Petrosian magnitudes (Petrosian 1976; Kron 1980), or on specific metrics such as the difference between PSF and model fluxes, as implemented in the SDSS (Lupton et al. 2001), Pan-STARRS (Farrow et al. 2014), and Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (Bosch et al. 2018, HSC-SSP;) large surveys.

Early studies based on photographic plates already exploited image moments and surface-brightness profiles to distinguish unresolved from extended sources (MacGillivray et al. 1976; Kron 1980; Heydon-Dumbleton et al. 1989; Yee 1991, e.g.). With the advent of CCD detectors, automated pipelines such as SExtractor (Bertin and Arnouts 1996) enabled efficient star–galaxy separation using morphological parameters including the flux radius or the stellarity index. In recent years, more sophisticated methods have been developed that exploit both morphological and colour information (Hildebrandt et al. 2012; Tachibana and Miller 2018; Sevilla-Noarbe et al. 2018, e.g.) and inject artificial objects into real data (e.g. Euclid Collaboration: Urbano et al. 2026; Hui et al. in prep.). Combined with Bayesian inference techniques (Fadely et al. 2012, e.g.) and supervised or unsupervised machine-learning algorithms such as deep neural networks (Breiman 2001; Gatto et al. 2026) and boosted decision trees, these methods have been successfully applied to improve classification accuracy at faint magnitudes (Clarke et al. 2020; Cunha and Humphrey 2022; Cook et al. 2024, e.g.). For example, this is used in the Euclid mission (Euclid Collaboration: Tucci et al. 2026), where a combination of supervised machine-learning classifiers and SED-fitting techniques is applied to multi-band photometry from both Euclid and ground-based surveys to separate stars, galaxies, and QSOs. papers.title: Halo spin-axis correlations in IllustrisTNG: Lagrangian-to-Eulerian separation mapping, baryonic effects, and redshift-space distortions
papers.abstract: We investigate correlations of halo and stellar spin axes in the TNG300 volume of the IllustrisTNG simulations and compare them with a model based on linear tidal torque theory (LTTT). Dark matter (DM) halo spin axes at $z = 0$ exhibit positive correlations as a function of Lagrangian pair separation. The LTTT-based model describes their separation dependence well, with weak variation in the fitted amplitude across mass thresholds. A Lagrangian-to-Eulerian separation mapping based on the conditional distributions of initial separations at fixed present-day separation, measured directly from the simulations, allows the model to reproduce the overall trends in both real and redshift space without additional fitting. The hydrodynamic and DM-only runs generally show similar DM halo spin-axis correlations, although the DM-only run exhibits a steeper rise at small real-space separations. In the hydrodynamic run, stellar spin-axis correlations are consistent with the same Lagrangian form as their DM halo counterparts, but with approximately 60% of the DM correlation amplitudes. Positive stellar correlations persist in both real and redshift space, and the mapped model captures their separation dependence. Initial spin-axis correlations of protohalos are substantially stronger than their present-day counterparts at the same Lagrangian separations, consistent with subsequent nonlinear spin evolution weakening these correlations. These results suggest that present-day halo and stellar spin-axis correlations retain signatures of the initial tidal field and that their general behavior can be understood through LTTT-based modeling combined with pair-separation mapping.

papers.intro:
The angular momentum of galaxies is thought to originate from gravitational tidal torques exerted by the surrounding matter distribution during the initial stages of structure formation. Within the framework of linear tidal torque theory (LTTT) Peebles (1969); Doroshkevich (1970); White (1984); Catelan and Theuns (1996), net angular momentum arises from the misalignment between the shape tensor of a protogalaxy and the local tidal shear field in Lagrangian space. Because the large-scale tidal field itself is spatially correlated, neighboring galaxies can experience correlated tidal torques, which can in turn induce correlations in their angular momentum vectors Lee and Pen (2000); Pen et al. (2000); Lee and Pen (2001). Spin correlations may provide a useful probe of this coherence imprinted in galaxy angular momenta at early times.

(2026), their correlations offer an additional way to constrain early-Universe physics using low-redshift galaxies, including, for example, tests of primordial parity violation Yu et al. Theoretical predictions for spin correlations based on LTTT are naturally formulated in Lagrangian space, while spin correlations at late times are measured as a function of the Eulerian separation between galaxies. As gravitational displacements move galaxies away from their initial Lagrangian positions, the initial separation of a galaxy pair does not in general remain the same as its separation at the present epoch Porciani et al. (2002b). It is therefore essential to account for this Lagrangian-to-Eulerian mapping when connecting LTTT-based spin correlations to late-time measurements.

Studies based on cosmological NN-body simulations have reported spatial correlations between the spins of neighboring dark matter (DM) halos, with the strength and scale varying across different halo samples Hatton and Ninin (2001); Porciani et al. (2002b); Faltenbacher et al. (2002); Lee and Pen (2008); Trowland et al. (2013). In contrast, correlations between galaxy stellar spins have been less explored in hydrodynamic simulations. Ref. Codis et al. (2015a) measured correlations between stellar spins at z=1.2z=1.2 in the Horizon-AGN simulation and found a significant signal for blue and low-mass galaxies. Subsequent work extended the analysis to investigate various forms of spin-related intrinsic alignments Chisari et al. (2015); Chisari et al. (2016); Soussana et al. (2020), but correlations between spins have received less attention, with grid-locking artifacts in Cartesian grid-based simulations further complicating their interpretation Codis et al. (2015a); Chisari et al. (2015). Cosmological simulations provide access to both the initial conditions and the subsequent evolution, making them well suited for examining the connection between spin correlations measured with respect to Lagrangian and Eulerian separations.

In particular, peculiar velocities distort the inferred pair separations in redshift space, thereby modifying two-point correlations (Jackson, 1972; Kaiser, 1987; Hamilton, 1992; Hamilton, 1998, e.g.,). papers.title: A Robust Optimization Framework for Energy System Capacity Expansion under Line Outage Uncertainty
papers.abstract: Capacity expansion models are widely used in climate and energy policy analysis to find optimal investments in generation, storage, and transmission. As the share of renewable generation grows, these models rely more on transmission lines to balance supply and demand across regions. Transmission lines, however, can fail due to aging, extreme weather, or accidents. Models that represent outages as time-dependent events come mainly from electrical engineering and are applied to small-scale systems, as they quickly become computationally intractable for inter-regional capacity expansion. We develop a capacity expansion model in which the risk of line failures shapes the investments in all parts of the system. We formulate it as a two-stage, scenario-based robust optimization problem that samples time-varying outage scenarios from a Markov model and hedges the investments against the most severe ones. To solve the model, we propose a memory-augmented Benders decomposition algorithm combined with Monte Carlo simulation that can handle thousands of scenarios. The selected plan is then evaluated with an out-of-sample simulation to bound the Value-at-Risk (VaR) of its system cost. In a 25-node case study of Germany and its neighboring countries, the gap between the lower bound and the simulated VaR bound is below 1%. We compare the robust plans with a deterministic plan, which assumes all lines are always available, and with a reserve-margin heuristic, which requires local firm capacity to be above peak demand. Like the heuristic, the robust plans nearly eliminate loss of load in 1000 simulated outage scenarios. Their mean system cost is within 0.2% of the deterministic plan and about 4.5% below the heuristic. Instead of adding more generation capacity, the robust approach mainly changes the type and location of capacity, for example, by spreading storage across the network.

papers.title: Out of Sight, Not Out of Clues: Can Video LLMs Guess from Partial Evidence?
papers.abstract: In real-world applications like egocentric recording, visual accessibility, and surveillance review, visual evidence for Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) is often only partially captured. A reliable model should match its response to the evidence: answering when sufficient, guessing from visible clues when partial, and abstaining when absent. Yet existing benchmarks enforce a binary answerable-or-unanswerable split, leaving partial evidence unmeasured and obscuring whether failures arise from missing evidence or misjudging sufficiency. We introduce ClueProbe, a diagnostic benchmark to (1) separate perceiving evidence from judging sufficiency, and (2) validate our diagnosis via targeted fine-tuning. ClueProbe comprises 1,721 human-annotated questions across 598 natural videos, labeled Answerable, Guessable, or Unanswerable, alongside controlled perturbations altering wording or visual input. Evaluating 10 open-source and proprietary Video LLMs reveals that failures stem from judgment rather than perception: models perceive the evidence yet lack graded sufficiency awareness, answering or refusing outright while rarely guessing from partial clues. Targeted fine-tuning shows that this reflects missing supervision rather than insufficient capacity: supervising the guess level lifts appropriate guessing from 1.6% to 40.4% without extra false refusals, whereas conventional refusal tuning rejects 92% of guessable questions. Data and code will be released at https://github.com/suat-llm/ClueProbe.

Qwen3-VL-8B states what work follows as a fact and, once offered a guess as well, refuses instead, although the finished floor narrows the answer. Such failures can stem from distinct causes: the model may not see the evidence, or may see it but misjudge whether it suffices, and a misjudgment may reflect missing capacity or missing supervision. A single accuracy or refusal rate cannot tell these causes apart.

Models see the evidence: they answer most Answerable questions, reject wrong candidate answers when the video is present, and reach the clue-supported answer on most Guessable questions. Yet by default they state that answer as fact and almost never guess. Even the models that flag many blank or mismatched clips without being asked miss most natural gaps, where the video shows the scene but not the answer. A prompt that offers a guess switches refusal on but sends partial evidence to refusal as well, and refusal is rarest for temporal gaps, which only video can pose.

papers.title: Length-scales and fractal scaling in dairy gels: comparisons of the insights from ultra-small angle neutron scattering and rheology
papers.abstract: A key structural parameter that dictates the textural properties of a particulate gel is the fractal dimension (Df) of the network indicating self-similarity within the spatial range defined by the correlation length (xi). In this study dairy gels are formed from reconstituted skim milk at defined CM volume fractions via two different mechanisms: acidification, and enzymatic (rennet)-induction. Oscillatory rheology is performed to obtain the gelation times, the time-scale for the maturation of mechanical properties of the gel, and the viscoelastic properties of the gel. A direct probe of gel structure is ultra-small-angle neutron scattering (USANS) examining length-scales from approximately 60 nm up to 15 microns. Structural information is extracted from USANS of matured gels by comparing the measured differential scattering cross-section with that calculated from a model constrained by the sample composition. Time-scales for structural equilibration from USANS perspective were shorter than the rheological gelation time for both gels. Rheological scaling theories are utilized to relate the microstructure to their bulk mechanical properties. We show that the fractal scaling at low-q (scattering vectors), due to aggregation of CM, extracted from the USANS at the longest timescales is described by a power-law density-density correlation function, and that rheology relates - through Shih-Wu-Morbidelli models - the local elasticity both within and between the fractal flocs formed by these particles over different size ranges to the bulk moduli of the gels. There are similar values of fractal dimensions from both techniques but different sizes attributed to the complex fractal evolution during dairy gelation, which leaves space to refinements of the models.
