papers.title: The confined discrete DLSS equation: gradient flow structure and long-time asymptotics
papers.abstract:
We propose and analyse a structure-preserving discretization of the fourth-order DLSS equation in dynamically rescaled variables leading to a linear confinement on the one-dimensional real line. The scheme is obtained as a discrete analogue of the Carrillo--Toscani splitting. It allows for a new interpretation of the DLSS equation as gradient flow of the relative entropy with respect to a combined diffusive and transport metric, extending the structure of the discretization introduced in our earlier work with Giuseppe Savar\'{e} for the unconfined equation.
  We prove global existence of positive solutions and, as the main analytical result, exponential decay of the relative entropy towards the discrete Gaussian equilibrium. The decay rate is obtained via a discrete modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality. The resulting rate is consistent with the continuum rate and converges to it from below in the vanishing mesh-size limit. Numerical results illustrate and confirm our findings.

papers.title: SPARC: Semantic Calibration with Latent Multimodal Knowledge for Robust Image-Text Retrieval
papers.abstract: Robust image-text retrieval aims to maintain accurate cross-modal matching when image or text queries are incomplete, supporting reliable information access in real-world applications. However, existing methods typically focus on adapting to distribution shifts, without adequately addressing candidate discrimination for incomplete queries and ranking instability. To this end, we propose semantic projection and alignment with relational constraints (SPARC), which elicits latent multimodal knowledge from frozen encoders to improve candidate discrimination and ranking stability. Specifically, we first devise a semantic calibration module on a product of spheres that refines incomplete visual and textual features through tangent-space updates, maintaining the unit-sphere structure used for cosine similarity. Second, we introduce a robust semantic guidance module that combines latent multimodal knowledge encoded in complete image-text features with cross-modal semantic anchors to promote semantic alignment of the calibrated features. Finally, we introduce a matching relation constraint module that fuses original query features with their calibrated counterparts and applies a soft ranking constraint to penalize reductions in initially positive matching margins, thereby limiting ranking perturbations. Extensive experiments on Flickr30K and COCO demonstrate that SPARC outperforms competing methods under various image occlusion and word deletion settings, while achieving consistent gains across different pretrained backbones.

papers.title: AgentLens: Graph-guided Security Auditing for LLM-based Agents
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents are emerging as a key paradigm for automating software engineering by coupling LLM-driven decision-making with external tools, files, APIs, and execution environments. However, weaknesses in agent implementations and insecure interactions between the agent and external resources can lead to severe consequences, including remote code execution, arbitrary file access, SQL injection, and data leakage. This makes pre-deployment auditing essential for systematically identifying implementation weaknesses and validating whether they can manifest as concrete security risks in realistic agent workflows. Existing approaches either focus on specific vulnerability classes or lack the capability to validate whether identified static weaknesses correspond to executable exploits. In this paper, we propose AgentLens, a systematic auditing framework for LLM-based agents. AgentLens analyzes the target agent's implementation, component interactions, and built-in defenses, and organizes them into an Audit Knowledge Graph that captures how these factors interact to expose potential security risks. Based on this graph, AgentLens derives candidate attack paths, generates path-specific validation payloads, and constructs realistic multi-turn audit scenarios that place these payloads in task-relevant contexts to validate whether suspected risks manifest as security-violating behaviors during execution. Across five widely-used agent applications, each with over 24,000 GitHub stars, AgentLens identifies 44 vulnerabilities, and every vulnerability is validated by being triggered during execution. Compared with the state-of-the-art approach (AgentFuzz), AgentLens detects 3.67$\times$ more vulnerabilities. To date, 12 reported issues have been assigned CVE IDs.

papers.intro:
LLM-based agents have become prevalent in software engineering workflows, including code generation [1], program repair [2], repository understanding [3], test generation [4], and security testing [5]. They have been integrated into IDE extensions [6], command-line development assistants [7], cloud coding platforms [8], automated maintenance workflows [9], and web-facing software services [10]. In such settings, agent decisions are no longer confined to textual responses; they can directly drive tool invocations, file operations, API calls, and other state-changing actions.

They have been integrated into IDE extensions [6], command-line development assistants [7], cloud coding platforms [8], automated maintenance workflows [9], and web-facing software services [10]. In such settings, agent decisions are no longer confined to textual responses; they can directly drive tool invocations, file operations, API calls, and other state-changing actions.

The growing deployment of LLM-based agents in diverse real-world scenarios, together with their expanding access to tools, memory, data, and external services, makes pre-deployment security auditing essential. Particularly, prior studies [11, 10, 12] on LLM-integrated applications have shown that insecure coupling between LLM-generated content and executable operations can lead to severe consequences, including remote code execution, arbitrary file access, SQL injection, and prompt leakage. These risks become more pronounced when agents iteratively observe context, plan actions, invoke tools, and update external states during task execution. Therefore, auditing is needed to identify implementation weaknesses and validate whether they can lead to security-violating behaviors in realistic workflows, thereby helping developers prioritize subsequent security hardening.

Prior security testing approaches for foundation LLMs [13] are insufficient for auditing agents. LLM-centric red-teaming approaches (HarmBench [14], garak [15], and PyRIT [16]) primarily evaluate whether adversarial prompts can elicit unsafe or policy-violating responses from a target LLM. However, agent security depends not only on the LLM response itself, but also on how the surrounding implementation interprets that response and translates it into tool calls, external requests, or other environment-changing actions. As a result, a semantically benign LLM output may still lead to an insecure operation, whereas a harmful LLM output may be blocked by guardrails before affecting the environment. Recent studies have examined specific vulnerability classes in LLM-integrated applications, which are closer to agent auditing. For example, AgentFuzz [17] detects taint-style vulnerabilities in agent systems, while Prompt-to-SQL injection [10] studies how prompts can induce insecure database queries. Different from them, agent auditing should focus on how to comprehensively assess the security of an LLM agent, rather than only detecting a predefined class of vulnerabilities. Particularly, for a complex agent, the security risks are often unknown beforehand: where they arise, what types they belong to, which component interactions cause them, whether they are affected by existing defenses, and how they should be tested.

Recently, Agent Audit [18] was proposed to audit agents by statically analyzing their code and deployment artifacts to detect risky tool implementations, insecure data flows, etc. However, vulnerability candidates found by static analysis do not guarantee that the reported issues can be triggered in an actual agent execution. Specifically, Agent Audit identifies no validated vulnerabilities in Langflow [19] (as shown in Sec. IV-C). This is because static approaches lack dynamic context-awareness: they cannot determine whether a vulnerable tool is reachable under the LLM’s non-deterministic task planning, nor can they assess whether built-in dynamic guardrails (e.g., intent filters, permission checks) would block the execution. This shows that effective agent auditing must account for not only the suspicious implementation weaknesses, but also whether the reported issues are feasible and can lead to security-violating outcomes within the agent’s executable workflow.

We highlight two technical fundamental challenges that need to be addressed for agent auditing: (C1) How to define the audit scope of a target agent? Agent risks are often implicit and relational: they arise from interactions among prompts, tools, files, APIs, configurations, execution environments, and built-in defenses, rather than isolated implementation flaws. Thus, the auditor must infer the target agent’s security-sensitive behaviors and formulate concrete audit objectives. Currently, the security boundary of an agent is not well defined. (C2) How to validate whether a suspected risk manifests in realistic agent workflows? A suspicious weakness is not necessarily exploitable: it may be unreachable from attacker-controlled inputs, depend on specific agent states, or be blocked by intermediate defenses. The auditor must therefore turn each suspected risk into an executable scenario and collect reliable evidence that it leads to a security violation.

papers.title: Fuel as Identity: Authenticating Inter-Satellite Laser Links after Total Key Compromise
papers.abstract: Optical inter-satellite links form the backbone of entire constellations in low Earth orbit, yet their security rests on keys alone. When an attacker obtains every key of a satellite, no secret is left to authenticate it again. Existing fixes fail, since ground rekeying encrypts new keys under the leaked ones, and post-compromise protocols assume an authenticated start. As a remedy, the satellite's orbit can take over as the trust anchor. The attacker then needs an impostor satellite that blocks and retransmits the beam, a chord beneath the curved orbit. Hence, the blocking point lies off free fall and costs the impostor continuous thrust. We formalize this position-gated adversary and prove, for satellites on a shared circular orbit, a tight lower bound on the propellant cost in delta-v of a point-mass craft that keeps blocking, however it moves. We present OrbitLock, a history-chained protocol that combines this position gate with ML-KEM. Each link authenticates on its own, and we sketch how combining links forces an impostor onto every link. Once the chain outlasts an impostor's propellant, every key back to the first is authenticated retroactively. A satellite thus needs no crosslink key before launch, so none can leak in the supply chain. The same mechanism heals the link after total key compromise, even without compromise awareness. A passive attacker is shut out at the next round, whereas an active one splits the chains and is exposed once its propellant runs out. The chain can then heal after an operator reset. As a result, every Starlink satellite has a partner on whose link a CubeSat-class impostor runs out of propellant in about two days. This holds against one rigid craft per link running the best attack we know, if each terminal enforces a 1 km exclusion zone, while the protocol only uses under 0.02% of the link.

Quantum computers would break current public-key exchange and reveal every key it agreed on. Today, a flaw in a widely used commercial off-the-shelf communication module hands its telecommand signing key to an unauthenticated attacker [3]. Satellite firmware and telecommand interfaces have proven exploitable [4], and operational satellites still send sensitive data unencrypted [5]. Closing such a flaw does not help, since every key the attacker read stays known to it. After a total key compromise, no one can visit the satellite to install a new secret. Nor can the operator certify a fresh key by radio, since the leaked keys let the attacker send its own. The satellite could confirm such a key by a maneuver that the operator tracks. Each such recovery costs propellant, and until the next one a leaked key is free to use.

Standard satellite key management cannot recover from a total key compromise. A satellite receives its first keys on the ground before launch, and every later key upload is encrypted under them [6]. An industry analysis of these CCSDS (CCSDS) procedures concludes that an attacker who learns all keys can never be shut out again, although no mission can exclude such a leak [6]. Existing solutions do not close this gap. Post-compromise protocols such as the double ratchet heal only from an authenticated start, and only once the attacker turns passive [7, 8]. On a network, it never has to. Quantum key distribution needs an authenticated classical channel [9]. Physical-layer authentication of satellites is statistical [10, 11, 12].

The orbit is a trust anchor that survives the leak of every key. The argument is a chain of four steps (Figures 1 and 2). First, an impostor that poses as Alice must remove her signal at her partner Bob, or her stream and its own add up at his detector. Second, light from off the line of sight cannot cancel her signal, because independent light adds in intensity at a direct-detection receiver. Third, the impostor must block her beam from a seat on the line of sight. Fourth, that line is a straight chord below the curved orbit, so the seat lies below free fall and needs continuous outward thrust. A passive reader of both directions also sits below free fall, but it gains nothing while ML-KEM holds. We state the thrust in Δv, the velocity change that propulsion delivers, so a bound tells an operator which fixed budgets afford an attack and for how long.

We build OrbitLock on this physical gate. Alice and Bob run rounds at random times, at most 10 s apart. Each round mixes fresh random bits, which only a receiver inside both beams observes, with a fresh ML-KEM key [18]. As in the double ratchet of Signal [7], every round authenticates under the secret of the previous one. The ML-KEM key never crosses the link, so a passive attack is never enough, even from inside both beams. Therefore, an impostor must substitute shares, which on a laser link needs a paid seat on the line of sight at every round. Breaking the cryptography spares it only the rounds before it entered. Each link authenticates on its own, and we sketch how to combine links. Position verification is impossible against collusion, so we allow one rigid craft per link. The cost grows with the standoff each terminal enforces, here 1 km.

This paper makes five contributions. • A security definition that prices position. We introduce budget-conditioned authentication, to our knowledge the first security experiment that bounds an attacker’s advantage by the propellant it spends. Position-based cryptography asks where a prover is, and we ask what it costs to stay there. Because off-axis light cannot erase the genuine signal, modification needs the on-axis seat (Sections III and VI-D). • A tight floor on a shared orbit. We prove that a point-mass craft holding a seat pays at least 3​n2​d​T3n^{2}d\,T, however it moves. Hovering attains the bound, and drifting, coasting, or leaving between rounds saves at most a fixed amount or a small fraction. Numerical arguments extend the floor beyond the shared orbit (Sections V and VII). • A quantified attack surface. We size every cone from measured flight hardware, including a secrecy cone and the acquisition phase, and show that for a Gaussian beam no free seat reads both directions on a link that decides a recovery. The zone that keeps the attacker off the cheapest seats is thus only about 440 m3 per terminal, in a known direction (Sections V and VI-E). • OrbitLock, specified in full. We give the full protocol, with fail-closed acquisition, retries, an independent chain per link, and in-band checks that need no secret, among them a direction check that defeats tracking capture. Staying accepted costs an impostor Δv even if the cryptography fails, and while ML-KEM and the authenticated encryption hold, lasting acceptance means that it paid since the leak. The chain heals against a passive attacker after total key compromise, even without compromise awareness (Section VI). • Evaluation on a real constellation. We price 17,433 possible Starlink crosslinks from public orbital data. With one attacking craft per link and a 1 km exclusion zone, about 99 percent of satellites have a link that exhausts a CubeSat-class craft within a week. The floor matches propagation with Earth’s oblateness (J 2 ) and drag to within 0.25 percent and NASA station-keeping practice to about 3 percent, and a released artifact recomputes every bound. Electric propulsion enlarges only the budget (Section VIII).

papers.title: A search and multi-frequency study of curved parsec-scale jets in active galaxies
papers.abstract: Very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations show that a fraction of active galactic nucleus (AGN) jets exhibit pronounced apparent bending on parsec scales, potentially strongly enhanced by projection effects. While individual sources have been studied in detail, the statistical properties of curved jets and the physical mechanisms responsible for their morphology remain poorly constrained. We aim to select a statistically robust sample of AGNs with significantly curved parsec-scale jets and to constrain the physical mechanisms responsible for jet bending. We analyse 123 456 VLBI images of 17 478 AGNs collected by the public Astrogeo database. After filtering for extended structure, we extract and stack multi-epoch, multi-frequency (1.2--86 GHz) ridge lines. We fit linear and logarithmic helices representing jet precession and resonant Kelvin--Helmholtz instability mode. We combine model-fits and Monte Carlo simulations to further constrain these physical models. We robustly identify 586 AGNs (7.4% of sources with resolved jets) with curved parsec-scale jets. Compared to straight jets, curved ones are less common at low redshifts, possibly due to the sample-related selection effects. In the precession scenario, the inferred periods span $P \sim$10--10 000 yr, with a logarithmic mean of $\sim 220$ yr. Solid-body disc precession in supermassive black hole binaries is broadly consistent with these periods, whereas geodetic precession requires extremely tight, near-equal-mass systems. Lense--Thirring precession remains viable for both thin and thick discs. Kelvin--Helmholtz instability also provides a potential explanation. However, identifying the preferred model for each individual source requires further investigation, including temporal analysis and jet kinematics.

papers.intro:
Decades of very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) have shown that a significant fraction of AGN jets exhibit bending, magnified by projection effects. A study by Lister et al. (2021) on a sample of 419 jets shows that about 42% of the 926 well-sampled features follow non-radial, curved trajectories, indicating the bending of the jets themselves since these features are expected to trace the outflow. Additionally, the study observed notable variations in the inner jet position angle, which may lead to pronounced bending on larger scales. This topic was further analysed by Kostrichkin et al. (2025), who studied a sample of 317 AGN jets with notable variations in the direction of the VLBI jet. The variability was also connected with possible further jet bending. The next important signature of the jet bending is a misalignment of directions on parsec and kiloparsec scales. This phenomenon is demonstrated and studied by Pearson and Readhead (1988) and Conway and Murphy (1993), suggesting a helical structure of the jets. In fact, curved jets are often presumed to be helical and, as proposed by Steffen (1997), are categorised into three groups: ballistic helical jets, helically bent jets, and internally helical jets. Ballistic helical jets, such as B0605−-085 (Kudryavtseva, N. A. et al., 2011), involve individual elements like plasma blobs following straight paths but collectively forming a helical structure due to periodic changes in ejection direction. Helically bent jets, exemplified by PKS 2136++141 (Savolainen et al., 2006), are bent as a whole with matter flowing along the helix. Internally helical jets may have internal matter flowing along several helical paths. Theoretical explanations for these phenomena include jet precession (Roos, 1988; Fendt and Yardimci, 2022; Dubey et al., 2024) and distortions caused by plasma instabilities such as Kelvin-Helmholtz (KH), current-driven instabilities (Hardee, 2000) and kink instabilities (Lalakos et al., 2024). Besides helical structures, jets can follow irregularly bent paths, like local bends due to the interaction with surrounding medium (Kosogorov et al., 2022; Sutherland and Bicknell, 2007; Choi et al., 2007), often exaggerated by projection effects which may play a crucial role in our perception of the source. As proven by Kovalev et al. (2025) on the example of jet in the blazar PKS 1424++240, some sources may have critically small angles between the directions of their jets and our line of sight, which virtually makes us look inside the jet cone. In such cases we may expect projection effects to be maximised, resulting in more prominent apparent bending of structures inside the jet.

The KH instability may also originate from slow precession of the jet nozzle (Lister et al., 2003).

The jet base precession may stem from two primary mechanisms: orbital revolutions within a supermassive black hole binary (SMBHB) system (Begelman et al., 1980) or the Lense-Thirring effect due to the misalignment of momenta vectors between a supermassive black hole (SMBH) and its accretion disc (Sarazin et al., 1980). The SMBHB hypothesis is particularly relevant due to the abundance of post-merger galaxies predicted by the hierarchical merger models of galaxy formation (White and Rees, 1978). After the merger, the central SMBHs move closer through dynamical friction and form close SMBHBs (Mayer et al., 2007). Alternatively, the disc-driven precession model, in which the black-hole spin is misaligned with the angular-momentum vector of the accretion disc, is supported by observations (Caproni et al., 2004; Caproni et al., 2006) and general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations (Liska et al., 2017). papers.title: An X-ray binary origin for the LHAASO peanut
papers.abstract: The LHAASO "peanut" source is a remarkably extended ($\gtrsim$4$^\circ$) ultra-high-energy gamma-ray emitter detected by the LHAASO observatory. While its angular extent and high-energy spectrum require a Galactic origin, its location at a Galactic latitude of $\approx$-17$^\circ$ limits the possible known counterparts to a nearby millisecond pulsar. However, models accounting for the emission solely with this pulsar require the transport properties to operate near extreme parameter limits. We propose an alternative explanation where the peanut source is produced through the past activity of a now quiescent X-ray binary located at a distance of 1-2 kpc. We draw an analogy with known X-ray binaries producing similar structures at high Galactic latitudes, and argue that the peanut emission could be explained by an almost identical physical scenario. We conclude that an X-ray binary origin of the emission is plausible and predict that sufficiently sensitive X-ray observations should be able to detect a quiescent X-ray binary in the central region of the peanut source. If our hypothesis is confirmed, it would be the first time an X-ray binary is identified in quiescence, opening a new avenue to detect such objects through their past gamma-ray emission.

papers.intro:
The study of very-high-energy (VHE, TeV-scale) and ultra-high-energy (UHE, >100 TeV-scale) gamma-ray sources has opened a new window onto the non-thermal universe. Wide-field instruments such as HAWC and LHAASO, and imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes (IACTs) such as H.E.S.S., MAGIC and VERITAS have revealed a population of gamma-ray sources whose origins remain poorly understood. Despite extensive cataloguing attempts, the majority of VHE and UHE gamma-ray sources remain unassociated - that is, the astrophysical object responsible for the emission has not been identified (H. E. S. S. Collaboration et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2024, e.g.). For the vast majority of unassociated sources this lack of confirmed counterpart is actually due to an over-abundance of potential candidates. Galactic gamma-ray sources are often extended, and since the distance to a gamma-ray source cannot be derived from its gamma-ray emission alone, it is often impossible to disentangle which astrophysical object is responsible for the emission in crowded Galactic environments.

There are, however, a handful of arguably more puzzling sources: those located at large Galactic latitudes. There, the reduced density of potential counterparts and the lower interstellar medium density mean that the source remains unassociated because no plausible counterpart is known. One such source is the so-called "peanut" source detected by LHAASO (LHAASO Collaboration et al., 2025b). Spanning 0.45°×\degree\times4.6°\degree this large, asymmetric structure lies -17.5°\degree below the Galactic plane (see Figure 1). The only known candidate counterparts are three pulsars. Two of them (PSR J0211+4235 and PSR J0209+4331) have spin-down energies on the order of E˙∼1030\dot{E}\sim 10^{30} erg/s, orders of magnitude lower than any pulsar detected in the gamma-ray band (E˙≳1033\dot{E}\gtrsim 10^{33} erg/s). The remaining object is a relatively powerful (E˙∼1035\dot{E}\sim 10^{35} erg/s) millisecond pulsar (MSP), MSP J0218+4232.

papers.title: CADENCE: Sensor-GroundedWorld-Consistent Gaussian SLAM for Collaborative Mobile Reconstruction
papers.abstract: Collaborative reconstruction with consumer phones promises faster and more complete indoor maps. However, heterogeneous devices introduce degraded observations and unreliable cross-device associations, so a single poor contributor or incorrect match can corrupt the shared Gaussian map. To address this, we propose \textbf{CADENCE}, a collaborative Gaussian simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) system that separates finding cross-device matches from deciding whether and how peer observations update the map. To find matches, a sensor-grounded regional memory summarizes committed observations and ranks candidate peer regions using appearance, relative pose, gravity, barometric altitude, and observation quality. Deterministic geometric verification and optional physical checks then decide which of the proposed matches are accepted. Once a match is accepted, separate cue-based confidences control how its observations contribute to pose constraints, geometry, appearance, and memory. As a result, useful depth can still contribute even when color is unreliable. Throughout this process, local tracking remains isolated from mapping, verification, and networking. We evaluate CADENCE on eight Matterport3D houses that were not used to train the memory. On these houses, regional memory achieves an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of $0.95$ to $0.97$ and thus outperforms appearance retrieval, while verification keeps false-link rates below $0.5\,\%$. Furthermore, soft confidence weighting reduces the mean receiver peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) loss from $2.66$ to $1.05$\,dB across eight degradations while retaining useful peer depth. Finally, using inertial and platform motion, CADENCE tracks all twelve held-out iPhone scans with a mean absolute trajectory error of $6.98$\,cm, and its refined maps achieve better average rendering quality than the baselines.

papers.intro:
When several phones scan the same environment, they can cover more areas than a single phone. However, different phones may capture different lighting conditions, exposure levels, motion blur, depth quality, and tracking reliability. As a result, one phone may correctly recognize a place but still provide unreliable data that reduces the quality of another phone’s map. A collaborative system must therefore do two things: identify matching places and decide which information from another phone is reliable enough to add to the map.

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) can create detailed 3D scene representations [27]. It has also been used in dense simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) systems [34]. Similar approaches include SplaTAM [23] and PhotoSLAM [21]. Collaborative Gaussian SLAM systems combine observations from multiple devices using appearance matching and geometric or photometric registration. Examples include the method presented in [53, 51]. However, finding the correct place does not mean that every type of information in the matched observation is reliable. Research on collaborative perception also shows that differences between contributing devices can reduce the quality of a shared result [14]. Therefore, a collaborative reconstruction system must check how useful each type of incoming evidence is for the receiving map, while allowing the phone to continue tracking its own movement.

CADENCE addresses this problem by separating three steps: ranking possible matches, checking whether a match is geometrically valid, and deciding which matched information can update the map (Fig. 1). It uses a sensor-grounded world-consistency memory (SG-WCM) to summarize committed observations within spatial regions. This memory ranks candidate regions from other devices using appearance, relative pose, gravity, barometric altitude, and observation quality. Deterministic geometric tests decide whether a proposed match can be accepted, with optional physical checks providing additional verification. Separate confidence values then control how accepted peer evidence affects pose constraints, geometry, appearance, and memory. The explicit map remains the main source of truth, while local tracking proceeds independently of background collaboration. On unseen Matterport3D [5] houses, the regional memory improves region ranking over appearance retrieval, achieving an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.950.95 to 0.970.97, while geometric verification limits false associations. Soft confidence weighting removes the 3.733.73 dB own-view peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) loss from a low-light peer while retaining its depth, and live iPhone sessions demonstrate collaboration with low tracking latency. The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows: 1. A sensor-grounded regional memory that ranks cross-device regions from committed appearance and sensor evidence, with capped embedding storage and single-stage training. 2. Collaborative fusion that verifies memory-ranked cross-device matches using feature correspondences and available depth before admitting peer updates, keeping false-link rates below 0.5%0.5\,\% on unseen Matterport3D houses. 3. Confidence-governed sharing that controls peer updates to pose constraints, geometry, appearance, and memory; soft weighting reduces mean receiver PSNR loss from 2.662.66 to 1.051.05 dB across eight degradations. 4. papers.title: Compact Vision-Language Navigation in Continuous Environmentsvia On-Policy Training and Route-Bearing Output
papers.abstract: Instruction-following robots need navigation policies that reach high accuracy and remain inexpensive to train and to run on a single graphics processing unit (GPU). The most accurate vision-language navigation policies for continuous environments rely on language models with 4 to 8 billion parameters, long observation histories, and large auxiliary corpora. Two properties of the standard training setup limit smaller policies. Imitation labels cover the states that an expert visits, whereas the running policy reaches states that its own errors produce. In addition, an image-plane waypoint exists only while the route lies inside the camera view. We present \textbf{\paper}, a monocular red-green-blue (RGB) policy with 2 billion (2B) parameters that addresses both limitations. \paper adapts Qwen3-VL-2B with low-rank adapters and processes an eight-frame memory and the current view in one forward pass. The policy predicts the route direction as a bearing in the body frame of the agent, which remains defined for every heading, and a deterministic controller converts this bearing into motion. This design allows training to relabel the states that the policy itself visits. On-policy correction improves success, while bearing decoding outperforms image-plane waypoint scanning across all evaluated start headings with identical weights. On the \valunseen split, \paper achieves \rFinSR\% success on Room-to-Room in Continuous Environments (\rtor), averaged over three seeds, and \rRxFinSR\% on its Room-Across-Room counterpart (\rxr). Instruction-following navigation enables a robot to cross an unfamiliar building by following a route description. Vision-and-language navigation in continuous environments (VLN-CE) formulates this task with low-level actions, namely 0.25 m forward steps, 15∘15^{\circ} turns, and a stop action [15]. On the standard Room-to-Room in Continuous Environments (R2R-CE) benchmark, video-language models predict these actions from sequences of red-green-blue (RGB) observations. NaVid [37] introduced this approach, Uni-NaVid [38] extended it to several navigation tasks, and NaVILA [8] and StreamVLN [34] scaled it further. These systems are built on language models with 7B-8B parameters and long observation histories, and their training adds web video, question answering, or synthetic navigation episodes to the benchmark data. StreamVLN and NaVILA report 270 and 595 ms per model call, respectively, on an RTX 4090 GPU, and training these 7B and 8B systems costs 544 to 2,816 data-center GPU-hours (details in Table 2).

papers.title: The Last Expectation: Sampling Measurement Outcomes in Value of Information Analysis
papers.abstract: In decision-making under uncertainty, additional information can improve decisions but is often costly to acquire. The Value of Information (VoI) quantifies the expected benefit of different information-gathering strategies. The main computational burden in VoI analysis arises from evaluating the expected utility of a strategy over possible outcomes. As each outcome entails solving a computationally expensive optimization problem under uncertainty to determine the optimal decision, efficient estimation of this expectation is crucial. This work focuses on sampling-based estimation and investigates three classical variance-reduction techniques, namely control variates, stratified sampling, and importance sampling, as well as combinations thereof. In particular, we establish a connection between two common VoI formulations through a control variate framework and show how this relationship can be exploited to obtain more efficient VoI estimators. The methodology is assessed using three test cases. The first is an analytical example with a known reference solution, the second involves a fatigue reliability and the third a slope stability application. Our results demonstrate that the relative performance of the sampling methods depends strongly on the problem characteristics. However, suitable combinations of variance-reduction techniques consistently improve efficiency and provide stable VoI estimates across a range of scenarios.

papers.intro:
Decision analysis entails applying principles from decision theory to make well-informed decisions (Raiffa and Schlaifer, 1961; Howard, 1966). Decision-makers navigate uncertainty, balancing the costs of actions against their associated risks and consequences. In practice, many decisions rely on uncertain parameters, such as soil properties in geotechnical engineering or the condition of machine components in mechanical engineering. While obtaining additional information on these uncertain parameters has the potential to decrease uncertainty and enhance decision outcomes, it often entails high costs. Hence, information acquisition strategies should be chosen carefully, a problem commonly addressed within the framework of pre-posterior decision analysis, where the expected benefit of acquiring information is evaluated before outcomes become available.

Hence, information acquisition strategies should be chosen carefully, a problem commonly addressed within the framework of pre-posterior decision analysis, where the expected benefit of acquiring information is evaluated before outcomes become available.

The Value of Information (VoI), rooted in Bayesian statistical decision theory (Raiffa and Schlaifer, 1961; Howard, 1966; DeGroot, 2005), serves to evaluate the advantages of acquiring additional observations for better informed decisions. It is also applied in sensitivity analysis by assigning decision-relevant metrics to reductions in uncertainty (Pörn, 1997; Oakley, 2009; Borgonovo and Cillo, 2017; Straub et al., 2022, e.g.,). In the realm of engineering applications, the VoI finds widespread use in quantifying the influence of monitoring and inspections on structural systems (Straub and Faber, 2005; Pozzi and Kiureghian, 2011; Malings and Pozzi, 2016; Thöns, 2018; Luque and Straub, 2019; Vereecken et al., 2020; Kamariotis et al., 2022; Giordano et al., 2023, e.g.,). Also in the field of geosciences, the applications of the VoI are diverse, extending to various areas such as geological exploration (Eidsvik et al., 2008; Athens and Caers, 2019; Dutta et al., 2019, e.g.,) and groundwater management (Liu et al., 2012; Trainor-Guitton, 2014, e.g.,). For a recent review of VoI in civil and infrastructure engineering, see Zhang et al. (2021).

We adopt the standard expected utility framework, in which the optimal decision under uncertainty is the one that maximizes expected utility (Von Neumann and Morgenstern, 2007). For simplicity, we assume that all consequences can be expressed as monetary costs and that utility is linear in cost. However, the findings of this work remain valid for more general utility functions. Here, the optimal decision is the one that minimizes the expected cost. Furthermore, we focus on measurements in a continuous space as the source of information. The resulting VoI of a measurement strategy is the expected reduction in cost that can be achieved by making decisions accounting for the additional information provided by the measurements. The optimal measurement system maximizes the net value of information, i.e., the VoI minus the measurement cost (Straub, 2014).

In practice, measurement systems provide only imperfect information about the underlying uncertain quantities. Bayesian updating is used to incorporate such information and revise the probability distributions of the underlying variables (Beck and Katafygiotis, 1998; Straub and Papaioannou, 2015). For a given measurement outcome, evaluating the minimum expected cost requires identifying the optimal action, which in turn involves assessing the system performance under the candidate actions, often through expensive reliability analyses (Dutta et al., 2019; Ehre et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2020, e.g., ). Depending on whether the action space is continuous or discrete, the optimization problem may be non-convex or combinatorial, leading to additional challenges (Malings and Pozzi, 2016; Dutta et al., 2019). The central challenge in VoI analysis, however, is that the outcome remains unknown when a measurement strategy is selected. Consequently, the benefit of the strategy must be averaged over all possible measurement outcomes. This outer expectation, which accounts for the uncertainty in future measurements, is referred to in the following as the “last expectation”.

In practical problems, this last expectation does not have a closed-form expression and must be approximated numerically. Although numerical integration may be feasible in some settings (Heath et al., 2016; Konakli et al., 2016, e.g.,), sampling-based methods are generally more flexible, particularly in high-dimensional parameter settings. Estimation of the last expectation requires a computationally expensive cost-minimization analysis for each sampled measurement outcome. Hence, the overall efficiency of VoI evaluation depends critically on the sampling strategy employed. The most widely used approach is Monte Carlo (MC) sampling (Eidsvik et al., 2008; Dutta et al., 2019; Vereecken et al., 2020; Kamariotis et al., 2022). However, MC sampling is inefficient when measurement outcomes that lead to changes in the optimal decisions occur only rarely (Straub, 2014). This issue becomes more pronounced when multiple measurements with several possible outcomes are considered.

To the best of our knowledge, the numerical estimation of the last expectation in VoI analysis has not previously been the subject of a systematic investigation. In particular, we show how two alternative VoI formulations are related through a control variate framework, and demonstrate that the resulting control variate estimator can provide improved robustness and efficiency. Furthermore, particular attention is given to importance sampling, for which a suitable proposal density must be constructed. To this end, we use Gaussian process (GP) models to approximate the optimal IS density. This approach is inspired by the work of Dubourg et al. We investigate the proposed methods on three test cases, all based on a binary decision between taking no action and a perfect action, where the latter completely eliminates the failure risk. The first test case is an analytical example that enables benchmarking against a known reference solution. The second and third test cases are adapted from Kanjilal et al. papers.title: Doppler RaDAR Single-Frame Anomaly Detection and Consistency Assessment by Velocity-Conditioned Gaussian Spectral Modeling
papers.abstract: Reliable speed-over-ground estimation is essential for automated railway vehicles. However, the accuracy of a velocity estimate alone does not indicate whether the underlying RaDAR measurement is physically plausible. This paper introduces a velocity-conditioned Gaussian spectral modeling framework for anomaly detection and velocity consistency assessment. A neural encoder estimates the vehicle velocity from complex Doppler spectra, while a Gaussian decoder models the expected spectral distribution conditioned on a velocity estimate. Three complementary inference-time online indicators are derived: the spectral anomaly score (SAS), conditional anomaly score (CAS), and absolute velocity disagreement (AVD). Experiments demonstrate the sensitivity of the scores to velocity deviations. Under controlled spectral anomalies, SAS and CAS outperform conventional spectral indicators in most conditions. Furthermore, AVD exhibits strong correlations with actual velocity estimation errors (Pearson $r>0.99$) for the investigated extra-peak and local anomalies. These results demonstrate the potential of online conditional spectral modeling to assess measurement plausibility and velocity estimation reliability without requiring ground-truth velocities during inference.
papers.intro:
Reliable velocity information is essential for railway odometry and the safe operation of increasingly automated rail vehicles: accurate estimates support localization and control, while unreliable measurements can compromise downstream functions [1]. Railway vehicles commonly rely on wheel-based odometry, inertial sensors, and satellite navigation, each with limitations under challenging operating conditions [2, 3]. Ground-facing Doppler RaDAR complements these methods with contactless speed-over-ground estimation using Doppler shifts of signals reflected from the track bed [4, 5]. Vehicle velocity can be inferred from the resulting Doppler spectra using conventional methods such as peak picking, center-of-mass estimation, and spectral cross-correlation [6], as well as learning-based approaches [5]. However, Doppler RaDAR measurements can be affected by track-bed conditions and multipath propagation [2], as well as radar interference [7], raising the question of how reliably individual measurements can be assessed.

However, Doppler RaDAR measurements can be affected by track-bed conditions and multipath propagation [2], as well as radar interference [7], raising the question of how reliably individual measurements can be assessed.

Disturbances in Doppler RaDAR measurements can alter spectral distributions through increased noise, additional peaks, or changes in dominant components. Detecting these deviations helps assess measurement plausibility independently of velocity estimation accuracy. Conventional indicators, including spectral entropy based on Shannon’s information measure [8] and previously applied to Doppler spectra [9], as well as peak-to-noise ratio [10], characterize selected spectral properties. Signal-based quality assessment has also been investigated for RaDAR-derived velocity measurements [11, 12]. However, these approaches are tailored to ocean-current measurements and require application-specific processing, limiting their direct applicability to single-frame railway Doppler spectra. Their use of spectral characteristics nevertheless motivates a velocity-conditioned spectral energy (VCSE) baseline considered here, which evaluates spectral energy relative to the predicted velocity. More elaborate Doppler spectral methods include machine-learning-based peak identification [13] and hierarchical representations of multiple spectral peaks [14].

Beyond RaDAR-specific methods, deep anomaly detection includes reconstruction-based, representation-based, and probabilistic approaches that learn characteristics of normal observations [15]. Anomaly detection in time-series data has also been studied [16]. Recurrent encoder-decoder networks [17] and stochastic recurrent models [18] exploit temporal dependencies to identify anomalies, while related approaches combine recurrent prediction with adaptive thresholds for spacecraft telemetry [19]. Alternatively, deep one-class classification learns representations of normal observations to distinguish anomalous samples [20]. Unlike these temporal approaches, frame-wise spectral assessment can detect deviations from expected spectral characteristics in individual Doppler measurements without relying on preceding frames.

Beyond detecting anomalous RaDAR measurements, assessing the reliability of the resulting velocity estimates is equally important. A spectrum may deviate from its expected characteristics without causing a large estimation error, while an erroneous velocity estimate may not be identifiable from simple spectral indicators alone. Research in neural classification considers erroneous predictions and out-of-distribution inputs as distinct but related problems [21]. Learning-based approaches distinguish aleatoric uncertainty arising from observation noise from epistemic uncertainty associated with the learned model [22], providing a framework for interpreting prediction reliability. However, predictive uncertainty can become less reliable under distribution shifts [23]. Selective prediction offers another perspective by rejecting predictions when their estimated reliability is insufficient [24]. For railway Doppler RaDAR, a reconstruction-based velocity estimator with an additional confidence head predicting frame-wise error bounds has been introduced [5]. However, these estimates do not explicitly assess spectral plausibility or consistency with the predicted velocity, particularly whether a velocity-conditioned spectral model can adequately explain the observation. To address these aspects, we introduce a generative approach based on a velocity-conditioned Gaussian model that learns the expected spectral distribution. This enables assessment of both the best achievable spectral fit and agreement with the encoder-predicted velocity. Comparing the encoder prediction with the velocity favored by the generative model further provides a ground-truth-independent consistency indicator that may reveal estimation errors.

Generative modeling offers a complementary approach by learning distributions of expected measurements rather than relying solely on handcrafted spectral features. Neural conditional density estimation allows probability distributions, including Gaussian models, to be parameterized by conditioning variables [25]. Gaussian mixture variational autoencoders have also been investigated for probabilistic anomaly detection in multivariate time series [26]. Other generative approaches identify anomalies through reconstruction-based models, including adversarial methods [27]. However, high generative likelihood does not necessarily imply that an observation is representative of the training distribution [28]. To address background statistics, likelihood ratios using a separate background model trained on perturbed observations have been proposed [29]. Direct application to Doppler spectra is less straightforward, since defining perturbations that suppress velocity-related signal structure while preserving background statistics is challenging. This motivates evaluating spectral consistency indicators without a separate background model. Conditioning a probabilistic spectral model on velocity enables evaluation across different candidate velocities. Building on the velocity encoder introduced in [5], this paper proposes a velocity-conditioned Gaussian model of Doppler spectra for anomaly detection and velocity consistency assessment. Three complementary test-time online indicators are derived: the spectral anomaly score (SAS), measuring the best achievable spectral fit across candidate velocities; the conditional anomaly score (CAS), evaluating spectral plausibility at the encoder-predicted velocity; and the absolute velocity disagreement (AVD), quantifying the difference between the encoder prediction and the velocity preferred by the generative model. We evaluate the sensitivity of learned spectral consistency to velocity deviations, compare the indicators with conventional spectral baselines using controlled synthetic anomalies, and investigate the relationship between AVD and actual velocity estimation errors.

papers.title: REE: A Scientific Research Entrance Exam for AI Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous research agents are emerging as a promising approach to scientific problem-solving across disciplines, owing to their growing ability to improve a solution through repeated experiments. Evaluating this ability requires benchmarks that pose open-ended research problems and measure improvements over established scientific methods. We introduce REE (Research Entrance Exam), a benchmark that tests AI agents on scientific research. It consists of 100 open-ended research problems spanning five broad scientific areas and 23 domains. To ensure high quality, every problem is drawn from active research in its field and individually reviewed by domain experts. Each problem is posed as a task of iterative improvement: an agent has up to 12 hours to improve a working starter solution, and REE scores the result on a common scale against an established expert solution evaluated under comparable conditions. By this measure, two of the four frontier agents we evaluate, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, outperform the expert solutions on 86% and 81% of problems, across all five scientific areas. Their runs also show how they do so: both agents surpass the expert solutions within the first two hours on average, and their best solutions mostly tailor or combine established methods of the field. REE thus provides a unified framework for evaluating autonomous scientific research, capturing both improvements over established methods and the research processes behind them.

Autonomous research agents are AI systems that propose methods, run experiments, and refine their solutions to a research problem with little human guidance. Their role in scientific research is growing, from supporting single steps, such as searching the literature or writing code, to carrying out this whole cycle. Results produced in this way have begun to hold up under experimental validation and peer review (Gottweis et al., 2026; Yamada et al., 2025). The longer-term aim is for such agents to work across scientific disciplines and advance the frontier problems of each.

One of the most effective modes of agent research is iterative improvement. The agent starts from a working solution and a measurable objective, proposes a change, tests it, keeps the change if the result improves, and repeats this cycle many times. AlphaEvolve applied this cycle to more than fifty open problems in analysis, geometry, combinatorics, and number theory, and it improved the best known solution on 20% of them (AlphaEvolve team, 2025; Novikov et al., 2025). The cycle is also effective in direct competition with humans: in a four-hour AtCoder Heuristic Contest, where participants refine a program against a score, an agent took first place ahead of 804 human participants (Sakana AI, 2026). In both cases the object being improved is a solution to a given problem. When it is the agent itself, the cycle is known as recursive self-improvement (RSI), a direction that now draws wide attention because an agent that improves itself could speed up all of its later work (Srikanth et al., 2026).

The problems cover 23 domains in five scientific areas: mathematics and computing, physical sciences and engineering, life and health sciences, earth and environmental sciences, and language, society and culture. We call REE an entrance exam because it asks an agent to do what a field expects of a new researcher, which is to take one of the field’s problems and improve on its established solution. To evaluate an agent, REE poses each of these problems as a task of iterative improvement. The agent receives a problem statement, a working starter solution, and development data on which it can develop and test its methods. It then has up to 12 hours to improve the solution, and a provided checker scores each revision on the development data. The final solution is evaluated on held-out test instances that the agent never sees. It receives a score from 0 to 100, where 0 is the starter solution and 100 is the upper bound of the problem’s metric, such as the highest F-score that any output can attain against the labels of two annotators. To relate this score to human work, each problem also has an expert solution, an established human-designed solution such as a competition entry or a method published for the problem. Because published results were obtained on other test data, we evaluate each expert solution ourselves on the same test instances and under comparable conditions. We also evaluate the intermediate solutions that an agent saves during a run, which shows how its progress develops over time.

papers.title: SceneDesigner3D: Agentic Evolutionary Search for Principled Rearrangement of 3D Indoor Scenes
papers.abstract: Scene rearrangement is an essential task for 3D content creation applications, requiring generation of diverse, aesthetic and functional scene rearrangements. We present SceneDesigner3D, an agentic evolutionary search method for 3D indoor scene rearrangement that systematically explores the design space of 3D scenes and generates multiple solutions according to common interior design principles. Given an input scene and a text prompt, SceneDesigner3D represents the rearrangement as an editable program and evolves a population of candidate layouts. Starting from distinct design ideas, a VLM agent mutates the programs by refining promising candidates, exploring new rearrangement strategies or redesigning from scratch, while verifying the layouts for physical validity. Proposals are scored by a VLM judge for adherence to the input prompt and satisfaction of design principles such as balance, zoning and emphasis, as well as numerically computed principles such as circulation and clutter. An archive of top-performing, structurally varied candidates further increases diversity of rearrangements. Experiments on the SAGE-10k and SceneSmith datasets show that SceneDesigner3D improves prompt adherence and computed design principle scores over baselines by up to 5.1% and 15.2%, respectively. Code will be made publicly available.

papers.intro:
3D indoor scene rearrangement is a central task for content creation applications such as interior design, games and movies, as well as embodied AI systems that need to plan and interact with the world around them. Given an input 3D indoor scene, the task is to rearrange the objects in the scene following the input prompt while keeping the scene physically plausible and functional without collisions or unusable objects. This task is challenging for several reasons: the solution space is combinatorial over tens to hundreds of input objects, and moving one object can affect the functionality and aesthetics of the scene both locally and globally. Moreover, the prompt, functionality and aesthetics often compete with each other and must be traded off. There are typically many desirable solutions, and committing to a single solution can miss better ones. Generating a diverse set of high-quality solutions can enable users and interior designers to choose the one that best fits their needs.

These principles depend on the overall layout and cannot be captured by local constraints. Further, existing methods are designed to generate a single rearranged layout following the input text prompt, and do not systematically search the space of possible solutions to optimize for such principles.

Principles that can be measured geometrically, such as circulation, focal point and clutter, are computed numerically from the layout. The computed scores give the mutator precise feedback across iterations, and together with the judge scores they determine the fitness.

papers.title: Proverbs As A Window On Collective Prescriptions
papers.abstract: Proverbs, as repositories of traditional wisdom, have informed human reasoning for millennia. Yet the collective prescriptions they encode have remained largely unquantified. We introduce a computational framework to analyze nearly 50,000 English-language proverbs. Using large language models, validated against human judgments, we map the topical landscape of proverbs, assess their prescriptive power, and quantify their recommendations on key dimensions of human judgment and behavior. We find that most proverbs are prescriptive, offering guidance in domains under individual control, such as preparation and prudent action, whereas proverbs about uncontrollable circumstances, such as fate and mortality, tend to describe rather than prescribe. When prescriptive proverbs take a consistent stance, they favor caution over risk, long-term over short-term outcomes, honesty over deception, and kindness over malice, and show a moderate tendency toward suspicion over trust. On dimensions involving genuine trade-offs, especially autonomy versus compliance, proverbs provide contradicting advice rather than a single recommendation. This analysis provides a quantitative map of the collective prescriptions in a culture's proverbial wisdom, revealing a core of prudent, honest, and forward-looking guidance alongside varied advice where circumstances dictate the best course of action.

The time-honored lineage, however, does not mean that they are on their way to extinction in a modern and complex world. “Another day, another dollar” or “Garbage in, garbage out” from the world of business and computers are of more recent vintage. According to Mieder 2004, proverbs are “indeed alive and well, and as sapient nuggets, they continue to play a significant role in the modern age” (Mieder, 2004, p. xi). Proverbs have indeed been extensively investigated from different disciplinary angles such as semiotics, linguistics, cognitive science, literature, media studies and their importance has even given rise to a field of proverb studies, called paremiology (see Hrisztova-Gotthardt and Aleksa Varga, 2015). It is devoted to collecting and classifying proverbs, and examine the form, structure, style, content, function, meaning, and value of proverbs.

It is this potential of proverbs that we study here. To open a window onto the collective consciousness expressed through proverbs, we introduce an analytical-computational framework for characterizing and quantifying their content (see Figure1). We address three research questions. First, using a sample of 49,528 English-language proverbs and large language models, we classify the topics addressed by each proverb based on both its wording and a description of its gist. This analysis identifies the situations represented in proverbs and their relative prevalence. Second, we examine the extent to which proverbs prescribe rather than describe how individuals should act or decide. This distinction parallels prominent accounts of social norms that differentiate social regularities (what people do”) from normative guidance (what people ought to do”) (Cialdini et al., 1990; Bicchieri, 2005). Third, we analyze the direction of these prescriptions across nine fundamental dimensions of human judgment and behavior. Three are central to economic research because they "affect such a broad range of economic decisions …. and [afford] the opportunity to better explain economic behavior" (Falk et al., 2023, p. 1935): risk preference (i.e., recommendation of taking risks or exercising caution), intertemporal preference (i.e., recommendation of actions favoring short-term or long-term consequences) and social preference (i.e., recommendation of own-interest or other-regarding behaviors). For each dimension, we assess which pole is favored by prescriptive proverbs.

papers.title: Stranger Things: When Objects Appear Without Their Typical Neighbors
papers.abstract: Visual context is a powerful cue for object recognition: scenes inform what, where, and at what scale objects are likely to appear. Yet over-reliance on context becomes a failure mode when models predict objects based on their typical neighbors rather than the objects' own visual features, which we call typicality bias. While extensively studied in the pre-Transformer era, it has often been assumed that architectural and scale improvements would naturally solve it, and a systematic diagnostic across the modern vision stack remains absent. We provide such a diagnostic framework. We measure typicality bias via normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) over object pairs, and introduce STRANGE-Bench (Synthetic Typicality-RANked Grounded Evaluation Benchmark): a photorealistic, layout-controlled benchmark spanning 17 sub-tiers from typical to never-co-occurring object pairs. Across five model families (specialist detectors, open-vocabulary detectors, self-supervised, vision-language, and multimodal large language models) and three recognition tasks (supervised detection, open-vocabulary detection, and classification), the bias is prevalent: gaps of 5-11 p.p. persist when objects appear outside their typical company, and do not consistently shrink with scale. To mitigate it, we turn to data augmentation: existing augmentations are designed for visual diversity, not for breaking co-occurrence shortcuts, and sample from the very distribution that produces typicality bias. We propose Anchor-Atypicality Sampling (AAS), a simple sampling rule for paste-based augmentations that uses the NPMI signal to tilt the training-time co-occurrence distribution toward atypical partners. AAS reduces the typicality gap by up to 1.6 p.p. on natural-image COCO splits and 23.0 p.p. on synthetic STRANGE-Bench across three model families, without sacrificing overall performance.

papers.title: The Splash population confined to the Milky Way bar region
papers.abstract: We investigate the chemo-dynamical properties of in-situ stars in the Galactic bar region (central $5$ kpc), specifically the inner Galactic counterpart of the solar-neighbourhood Splash population (in situ halo). We use a sample of APOGEE DR17 red giants with Gaia astrometry and AstroNN distances, and separate bulge/bar stellar populations dynamically using a normalised time-averaged bar-frame angular momentum, $\mathcal{V}_{\phi}$. Chemo-dynamical maps in the $\mathcal{V}_{\phi}$-[Fe/H] plane reveal a pronounced extension of the bar population towards $\mathcal{V}_{\phi}<0$ (non-bar-following orbits) within $-1.0<{\rm [Fe/H]}<-0.3$, characterised by high eccentricities, large $z_{\rm max}$ and an extended spheroidal orbit density distribution, and accounting for $\sim 30\%$ of all stars at these metallicities. These $\mathcal{V}_{\phi}<0$ stars have [Mg/Fe] and [Al/Fe] abundances similar to those of stars on ${\rm x_1}$ orbits at the same [Fe/H], and they match the solar-neighbourhood Splash in its metallicity and abundance ratio distributions. We therefore refer to them as the $\textit{central Splash}$. The presence of a significant central Splash underscores the role of the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus merger in the early history of the Galaxy. We find a similar, weaker extension in the $\mathcal{V}_{\phi}$-[Fe/H] maps for extremely metal-rich stars, which are confined to the bulge. At metallicities [Fe/H] $<0.3$, we find no additional classical bulge population in these maps beyond the central Splash and proto-Galactic populations $-$ the high-$\alpha$ bulge appears to have evolved from the early high-$\alpha$ disc.

Major progress has recently been made in identifying key stages in Galactic history, using stellar kinematics and stellar abundances from Gaia and spectroscopic surveys. Studies of nearby stars have provided evidence for the primordial spin-up signalling the formation of the Galactic disc (Belokurov and Kravtsov, 2022; Rix et al., 2022), and for the early merger of the Milky Way with the Gaia-Sausage-Enceladus (GSE) satellite (Helmi et al., 2018; Belokurov et al., 2018), which created both the anisotropic accreted inner Galactic stellar halo, as well as an in situ halo of kicked out disc stars, the Splash (Gallart et al., 2019; Di Matteo et al., 2019; Belokurov et al., 2020).

The Galactic bar region, commonly taken to be inside ∼5\sim 5 kpc, is the region inside corotation where the bar dominates the dynamics. The presence of an additional spheroidal dispersion-dominated classical bulge has not been excluded (Barbuy et al., 2018; Queiroz et al., 2021).

The goal of this paper is to study the Splash population in the bar region and to disentangle it from the bulge and the bar.

N-body models compared with observations of nearby galaxies, including the Milky Way, suggest that b/p bulges arise from so-called secular evolution of the disc, whereby a bar first forms and then evolves into the b/p bulge (Combes et al., 1990; Bureau and Athanassoula, 2005; Shen et al., 2010). On the other hand, a classical bulge forms rapidly by gravitational collapse or hierarchical merging of smaller objects and dissipative gas processes (Steinmetz and Muller, 1995; Brooks and Christensen, 2016). Composite bulges are not unexpected (Athanassoula, 2005) and have also been observed (Erwin et al., 2015; Erwin et al., 2021; Blaña Díaz et al., 2018). The composition of the Galactic bulge therefore provides crucial insights into the formation history of the Milky Way.

papers.title: An oxygen-rich supernova remnant in NGC 253 with narrow [N II] emission lines
papers.abstract:
Context. Supernova remnants (SNRs) are the final evolutionary stage of supernovae. In rare cases, the remnant persists as an optically luminous remnant decades after the explosion. We report the discovery of an unusual oxygen-rich (O-rich) SNR that was serendipitously discovered in the MUSE mosaic of the nearby (D $\sim$ 3.5 Mpc) galaxy NGC 253 released by arXiv:2506.14921.
  Aims. We search for SNRs in MUSE integral field spectroscopy data of NGC 253.
  Methods. We search for unresolved point sources with broad and strong [O III]$\lambda$$\lambda$4959,5007, [O I]$\lambda$$\lambda$6300,6364 or [O II]$\lambda$$\lambda$7320,7331 emission lines. We also search for possible counterparts at other wavelengths in archival data.
  Results. We find a single O-rich SNR in NGC 253 with [O III]$\lambda$$\lambda$4959,5007. For this object, we report a coincident X-ray source detected by Chandra and a non-detection at mid-infrared wavelengths by JWST. Additionally, we identify [N II]$\lambda$$\lambda$6548,6583 emission lines and no detectable hydrogen or [SII]$\lambda$$\lambda$6716,6731 emission. The [N II] emission lines are broader (230 km/s) than the surrounding interstellar medium lines but still narrow in comparison to the [O III] emission (>1500 km/s) from the SNR. No detections of [O I]$\lambda$$\lambda$6300,6364 and [O II]$\lambda$$\lambda$7320,7331 were made.
  Conclusions. The discovery of a single O-rich SNR after a systematic search of NGC 253 highlights their scarcity in nearby galaxies. The structure of [O III] emission indicates complex structure in the O-rich ejecta. The relative narrowness of [N II] emission lines compared to the [O III] lines and the non-detection of hydrogen show that the remnant is surrounded by an N-rich circumstellar medium. The ejecta is currently interacting with this material of the preceding supernova explosion.

papers.intro:
A supernova remnant (SNR) is the final evolutionary phase of a supernova (SN) before it disperses into the interstellar medium. In the Milky Way, they are observed at a full complement of wavelengths from radio to gamma rays (e.g. Ranasinghe and Leahy 2023; Vink et al. 2021). In external galaxies, the radio emission often becomes too faint, and historically extragalactic SNRs have been identified via the use of optical emission lines, namely the ratio of [SII]λ​λ\lambda\lambda6716,6731/Hα\alpha, which is enhanced in the shocked gas found in SNRs with respect to other nebulae such as H II regions (Mathewson and Clarke, 1972; Blair and Long, 2004). Recently, new techniques have been implemented for a more complete detection of SNRs. These include [OI]/Hα\alpha line ratio mapping (Kopsacheili et al., 2020), which has been successfully implemented to detect hundreds of extragalactic SNRs by Li et al. (2024). With the advent of high spatial resolution integral-field spectroscopy, shocked regions in galaxies, such as SNRs, may also be identified from their kinematics together with their spectral properties (Congiu et al., 2023). However, SNRs detected using these line-ratio methods are typically old, from at least thousands of years up to a million years (Micelotta et al., 2018).

With the advent of high spatial resolution integral-field spectroscopy, shocked regions in galaxies, such as SNRs, may also be identified from their kinematics together with their spectral properties (Congiu et al., 2023). However, SNRs detected using these line-ratio methods are typically old, from at least thousands of years up to a million years (Micelotta et al., 2018).

Detected emission from SNRs is typically caused by the radiative cooling during a SNR’s “snowplough” phase, where the ejecta and the ambient medium are piled into a dense cooling shell (Micelotta et al., 2018). There is usually a “dark age” period between the SN phase and its proceeding radiative SNR phase (Yasuda et al., 2021). For example, the initial phase of an H-rich Type II SN is powered by recombination of hydrogen with possible additional energy coming from the ejecta interacting with the circumstellar medium (CSM). After recombination, the SN enters its nebular phase powered by the radioactive material produced by the explosion. As the radioactive material decays, the nebular emission weakens; the SN enters a freely expanding non-radiative phase for thousands of years, and observing it becomes a challenge. Finding young SNRs that are interacting and emitting light through other means is key to understanding their evolution during this “dark age”.

Oxygen-rich (O-rich) SNRs are a rare and young subtype of SNRs, of which only a handful of examples are known; these include Cassiopeia A (Cas A), Puppis A in the Milky Way, LMC N132D in the Large Magellanic Cloud, and the luminous remnant SNR 4449-1 in NGC 4449 (Blair et al., 2000; Ghavamian et al., 2023). Their visible light spectra are dominated by the emission lines of oxygen originating from the inner parts of the remnant. In the case of SNR 4449-1, the reverse shock is thought to be interacting with the oxygen-rich layer within the ejecta originating from the carbon-burning process. The reverse shock itself originates from nitrogen-enriched CSM (Milisavljevic and Fesen, 2008). Additionally, the fast shocks also produce extremely strong X-ray emissions in the ejecta (Patnaude and Fesen, 2003). Recently, several new O-rich SNRs were discovered in nearby galaxies using integral-field spectroscopy (Kravtsov et al., 2025). The method used in the discovery was based on the isolation of the wings of broad emission lines from the continuum and narrow emission lines. This allowed for the effective detection of SNRs, which tend to have broadened shock-excited emission lines compared to the narrow photoionised emission lines of H II regions. Motivated by these discoveries, in the current work we carried out a similar search in NGC 253 (the Sculptor Galaxy), which is a nearby galaxy with an accurately defined distance of 3.5 Mpc based on the tip of the red giant branch method (e.g. Newman et al. 2024; Radburn-Smith et al. 2011). NGC 253 is a well-known starburst galaxy with numerous radio SNRs detected in the central 300 pc region (Rampadarath et al., 2014). These findings indicate a SN rate of up to 0.2 yr-1, which is high compared to normal star-forming spiral galaxies.

papers.title: AnyCam4D: Ray-Based 4D Gaussian Rendering for Arbitrary Camera Models
papers.abstract: Real cameras are not pinholes, yet most dynamic Gaussian splatting assumes they are. Footage is therefore undistorted first, losing field of view or detail, especially with wide-angle and fisheye cameras. Static Gaussian splatting has largely solved this with ray-based rendering, which suits any camera. Native 4D Gaussians, which model motion in space-time, cannot use it directly: each Gaussian's orientation and size cannot be recovered reliably from its covariance. We present AnyCam4D, which trains native 4D Gaussians on original footage by ray-based rasterization, preserving field of view and resolution at about the per-step cost of standard projection. Our key contribution is a numerically stable way to obtain orientation and size: we condition a square root of the 4D covariance. Trained models render through other cameras, with rolling shutter, depth of field or chromatic aberration. With a synthetic 170-degree fisheye camera, training on original images improves peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) by 3.0-8.1 dB. On real footage, AnyCam4D has lower perceptual error than the standard projection adapted to each camera, at comparable PSNR and without camera-specific derivations. With the synthetic camera rotated 60-80 degrees away from the capture rig's view, it leads by 6.2 dB against ground truth.

papers.intro:
Dynamic Gaussian splatting [43, 37, 23, 35] reconstructs moving scenes from multi-camera video and renders new views photorealistically in real time, but usually assumes pinhole cameras. Its projection, EWA splatting [50], linearizes the camera at each Gaussian’s mean and orders Gaussians by depth along the optical axis, which is accurate only near the axis of an undistorted camera. Real lenses distort, from the mild radial distortion of standard lenses to fisheye lenses that see 180∘180^{\circ} and more, and rigs, for example in robotics, often combine several.

Dynamic Gaussian splatting [43, 37, 23, 35] reconstructs moving scenes from multi-camera video and renders new views photorealistically in real time, but usually assumes pinhole cameras. Its projection, EWA splatting [50], linearizes the camera at each Gaussian’s mean and orders Gaussians by depth along the optical axis, which is accurate only near the axis of an undistorted camera. Real lenses distort, from the mild radial distortion of standard lenses to fisheye lenses that see 180∘180^{\circ} and more, and rigs, for example in robotics, often combine several.

Footage is therefore undistorted first, at the cost of field or resolution. At equal resolution a pinhole image either crops the field of a wide lens or samples its center more coarsely: undistorting a 170∘170^{\circ} fisheye to keep 150∘150^{\circ} across the image samples its center 3.4 times more coarsely per axis, keeping the center’s resolution leaves 95∘95^{\circ}, and beyond 180∘180^{\circ} no pinhole image exists.

For static scenes, ray-based renderers [29, 38, 15] have removed this limitation: they evaluate each Gaussian along the ray of a pixel, so the camera only has to provide rays, and 3DGUT [38] keeps rasterization speed by selecting tiles with an unscented transform (UT). Dynamic scenes cannot simply swap in such a renderer: the 3D Gaussian that a native 4D Gaussian [43] draws at time τ\tau comes from conditioning, which yields a covariance but not the rotation and scale that the UT and the ray evaluation are built from. Recovering them is unreliable: an eigendecomposition has no usable gradient at the usual isotropic initialization, at any precision, and in the single precision (fp32) of GPU rasterizers the conditioned covariance loses the thin axis of fast, thin Gaussians.
