papers.title: One, two, three, and a tilting frisbee: a transient state of some Be stars
papers.abstract:
A recent reanalysis of the extreme variability of {\gamma} Cas in the 1930s/40s and 59 Cyg in the 1970s concluded that the disks of these two Be stars have each made a full turn over the poles (Baade+ 2023). For a better understanding of the underlying physics, more examples need to be identified, including less spectacular events, in which the disk was just tilted or warped. This paper discusses PZ Gem and HD 120678 as additional stars with spectroscopic evidence of a tilting disk: during extended line-emission periods intermittent shell phases occurred. In V1294 Aql, the symptoms of a tilting disk concerned H{\alpha} only. Three stars displayed heartbeat-like light variations. Unlike the original heartbeats resulting from distortions of red giant stars on an eccentric orbit, the much-larger-amplitude heartbeats in Be stars are due to changing orientations of the circumstellar disk. Two stars, Pleione and HD 120678, have exhibited both symptoms so that there is probably just one population of Be stars with tilting disks. The small number of candidates suggests that large-amplitude tilts/warpings of Be disks are not common. There is an extreme dominance of spectral types of B1 or earlier.
  In Be binaries resulting from previous mass transfer, spin-orbit misalignments and any torque on the Be disk should not be large. The necessary tilting force could be provided by a putative third star on an orbit highly inclined with respect to the inner binary (or just passing the B star) and be exerted either directly or indirectly via tilting the inner orbital plane. Beyond a refined knowledge of the multiplicity of Be stars, this would not promise much new insight into Be stars at large (except, perhaps, for some independent estimates of the viscosity parameter and a more 3D view of stellar winds). However, pruning the Be-star saga of such peculiarities may help reduce the level of confusion.
papers.intro:
The picture widely associated with Be stars resembles Saturn: a sphere surrounded by an equatorial disk. This is Otto Struve’s heritage (Struve, 1931), who noticed the correlation between the stellar vv sin ii and the width of the emission lines. Hanuschik (1989) and Arias et al. (2006) repeated the analysis with non-photographic data, and, in a higher-level comparison, Sigut and Ghafourian (2023) found agreement between stellar inclination angles derived from rotational gravity darkening and disk inclination angles obtained from Hα\alpha emission profiles.

(2006) repeated the analysis with non-photographic data, and, in a higher-level comparison, Sigut and Ghafourian (2023) found agreement between stellar inclination angles derived from rotational gravity darkening and disk inclination angles obtained from Hα\alpha emission profiles.

The existence of such a stellar-circumstellar correlation requires that the disks are generally coplanar with the respective stellar equator. Interferometry (Berio et al., 1999, e.g.,) and polarimetry (e.g., Reis Querido et al., these proceedings) have confirmed for many stars that the aspect angles of Be disks are ∼\siminvariant over many years or even decades. This is less simple for Saturn, the rings of which can be viewed from below, from above, and even edge-on. However, the tilting is only apparent and results from the relative orbital motions of Saturn and Earth. If the disk around a Be star seems to tilt, this explanation is not applicable, and the variation must correspond to a physical change in the angular momentum vector of the disk. A tilting of Saturn’s rings can also be physical in the hypothetical case that another planet passes Saturn closely, in particular if the rings and the motion of the other planet are not coplanar.

A Be disk (the frisbee in the title) can experience similar encounters. Obviously not in isolated Be stars, but companion stars on misaligned orbits (or a star just passing as in the above planetary example) can inflict transient tilts on Be disks. If the central B star has received a substantial mass and angular-momentum donation from what now is the secondary star, the spin-orbit misalignment may be small. That is, "one" (see title) is not an option, "two" may be, and "three" certainly is. The foundation to the suspicion that Be disks may tilt was laid by γ\gamma Cas and 59 Cyg, which in the 1930s/1940s and 1970s, respectively, underwent two transitions each between (i) continuous strong emission and (ii) transient shell phases that are not foreseen in Struve’s paradigm and were explained by Hummel (1998) and Baade et al. (2023) as a temporary tilting of the disks into the line of sight.

papers.title: periapsis: A Comprehensive Orbital Fitting Package
papers.abstract: We introduce a new Python package \texttt{periapsis}, which computes posterior distributions for a variety of orbital parameters given astrometric and/or radial velocity data. \texttt{periapsis} not only returns posterior distributions, but also a variety of statistics assessing convergence and fit metrics as well as plotting capabilities for visualizing the orbital systems. In this paper, we describe our various methods for fitting Keplerian orbits to both astrometric and radial velocity data. We then show the breadth of binary systems that \texttt{periapsis} can characterize by comparing our computed parameters with known orbital systems. Finally, we discuss how \texttt{periapsis} will be a helpful tool for future data releases like \textit{Gaia} DR4 and \textit{Roman}.

papers.intro:
A large fraction of stars along the main sequence are believed to form and reside in binary or higher-order systems (Offner et al., 2023; Moe & Di Stefano, 2017). These systems are rich with interesting astrophysical phenomena enabling us to learn more about stellar evolution (Moe & Di Stefano, 2017), compact object formation and populations (Andrews et al., 2019; Müller-Horn et al., 2026a), planetary systems (Butler et al., 2006), progenitors to gravitational wave sources (Abbott et al., 2016), and much more. The last few decades of astronomy have seen a dramatic increase in the number of spectroscopic surveys, providing a large number of radial velocity measurements on stars across the Milky Way (De Silva et al., 2015; Majewski et al., 2017), and with the advent of Gaia, astrometry for over a billion sources has been recorded (Gaia Collaboration et al., 2023; Halbwachs et al., 2023). These datasets have led to the discovery of many interesting stellar, planetary, and compact object companions, greatly increasing our knowledge on their populations (Müller-Horn et al., 2026b; Butler et al., 2006; El-Badry et al., 2023a; El-Badry et al., 2023b; Gaia Collaboration et al., 2024; Whitaker et al., 2026). Being able to accurately characterize these systems and their uncertainties is important to further our understanding of these populations and phenomena.

Many different approaches have been taken to characterize binary systems, with Bayesian inference being highly favored to obtain posterior distributions of orbital parameters that encapsulate their uncertainties (Lucy, 2018). Different ways of doing this have been presented in a variety of orbital fitting packages and custom made codes, made to fit astrometry, radial velocity, or joint measurements (Price-Whelan et al., 2017; Blunt et al., 2020a; El-Badry et al., 2024). However, it can be difficult to find a package that works for a variety of observational scenarios and that is easy and intuitive to use.

However, it can be difficult to find a package that works for a variety of observational scenarios and that is easy and intuitive to use.

We here present our comprehensive orbital fitting package periapsis11 1 https://github.com/Evank2004/periapsis, which is capable of fitting orbits to a wide variety of observational data, whether that be 2D astrometry, scanning-plane astrometry (like Gaia), radial velocities, or any combination of the three. The package can also accommodate the case where both components of the binary system have been observed, performing a joint fit on both. The package has been designed to fully characterize a binary system with a minimal amount of manual tuning done by the user. This “plug and play” design allows for easy analyses of interesting systems, where users can obtain detailed orbital constraints on their system with a minimal amount of code. The package can return a large variety of statistics on the behavior of the sampler and the parameter values and uncertainties. To visualize the orbital fit and the sampler behavior, multiple plotting options are included.

We then show the effectiveness of periapsis by fitting known orbital systems in Section 4. papers.title: CHEX-MATE: Probing the thermal$-$non-thermal connection in radio halo clusters with LoTSS-DR2
papers.abstract: The main baryonic component of galaxy clusters is in the form of a hot plasma observed in the X-rays. In addition, clusters host a non-thermal component (relativistic particles and magnetic fields) which is studied mainly via radio telescopes and is dynamically coupled to the thermal plasma. These two components evolve together within the system and are subject to both micro and macro-physical processes which can be traced only with deep and detailed observations. We present the first homogeneous spatially resolved radio--X-ray study of 18 radio halo clusters combining CHEX-MATE and the LOFAR Two metre Sky Survey DR2. Radio ($I_R$) and X-ray ($I_X$) surface brightness are clearly correlated (Spearman coefficient $r_s \ge 0.5$), following a typically sublinear $I_R-I_X$ relation ($67 \pm 5\%$ of the sample) that appears to be independent of other cluster properties, although a tentative trend with mass/redshift may be worth exploring with larger samples. When inspecting such a relation as a function of the radius, we observe a variety of behaviours, which suggest that the interplay between the thermal and non-thermal plasma components varies with radius. We find the averaged slope profile of dynamically disturbed clusters to be consistent with expectations from turbulent re-acceleration models where a constant ratio between cosmic-ray electron and thermal energy densities is assumed. Differently, less perturbed clusters require an increasing cosmic-ray-to-thermal energy ratio with radius. Finally, we show that radio halo surface-brightness profiles can be effectively rescaled using X-ray information and theoretical expectations. This procedure significantly reduces their scatter and reveals common underlying trends based on the cluster dynamics, resembling what is observed for the thermal ICM, and strengthening the idea of a strong interplay between these two plasma components.

papers.intro: Galaxy clusters allow us to study a wide range of processes, from structure formation and cosmology to particle re-acceleration processes and radiative mechanisms. These two latter subjects are mainly explored through radio and X-ray observations. In fact, it is well established that within the cluster environment, many sources of radio synchrotron emission are present (see e.g. van Weeren et al., 2019, for a review). Among the most puzzling and extended cases of such emission are giant radio halos. They are megaparsec-scale sources characterised by a steep spectral index (α<−1\alpha<-1, where the flux density Sν∝ναS_{\nu}\propto\nu^{\alpha}) mainly found in massive merging clusters. Although two main mechanisms for the production of radio halos have been proposed (hadronic and leptonic origin), past gamma ray observations have discarded a pure hadronic origin of the cosmic ray electrons (CRe, see Brunetti and Jones 2014 for a review). Instead, statistical studies on radio halos at low frequencies showed an agreement with the expectations from the (re-)acceleration of CRe operated by merger-induced turbulence (Cassano et al., 2023, e.g.). In fact, during the structure formation process, galaxy clusters experience the accretion of sub-clusters and groups through mergers, which release up to ∼1064\sim 10^{64} ergs in the Intra Cluster Medium (ICM) in a cluster crossing time (Tormen et al., 2004, ∼\sim Gyr, e.g.). Such energy is mainly dissipated into gas heating through shocks, enhancing the ICM thermal Bremsstrahlung emission in the X-rays. A small fraction of this energy can be channelled into turbulence that re-accelerates relativistic electrons via a Fermi-II like mechanism, originating synchrotron emission (Brunetti et al., 2001; Petrosian, 2001). Since cluster mergers are ultimately driven by gravity, the energy available for particle acceleration is expected to scale with the cluster gravitational potential, and hence with its mass. Consequently, the most massive mergers are expected to generate bright radio halos observable up to GHz frequencies, whereas less energetic mergers should preferentially produce fainter halos with steeper spectra, detectable mainly at low radio frequencies. These latter objects have indeed been studied in both targeted observations (Macario et al., 2013; Wilber et al., 2018, e.g.) and large samples (Cassano et al., 2023). This turbulent mechanism for halo production reproduces well the general properties of radio halos, like their number and redshift distribution or the expected flux (Cassano et al., 2023). It also provides a natural explanation for the observed radio power - mass relation and the halo merger connection (Cassano et al., 2010a; Cuciti et al., 2023; Di Gennaro et al., 2025, e.g.). However, the spatially resolved properties of such a process remain poorly understood. In fact, different turbulence re-acceleration mechanisms (transit time damping; Alfven resonant scattering, etc.) predict different spatial distributions of relativistic particles, magnetic fields, and thermal plasma, leading to a variety of observational signatures and physical scenarios (Brunetti and Lazarian, 2007; Brunetti and Lazarian, 2011; Miniati and Beresnyak, 2015; Brunetti and Lazarian, 2016, e.g.). Thanks to the high sensitivity of current radio facilities (e.g., LOFAR, van Haarlem et al. 2013, MeerKAT, Jonas and MeerKAT Team 2016, ASKAP, Hotan et al. 2021), spatially resolved studies of radio and X-ray derived quantities are becoming possible for large samples of objects. They have the great potential to infer the details of the radio emission mechanism (e.g. CRe distribution, acceleration rate, magnetic field) and to put constraints on the microphysics of the ICM (Govoni et al., 2001; Rajpurohit et al., 2021b; Balboni et al., 2024, e.g.). Recent works exploited the correlation among radio and X-ray surface brightness in the centre and in the periphery of clusters to derive constraints on the non-trivial distribution of the synchrotron emitting electrons (Biava et al., 2021; Biava et al., 2024, e.g.). Similarly, from radio spectral index profiles it is now possible to constrain some of the crucial parameters of the model, such as the typical re-acceleration time (Rajpurohit et al., 2023; Kale et al., 2025, tacct_{\text{acc}}, e.g.). Studies on large samples of halos have shown that their global properties are broadly consistent with the predictions of homogeneous re-acceleration models, based on cluster-averaged physical quantities (Cassano et al., 2023). However, when radio spectral index profiles are available and allow to constrain some of the crucial parameters of the model such as ta​c​ct_{acc}, radial variations emerge, indicating that these averaged descriptions may not fully capture the underlying physics (Rajpurohit et al., 2023; Bonafede et al., 2022, e.g.). Only a handful of detailed studies combining spatially resolved radio and X-ray observations have so far explored these effects. Bonafede et al. (2022) (and subsequently Bruno et al. 2023 and Balboni et al. 2024) investigated the radial trend of the radio and X-ray surface brightness relation, finding evidence that the ratio between thermal and non-thermal energy densities may vary with radius. Similarly, Santra et al. (2024) and van Weeren et al. (2026) also provided evidence for a non-trivial distribution of CRe throughout the cluster extension, and for different CRe production scenarios. These studies demonstrate the potential of spatially resolved analyses, but remain limited to a small number of individual clusters. A homogeneous analysis of a statistically representative sample is therefore still lacking. With the present work, we aim to perform the first systematic study of radio halo resolved brightness properties and their correlations with thermal ICM emission. In particular, we aim to study a well selected sample of objects, for which we have uniform and homogeneous coverage in both radio and X-ray bands. This is possible by matching the Cluster HEritage project with XMM-Newton - Mass Assembly and Thermodynamics at the Endpoint of structure formation (CHEX-MATE Collaboration et al., 2021, CHEX-MATE,) and the LOFAR Two-meter Sky Survey Data Release 2 (Shimwell et al., 2022, LoTSS-DR2,) datasets. They provide the necessary data in the two requested bands and for a wide sample of Planck 2nd Sunyaev-Zeldovich Source Catalog objects (Planck Collaboration et al., 2016). The paper is organized as follows: in Section 2 we present the sample observations and data reduction; in Section 3 we describe the data analysis; in Section 4 we comment on our results. In Sections 5 we summarise the results. In this work we assume a flat, Λ\LambdaCDM Universe cosmology with H0=70​km​s−1​Mpc−1H_{0}=70\rm\penalty\ km\penalty\ s^{-1}\penalty\ Mpc^{-1}, Ωm,0=0.3\Omega_{m,0}=0.3, ΩΛ=0.7\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.7, Hz/H0=Ez=[Ωm,0​(1+z)3+ΩΛ]1/2H_{z}/H_{0}=E_{z}=[\Omega_{m,0}(1+z)^{3}+\Omega_{\Lambda}]^{1/2}.

papers.title: AT2024dky as an Off-nuclear Tidal Disruption Event Candidate
papers.abstract: Through a retrospective search for tidal disruption events (TDEs) in the ZTF archives agnostic to their location within their host galaxies, we identify AT2024dky/ZTF24aagksvd as a promising off-nuclear TDE candidate. At $z=0.0592$, it lies at a projected offset of $3.72^{\prime\prime}$ (4.26 kpc) from the center of a massive ($M_{\rm gal}\sim10^{11}\,M_\odot$), quiescent galaxy. We present early-time ZTF and ATLAS optical photometry and late-time follow-up observations with Keck-I/LRIS, VLA, EP, and Chandra. With $M_{g,\rm peak}=-18.50$ mag, AT2024dky exhibits persistently blue color ($g-r\sim-0.1$ mag) through 80 d after peak. At $\delta t=858$ d, Keck reveals $M_{u'}=-13.07\pm0.09$ mag and $M_R > -14.15$ mag. At $\delta t=866$ d, VLA detects the transient at $\nu L_{\nu,10\,\rm GHz}=(1.26\pm0.17)\times10^{38}\,\mathrm{erg\,s^{-1}}$. The combination of early photometric evolution, detected late-time radio and UV emission strongly favor a TDE interpretation. The properties of its host galaxy also bear remarkable similarities to the parent galaxies of known off-nuclear TDEs. Based on the low values of peak-time and late-time UV/optical luminosities, we favor a black hole mass of $\sim 10^5$--$10^6 M_\odot$. Together, these observations strongly favor an off-nuclear TDE.

papers.intro:
Massive black holes (MBHs) residing outside galactic nuclei, including both supermassive black holes (SMBHs; MBH≳105​M⊙M_{\rm BH}\gtrsim 10^{5}\,M_{\odot}) and intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs; 102≲MBH≲105​M⊙10^{2}\lesssim M_{\rm BH}\lesssim 10^{5}\,M_{\odot}), can arise through several formation channels. During galaxy minor mergers, tidal stripping can leave the central MBH of the secondary galaxy embedded in a stripped nucleus, while long dynamical friction timescales delay its migration toward the center of the parent galaxy [37, 69]. MBHs can also be ejected from galactic nuclei by gravitational-wave recoil following black hole coalescence or by gravitational slingshot interactions involving multiple black holes [14, 64, 103]. Off-nuclear IMBHs may also form in dense stellar clusters through runaway stellar collisions [99, 48]. The abundance, spatial distribution, and stellar environments of these off-nuclear MBHs provide constraints on black hole formation, the accretion and disruption of satellite galaxies, and the efficiency with which MBHs pair and merge. They therefore offer a complementary perspective on the connection between black hole growth and galaxy assembly beyond that provided by central MBHs.

At larger distances, off-nuclear MBHs have been searched for as offset active galactic nuclei (AGNs) or AGN pairs (either dual or binary). A literature compilation covering studies published through 2020 contains 156 confirmed dual AGNs and one confirmed binary AGN [98]. Complementary searches have identified individual spatially offset AGNs and larger samples of candidates in merging galaxies [10, 11, e.g.,]. However, AGN searches preferentially reveal MBHs with sufficient gas to sustain persistent accretion.

Tidal disruption events (TDEs) provide a complementary approach: the disruption of a star can temporarily illuminate an otherwise dormant black hole in a gas-poor, quiescent environment, making it detectable over a much larger volume. This method potentially favors MBHs embedded in dense stellar systems that can supply stars and replenish the loss cone [23]. Nevertheless, theoretical studies suggest that off-nuclear black holes could contribute a significant fraction of the TDE population. Recoiling black holes alone may account for ∼1\sim 1% of all disruptions [122], while merger-driven wanderers could contribute substantially more [100].

A few off-nuclear TDEs have been established. The first two, 3XMM J2150-05 and EP240222a, were identified in X-rays and are consistent with disruptions by IMBHs of 10410^{4}–105​M⊙10^{5}\,M_{\odot}. Whereas 3XMM J2150-05 was discovered through archival observations [77], EP240222a was detected in real time, enabling prompt multi-wavelength follow-up [66]. The remaining three events were discovered optically by the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF; Graham et al. 53, Bellm et al. 12, Dekany et al. 32). TDE 2024tvd initially passed a nuclear-transient selection, but its significant (∼1​″\sim 1\arcsec) offset from the host nucleus, together with its low peak luminosity relative to nuclear TDEs in comparably massive galaxies, motivated high-resolution follow-up, which confirmed its off-nuclear nature [139]. This discovery motivated complementary efforts to identify off-nuclear TDEs: real-time searches that relax the nuclear-location requirement lead to TDE 2025abcr [119], and reexamination of the known ZTF nuclear TDE sample for previously unrecognized offsets identified TDE 2023mfm [119, 76, 112].

In this Letter, we report AT 2024dky. Its displacement from the host-galaxy nucleus is unambiguous. Although the absence of early-time spectroscopy initially limits the certainty of its TDE classification, our late-time optical and radio observations, together with the resemblance of its host environment to those of known off-nuclear TDEs, strongly favor a TDE interpretation. We present observations of the transient and its host galaxy to assess its nature and motivate further follow-up.

papers.title: Effect-Driven Skill Abstractions for Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: We seek to learn discrete skill abstractions to facilitate long-horizon, goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning (RL) tasks. Recent approaches have shown success by quantizing actions via clustering or reconstruction. However, these objectives lead to skills that are not directly related to what the current state affords or what the goal requires. Instead, we argue that goal-directed skills should be driven by \emph{how they affect the state} of the agent. To realize this, we introduce a novel quantization method for action chunks that optimizes next-state predictions conditioned on the current state and action. This objective encourages skills to be distinguished by the future states they lead to, resulting in a vocabulary that spans diverse outcomes reachable from a given state. Our framework can easily be paired with common offline RL methods by replacing their continuous actor head with a discrete one that selects among the learned skills. We can execute these skills in the environment by converting them back to continuous actions using a trained low-level controller. Experiments on benchmark navigation and manipulation tasks largely show substantial and consistent improvements over both the continuous-actor baselines and reconstruction-based discretizations. Our project page can be found at: https://burcukilic.github.io/projects/effect-driven-skill-abstractions/.

papers.intro:
Offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) aims to learn decision-making policies from collected interaction data to eliminate the safety and sample-efficiency issues of online exploration Levine et al. (2020). This paradigm is especially useful in goal-conditioned settings Kaelbling (1993); Park et al. (2025); Schaul et al. (2015) where a single policy must reach various targets in the environment, making online exploration unsafe and expensive. However, training stable goal-conditioned policies remains challenging for long-horizon tasks in sparse-reward settings, especially in high-dimensional continuous action spaces, where the policy may output actions outside the training dataset’s support, leading to unstable training and unreliable value estimates.

(2020). This paradigm is especially useful in goal-conditioned settings Kaelbling (1993); Park et al. (2025); Schaul et al. (2015) where a single policy must reach various targets in the environment, making online exploration unsafe and expensive. However, training stable goal-conditioned policies remains challenging for long-horizon tasks in sparse-reward settings, especially in high-dimensional continuous action spaces, where the policy may output actions outside the training dataset’s support, leading to unstable training and unreliable value estimates.

One way to mitigate this is to convert the continuous problem into a discrete one. It is generally more straightforward to optimize a policy over a finite set of actions than over an uncountable set Dadashi et al. (2022). The simplest approach to discretizing a continuous action space is to uniformly partition each dimension into discrete bins. However, such a partition would suffer from the curse of dimensionality in high-dimensional spaces. A better alternative is to learn the discretizations from data. AQuaDem Dadashi et al. (2022) and SAQ Luo et al. (2023) learn state-conditioned action discretizations, improving both training stability and task performance over continuous baselines. These methods discretize actions at the level of a single timestep. However, for long-horizon tasks, behavior should be temporally extended as a prerequisite for tractable learning and reasoning Sutton et al. (1999); Konidaris (2019). Recent studies quantize action chunks rather than single-step actions to produce discrete skills Shafiullah et al. (2022); Lee et al. (2024); Zheng et al. (2024); Mete et al. (2024). These methods perform quantization by reconstructing or clustering actions, which is a sensible objective to capture the multimodality of the demonstrator’s behavior.

We argue that for goal-conditioned tasks, what makes a learned skill useful is the effect it has on the state, not the particular sequence of low-level control commands that produces it. In this respect, in the unsupervised skill discovery literature, DIAYN Eysenbach et al. (2019) learns diverse skills by making the states they visit distinguishable, and DADS Sharma et al. (2020) trains skills whose next state, given the current state, is predictable. However, neither approach performs explicit discretization; they observe diverse behavioral patterns in the data but do not represent them as separate entities or leverage them as reusable primitives. Inspired by this consequence-driven perspective, we quantize action chunks based on next-state predictions, grounding each discrete skill in its effect on the state rather than in its low-level execution. Conditioning this effect prediction mechanism on the current state further ensures that each discrete skill corresponds to an outcome that the state already offers in the dataset. In this sense, the resulting skill codes behave as state-dependent affordances Gibson (1977); Khetarpal et al. (2020), which are skill possibilities available to the agent in the current state provided by the environment. Through this quantization framework, we aim to discover a discrete vocabulary of skills that yield meaningful outcomes, i.e., outcomes that allow the system to effectively sequence these skills to achieve given goals.

In summary, we introduce a novel action chunk quantization method that discovers goal-driven discrete skills by predicting the outcomes they generate. Our system also learns a separate low-level controller network to translate the discrete skills back to continuous actions. Both the skill vocabulary and the controller are policy-independent, meaning that they can be paired with various offline RL methods. To demonstrate policy independence, we derive discrete variants of four standard offline RL methods, which are trained as high-level policies that output discrete skills instead of continuous actions. We evaluate our method across state- and pixel-based navigation and manipulation domains, including Maze, Puzzle, and visual tasks from the Offline Goal-Conditioned RL Benchmark (OGBench) Park et al. (2025), Push-T dataset Chi et al. (2023), and D4RL Kitchen Fu et al. (2021) against both continuous baseline policies and reconstruction-based or single-step action quantization alternatives, demonstrating that our method consistently outperforms all baselines.

papers.title: Will national renewable costs continue declining?
papers.abstract: Since the 1980s, the global average solar photovoltaic (PV) cost has decreased by about two orders of magnitude while the global average onshore wind cost has decreased by about one order of magnitude. But global averages are only part of the story: For both solar and wind, costs vary between countries by about an order of magnitude. We curate a comprehensive database of national costs and build predictive models for future costs by decomposing the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) into its components at the national level and modeling them separately. For solar we find that since 1990 the module cost and the balance of system (BOS) cost have both declined roughly exponentially at rates of 12% per year. In contrast, wind turbine cost has declined roughly exponentially by 4% per year, while BOS cost has not declined at all. This suggests that total global wind cost will approach a floor cost of about 35 USD/MWh, reaching about 43 USD/MWh in 2050, whereas global solar cost will continue to decline exponentially, reaching about 8 USD/MWh in 2050. For solar, about half of the cross-sectional variations in national LCOE costs is due to variations in capacity factors, though capital costs also play an important role. For wind, the cross-sectional variations are split approximately equally between capacity factor, capital costs, and investment costs. National BOS costs revert to global costs with a timescale of about 5-7 years, while variations in other factors are more persistent. We develop a simple model for predicting the deviations from global costs and show that it makes reasonable predictions with predictable errors. Finally, we compare our predictions to recent projections of integrated assessment models, and show that China has only accounted for about 0.05% of the overall decline in solar energy costs.

papers.intro:
The rapid decline of the costs of solar and wind energy over the last sixty years or so has changed views about the feasibility of the energy transformation, injecting a rare note of optimism into the climate debate. In hindsight, it is clear that this could have been predicted much earlier by extrapolating past statistical trends; a few did this, but their voices received limited attention.[farmer_us_2010, farmer16, way22] Paying more attention to such forecasts would have made it possible to anticipate which technologies were likely to be cheap and plan and invest accordingly.[creutzig17, bolinger22, way22]

Today, with significantly more granular data available for renewable costs, we can improve on these simple statistical models and investigate if and when future renewable costs may deviate from past trends. A number of studies have investigated granular trends in renewable costs. Examples include more granular assessment of cost declines in solar modules,[nemet06, kavlak18] balance of system,[elshurafa18, kothari_drivers_2023] wind turbines,[elia_wind_2020] operation and maintenance,[wiser_assessing_2019, riva_iea_2018, steffen20a, raupach-sumiya_regional_2015] or financing.[steffen18] Furthermore, increasing attention is being paid to understanding empirical and theoretical drivers of cost declines in renewables, and how these may translate to other technologies.[wilson_granular_2020, malhotra_accelerating_2020] Nonetheless, there is an important need for better out-of-sample statistical testing, as there has been a tendency toward overfitting and in hindsight many previous forecasts (that didn’t do this) are wrong.[baumgartner_need_2024]

Here we develop reliable forecasts for solar and wind costs by decomposing national costs into their components and studying their statistical properties in detail. Leveraging much of the previous academic work in this space, we have aggregated a novel dataset of renewable costs in 65 countries for solar PV and 68 countries for onshore wind. The dataset spans time-series data for different national cost components over the past 70 years (though albeit some of these are sparsely populated). Our dataset contains approximately 20,000 data points and is the largest academic dataset currently available. Due to data availability, the dataset is skewed towards developed economies. There are, however, a number of emerging markets represented that do not exhibit statistically different properties to developed counterparts.

National costs of renewables vary widely, so forecasts need to take this into account.[lutz_economic_2015] As we show here, the deviations across countries can be understood by decomposing the costs of renewables into their components. This turns out to also have implications for global costs; as we will see, extrapolating the revealed trends suggests that wind power will drop in cost more slowly and reach a floor, whereas solar will continue to drop exponentially for some time. This suggests that twenty years from now, solar energy will be substantially cheaper than wind energy.

The standard way to compare the costs of capital-intensive renewable technologies with those of more operationally intensive technologies such as fossil fuels is based on the levelized cost of electricity (LCOE), which is defined as the average annualized cost of generating one unit of electricity.[irena_renewable_2024, bolinger22] Here we decompose the formula for LCOE into its different components and develop a forecasting model for each component separately. This allows us to forecast national renewable electricity costs and better understand the drivers that determine them.

It is worth mentioning that the LCOE is not without limitations. The LCOE has been criticized for dismissing the intermittency of renewable electricity sources.[wang_cost_2022, smil_examining_2016, ueckerdt_system_LCOE_2023] Energy systems with large shares of renewables also require sufficient short- and long-term energy storage to provide reliable power in the absence of sunshine or wind.[way_empirically_2022, creutzig17, luderer_impact_2021] Forecasting LCOE components is therefore helpful in applications where the LCOE is inappropriate.

papers.title: State of the UNIONS: Four Milky Way companions discovered in a systematic search for northern Local Group satellites
papers.abstract: We present four newly discovered Milky Way satellites from a systematic search through the $gri$ photometry from the Ultraviolet Near-Infrared Optical Northern Survey (UNIONS). Two of these satellites are likely ultra-faint dwarf galaxies that we have named Bo\"otes VI and Draco III. Both galaxy candidates are $\gtrsim 100$ kpc from the Galactic center and have absolute $V$-band magnitudes ($M_V$) of $-2.7^{+0.6}_{-0.5}$ and $-4.0\pm0.6$, respectively. Bo\"otes VI and Draco III have physical half-light radii ($r_{\rm h}$) of $\sim 50$ pc, or about twice as large as the most extended Milky Way globular clusters with similar luminosities. They are therefore candidate galaxies, though chemodynamical analyses will be needed to secure these classifications. We name the two other systems UNIONS 2 and UNIONS 3. They are extremely faint ($M_V = +0.4^{+0.6}_{-0.9}$ and $-0.7^{+0.6}_{-0.8}$) and compact ($r_{\rm h} = 5\,\pm\,1$ and $10^{+3}_{-2} pc), and zero giant stars are identified in either of their present-day stellar populations. Morphological measurements alone are not sufficient to assess the presence of dark matter in either system, so do not provide definitive classifications. We discuss the challenges in either detecting or refuting the presence of dark matter in UNIONS 2 and UNIONS 3, two systems that are archetypal of the faintest satellites that will be discovered in increasing numbers in upcoming wide-field surveys.

In the Milky Way halo, the faintest confirmed satellite galaxies known have total luminosities less than 300 L⊙\textup{L}_{\odot} [141, 120, 129, Tucana V, Segue 1, Triangulum II;]. These are the most extreme examples from a class of galaxies referred to as ultra-faint dwarfs (UFDs), defined as galaxies with MV>−7.7M_{V}>-7.7 [26, 144]. They are ancient (age, τ≳10\tau\gtrsim 10 Gyr), metal-poor (⟨[Fe/H]⟩≲−2\langle{\rm[Fe/H]}\rangle\lesssim-2), and have large implied dynamical mass-to-light ratios (Mdyn/L ≳103\gtrsim 10^{3} M⊙\textup{M}_{\odot}/L⊙\textup{L}_{\odot}).

In the context of Λ\Lambda Cold Dark Matter (Λ\LambdaCDM) cosmology, UFDs are highly dark matter dominated and situated as the lowest mass fossils of galaxy formation in the early universe [22, 24, 25, 61]. Individual UFDs have become premier laboratories for investigating baryonic processes such as self-enrichment [89, 101], chemical evolution [60, 84, 85, 133, e.g.], the local and environmental impacts of reionization [27, 130, 21], and low mass galaxy mergers [43, 36, 159], as well as open questions in dark matter theory, like the shape and density of small dark matter halos [135, e.g.], and their modification in a halo environment [54, 52, 51]. On a population level, the number and distribution of UFDs has spurred progress in the understanding of the galactic luminosity function [142, 91, 156, 160, 123, 47], the halo occupation function [83, 121, 136] and the viability of alternate dark matter models [122, 124, 41, 116], as well as tidal stripping [54, 82, 131] and the accretion history of the Milky Way [42, 136, 139].

The challenge of uncovering galaxies at ever fainter limits, and thereby extending galactic evolution models to lower masses and smaller length-scales, has been enabled by the era of digital sky surveys and wide-field photometry performed over the extragalactic sky. Only nine “classical” dwarf galaxies (MV<−7.7M_{V}<-7.7) were known prior to the turn of the millennium. The Sloan Digital Sky Survey [166, 1, SDSS,] saw ∼\sim15 Milky Way satellite dwarf galaxies discovered [164, 163, 16, 15, 14, 13, 167, 168, e.g.], revealing the first UFDs and more than doubling the known population of Milky Way dwarf galaxies. The Dark Energy Survey [2, DES,] and the 3π\pi survey with the Panoramic Survey Telescope and Rapid Response System [35, Pan-STARRS,] enabled the discovery of another ∼\sim25 UFDs [12, 48, 92, 96, 95]. Most recently, the DECam Local Volume Exploration survey [49, 50, DELVE,] has been particularly productive hunting grounds [110, 31, 32, 29, 28, 152, 153] while additional discoveries [76, 77, 74, 75, 67, 147] in the Hyper-Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program [3, 4, HSC-SSP,] and the Ultraviolet Near-Infrared Northern Survey [70, UNIONS,] have brought the total number of confirmed or suspected Milky Way satellite UFDs to 57 [127, 34].

Looking beyond the Milky Way, our largest neighbor Andromeda (M31) hosts a larger population of dwarf galaxies per luminosity bin, with 43 galaxies known brighter than MV=−5M_{V}=-5, 15 of which are UFDs. The Pan-Andromeda Archaeological Survey [113, PAndAS;] discovered many of M31’s satellites within 150 kpc while the outer region of the halo population has been added to by SDSS, Pan-STARRS, UNIONS, and the DESI Legacy Imaging surveys [46]. In the rest of the Local Group, the galactic region surrounding the Milky Way and M31, there are roughly 65 known galaxies out to 3 Mpc. Only a handful are UFDs (∼5\sim 5), reflecting the difficulty of detecting the the lowest mass, least evolved galaxies beyond the halo environment.

Returning to the Milky Way halo, the dark matter-dominated dwarf galaxies are contrasted by nearly 200 self-gravitating star clusters (SCs), the majority of which (∼\sim150) are the classical globular clusters [GCs, 72, 2010 edition]. Most GCs can be easily distinguished from dwarf galaxies via imaging: in the magnitude range of typical GCs (−10<MV<−5-10<M_{V}<-5), they are far more compact (half-light radii, rhr_{\text{h}} ≲10\lesssim 10 pc in scale radius) than dwarfs (rhr_{\text{h}} ≳100\gtrsim 100 pc). Stellar spectroscopy has also revealed key differences: line-of-sight velocities imply that GCs have 1<1< Mdyn/L <3<3 M⊙\textup{M}_{\odot}/L⊙\textup{L}_{\odot} [11, e.g.] and chemical analyses show little spread in iron abundance [97, e.g.], implying short star formation histories and negligible self-enrichment [10, 162]. This difference is thought to reflect the fundamental distinction between the populations, namely that dwarf galaxies form at the centers of their own dark matter halos, whereas GCs do not [see 94, and citations therein].

papers.title: Anatomy-Aware Pseudo-Labels and Homotopy-Annealed Hausdorff Supervision for Semi-Supervised Pancreas Segmentation
papers.abstract: Confidence-gated co-training assumes that pseudo-label errors are uncertain and concentrated at organ boundaries. We argue that for pancreas CT, where the target organ is a single connected structure and detached fragments are anatomically implausible, the dominant failures arise at three levels: where the organ is, what its boundary should look like, and how a correct boundary is penalized. Anatomical Rectification relabels implausible fragments of a teacher prediction as confident background, without adding any loss or parameter; an audit confirms that its rejections are overwhelmingly detached hallucinations and that thin, tail-like slices are not eroded. Boundary Grafting transplants labelled surface regions with their annotation into unlabeled volumes, replacing unreliable boundary pseudo-labels with ground truth. The residual error is coherent surface displacement, weakly penalized by permutation-invariant Dice and cross-entropy losses. Homotopy-Annealed Hausdorff (HAH) supervision anneals a distance-weighted penalty from an annotation-anchored objective that is convex in the prediction to a Hausdorff surrogate, admitting the prediction-dependent distance term only after the predicted surface becomes reliable. On NIH pancreas CT, under the standard semi-supervised split, the full method reaches 84.60% Dice and 4.97 voxels 95HD, improving all four metrics over compared methods; on MSD Task07, 78.90% Dice and 4.19 voxels 95HD. We further contribute PanTS-SSL, a semi-supervised evaluation protocol derived from the public 9,901-case PanTS corpus, with a curated 1,015-volume main pool, labelled tiers of 50, 100 and 250 volumes, an 80-case tumor track, shift probes for acquisition and anatomy change, and a fixed 901-volume test set. On it, the method exceeds the co-training baseline at 100 labels, scales to 85.29% Dice at 250 labels, and reaches 85.50% Dice at 100 labels with HAH.

papers.intro:
Voxel-level annotation of abdominal CT is costly, and the pancreas is among the hardest organs to delineate: it tapers from centimetres at the head to millimetres at the tail, borders fat and bowel at low contrast, and varies across patients [27]. Semi-supervised learning answers with consistency: a network agrees with its own perturbed or temporally averaged predictions [32], or two independently initialized networks supervise each other [5], keeping their trajectories distinct and avoiding the confirmation bias of a single teacher-student pair [4]. We adopt translation-consistent co-training [18], a strong instance of this family on pancreas CT, unmodified as our starting point.

Voxel-level annotation of abdominal CT is costly, and the pancreas is among the hardest organs to delineate: it tapers from centimetres at the head to millimetres at the tail, borders fat and bowel at low contrast, and varies across patients [27]. Semi-supervised learning answers with consistency: a network agrees with its own perturbed or temporally averaged predictions [32], or two independently initialized networks supervise each other [5], keeping their trajectories distinct and avoiding the confirmation bias of a single teacher-student pair [4]. We adopt translation-consistent co-training [18], a strong instance of this family on pancreas CT, unmodified as our starting point.

These recipes share one instrument, a confidence gate that decides which pseudo-labels enter training [30], sometimes sharpened by uncertainty [37], and one tacit assumption: the errors it must catch are uncertain and concentrated at organ boundaries. For the pancreas this assumption is misplaced, for anatomical reasons: the pancreas is a single connected structure, so a prediction splitting into disjoint fragments is impossible however confident, yet a confidence gate is blind to this because it reads each voxel only through the peer’s confidence. We therefore hypothesize that confidence-gated co-training fails at three levels the gate cannot see: where the organ is, since confidently detached fragments are reinforced throughout training; what its boundary should look like, since the two networks converge on shared boundary mistakes that no voxel-wise rule can separate; and how a correct boundary is penalized, since permutation-invariant losses such as Dice and cross-entropy charge a boundary displaced by a few voxels no more than an interior flip. The admission statistics and the rejection audit supporting this account are in Secs. 3 and 4.4.

Each level suggests a correction; the first two act on the pseudo-label distribution, not on the objective. Anatomical Rectification (AR) supplies the missing criterion: fragments small relative to the main component of a teacher prediction are relabeled as confident background, telling the student where the organ cannot be rather than merely withholding the voxel, in the spirit of negative learning [9]; when the prediction is already connected the edit vanishes. Boundary Grafting (G) supplies the missing targets: a targeted fraction of admitted boundary supervision is wrong and correlated across the two networks, so no reweighting recovers it; G instead transplants a cuboid sampled on the surface of a labelled volume, with its annotation, into an unlabeled volume, replacing the stagnant part of the boundary supervision with ground truth that is correct by construction [3]. What AR and G cannot supply is geometry in the penalty itself: Homotopy-Annealed Hausdorff Supervision (HAH) anneals a distance-weighted loss from an annotation-anchored objective to a full Hausdorff surrogate [10], admitting its prediction-dependent term only once the predicted surface is reliable, so that this term does not act while AR and G are still stabilizing the targets. HAH is the only component that modifies the objective; AR and G remain loss-free and leave the target unchanged when their trigger is absent.

Methods validated only on small benchmarks prove little about generality, and the semi-supervised pancreas literature lives on a 62-volume NIH training pool (12 labelled) [27] and a 224-volume MSD pool [2], where gains are fragile to split and seed. We therefore derive PanTS-SSL from the public PanTS corpus [16]: a curated protocol with a homogeneous portal-venous main pool, labelled tiers of 50, 100 and 250 volumes, a tumor track stratified by lesion size, seed replicates, and probes for contrast phase, slice thickness and organ atrophy, scored against a fixed 901-volume test set touched once. The images and masks belong to PanTS; our contribution is the protocol, which measures how gains change with the label budget on a fixed, unscreened test set and releases shift probes, in the spirit of standardized benchmarks [8].

papers.title: Computing Optimal Graph Mappings
papers.abstract: The weak graph distance is a distance measure for comparing two embedded graphs, which takes into account both the topology and the geometry of the graphs. The algorithm for computing this measure produces a mapping from one graph to the other that minimises the maximum distance; however, it maps all other distances only well enough to ensure that the maximum distance is not exceeded. In practical applications, it may be of interest to map the parts of the graph beyond the bottleneck as accurately as possible. We propose two different criteria for optimal mappings and also provide algorithms to compute them.

papers.intro:
There are many applications that can be modeled as embedded graphs, for example, representations of road maps, protein alignment, and river networks. In these applications one may need to compare two such embedded graphs with one another, for example to compare a road network graph reconstructed from GPS data with an existing graph of the network. As different applications require different interpretations of similarity, many different measures of graph similarity have already been proposed. These include a geometric graph edit distance [10], traversal distance [4], contour tree distance [7], graph sampling distance [1] and local persistent homology distance [2], which are also surveyed in [8]. We are interested in a measure that maps one graph onto the other, and in doing so considers both the geometric and topologic error of the mapping. For this we use the weak graph distance introduced by Akitaya et al. [3].

The weak graph distance is based on the Fréchet distance [5], which is a well-known distance measure for curves. It provides us with a measure of what the maximum deviation would be if we were to optimally map one graph onto the other. Although the computation of the weak graph distance is generally NP-complete, there are some graph classes for which the computation can be done in polynomial time. This is the case, for example, for planar, spike-free graphs, for which Akitaya et al. [3] have introduced an algorithm. papers.title: Homogenization with Shape-Evolving Microstructures: A Two-Phase Membrane Problem
papers.abstract: We study a diffusion problem in a highly heterogeneous periodic medium (characterized by a small scale parameter $0<\varepsilon\ll1$) where small inclusions are separated from the surrounding connected area by solute-impermeable membranes. These membranes are allowed to grow and deform under surface tension and osmotic pressure (driven by the concentration difference across the membrane). We prove existence of weak solutions on a time interval which is independent of the microscopic scale via a Schauder fixed-point argument by establishing spatial boundary H\"older estimates. For the homogenization limit $\varepsilon\to0$, we establish strong compactness of the outer concentration via time translates and then derive a stability estimate for the driven inner cell problems. The limit couples a macroscopic conservation law, with shape-dependent effective diffusion, to inner diffusion and membrane motion in each cell.

papers.intro:
Transport of chemical substances through heterogeneous media can heavily depend on the geometry of the microstructure and when this geometry changes in response to the transported substances, the effective material properties may change as well. One natural example of such a feedback is osmotic swelling: local concentration differences across a semipermeable membrane11 1 Here, this means permeable to the solvent but impermeable to the dissolved substances. exert an osmotic pressure that drives the membrane’s motion, while surface tension opposes the increase of interfacial area. Free-boundary models describing this mechanism have been studied for one- and two-phase configurations in [22, 23]; for corresponding models using phase-field approximations, we refer to [28, 31]. In a medium containing many small inclusions, each separated from a connected surrounding phase via such a membrane, an effective description of the transport processes should take into account the size and shape of the membranes without resolving every individual membrane at the macroscopic scale. Such heterogeneous configurations can be found, e.g., in biological tissues, where cell volume changes in response to osmotic gradients, in suspensions of vesicles, or in swelling hydrogels [17, 30, 31].

In all these works above, the geometry may vary substantially over time, but its evolution is given a priori and does not depend on the transport process.

papers.title: Clouds as near-horizon backgrounds in the radio detection of air showers
papers.abstract: Stand-alone radio detection of air showers from cosmic rays or neutrinos relies on effective and efficient suppression of human-made noise sources. We propose here that reflections of human- made transmitters on clouds or other atmospheric phenomena, can cause confusion backgrounds that have not been studied previously. Given the absence of prior modelling, we have developed a simplified model for the reflection strength of clouds in the MHz regime. The results indicate that such reflections are, in principle, detectable, in particular in extremely horizontal geometries with typical experimental set-ups.

papers.intro:
While radio detection of air showers has matured as a technique, the problem of a highly efficient and pure self-trigger has not been universally solved. This is mostly due to the abundance and variety of radio background signals (RFI) as a function of location and time that cause false-positive triggers, often at rates that saturate data-acquisition systems. While this fact has caused radio detection of air showers to be almost abandoned in times of analogue-only electronics, the advent of digital electronics and the feasibility of more complex triggers have enabled vetoing backgrounds on-the-fly [22]. Still, the horizon, here referring to a couple of degrees above the physical horizon, is often excluded in triggers or analysis, simply because the background is overwhelming. If looking for cosmic ray induced air showers, this is certainly a viable path forward, given that the effective area lost is minor. However, for experiments looking for the radio emission of neutrinos, by detecting showers stemming from Earth-skimming (tau-)neutrinos [35], this exclusion is no longer feasible.

Radio detection of Earth-skimming neutrinos relies on the fact that detectors are constructed with superior angular resolution in mind that will be able to tell the difference between a background from or just above the horizon and the true signal from below the horizon. Many of the proposed instruments also exploit the topography of the Earth to provide a good view of below-horizon Earth [7, 46, 30]. One should remember that a location on top of a mountain changes where the horizon is, and we have tried to be very careful in this article when converting coordinate systems to one where 0∘0^{\circ} is horizontal.

Many experiments also report that these backgrounds are time-variable, impulsive, and often remain in the data after known terrestrial sources, airplanes, and thunderstorms have been removed.

Here, we want to propose that clouds reflecting terrestrial emissions in skimming geometries may be the cause of backgrounds appearing as above-horizon sources. In this article, we infer the radar cross-section of clouds at MHz frequencies using simplified droplet models. Together with basic geometric considerations, we find that the hypothesis is not so easily rejected and in fact consistent with general assumptions about experimental sensitivity and cloud properties. papers.title: PreserveReward: Reliable Consistency Reward Modeling for Image Editing via Dual-Teacher On-Policy Self-Distillation
papers.abstract: Instruction-guided image editing has a wide range of applications, yet existing models may inadvertently alter content that should remain unchanged. Reliable consistency evaluation is therefore essential for assessing content preservation and providing reward signals for Reinforcement Learning (RL). However, existing reward models may overlook subtle visual changes or fail to distinguish necessary modifications from unintended alterations, limiting the reliability of consistency assessment. To address this challenge, we propose PreserveReward, a consistency reward model for image editing that integrates visual On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) to enhance fine-grained visual perception and consistency assessment. PreserveReward learns from reference preservation scores through a regression-based scoring loss and employs two complementary teacher views for self-distillation. The local teacher uses matched crops to identify subtle visual changes, while the joint teacher combines local details with global context to determine whether these changes align with the editing intent. To improve the reliability of distillation supervision, we calibrate teacher score distributions via minimum-KL projection under reference-score error constraints and adaptively select teacher process supervision based on gradient alignment with the scoring objective, mitigating scoring bias and optimization conflicts. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that PreserveReward achieves strong alignment with human preference on non-edited content preservation and generalizes well across diverse editing scenarios.

papers.intro:
Instruction-guided image editing supports a wide range of applications, from photo retouching to creative design [40]. Although recent models have made substantial progress in modifying target objects according to user instructions [30], they can still inadvertently alter objects that should remain unchanged [22]. This limitation calls for reward models that accurately assess non-edited subject consistency, enabling reliable evaluation of content preservation and providing reward signals for Reinforcement Learning (RL) to improve editing fidelity [13]. Developing such models is challenging because consistency may depend on fine-grained object attributes or spatial relationships across the scene [39]. An evaluator must detect subtle changes in these properties and interpret them in light of the editing instruction, drawing on global context when needed to distinguish necessary modifications from unintended alterations [8].

Developing such models is challenging because consistency may depend on fine-grained object attributes or spatial relationships across the scene [39]. An evaluator must detect subtle changes in these properties and interpret them in light of the editing instruction, drawing on global context when needed to distinguish necessary modifications from unintended alterations [8].

Guiding policy optimization toward instruction following and content preservation requires reliable reward signals. EditReward [31] learns to score edits from human preferences, while EditScore [13] generates reasoning before scoring to support online RL. FIRM [39] explicitly assesses edit execution and consistency separately. Despite these advances, reliable consistency evaluation remains challenging. Evaluators emphasizing global semantics may overlook subtle changes to the markings, textures, or identity cues of non-edited subjects, underestimating the resulting loss of fidelity [39, 33]. Meanwhile, consistency also encompasses object counts, spatial relationships, and scene layout, requiring a joint assessment of local details and global structure, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Crucially, comparing source and edited images also requires interpreting these changes in light of the editing instruction and scene context to distinguish necessary modifications from unintended alterations. Without complementary evidence across scales, reward models may overlook damage to content that should remain unchanged or incorrectly penalize intended edits, producing unreliable optimization signals. These challenges persist even in advanced open-source vision-language models (VLMs), which can exhibit substantial errors in assessing content preservation; increasing model size alone does not necessarily ensure reliable consistency judgments [13, 21]. Although proprietary VLMs can offer more accurate assessments, the cost and latency of repeated reward queries constrain their practical use in online RL. These limitations motivate consistency reward models that integrate fine-grained visual perception with global contextual reasoning, improve scoring reliability, and maintain efficient inference for large-scale policy optimization.

Although proprietary VLMs can offer more accurate assessments, the cost and latency of repeated reward queries constrain their practical use in online RL. These limitations motivate consistency reward models that integrate fine-grained visual perception with global contextual reasoning, improve scoring reliability, and maintain efficient inference for large-scale policy optimization.

To address these challenges, we propose PreserveReward, a consistency reward model for image editing that builds on On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD) to improve fine-grained perception of non-edited visual content and scoring reliability. Given an editing instruction and the source and edited images, the model generates a consistency rationale and a numerical score. We supervise score predictions with a Score-MSE loss, which weights each candidate score’s squared error relative to the reference target by the probability assigned to that score. However, score supervision alone provides limited guidance on identifying and interpreting visual evidence relevant to consistency. We therefore introduce two complementary teacher views, local and joint, to enhance the student’s visual perception and reasoning through self-distillation. The local teacher examines matched crops from the source and edited images to identify subtle changes in subject identity and texture. The joint teacher additionally observes the full image pair, considering object counts, spatial relationships, and scene layout to assess whether local changes are consistent with the editing intent. The teachers supervise both reasoning and score prediction along student-generated trajectories, transferring the benefits of additional visual evidence to the student’s full-image inference.

papers.title: AI-human hybrid conversations: Can AI Agents Improve Discourse Quality?
papers.abstract: Conversations are central to how people exchange information, share experiences, and develop collective understanding. Yet, across conversational settings, discussions often suffer from uneven participation, unanswered contributions, and a narrow range of perspectives. As generative AI agents increasingly participate alongside humans, hybrid human-AI conversations present a new opportunity to address these challenges. We investigate whether AI agents can serve as catalysts for human interaction, improving conversational engagement and broadening collective discourse. We develop a framework for introducing generic and persona-conditioned AI agents into evolving discussions and evaluate it through two complementary studies. First, using agent-based simulations grounded in Reddit discussions across four domains, we find that AI-generated conversations are more positive and less toxic than human conversations, but substantially less semantically diverse. Persona conditioning produces more human-like contributions and narrows this diversity gap, while increasing the representation of underrepresented personas can shift which perspectives emerge without necessarily increasing overall diversity. Second, we conduct a pre-registered experiment with 221 participants across nine discussion threads, comparing human-only conversations with those involving generic or persona-conditioned AI agents. We find that AI participation increases responsiveness, reduces unanswered contributions, and broadens the range of ideas expressed by human participants, even though the AI agents themselves do not fully reproduce human conversational diversity. These findings suggest that the value of hybrid human-AI conversations lies not simply in the content AI agents generate, but also in their potential to stimulate more responsive and diverse interactions among humans.

papers.intro:
Conversations are central to how people exchange information, share experiences, and develop collective understanding. From focus groups used to elicit consumer insights in market research and classroom discussions that facilitate learning to online communities where individuals exchange opinions and seek advice, conversations provide opportunities for people to engage with ideas and perspectives beyond their own. Yet, across these settings, productive participation is difficult to sustain. Discussions often suffer from uneven engagement, with a few individuals dominating while others remain silent (Alimoradi et al., 2025), contributions receiving limited responses, and group dynamics restricting the range of perspectives expressed (Farnsworth and Boon, 2010; Sedova and Sedlacek, 2023). Infact, one of the top reasons for not participating actively in a discussion have been linked to feeling unwelcome, not fitting in and not getting enough response from the community (Preece et al., 2004). These challenges are amplified on digital platforms, where discussions occur at scale and can be further characterized by echo chambers that reinforce existing viewpoints, polarized exchanges, and toxic interactions that undermine constructive dialogue and increase entry barriers for traditionally under-represented groups in a conversation (Li and Hitt, 2008; Hu et al., 2017; Chmiel et al., 2011; Garcia et al., 2016; Cheng et al., 2017; Lu and Liang, 2024; Sibai et al., 2024).

Crucially, conversations are not simply collections of independent contributions; they are dynamic, path-dependent processes in which each interaction shapes what comes next. An early response can influence who participates, the tone of subsequent exchanges, and the perspectives that enter the discussion (Muchnik et al., 2013; Cheng et al., 2017). Consequently, even a single strategically introduced contribution has the potential to redirect the course of a conversation. This raises an important possibility: rather than merely observing how conversations unfold, can we actively intervene to improve their outcomes?

Recent advances in generative AI create a new opportunity to both study and potentially shape conversational trajectories. AI participation in online conversations is rapidly moving from a theoretical possibility to a practical reality. Platforms such as Character.AI and Meta’s AI Studio have introduced AI characters that interact with humans, including in group conversations, while emerging AI-native communities such as Moltbook illustrate the possibility of discussions among autonomous AI agents. Unlike approaches that analyze conversations after they have occurred, AI agents can participate directly in evolving discussions, responding to overlooked contributions, introducing alternative perspectives, and potentially influencing subsequent interactions. Large language models (LLMs) can generate context-dependent natural language, condition their behavior on empirically derived persona characteristics, retain information about their own prior contributions, and respond sequentially to an evolving discussion. Prior work has established that LLMs can represent heterogeneous synthetic respondents (Argyle et al., 2023; Arora et al., 2025) and can also interact as agents in multi-turn social environments (Park et al., 2022; Park et al., 2023; Zhou et al., 2024). However, these streams have developed largely in parallel: persona-based work has focused primarily on whether individual synthetic actors reproduce characteristics of target populations, while multi-agent work has focused more on emergent interaction among generative agents. Less is known about how introducing AI agents into ongoing human conversations influences conversational outcomes, and whether the characteristics of these agents matter. In particular, generic AI agents may encourage engagement and civility while contributing a relatively narrow range of perspectives. Conditioning agents on empirically grounded, heterogeneous personas offers a potential way to introduce greater variation in communication styles and viewpoints, including perspectives associated with groups that are typically underrepresented in a discussion.

Building on these possibilities, our primary research questions are: (1) How does introducing AI participants affect conversational tone, human engagement, and opinion diversity? (2) Does the type of AI participant (generic versus persona conditioned), shape these conversational outcomes? We examine three complementary dimensions of discourse quality. Conversational tone captures the sentiment and toxicity of exchanges; human engagement reflects participation, responsiveness to contributions, and the continuation of discussions; and opinion diversity captures the breadth of ideas, topics, and perspectives expressed. These dimensions are related but distinct: a conversation may generate substantial engagement while remaining toxic or dominated by a narrow set of viewpoints. Examining them jointly allows us to assess how AI participation affects not only the volume of interactions but also their quality and the range of perspectives represented.

To address these questions, we adopt a two-part empirical approach combining agent-based simulations with a human–AI discussion experiment. Each approach serves a complementary purpose. Because conversations are path-dependent, observing a discussion reveals only one of many possible trajectories. Agent-based simulations provide a controlled testbed in which we can systematically vary the presence, characteristics, and composition of AI participants while holding the initial discussion context fixed. However, simulations alone cannot establish how real people respond to AI participation, particularly whether AI-generated contributions encourage subsequent human engagement or broaden the range of perspectives expressed by humans. We therefore complement the simulations with an experiment in which real participants engage in asynchronous discussions alongside AI agents. These two studies, together, allow us to examine both how AI agents generate conversations and how their participation shapes human conversational behavior.

papers.title: Large deviations for integrated exponentials of Gaussian Volterra processes - application to variance options
papers.abstract: We prove small-time large deviations for the normalised time integral of the exponential of a Gaussian Volterra process, and complement it with a central limit theorem and moderate deviations. As an application, we obtain short-maturity asymptotics for out-of-the-money and at-the-money variance options in rough volatility models, as well as implied volatility expansions which we validate numerically.

papers.title: The asymptotics of maximal rank of three-way tensors
papers.abstract: We prove that the maximal rank of an $n\times n\times n$ tensor is $n^2/3+O(n^{3/2})$, over the real numbers and over every algebraically closed field. More generally, in format $\lfloor an\rfloor\times\lfloor bn\rfloor\times\lfloor cn\rfloor$, with $a,b,c>0$ fixed, the leading term is $\frac{abc}{a+b+c}n^2$. The argument starts with a criterion for rank with respect to an arbitrary projective variety: a decomposition of zero with surjective differential, from a smooth parameter space, bounds the rank of every point. For Segre varieties, we construct such decompositions using a basis of units in a split algebra. We also give an optimized finite bound and a closed estimate with explicit constants for the maximal rank.

papers.intro:
How much larger can the rank of an exceptional tensor be than the rank of a general tensor? For matrices there is no difference. For tensors of order three, the two ranks can differ, and a generic decomposition does not give a decomposition of every tensor. We show that this difference disappears in the leading term when the dimensions grow in fixed proportions.

papers.title: From Data Room to Report: End-to-End AI Support for M&A Legal Due Diligence
papers.abstract: Legal due diligence in mergers and acquisitions requires lawyers to organize heterogeneous virtual data room documents, extract transaction-relevant information and consolidate reviewed findings into a due diligence report. We present LEXI (Legal Extraction and Intelligence), a work-in-progress system that demonstrates how large language models can support this process from document ingestion to report preparation. LEXI classifies documents under a configurable due diligence taxonomy, assigns relevant target entities, extracts predefined information with supporting passages and page-level provenance and prepares report content from reviewed findings. Structured outputs connect these stages and allow model-generated results to be passed through the workflow in a controlled form. Lawyers review and correct classifications and extractions and retain responsibility for legal assessments, recommendations, risk ratings and final report wording. Initial evaluations of the classification and extraction components provide preliminary evidence that the approach is feasible. LEXI illustrates how AI can be integrated across the legal due diligence workflow while preserving lawyer control over substantive legal judgment.

papers.title: Foundation interatomic potentials capture structural disorder in metallic glasses
papers.abstract: Foundation machine-learning interatomic potentials transfer well across chemical and structural space, yet their reliability for highly disordered metallic states is less established. Metallic glasses are a demanding benchmark: they have traditionally been modeled with Embedded Atom Method (EAM) potentials fitted to specific compositions, while ab initio molecular dynamics remains too expensive at the required sizes and timescales. Using the prototypical Cu-Zr-Al glass, we show that foundation potentials capture structural disorder, reproducing the structure, quenching dynamics, and elastic, mechanical and thermal properties of the amorphous state at near first-principles accuracy. We benchmark MACE foundation models against a classical EAM potential along molecular dynamics quenches, validating against density functional theory and experiment, first at Cu46Zr46Al8 and then across the good glass-forming region of the ternary. We further test two specialization routes: fine-tuning on glass structures generated with Lennard-Jones surrogate models, and on automatically generated small periodic cells (ASSYST). Models pre-trained on databases that include non-equilibrium liquid and amorphous configurations, such as OMAT, are accurate and transferable across composition out of the box, clearly outperforming the composition-specific EAM potential. Fine-tuning on target glass structures brings only modest gains, while specialization on small crystalline cells degrades the description of disorder. The readiness of foundation potentials for disordered metals is therefore set mainly by the diversity of their pre-training data rather than by system-specific fine-tuning, shifting the modeling effort from bespoke dataset generation to pre-training coverage and careful validation of the resulting dynamics.

papers.intro:
Machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) have transformed atomistic modeling by mapping the high-dimensional configuration of a material directly onto its quantum-mechanical potential energy surface (PES), from which atomic forces are obtained as the analytical gradient of the predicted energy[1]. Trained on high-fidelity Density Functional Theory (DFT) data, they capture intricate many-body interactions within the classical Molecular Dynamics (MD) framework. Their most recent evolution is that of foundation MLIPs[2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9]: pre-trained on extremely large and diverse datasets[10, 11], they aim to act as zero-shot force evaluators across nearly the entire periodic table.

These models are, however, intrinsically bound by their training distributions and often struggle to extrapolate to out-of-distribution scenarios. The amorphous state is emerging as a central challenge in this respect, since early pre-trained models and benchmarks have largely targeted ordered, crystalline structures, and their transferability to non-crystalline solids is far from established[12]. The difficulty is compounded by the fact that accuracy on single-point energies and forces does not necessarily translate into a faithful description of structural and dynamical observables at finite temperature, as recent finite-temperature benchmarks such as Dyna-Mat have highlighted[13]. To mitigate this distributional gap, fine-tuning strategies are increasingly adopted to specialize pre-trained models[14, 15, 16].

Metallic glasses (MGs)[17, 18] provide an especially demanding test of such transferability. Lacking long-range crystalline periodicity and microstructural defects such as grain boundaries and dislocations, they combine low elastic moduli with high yield strengths, large elastic limits and good thermoplastic formability[19]; more importantly for the present purpose, their disordered structure probes exactly the local chemical environments that a general-purpose potential must learn rather than memorize. Traditionally, MGs have been modeled with classical MD driven by Embedded Atom Method (EAM) potentials[20]; the Mendelev Cu-Zr potential[21], for instance, was parameterized against experimental diffraction data and first-principles liquid mixing enthalpies, reproducing the liquid-to-glass transition temperature in good agreement with calorimetry. Such empirical potentials, however, have limited transferability outside their parameterization domain and are ill-suited to explore the wide compositional space of MGs, while ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) remains prohibitively expensive at the system sizes and timescales required for amorphous metals.
