For the specific problem of disorder, the composition of the pre-training corpus is decisive: databases that explicitly include high-temperature dynamics and non-equilibrium amorphous states, such as the Open Materials (OMAT) database[10], offer a promising route to model MGs directly. Building a representative training set for these systems is itself non-trivial. Modern workflows integrate active learning with advanced thermodynamic sampling—using Lennard-Jones (LJ) surrogate models combined with swap Monte Carlo (swap-MC) moves to computationally age the glass toward deeply relaxed states[22]—but require DFT on large supercells and must be repeated for each composition of interest. Alternatively, automated pipelines built on small periodic cells, such as ASSYST[23], yield reliable potentials for the energetics of complex crystalline systems, although their ability to capture the dynamics of structurally disordered phases is less clear.

Complementary to broad, multi-system surveys of the amorphous challenge[12], we provide an in-depth study of a glass-forming family: we assess the capability of MACE foundation potentials[6] to reproduce the quenching dynamics and the structural, elastic, mechanical and thermal properties of a reference stoichiometry, as well as their extrapolation across composition. Together, these comparisons address the practical applicability of general-purpose potentials to MGs—based both on their pre-training databases and on modern data-generation workflows—delivering an overview from composition-specific to composition-dependent properties.

papers.title: BOP-Refer: Benchmark for Monocular 3D and 2D Object Grounding
papers.abstract: We introduce BOP-Refer, the first benchmark for monocular 3D and 2D grounding of everyday and industrial objects sourced from 9 diverse BOP datasets. We pair images from these datasets with VLM-generated and human-verified referring expressions, and derive accurate ground-truth 3D and 2D bounding boxes of the referred objects from their 3D models and 6DoF pose annotations. Our systematic evaluation of 17 frontier VLMs across the major proprietary and open-weight families (Gemini, GPT, Claude, Qwen, Gemma) shows that the best model, Gemini 4 Carbon, reaches 72.6% AP_IoU2D in 2D but only 12.4% AP_IoU3D in 3D, despite the more lenient IoU thresholds in 3D. The predicted 3D boxes are usually centered on the target objects in the image but often off in depth by more than the object's size, suggesting that metric scale estimation, which needs reliable object size priors, is currently by far the main source of error.

papers.intro:
3D object grounding, which is the task of 3D localization of objects referred to by a natural-language expression from visual or 3D input, is important for systems that act in the physical world [16, 1]. Robots need 3D information for grasping, AR systems for augmenting objects with virtual content, and navigation systems for reaching named targets. We focus on the monocular variant [99], predicting 3D bounding boxes from a single image with known intrinsics rather than from the reconstructed point cloud assumed by most 3D grounding methods. This variant needs only a calibrated camera, as found on phones, robots, and AR/VR headsets.

Robots need 3D information for grasping, AR systems for augmenting objects with virtual content, and navigation systems for reaching named targets. We focus on the monocular variant [99], predicting 3D bounding boxes from a single image with known intrinsics rather than from the reconstructed point cloud assumed by most 3D grounding methods. This variant needs only a calibrated camera, as found on phones, robots, and AR/VR headsets.

While 2D grounding has been studied extensively, with task-specific detectors [58, 68] and more recently general-purpose vision-language models (VLMs) [80, 6, 36], the 3D counterpart remains underexplored. Three factors make it harder: (1) the expected output is an oriented 3D box rather than an axis-aligned rectangle, (2) ground truth is hard to obtain at scale, and (3) a single monocular view leaves object scale and distance jointly underdetermined. Existing 3D grounding benchmarks focus on room-scale indoor or traffic scenes [16, 1, 99, 48], open-vocabulary 3D detectors are evaluated with category-level queries rather than free-form referring expressions [93, 56, 71], and few evaluate 2D and 3D grounding together [23, 27], leaving it unclear whether errors arise in localizing the referred objects in the image or in estimating their 3D position, size, or orientation.

papers.title: A second-order relaxation system for a degenerate-parabolic quasilinear fourth-order rimming-flow equation with critical spectrum
papers.abstract: For a spectrally critical nonlinear degenerate-parabolic PDE of fourth-order, describing a capillary-driven fluid flow in a rotating cylinder, we propose a second-order relaxation system of parabolic-elliptic type. For positive initial data, we prove local existence and uniqueness of solutions to the relaxation system. Thereby, the lifespan of the approximate solutions turns out to be independent of the relaxation parameter. Moreover, we prove convergence of non-negative weak solutions of the relaxation system to weak solutions of the original equation on compact time intervals. We classify positive steady states of the relaxed system, prove a stability result yielding global strong solutions, and show that the long-time dynamics remain consistent under the relaxation limit.

papers.title: First detection of s-cis-acroleine (sc-CH2CHCHO) in the interstellar medium
papers.abstract: We report the first interstellar detection of the higher-energy $s$-cis conformer of acrolein (CH2CHCHO) toward TMC-1 using the Quijote line survey. Local thermodynamic equilibrium modeling, assuming a rotational temperature of 7.5 K, yields a column density of $(1.0\pm0.2)\times10^{11}$~cm$^{-2}$ when fitting the observed lines. The s-cis/s-trans abundance ratio is $0.45\pm0.11$, despite an energy separation of approximately 1025~K, indicating a strongly nonequilibrium conformational distribution. An exploratory gas--grain chemical model identifies C3H5 + O as the dominant acrolein formation route, pointing to this reaction as a first entry to consider when explaining the isomeric ratios. The observed ratio provides a new constraint on conformer-specific formation, destruction, and interconversion processes in cold interstellar clouds.

papers.intro:
The detection of interstellar isomers, molecules with the same chemical formula but different structural arrangements, provides valuable insights into the chemistry of astronomical environments. Their abundance ratios can serve as probes of the physical and chemical conditions of the regions where they are observed (Goicoechea et al., 2009; Cuadrado et al., 2016; Hacar et al., 2020; Loison et al., 2017, e.g.,). Particularly sensitive to these conditions are stereoisomers, which share the same atomic connectivity but differ in their three-dimensional arrangement. Their relatively small energy differences and largely similar chemistry make their abundance ratios highly sensitive to even modest changes in physical or chemical conditions (Cuadrado et al., 2016; Shingledecker et al., 2020; Shingledecker et al., 2022; Molpeceres et al., 2022; García De La Concepción et al., 2023; Sanz-Novo et al., 2025; Molpeceres et al., 2025). A recent review of interstellar isomerism is provided by Rivilla et al. (2026).

papers.title: Minimizing Optical Circuit Reconfigurations for Concurrent Collectives
papers.abstract:
Optical circuit switches (OCSes) provide high-bandwidth point-to-point circuits in GPU clusters, but each optical port attaches to only one peer at a time, and reconfiguring a connection interrupts transmission. In large-model training, these ports are shared by many communication domains, each running its own collective instance, called a CCL kernel; often, several of these kernels execute the same collective at the same time. Because each step of the collective can reach a different peer, domains advancing through the steps in the same order may require a reconfiguration at every step.
  We introduce the mega CCL kernel to schedule these kernels jointly. When a collective permits its steps to be reordered, different domains can take different legal steps in the same round, letting consecutive rounds share the same circuits and reducing the number of reconfigurations. Because the kernels are interchangeable, we need not decide the steps of every kernel separately. Instead, in each round we count how many kernels run each pattern, and then use bipartite matching to turn those counts into a concrete schedule for each kernel. We call this the count model, as opposed to the direct formulation that decides each kernel separately, and prove that the two give the same configuration sequences and the same optimum while the count model is substantially easier to solve.
  On a fully loaded 64-supernode, 64-domain scheduling instance, joint scheduling cuts pairwise-AlltoAll reconfigurations from 62 to 3 and HD AllReduce from 10 to 2. In synthetic training replays parameterized by eight real models, it reduces iteration time by up to about 34%; on a 64-GPU test case, the count model solves over six orders of magnitude faster than the direct formulation.

papers.intro:
Optical circuit switching (OCS) has been deployed at scale in large-model training clusters, most notably in Google’s TPU v4 [12]. An OCS connects its ports as point-to-point pairs, so each port serves at most one peer at a time, and changing that peer requires a reconfiguration that interrupts transmission for nanoseconds to milliseconds. A training collective often contacts several peers in one call, and switching among these peers can interrupt transmission repeatedly and waste bandwidth, and this paper studies how to minimize such interruptions under a fixed port budget.

A collective communication library (CCL), such as NCCL, runs a collective on a group of GPUs, which we call a communication domain. The collective instance executed on a domain is a CCL kernel. Large-model training combines tensor, data, expert, and pipeline parallelism, as in Megatron-LM [36], which divides the GPUs into many domains sharing one set of optical ports. Such a deployment is highly regular: several domains of one type run the same collective at the same time on the same supernodes, with each domain using the same number of GPUs on every supernode. Many collectives contact different peers in different steps; pairwise AlltoAll, for example, exchanges data with each peer in turn. If all domains advance through these steps in the same order, they all request the same kind of connection in one round and switch together in the next, so the circuits may need reconfiguring at every step.

papers.title: Collective relaxation dynamics and vitrification in hexatic smectic binary equimolar mixtures containing component with varying C$_3$F$_7$CH$_2$OC$_m$H$_{2m}$- chain length
papers.abstract: Differential scanning calorimetry, polarizing optical microscopy, and broadband dielectric spectroscopy are applied for investigation of phase transitions in equimolar binary mixtures consisting of the MHPOBC liquid crystal as one component and 3FmHPhH6 homologs as a second component with different C$_3$F$_7$CH$_2$OC$_m$H$_{2m}$- chain length (m = 2-7). The paraelectric smectic A* - ferroelectric smectic C* - antiferroelectric smectic C$_A$* - hexatic smectic X$_A$* - glassy smectic X$_A$* sequence is observed for all mixtures. The appearance of the bond-orientational order in smectic X$_A$* is accompanied by an additional relaxation process P$_{hex}$ in dielectric spectra at the low-frequency side of the P$_H$ phason, consistent with its assignment to bond-orientational fluctuations. The empirical exponential-power relationship is proposed for the ratio between the relaxation times of P$_{hex}$ and P$_H$. The behavior of the structural $\alpha$-relaxation and secondary $\beta$-relaxation in smectic X$_A$* depends on the m parameter, changing from overlapping $\alpha$ and $\beta$ processes for m = 2 to well-separated for m = 6, 7. A double glass transition is observed by calorimetry on heating for m = 5-7. The calorimetric glass transition temperature shows a composition-dependent correspondence with temperatures at which either the P$_H$ or $\alpha$-relaxation time reaches 100 s, suggesting that different relaxation processes may contribute to vitrification.

papers.title: Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces for Hard Math Problems
papers.abstract: Post-training large language models (LLMs) for mathematical reasoning often relies on accepted traces whose final answers pass a verifier. For hard math problems, however, such traces can be rare under independent Monte Carlo (MC) sampling. To address this, we propose Diverse Alternative Reasoning Traces (DART), a trace-mining method that starts from a rejected trace, decomposes it into reasoning steps, and ranks them by position-weighted uncertainty. It then generates deliberately distinct alternative candidates for highly ranked steps using reference-answer guidance and a meta-thought before completing the resulting traces. On greedy-unsolved DeepMath-103K problems, DART recovers 37% more problems than MC sampling at a matched number of generated traces. Its estimated generation cost per recovered problem is nearly identical, while its cost per accepted trace is 30% lower. Post-training Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on traces mined by DART achieves the highest point estimate in five of six evaluations across MATH-500 and AIME benchmarks. These results demonstrate that revisiting rejected traces with DART can expand problem coverage and provide effective post-training data.

papers.intro:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed in tasks that require complex, multi-step problem solving (Srivastava et al., 2023). One such task is mathematical reasoning, where prompting LLMs to generate intermediate reasoning steps rather than directly predicting the final answer has been shown to substantially improve their problem-solving performance (Wei et al., 2022).

One such task is mathematical reasoning, where prompting LLMs to generate intermediate reasoning steps rather than directly predicting the final answer has been shown to substantially improve their problem-solving performance (Wei et al., 2022).

To further improve their reasoning capabilities, LLMs are commonly post-trained on reasoning traces (Lightman et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024; Muennighoff et al., 2025). Since high-quality traces are generally difficult to obtain at scale, a common approach is to generate them from the model itself using Monte Carlo (MC) sampling at nonzero temperature. The generated traces can then be evaluated using verifiable rewards, based on whether the final answer to a mathematical problem matches a known reference answer, and subsequently used for post-training (Zelikman et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2025). We refer to traces as accepted if they pass the verifier and rejected otherwise.

A problem contributes post-training data only if the model generates at least one accepted trace. This creates a model-dependent data collection process that can underrepresent problems for which the model has a low probability of generating an accepted trace.

papers.title: Convergence of Residual-driven Adaptive Kernel-based Multilevel Approximation
papers.abstract: Kernel-based multilevel methods combine compactly supported radial basis functions with a residual correction scheme and are known to converge linearly in the number of levels. In this paper we study an adaptive version of the multilevel method, in which the interpolation on each level only uses those sites at which the residual of the preceding level exceeds a given threshold. Although this method has been proposed some time ago and converges in all numerical tests, a convergence proof has been missing so far. We close this gap. We derive an a priori error bound, an a posteriori error bound valid for arbitrary point selections, and extend the analysis to penalized least-squares approximation and to target functions outside the native space of the kernel. For a variant with an additional check-loop per level, we show convergence with the rate of the classical multilevel method. We illustrate our findings with three numerical examples.

papers.intro:
Kernel-based methods offer a versatile tool for the reconstruction of an unknown function from scattered data. Their applications range from approximation [16, 37] to meshless numerical methods for partial differential equations [18, 19, 36] and machine learning [12, 34], most recently in application to operator learning [5, 24]. The great advantage they offer is the flexibility, stability, and deterministic error analysis [30, 31, 32].

Kernel-based methods offer a versatile tool for the reconstruction of an unknown function from scattered data. Their applications range from approximation [16, 37] to meshless numerical methods for partial differential equations [18, 19, 36] and machine learning [12, 34], most recently in application to operator learning [5, 24]. The great advantage they offer is the flexibility, stability, and deterministic error analysis [30, 31, 32].

If compactly supported radial basis functions are used, a trade-off between stability and accuracy has to be made: a fixed support radius leads to ill-conditioned systems if the number of data becomes large [32], while a support radius coupled to the fill distance does not lead to convergence. This is known as the trade-off principle [33]. The kernel-based multilevel method, first suggested in [17], resolves this dilemma by computing a coarse approximation first and then successively correcting the residual on finer and finer sets of sites with kernels of smaller support, effectively representing multiple scales within the data. Although the method was established early and its convergence was demonstrated numerically, a proof of convergence for approximation on bounded domains is due to [38], see also [26] for the sphere and [39] for an overview. It is also used in collocation for partial differential equations [15] and high-dimensional problems [9, 23, 25]. For globally supported kernels, the multilevel method can be realized efficiently in samplet coordinates [4].

On many levels, however, the residual is already small in large parts of the domain. Hence, it is natural to use only those sites on which the residual is still non-negligible. Two such adaptive versions have been introduced in [27, 39]. The first one, discarding small coefficients after the computation of each local interpolant, goes back to [27] and its convergence is well-understood. The second one is a truly adaptive method: it evaluates the residual on the sites of the upcoming level and only uses those sites at which the absolute value of the residual exceeds a level-dependent threshold. This reduces the size of the linear systems and potentially the computational cost. Although all numerical tests indicate convergence, a proof has been missing so far. The difficulty is that the techniques of [38] require control of the residual on the full set of sites, whereas the adaptive method only enforces the residual to vanish on the selected subset, and we have no information about the residual on the remaining sites.

Recently, the idea of adaptive multilevel approximation has again gained interest and two related approaches have been proposed. The three approaches [28], [3], and [39] differ in what is selected and when. In [28], the sites are selected before the local approximation is computed, using the function values on the finest level, and the interpolant on the full set of sites is evaluated with the data at the removed sites set to zero. In [3], the centers of each level are chosen one by one by a greedy algorithm, which yields a bound on the number of centers. We follow the ideas of [39] described above.

The contribution of this paper is the first convergence analysis of the truly adaptive multilevel method of [39]. We derive an a posteriori error bound in Ht​(Ω)H^{t}(\Omega) and L∞​(Ω)L_{\infty}(\Omega), which holds for arbitrary selections of sites, in particular for the sets selected by the adaptive method itself. Besides the a priori term of the classical method, it only involves the residual at the dropped sites, measured in a discrete ℓ2\ell_{2}-norm, and for the L∞​(Ω)L_{\infty}(\Omega) bound additionally its maximum on the dropped sites of the last level. These quantities can be evaluated at negligible cost for nested sites. Building on the same recursion, we prove an a priori error bound for the adaptive method, which shows linear convergence up to the thresholds. papers.title: A Hierarchy of Risk Certificates for Representation-Based Prediction
papers.abstract: Representation-based prediction underlies many machine-learning systems. Yet a fitted predictor's failure to meet an accuracy requirement does not establish that its representation-decoder class cannot meet it. We study optimal population mean squared error (MSE) over Lipschitz decoders acting on a fixed representation. For blocks of $b\geq2$ independent and identically distributed (iid) observations, we minimize total squared error (normalized by $b-1$) under pairwise Lipschitz constraints. We prove that expected block scores form nondecreasing lower bounds on optimal class risk and converge to that risk on compact metric feature spaces, although no fixed block size provides a uniform relative guarantee. Verified dual lower bounds and iid calibration observations independent of model development, with bounded targets and predictions, yield simultaneous lower confidence bounds on optimal class risk and upper confidence bounds on fitted-predictor risk. These bounds can establish that every admissible decoder exceeds a prescribed MSE threshold or that an admissible fitted predictor meets it. Controlled experiments illustrate population-risk certification; fixed PTB-XL and Bike Sharing experiments provide deterministic empirical-risk conclusions. The results support principled assessment and selection of representation-decoder configurations. Efficient certification at scale and extensions to dependent observations remain open problems.

papers.intro:
Many prediction systems transform their inputs into feature representations and fit decoders to those features. A fitted predictor may have population mean squared error (MSE) above a prescribed threshold even when another decoder in the same representation-decoder class meets that threshold. We study the infimum of population MSE over decoders using a fixed representation and satisfying a prescribed Lipschitz constraint. We construct a hierarchy of lower bounds on this optimal class risk. If a certified lower bound exceeds the prescribed threshold, no decoder in the class can meet the requirement. In industrial predictive maintenance, such a certificate could motivate revising the sensor-history representation or decoder constraint used to forecast a machine-condition indicator rather than fitting further decoders within the excluded class. To illustrate the exclusion mechanism, consider the representation Γ⁡(x)=(|x1|,|x2|)\Gamma(x)=(|x_{1}|,|x_{2}|) of a two-observation history x=(x1,x2)x=(x_{1},x_{2}). Suppose the histories (−1,1)(-1,1) and (1,−1)(1,-1) each occur with probability 1/21/2, with respective deterministic targets 11 and −1-1. Both histories have representation (1,1)(1,1), so every decoder assigns them the same prediction cc. Its population MSE is (1−c)2+(−1−c)22=1+c2≥1.\frac{(1-c)^{2}+(-1-c)^{2}}{2}=1+c^{2}\geq 1. No decoder using this representation can meet an MSE threshold below one. Even without identical feature values, a Lipschitz constraint limits prediction differences between nearby feature vectors. If their targets differ by more than this limit, their two squared errors cannot both be zero. Our hierarchy applies these constraints jointly to blocks of independent and identically distributed (iid) observations.

papers.title: Energy cascade spectrum in wave turbulence of a two-dimensional quantum fluid
papers.abstract: In the two-dimensional (2D) Gross-Pitaevskii model for a Bose gas, the naive dimensional non-equilibrium wave-turbulence power-law prediction for the direct energy cascade coincides with thermal equilibrium and therefore carries no energy flux. We resolve this degeneracy by deriving a logarithmically corrected spectrum that supports a positive, constant energy flux toward small scales. A systematic asymptotic expansion of the wave-kinetic collision integral determines the logarithmic exponent to be 1/3, while the small-scale dissipation scale sets the upper cutoff in the logarithmic correction. Regularization of a marginal infrared divergence at the forcing scale yields an estimate of the spectral prefactor for asymptotically well-separated forcing and dissipation scales. Simulations of the Gross-Pitaevskii and wave-kinetic equations support the predicted spectral shape. Over finite spectral ranges, the correction produces apparent power laws steeper than the dimensional prediction, offering a possible explanation for the steep spectra observed in 2D Bose gas experiments. Our approach provides a systematic framework for constructing wave turbulent cascade spectra when the power-law prediction is degenerate with thermodynamic equilibrium.

papers.title: Strategic and Robust Task Allocation for Combat Objectives in Adversarial Multi-Agent Environments
papers.abstract: Task allocation in contested-objective team games requires coordinated decisions under uncertainty, spatial constraints, and changing tactical conditions. In such settings, multiple agents must anticipate both teammate behavior and opponent actions. We study a hybrid predict-then-optimize approach for assigning controllable agents to objectives in real time. A masked multi-head model predicts tactical signals for each agent, including survival chance, local superiority, combat interaction, travel time, and objective contribution. These signals are combined with rule-based terms in a score matrix, and a minimum-cost flow solver computes coordinated global assignments constrained by capacity, occupancy, stability, and defensive strategies. Learning is limited to tactical scoring, while explicit rules and solver structure preserve controllability and interpretability. We evaluate the system using predictive metrics, offline assignment diagnostics, online A/B evaluation, and latency measurements. The system is an R\&D research prototype built on a commercial game and is not deployed in the shipped game. The results indicate that learned tactical estimates can support stable, feasible, and inspectable objective allocation under strict real-time constraints.

papers.intro:
In many team-based adversarial games, players compete over spatial objectives that must be captured, defended, or contested. Teams win not only by eliminating opponents, but also by controlling objectives that generate score or other strategic advantages. A central decision problem in such games is therefore to determine which agents should move to which objectives and how limited team resources should be distributed across the map. However, task allocation in multi-agent environments is difficult because agents must be assigned to tasks under utility, resource, and coordination constraints [13, 8]. The problem becomes especially challenging when the value of objectives is dynamic, contested, and strongly influenced by other agents. In objective-control games, where teams compete over shared objectives, assigning one agent to a capture objective not only changes its own impact, but also the value of other agents through force concentration, exposure, and shifts in opportunities. Similar inter-agent dependencies are also central in multi-robot task allocation and market-based coordination, where local utility estimates alone are often insufficient for globally coherent team behavior [5, 4].

Artificial intelligence (AI) for commercial games often uses hand-authored heuristics for capture and defense decisions. While these systems are fast, they are difficult to maintain across map changes, rule updates, and evolving player behavior. Classical assignment methods provide efficient solutions when utilities are fixed and tasks are independent [14], but they do not encode many-to-one allocation, objective capacities, human occupancy, or game-specific stability constraints out of the box. Network-flow formulations extend this view to capacities and richer feasibility constraints [3, 10]. However, local game-AI heuristics can fail in contested settings because they favor short-term value over global coverage, force balance, and simultaneous objective pressure. This motivates methods that maintain the speed and controllability of heuristics while also adding global coordination over capacity, force balance, and simultaneous capture objectives.

In this paper we study the application of a learning-assisted constrained optimization pipeline to strategic task allocation in team-based contested-objective battle. This work and described system is an internal research and development (R&D) project and is not part of the released game. As a use case we focus on the game World of Tanks: HEAT [26], a team-based vehicle shooter in which two teams compete for certain objectives. In particular, we study whether this pipeline can produce coordinated, stable, and real-time feasible recommendations. The primary strategic outcome is match win rate, and a recommendation is considered strategic if it improves long-term win probability rather than producing a locally attractive move only. The central comparison is against the game’s built-in closest-base AI baseline, using offline evaluation on logged battles and battle-level outcome metrics where available.

We evaluate the resulting recommender using predictive metrics, offline assignment diagnostics, online evaluation, and latency measurements.

papers.title: Beat This! Live - Online Beat and Downbeat Tracking by Predicting the Future
papers.abstract: Beat and downbeat tracking have seen multiple improvements through recent deep learning approaches, but most target an offline setting, precluding their use in real-time scenarios. We adapt a recent offline beat tracking model, Beat This, for online, low-latency operation and propose Beat This! Live, a causal variant designed for real-time beat and downbeat tracking. We present the architectural modifications required to obtain a causal system suitable for streaming inference and measure their impact on accuracy. By training our model with temporally shifted labels, it produces predictions slightly ahead of the current frame, which not only reduces latency, but enables much more effective peak-picking. Evaluation on the GTZAN dataset shows the F1-score improves from 80.6 to 86.7 for beats and 56.5 to 74.1 for downbeats compared to BeatNet+, the current state of the art in online beat tracking.

papers.title: Music Similarity Estimation from Jukebox Embeddings
papers.abstract: Content-based music similarity estimation aims to provide a measure of similarity between music audio recordings, disregarding any associated metadata. This has potential applications in e.g. cold-start music recommendation scenarios, where there is no user interaction data. In this work, we propose JukeSim, a new approach to estimating musical similarity based on embeddings created by Jukebox, a generative music model. In evaluations on multiple datasets, we find that JukeSim performs on par with an existing learning-based approach, and both outperform the best hand-designed approaches, which had never been compared to recent work before. Even though the required compute for JukeSim is higher than for other measures, we demonstrate the viability of utilizing generative embeddings for this task, encouraging further research.

papers.intro:
Automated content-based music similarity estimation aims to predict the perceptual similarity of two musical pieces based purely on their audio content, not using any metadata. Although the problem is ill-defined, forcing different facets of similarity into a single dimension and not having a clear objective notion of what should be counted as correct, it is still a useful problem to tackle. In particular, it allows side-stepping the cold start problem in music recommender systems, when not enough users have interacted with an item for collaborative filtering to work.

Lately, generative music models have also gained popularity in academic research, exploring their potential for several downstream tasks in music information retrieval (MIR), with promising results.

papers.title: Controlability of the 1D wave equation by point sources: outgoing states, circle rotations and small divisors
papers.abstract: We characterise the states reachable from rest for the one-dimensional wave equation on the real line driven by finitely many fixed point sources. The characterisation reduces the control problem to a cohomological equation on a circle whose length is twice the distance between the outermost sources, with support constraints determined by the control time. For two sources, the reachable set is closed and the controls are unique at every finite time. For three sources, we give a complete classification in terms of the control time and the ratio of the two relevant travel times. Below the time needed to traverse the outer interval twice, reachability is described by finite orbit sums. At and above this threshold, an irrational ratio produces a dense, non-closed reachable set in the compatible outgoing-state space, and exact reachability is determined by a small-divisor condition. We also quantify the cost of control. The minimum control norm is equivalent to the energy norm of the target plus a weighted Fourier norm of its periodised defect. For a badly approximable irrational ratio, the worst cost for defects of Fourier degree at most $N$ grows linearly in $N$, i.e. Liouville ratios produce superpolynomial growth along subsequences. We derive constructive approximation estimates and sharp worst-case cost--accuracy rates on Sobolev classes of defects. For an arbitrary number of sources, the long-time classification and the quantitative estimates are governed by simultaneous Diophantine approximation of the source positions.

papers.title: List coloring degenerate graphs with requests
papers.abstract:
We prove three results on the flexible list coloring of $d$-degenerate graphs. Following Dvo\v{r}\'{a}k, Norin and Postle [J. Graph Theory 2019], a graph $G$ is $(k,\epsilon)$-flexible if for any assignment $L$ of lists of size $k$ to its vertices and any choice of requested colors by a set $\widehat V$ of the vertices from their respective lists, there is an $L$-coloring satisfying at least $\epsilon|\widehat V|$ of the requests. The complete graph on $d+1$ vertices shows that if all $d$-degenerate graphs are $(k,\epsilon)$-flexible for some list size $k$ and satisfaction ratio $\epsilon$, then $k \geq d+1$ and $\epsilon\leq\tfrac1{d+1}$.
  Our results concern values at or near these extremes. For list size $d+2$, we improve the satisfaction ratio from an inverse exponential to an inverse polynomial function of $d$. Although list coloring captures restrictions on admissible choices, it does not explicitly account for preferences among those choices. In applications such as scheduling and network design, certain admissible choices may be preferred because of cost, quality-of-service requirements, or user preferences. This motivates the study of flexible list coloring, introduced by Dvořák, Norin and Postle [8]. Here, each vertex in a specified subset has a preferred color from its list, and the objective is to find a proper list coloring that assigns the preferred color to as many of these vertices as possible. This can be viewed as a relaxation of the classical precoloring extension problem [1].

papers.title: Propagation failure for bistable differential equations on periodic trees
papers.abstract: We study traveling fronts for bistable reaction-diffusion equations on periodic heterogeneous trees. We use comparison principles to estimate the pinning and propagation regions for both cubic and general bistabilities. Our analytical results and numerical simulations show that the interesting propagation reversal effects found in homogeneous trees become more pronounced in the heterogeneous setting, paving the way towards understanding more general graphs. As the diffusion strength increases, the waves end up moving in the same direction irrespective of the bistability. This direction is determined solely by the underlying structure of the heterogeneous tree. Our techniques also lead to sharper results for the homogeneous setting.

Front propagation in spatially discrete bistable systems is strongly influenced by both the coupling strength and the underlying geometry of discrete media. Already on one-dimensional lattices, spatial discreteness may prevent a front from propagating and produce pinning over nontrivial parameter regimes; see, for example, [12]. papers.title: Interpretable identification of constitutive parameter field for three-dimensional heterogeneous and graded hyperelastic materials from full-field displacements
papers.abstract: The inverse problem of identifying spatially varying material properties of heterogeneous solids using experimentally available displacement fields and boundary reaction forces alone remains challenging. Being able to characterize heterogeneous and graded solids would be advantageous in the design and manufacturing of functionally graded materials and composites. Additionally, an efficient technique for identifying heterogeneous material properties from in vivo measurements would be useful in biomedical contexts to characterize heterogeneous biological tissues. Although several techniques developed over the past two decades have addressed inverse identification for homogeneous materials, including linear elastic, hyperelastic, viscoelastic, and elastoplastic solids, comparatively fewer studies have considered heterogeneous and graded materials. Furthermore, several recent approaches to characterizing heterogeneous and graded materials employ parameter-heavy, deep learning-based frameworks trained to enforce force equilibrium at specified collocation points within the material. In this work, we propose an interpretable and time-efficient framework that predicts the three-dimensional relative spatial variation of a constitutive parameter field for multiple parameters of a heterogeneous hyperelastic material, using only displacement-field data. In this work, we validate our framework on 3D synthetic and 2D experimental benchmarks involving heterogeneous, graded, and anisotropic hyperelastic materials. By leveraging the linear nature of the inverse problem for hyperelastic materials and directly optimizing for the constitutive parameters at the finite-element level, we achieve acceptable prediction accuracy with significantly lower computational time compared to recently reported deep-learning-based frameworks.

papers.intro:
Functionally graded materials (FGMs) are a class of heterogeneous materials in which composition, microstructure, and mechanical properties vary continuously across the specimen rather than changing abruptly between distinct material regions [Birman and Byrd, 2007, Li et al., 2020a]. Such spatial grading of mechanical properties is often encountered in engineered composites, architected materials, and biological tissues, where it can arise either by design or through the underlying material architecture [Li et al., 2020a, Bayar et al., 2026]. However, their constitutive characterization is challenging because the material property varies with position, especially in case of anisotropic FGMs such as fiber-reinforced composites and biological tissues containing collagen fiber networks. Oriented micro- and mesoscale fibers impart directional stiffness to anisotropic hyperelastic materials at the macroscopic scale [Holzapfel et al., 2019]. A method to accurately, reliably and rapidly characterize the spatially varying constitutive model of FGMs would enable their use in various engineering applications. For example, accurately designed fiber-reinforced composites with desired spatial and directional variations could be used to make lighter, stronger, and more fracture-resistant airplane wings [Brooks et al., 2019]. Similarly, well-designed anisotropic elastomers can be used for direction-specific morphing in soft robotics [Connolly et al., 2015, Sydney Gladman et al., 2016]. In biological materials, methods for modeling graded hyperelastic materials can better aid modern elastography techniques. Such techniques are frequently used to characterize pathological changes in tissue mechanics, as malignant tissues are commonly associated with increased stiffness and exhibit different anisotropies compared to softer healthy tissues [Skerl et al., 2016, Nia et al., 2020, Micalet et al., 2021, Koorman et al., 2022].

Such spatial grading of mechanical properties is often encountered in engineered composites, architected materials, and biological tissues, where it can arise either by design or through the underlying material architecture [Li et al., 2020a, Bayar et al., 2026]. However, their constitutive characterization is challenging because the material property varies with position, especially in case of anisotropic FGMs such as fiber-reinforced composites and biological tissues containing collagen fiber networks. Oriented micro- and mesoscale fibers impart directional stiffness to anisotropic hyperelastic materials at the macroscopic scale [Holzapfel et al., 2019]. A method to accurately, reliably and rapidly characterize the spatially varying constitutive model of FGMs would enable their use in various engineering applications. For example, accurately designed fiber-reinforced composites with desired spatial and directional variations could be used to make lighter, stronger, and more fracture-resistant airplane wings [Brooks et al., 2019]. Similarly, well-designed anisotropic elastomers can be used for direction-specific morphing in soft robotics [Connolly et al., 2015, Sydney Gladman et al., 2016]. In biological materials, methods for modeling graded hyperelastic materials can better aid modern elastography techniques. Such techniques are frequently used to characterize pathological changes in tissue mechanics, as malignant tissues are commonly associated with increased stiffness and exhibit different anisotropies compared to softer healthy tissues [Skerl et al., 2016, Nia et al., 2020, Micalet et al., 2021, Koorman et al., 2022].

The increasing availability of full-field deformation measurements through techniques such as Digital Image Correlation (DIC) [Genovese et al., 2021, Chen and Pan, 2022, Çapunaman et al., 2026, Abbasi et al., 2026], Digital Volume Correlation (DVC) [Bay et al., 1999, Wang et al., 2024, Grega et al., 2025] and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) [Avril et al., 2008a, Estrada et al., 2020] has motivated a wide range of inverse approaches to obtain constitutive models for homogeneous materials. These include the Finite Element Model Updating (FEMU) [Kavanagh and Clough, 1971, Avril et al., 2008b, Marwala, 2010, Pottier et al., 2011] approach, the Virtual Fields Method (VFM) [Grédiac et al., 2006, Promma et al., 2009], Equilibrium-Gap based Methods [Ikehata, 1990, Claire et al., 2004, Claire et al., 2007, Geymonat et al., 2002, Geymonat and Pagano, 2003, Florentin and Lubineau, 2010], and the EUCLID framework [Flaschel et al., 2021, Marino et al., 2023, Flaschel et al., 2022, Thakolkaran et al., 2022, Joshi et al., 2022]. Some of these frameworks have been adapted to identify the spatial variation of Young’s Modulus (Poisson’s ratio usually assumed to be 0.5) in linear elastic materials using surface displacement and boundary force data [Toussaint et al., 2006, Avril et al., 2008a, Haustrate et al., 2025, Tan et al., 2017]. More recent works [Chaurasiya et al., 2026, Shi et al., 2025] extend the Bayesian-EUCLID [Joshi et al., 2022] framework and the NN-EUCLID framework to model heterogeneous hyperelastic solids with clear segment boundaries between the heterogeneities. These works use residual forces to highlight inter-segment boundaries and model each segment separately, and thus are unable to model graded materials (such as FGMs) which have no clear distinct boundaries between materials.

The increasing availability of full-field deformation measurements through techniques such as Digital Image Correlation (DIC) [Genovese et al., 2021, Chen and Pan, 2022, Çapunaman et al., 2026, Abbasi et al., 2026], Digital Volume Correlation (DVC) [Bay et al., 1999, Wang et al., 2024, Grega et al., 2025] and Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) [Avril et al., 2008a, Estrada et al., 2020] has motivated a wide range of inverse approaches to obtain constitutive models for homogeneous materials. These include the Finite Element Model Updating (FEMU) [Kavanagh and Clough, 1971, Avril et al., 2008b, Marwala, 2010, Pottier et al., 2011] approach, the Virtual Fields Method (VFM) [Grédiac et al., 2006, Promma et al., 2009], Equilibrium-Gap based Methods [Ikehata, 1990, Claire et al., 2004, Claire et al., 2007, Geymonat et al., 2002, Geymonat and Pagano, 2003, Florentin and Lubineau, 2010], and the EUCLID framework [Flaschel et al., 2021, Marino et al., 2023, Flaschel et al., 2022, Thakolkaran et al., 2022, Joshi et al., 2022]. Some of these frameworks have been adapted to identify the spatial variation of Young’s Modulus (Poisson’s ratio usually assumed to be 0.5) in linear elastic materials using surface displacement and boundary force data [Toussaint et al., 2006, Avril et al., 2008a, Haustrate et al., 2025, Tan et al., 2017]. More recent works [Chaurasiya et al., 2026, Shi et al., 2025] extend the Bayesian-EUCLID [Joshi et al., 2022] framework and the NN-EUCLID framework to model heterogeneous hyperelastic solids with clear segment boundaries between the heterogeneities. These works use residual forces to highlight inter-segment boundaries and model each segment separately, and thus are unable to model graded materials (such as FGMs) which have no clear distinct boundaries between materials.

All of the aforementioned frameworks– FEMU, VFM and Equilibrium Gap-based methods such as EUCLID, rely on enforcing the weak-form of momentum balance on the underlying geometry to obtain an appropriate constitutive model for the material of interest. An alternative approach has been to represent the spatial distribution of material properties (usually Young’s modulus) using neural networks (NNs) or neural operators, which are then trained to minimize the residual of the strong form of momentum balance at every collocation point [Zhang et al., 2020, Mallampati and Almekkawy, 2021, Chen and Gu, 2021, Tripura et al., 2023]. ElastNet and El-UNet [Chen and Gu, 2023, Kamali et al., 2023, Kamali and Laksari, 2024], introduced deep-learning-based inverse frameworks that map spatial coordinates to a heterogeneous elastic-modulus and Poisson’s ratio field. Another work similar to ElastNet [Liu, 2025], provided a framework for 3D elastography for linear elastic solids. PIE-PINN model [Srikitrungruang et al., 2025, Srikitrungruang and Lee, 2026] employs a probabilistic formulation combining a B-spline-guided displacement approximation, neural correction, and adaptive residual weighting to recover spatially varying Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio from noisy and low-resolution displacement measurements. Similarly, AR-PINN [Zhu et al., 2026] extends the technique to the large deformation regime, reconstructs an unknown heterogeneous field from sparse Green–Lagrange strain observations, and uses residual-adaptive collocation to resolve sharp interfaces. Alternatively, Kim et al. [Kim et al., 2026] devised a supervised Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) [Li et al., 2020b] architecture to map ultrasound-derived axial displacement fields directly to spatial elastic modulus distributions. Once trained, the FNO-based model provides rapid inference and exhibits robustness to measurement noise. These studies demonstrate the potential of deep learning techniques to reconstruct material-property fields directly from deformation measurements. However, it remained predominantly two-dimensional and restricted to isotropic linear-elasticity: ElastNet, El-UNet, PIE-PINN, and FNO-based models consider small-strain, linear-elastic, incompressible behavior under plane stress/strain conditions, whereas the AR-PINN considers a scalar Neo-Hookean form, with the bulk parameter held fixed in a two-dimensional isotropic setting.

papers.title: Intrinsically nonlinear nanomechanical resonator toward the single-phonon Kerr regime
papers.abstract: Manipulating a physical system at the single-quantum level typically requires an anharmonic energy spectrum. Nanomechanical resonators, however, are commonly admitted to be linear objects in the single-phonon regime, thus motivating most efforts to employ external sources of nonlinearity at the cost of added relaxation and decoherence channels. Here, we take a radically different approach by directly exploiting strong intrinsic mechanical nonlinearities. We quantify this nonlinearity using a novel method based on the coupling between bending modes. Using this technique, we establish an upper bound of 34.0 +/- 9.7 phonons for the onset of intrinsically mechanical bistability. In addition, we highlight a new tuning mechanism based on a mechanical polarization angle of an upward-buckled nanotube resonator allowing us to reach an optimal working point. Extrapolating this level of intrinsic nonlinearity to realistically shorter resonators shows that the single-phonon Kerr regime is within reach, allowing for the realization of purely mechanical Schr\"odinger-cat states and highly coherent mechanical qubits.

papers.title: Autonomous Ergodic Robotic Palpation for Elastic Mapping of Curved Soft Tissues
papers.abstract:
Autonomous robotic palpation offers repeatable, quantitative
  estimates of tissue properties for stiff inclusion
  localization. However, existing methods often rely on prior mesh
  models or planar surface assumptions that do not generalize to
  complex human anatomy. We propose an ergodic palpation framework that
  operates directly on curved soft surfaces using point cloud
  data. Central to our approach is the Laplace--Beltrami operator,
  which grounds both online estimation and exploration in the surface
  intrinsic geometry. We estimate local viscoelastic parameters using
  an Unscented Kalman Filter (UKF) and fuse them into a surface-aware
  Gaussian Process (GP). This probabilistic model drives a
  diffusion-based ergodic motion planner, generating a continuous
  exploration trajectory that feeds the new informative samples back
  to the GP in a closed loop. Throughout this process, a hybrid
  force-impedance controller regulates interaction forces to maintain
  contact. We evaluate the approach against existing methods in
  simulation and validate it in physical experiments on
  tissue-mimicking silicone phantoms with varying geometries and
  viscoelastic properties, demonstrating geometry-consistent mapping
  and stiff inclusion localization under contact-rich conditions.

papers.intro:
Palpation is a clinical procedure in which physicians assess possible anomalies from the mechanical response of the patient’s tissues to touch. When performed manually, it is subjective and varies across practitioners, which limits diagnostic repeatability, particularly for small, deep-seated, or weakly contrasted lesions. Clinical workflows therefore complement palpation with imaging modalities such as mammography (Eisemann et al., 2025) and ultrasound (Dan et al., 2024), which are costly, require specialised staff and equipment, and can burden the patient (e.g., through ionising radiation). Robotic palpation promises a more repeatable and objective interaction. Beyond revealing possible lesions, it can also quantify elasticity and viscosity (Palacio-Torralba et al., 2015), which are useful for instance to regulate robot–tissue interaction forces in robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery and ultrasound-guided procedures.

Approaches to tissue mechanical characterisation fall into imaging-based elastography and contact-based sensing. Ultrasound (Zhang et al., 2025) and magnetic resonance (Sack, 2023) elastography estimate spatial stiffness distributions, but integrating them into robot-mediated, contact-rich procedures requires dedicated hardware, accurate registration between imaging and robot frames, and workflow adaptations. Contact-based approaches instead infer tissue properties from force and deformation at the tool-tissue interface, providing local mechanical feedback in real time. Force feedback during probing has been shown to reduce applied forces and procedure time (Trejos et al., 2009; Enayati et al., 2016), and force-based estimation can recover meaningful stiffness information without specialised tactile arrays (Haddadi and Hashtrudi-Zaad, 2012; Roveda et al., 2022). This motivates using a single wrist-mounted force-torque (F/T) sensor both to regulate the interaction and to estimate local viscoelastic properties.

However, these methods are typically formulated and validated on planar or locally flat surfaces (Garg et al., 2016) and assume rectangular exploration patches (Nichols and Okamura, 2015; Garg et al., 2016; Ayvali et al., 2017; Beber et al., 2026). This limits their applicability to curved anatomical surfaces and to irregular or non-convex admissible contact regions arising from safety constraints, anatomy, or kinematic limits.

We address these limitations with an autonomous palpation framework for elastic mapping on curved soft surfaces represented as point clouds, without requiring an anatomical mesh, a volumetric model, or a global surface parameterization. Figure 1 provides an overview of the framework. Local viscoelastic parameters are estimated online from force-displacement measurements using our previous force-based framework (Beber et al., 2025), in which a contact model based on the Dimensionality Reduction Method (DRM) (Popov and Heß, 2015) is embedded in a Kalman filter. These estimates are fused into a manifold-aware Gaussian Process (GP) (Borovitskiy et al., 2020) defined directly over the point cloud, whose posterior drives an ergodic planner in the spirit of HEDAC (Bilaloglu et al., 2025). The ergodic planner, point cloud HEDAC (PC-HEDAC), is updated at a high rate and requires neither surface flattening nor discrete waypoint planning. Its Expected Information Density (EID) combines attraction towards regions of high estimated apparent stiffness with exploration of regions of high posterior uncertainty, progressively refining the map around mechanically informative areas, according to the prescribed ergodic metric. The framework is evaluated through systematic simulation studies and repeated physical experiments. The results demonstrated that the proposed method achieves lower reconstruction RMSE than all evaluated baselines under the same travel budget and requires approximately five times less travel than BO to reach the same RMSE. In addition, the proposed stopping criterion reduces exploration time by approximately 30%30\% compared with full exploration runs, with comparable reconstruction and localization performance.

papers.title: Black holes in little red and blue dots drive no superwinds in the first 1.5 billion years
papers.abstract: Galaxy-formation models rely on accreting black holes to expel gas from their hosts. We test this prediction in 67 little red dots (LRDs) and little blue dots (LBDs) in the first 1.5 billion years, selected from 80,367 NIRSpec spectra in the DAWN JWST Archive. We detect no [O III] wind, against lower limits of 7.2 and 7.5 expected detections for local sub-Eddington and super-Eddington active nuclei. For winds narrower than 1,500 km/s, the corresponding incidence limits are 13% and 19% at 95% confidence, compared with 31% and 49% locally. Broad Balmer lines are centred on the narrow lines, and Balmer absorbers move below 8% of the escape speed. Published super-Eddington fountain, black-hole-star and quasi-star models each fail a measured property of the spectra. LRDs and LBDs drive no superwinds, and their black holes grow without the wind feedback invoked to regulate galaxies.

papers.title: Generation as Reverse Encoding
papers.abstract: Pretrained visual representations accelerate generative learning by abstracting away appearance and spatial detail. Yet the same abstraction makes the return to pixels far harder, shifting much of the burden onto a larger decoder. We ask why the representation-to-pixel path should be learned independently when the encoder already provides a learned pixel-to-semantics path (the semantic encoding path). We introduce RevFlow, based on the principle of generation as reverse encoding. RevFlow uses intermediate representations of a frozen encoder as successive generative targets, first generating deep semantic representations, then shallow representations that retain appearance and spatial detail, before decoding to pixels. To learn these transitions without training a separate generator for each stage, we develop HyC-DiT, a unified generative model with a standard DiT backbone shared across stages and stage-specific condition injection. We further show that native matching in semantic representation space enables few-step generation. RevFlow accelerates both learning and sampling. On ImageNet $256 \times 256$, RevFlow reaches 1.96 FID at 690M and 1.74 FID at 1.55B after only 5 training epochs. It also achieves 30.25 dB reconstruction PSNR with an 89M decoder. After a short native-matching adaptation phase, RevFlow-XL achieves 2.85 FID using a single sampling step in each stage. Our code repository is at https://github.com/ChengShiest/RevFlow

papers.intro:
Visual encoding and image reconstruction/generation can be viewed as opposite processes. A pretrained visual encoder progressively transforms an image into increasingly abstract representations, whereas image reconstruction/generation maps such representations back to concrete visual realizations. In conventional autoencoding [61, 46], the reverse problem is posed as reconstruction: a representation is paired with the particular image that produced it, and the decoder is trained to recover that image. Generation poses a harder reverse problem. Once abstraction makes different images share similar representations, the inverse becomes underdetermined: a representation can correspond to multiple images rather than a fixed target.

This distinction becomes especially pronounced for representations pretrained for visual understanding11 1 In this paper, unless otherwise specified, encoder refers to a frozen pretrained visual representation encoder, such as DINO or CLIP, rather than to a reconstruction-oriented VAE encoder.. Reconstruction-oriented representations, such as VAE latents, retain appearance and spatial detail for faithful recovery, whereas semantic representations learned for visual understanding suppress variations less relevant to semantic discrimination. Such abstraction accelerates generative learning, as exploited by REPA [63] and RAE [66], but leaves more appearance and spatial detail to be generated on the way back to pixels. In RAE-style models, this burden is delegated to a separately learned decoder, which is typically around 10×\times larger than those in conventional latent diffusion [48]; Figure 2 further shows that RAE can reconstruct a gray Christmas hat as red. Abstraction therefore shifts, rather than removes, the difficulty: generation in a semantic representation space is easier to learn, while decoding becomes more demanding and absorbs an increasing share of generative modeling.

Recent methods mitigate this tension by making the generated representation retain more appearance and spatial detail. VA-VAE [61] enriches reconstruction-oriented latents with semantic structure, while RAEv2 [51] combines multiple encoder levels into a single target containing both semantic and spatial information. These methods improve the target through alignment or feature aggregation, then learn a separate decoding path from that target to pixels.

We take a different view. Here we define the semantic encoding path as the progression of representations from pixels to abstract semantics that semantic pretraining forms within an encoder. If generation ultimately reverses semantic encoding, why learn a separate decoding path back to pixels when the semantic encoding path already connects pixels to semantics? We propose to reverse this path itself. Along the semantic encoding path, shallow representations retain more appearance and spatial detail, while deep representations emphasize semantics. The path thus acts like the forward process of diffusion models, which removes information gradually so that generation can recover it through simple reverse steps [52, 21]. Unlike data-agnostic Gaussian corruption, which removes information roughly by spatial frequency [47], the encoder removes it in a learned order: appearance and spatial detail first, semantics last [38, 1]. Its reverse resolves semantics first, from deep representations that largely reveal the class, leaving representation learning, a main bottleneck of diffusion training [63], to the pretrained encoder. Directly predicting clean shallow features from a class label faces an uninformative conditional mean and wide residual variance, forcing stiff jumps onto dispersed clean Dirac targets rather than smooth score refinement. Reversing the path keeps training smooth: the deep stage first models a lower-variance semantic space, and its output then provides spatial mean guidance that leaves only a narrow residual variance for the shallow stage (Appendix A, Sec. 4.3). This suggests a different principle: intermediate representations along the semantic encoding path should serve as successive generation targets, defining how generation unfolds. Generating each target, from the class label or from the next deeper representation on the path, forms a stage. How to learn stages that differ in conditions and representation spaces within one model, however, remains open.

We propose RevFlow (generation as reverse encoding), which carries out multiple stages of generation along the reversed semantic encoding path with a single Transformer backbone. The generation targets of all stages are representations of the same image along the path. Generation proceeds from class labels to deep semantic representations, then shallow representations, and finally pixels. Sharing a backbone across stages requires accommodating different conditions and addressing optimization interference across representation spaces. We therefore introduce HyC-DiT, which adapts a standard DiT [42] in both architecture and training: global class conditioning is used in the first stage and spatial feature conditioning in the second, while clean-target prediction enables effective weight sharing across stages. Crucially, the deep-to-shallow stage models appearance and spatial detail before pixel decoding, reducing the generative modeling burden on the decoder. The complete pipeline pairs a lightweight decoder with better generation and reconstruction.

Beyond reverse encoding, we study native distribution matching for few-step adaptation of semantic representation generators. Existing methods such as FD-loss [59] and representation distribution matching [15] improve few-step generation by aligning generated and real samples in pretrained feature space, but conventional VAE-based generators typically need to decode latents into images and re-encode them for matching. Generating encoder representations allows native matching without this decode–encode loop. Native matching (NM) improves both single-stage RAE and two-stage RevFlow, demonstrating applicability beyond our reverse-encoding architecture.

papers.title: Passivity Shaping over Frequency Bands: A Differentiable Optimization Approach
papers.abstract: The energy transition replaces traditional inertial synchronous machines with power electronic converters, introducing new grid stability challenges. Passivity provides a compositional input-output framework for assessing stability in interconnected grid subsystems, yet tuning controllers for this property over specific frequency ranges - a practical requirement in converter-dominated grids - still relies largely on practitioners' experience, typically based on intuition or trial and error. We address this gap in three steps: (i) we formulate the passivity index over arbitrary frequency bands as the optimal value of a parametric Semidefinite Program (SDP) using the generalized KYP (gKYP) lemma; (ii) we derive analytical sensitivities of this optimal value with respect to controller parameters via the Envelope Theorem; and (iii) we embed these elements in a bilevel optimization scheme that tunes controller parameters to maximize the passivity index. We validate the proposed method on two case studies of increasing complexity: a grid-following converter and a multi-converter microgrid.

Power systems are undergoing a fundamental transition from synchronous-machine-dominated grids to converter-based grids, driven by the large-scale integration of renewable energy sources [3]. This shift introduces new challenges in stability analysis. The mechanical inertia of synchronous generators, which has traditionally contributed to moderating the rate of change of system frequency and shaping electromechanical oscillatory behavior, is progressively diminishing. Consequently, power systems become more sensitive to fast dynamics, and higher-frequency interactions that were previously less significant may gain importance [10, 17]. Dissipativity [30], and more specifically passivity [32, 33], is widely regarded as a promising tool for the stability analysis of such power systems. The key advantage is that it offers a compositional framework to guarantee stability under interconnection at the subsystem level. Thus, the need for deriving and analyzing a model of the whole system, which is impractical or even impossible due to privacy considerations, is alleviated.

The practical relevance of passivity-based requirements is starting to be recognized at the regulatory level. In August 2024, the non-passive behavior of an offshore converter connection triggered a harmonic instability event in the German transmission system [8]. The German regulator consequently recommended introducing passivity over the relevant frequency range as a mandatory grid-connection requirement for all new assets [8, p. 53]. This trend extends beyond Germany: the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Electricity (ENTSO-E) recommends in its technical guidance on grid-forming requirements that power generating units exhibit passive impedance behavior over a frequency range specified by the transmission system operator [11, p. 21]. Likewise, NERC recommends that grid-forming inverters should be passive at 0−3000-300 Hz [23], and UNIFI recommends a combination of passivity and low gain in that frequency range [19]. Fingrid, Finland’s transmission system operator, has already updated its grid code to require grid-forming battery energy storage systems to exhibit passive behavior in the frequency ranges of 0-47 Hz and 53-250 Hz as a condition for grid connection [12].

In many practical designs, controller parameters are still selected through engineering intuition or parameter sweeps [27], even though passivity violations at specific frequencies often lead to instability in grid-connected converters [13]. The difficulty is inherent to Voltage Source Converters, which exhibit negative-conductance behavior in certain frequency ranges, making full-spectrum passivity unattainable. Moreover, passivity margins depend on controller gains in non-monotonic and counterintuitive ways [9], which makes parameter sweeps unreliable and manual tuning impractical, especially when many parameters must be adjusted at the same time.

Moreover, passivity margins depend on controller gains in non-monotonic and counterintuitive ways [9], which makes parameter sweeps unreliable and manual tuning impractical, especially when many parameters must be adjusted at the same time.

Several prior works address passivity-oriented controller design, each focusing on a specific problem setting. Feedback passivation has been formulated as a convex optimization problem with theoretical guarantees [29]; however, this approach considers only the standard feedback interconnection and is not applicable to more complex control structures composed of inner and outer loops, as is typical in power system applications. Furthermore, it targets passivity over the entire frequency axis, not over specific frequency bands. The passivity sensitivity methodology based on admittance models presented in [20] computes how individual parameters influence the passivity index at each frequency. However, this approach provides only pointwise sensitivities and does not capture the worst-case passivity margin over a frequency band. Recently, the authors of [18] derived two frequency-dependent passivity-based stability criteria for the converter–grid interconnection, further motivating passivity shaping over targeted frequency bands rather than over the entire frequency spectrum. Moreover, the work in [24] formulates finite-frequency passivity requirements as Linear Matrix Inequality constraints via the Generalized KYP lemma and provides a visual tool for analyzing the feasibility of passivization. We build on these advances: we formalize the general problem of tuning controllers to maximize passivity over targeted frequency ranges as an optimization problem, exploit its structure, and derive a gradient-based algorithm applicable to any differentiable controller parameterization. The proposed optimization-based formulation results in a non-convex problem: while the passivity index computation for fixed parameters constitutes a convex problem, jointly optimizing over the controller parameter space introduces non-convexity. The passivity index is not an explicit function of the controller parameters; rather, it is the optimal value of a parametric Semidefinite Program. Consequently, passivity-oriented tuning requires computing how the optimal value of the Semidefinite Program changes when the controller parameters vary.

Differentiable optimization [7] provides a natural framework for this task, offering tools to compute how optimal values change with problem parameters. Recent work has used these ideas to embed optimization problems inside larger learning and control architectures. For example, quadratic programs have been implemented as differentiable layers in neural networks [2], and this idea has been extended to disciplined convex programs together with open-source software support [1]. In control, related techniques have been used to differentiate through predictive-control policies, enabling controller parameters to be tuned through the policy’s underlying optimization problem [35]. We build upon these advances to address a different objective: tuning controller parameters to improve passivity margins for Linear Time-Invariant systems.

papers.title: Deep Learning-Based Mesoscopic Emission Modeling
papers.abstract: Traffic-related emissions are a major contributor to urban air pollution. However, existing emission models face a fundamental trade-off: macroscopic models are computationally efficient but rely on average speeds, leading to systematic errors, while microscopic models achieve high accuracy but are computationally prohibitive for large scale simulations. To bridge this gap, this study introduces Direct Emission Prediction (DEP), a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU)-based deep learning model. DEP was trained on over one million synthetic trips generated by coupling real-world GNSS speed profiles with the microscopic emission model MOBSim. By processing sequential link-level inputs, including vehicle characteristics, road attributes, and ambient temperature, DEP predicts CO$_2$ and NOx emissions. We integrated DEP into a MATSim-based workflow and applied it to the Ile-de-France region. DEP matches the accuracy of SPG-M, a hybrid mesoscopic-microscopic reference model, within 0.35% for CO$_2$ and 1.87% for NOx across both hot and cold-start scenarios, while reducing computational runtime to just 2.2%. Furthermore, validation against empirical remote sensing data confirms that DEP accurately reproduces real-world NOx emission levels across Euro 2-6 diesel vehicles, whereas traditional macroscopic tools like COPERT and HBEFA systematically underestimate them. Finally, DEP effectively captures the spatial distribution of cold-start emissions, identifying key hotspots in dense urban areas. This work demonstrates that deep learning-based mesoscopic frameworks can achieve microscopic accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost, enabling scalable, high-resolution urban emission modeling without relying on pre-computed emission factor databases.

papers.intro:
Outdoor air pollution is one of the most pressing public health challenges of our time. It causes at least 4.2 million deaths annually worldwide according to the World Health Organization (2024), and more than 350 000350\,000 deaths in the European Union (EU) in 2022 alone (European Environment Agency, 2024). When indoor air pollution is included, the two together account for approximately 10% of all deaths worldwide, making air pollution the fourth leading mortality risk globally (Shaw and Van Heyst, 2022). Beyond mortality, the consequences extend across multiple dimensions of human wellbeing: exposure to particulate matter (PM) and nitrogen oxides (NOx) impairs cognitive function and is associated with mental health disorders, sleep disturbances, anxiety, depression, and suicide (Chang et al., 2019; Ebenstein et al., 2016). The economic toll is equally significant, a 10% reduction in fine particulate pollution is estimated to increase EU economic output by between 0.5% and 1.5%, while the benefits of the U.S. Clean Air Act Amendments over the period 1990–2020 are estimated at 12 trillion USD (Dechezleprêtre et al., 2019).

Top-down models rely on aggregate data and statistical techniques to estimate emissions at large spatial scales. They correlate historical emission levels with macro-level variables such as fuel consumption, population trends, economic indicators, and vehicle fleet composition (Muratori et al., 2013; Pinto et al., 2020). While suitable for national or regional inventories, their limited spatial resolution makes them unsuitable for evaluating localized pollution patterns or targeted interventions.

In contrast, bottom-up methods utilize fine-grained data to offer more accurate emission estimates across multiple dimensions (Zhang et al., 2019). This enhanced capability is vital for a comprehensive understanding of the environmental impact of traffic in specific areas or districts, and facilitates precise modeling of diverse traffic scenarios (Piccoli et al., 2024; Dib et al., 2025). However, their implementation at larger scales presents significant challenges.

Traffic simulations model the dynamic interactions between populations and transportation systems (Dorokhin et al., 2020). These simulations produce data that are integrated into emission models to estimate pollutant levels across both space and time. However, there is a trade-off between the level of detail provided by these models and their computational efficiency.

These simulations produce data that are integrated into emission models to estimate pollutant levels across both space and time. However, there is a trade-off between the level of detail provided by these models and their computational efficiency.

For instance, the computational demands of microscopic traffic simulations paired with microscopic emission models, while providing highly detailed estimates for various kinds of studies (Misra et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2009; Mądziel and Campisi, 2023), effectively limit their application to small geographic areas such as individual intersections or specific traffic corridors (Tu et al., 2018). Conversely, mesoscopic and macroscopic approaches offer greater computational efficiency for large-scale networks, though less detailed. For example, Airparif uses a macroscopic traffic model combined with COPERT (COmputer Programme to calculate Emissions from Road Transport, Ntziachristos et al. (2009)) to estimate emissions in its Île-de-France inventory (Airparif, 2022). Similar methods have been applied in cities like Madrid (Borge et al., 2012), Barcelona (Rodriguez-Rey et al., 2021), Paris (Elessa Etuman and Coll, 2018), and New York City (Schnieder et al., 2022), where macroscopic traffic models are paired with emission models to estimate road traffic emissions.
