Although macroscopic models are computationally efficient for large-scale simulations, they often produce less accurate emission estimates (Rodriguez-Rey et al., 2021; Tu et al., 2018), particularly when trying to capture local emission peaks. For instance, comparisons between COPERT and HBEFA (Handbook Emission Factors for Road Transport, Notter et al. (2019)) models combined with macroscopic traffic models revealed significant differences in outputs (Borge et al., 2012). Similarly, in Gräbe and Joubert (2022), a model based on MATSim combined with HBEFA underestimated emissions compared to real-world Portable Emission Measurement Systems (PEMS) measurements. In addition, multiple studies like Rodriguez-Rey et al. (2021); Tu et al. (2018), and Lejri et al. (2018) highlight discrepancies between macroscopic and microscopic approaches, especially in urban areas with heavy traffic. Even when macroscopic models provide reasonable aggregate estimates, they struggle to capture the spatial distribution of emissions (Thibault et al., 2018; Laraki et al., 2022a). This is largely due to the fact that macroscopic emission models primarily rely on either average speed or discrete traffic situations, neither of which can always accurately reflect actual driving dynamics. Traffic-situation models, such as HBEFA, face challenges due to the level of data aggregation and the inherent ambiguity in defining traffic conditions (Le Cornec, 2021; Samaras et al., 2019). For average-speed-based models, such as COPERT, it has been shown that relying on average speed alone, without accounting for congestion or acceleration patterns, can lead to significant inaccuracies in emission estimates (Samaras et al., 2019; Smit et al., 2008). For instance, a speed of 45 km/h may represent free-flow conditions in urban areas, yet indicate heavy congestion on highways, resulting in fundamentally different emission profiles.

papers.title: Brand Recall and Category Accuracy in Language Models: An Audit of 1,000 B2B SaaS Brands
papers.abstract: A language model can name a brand without classifying it correctly. This study measures these outcomes separately for 1,000 B2B SaaS brands across 333 product categories. On Gemma 4 12B, with no external retrieval, category prompts elicit 510 brands (51.0%). A separate five-candidate category probe ranks the reference label first for 787 brands, a distractor first for 194, and yields little separation for 19. Among the 981 separated rankings, the error rate is 19.8%. It falls to 3.5% for the 547 brands with a winner-to-runner-up log-probability margin above 0.6. These are within-cohort measurements, not calibrated confidence estimates. Exploratory regressions associate technical coverage with recall and an owned-properties composite with category accuracy, but the composites use different adjustment sets and do not establish causal effects. Across four Gemma generations, measured recall is 39.8%, 44.3%, 51.1% and 51.0%. A separate representation-based sentiment measure has little linear association with customer ratings (r=0.03, n=921). The findings support reporting recall and category accuracy separately. Failure to elicit a brand does not establish its absence from model parameters or training data.

When a language model is used for product research, two questions matter: does it name a relevant company, and does it identify what that company does? Measuring mentions alone cannot distinguish these outcomes. Retrieval-enabled assistants add another source of variation because their answers may depend on newly retrieved documents as well as model parameters.

papers.title: FOCI: Trajectory Optimization on Gaussian Splats for Gaussian Robots
papers.abstract: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has recently gained popularity as a faster alternative to Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) in 3D reconstruction and view synthesis methods. Leveraging the spatial information encoded in 3DGS, this work proposes FOCI (Field Overlap Collision Integral), an algorithm that is able to optimize trajectories directly on the Gaussians themselves. FOCI leverages a novel and interpretable collision formulation for 3DGS using the notion of the overlap integral between Gaussians. The formulation presented applies to different robot morphologies (e.g., fixed and mobile base manipulators, legged robots, UAVs) and handles both static and dynamic Gaussian-Splat environments. Contrary to other approaches, which represent the robot with conservative bounding boxes that underestimate the traversability of the environment, we propose to represent the environment and the robot as Gaussian Splats. This not only has desirable computational properties, but also allows for orientation-aware planning, allowing the robot to pass through very tight and narrow spaces. We extensively test our algorithm in both synthetic and real Gaussian Splats, showcasing that collision-free trajectories for legged, aerial and manipulator robots can be computed in seconds, even with hundreds of thousands of Gaussians making up the environment. The code is available at https://github.com/leggedrobotics/foci

Trajectory planning is integral to autonomous mobile robotics to ensure guided and safe operation. However, in order to make an informed decision, these planning algorithms heavily depend on the underlying environment representations. Popular representations include occupancy grids, signed distance fields, 3D Meshes, and point clouds.

However, in order to make an informed decision, these planning algorithms heavily depend on the underlying environment representations. Recently, Neural Radiance Fields [27] have been proposed as a novel neural representation of the environment. However, they suffer from having slow inference speeds because new views have to be created using a computationally expensive ray-casting procedure. More recently, 3D Gaussian Splatting [22] has been proposed as a promising alternative to Neural Radiance Fields. Instead of using a neural network to represent the radiance field, it is defined explicitly by a set of 3D Gaussian ellipsoids. Because of this, new views can be efficiently generated by projecting these ellipsoids into the view plane.

Instead of using a neural network to represent the radiance field, it is defined explicitly by a set of 3D Gaussian ellipsoids. Because of this, new views can be efficiently generated by projecting these ellipsoids into the view plane.

Given the advantages that 3D Gaussian Splatting offers when compared with Neural Radiance Fields, the natural question is how a robot can leverage this Gaussian representation for navigation. In this paper, we propose an algorithm that enables a robot to perform trajectory optimization directly on the 3D Gaussians. Furthermore, the proposed formulation is robot-agnostic and makes no assumption of a static environment, enabling trajectory optimization across a wide range of robotic platforms and in dynamic scenarios (see Figs. 1 and 2). Although some steps have been taken in this direction [6, 23, 14, 25], the huge number of Gaussians a scene can have, together with the specific formulation of an explicit collision measure, makes this problem especially hard.

In this paper, we propose an algorithm that enables a robot to perform trajectory optimization directly on the 3D Gaussians. Furthermore, the proposed formulation is robot-agnostic and makes no assumption of a static environment, enabling trajectory optimization across a wide range of robotic platforms and in dynamic scenarios (see Figs. 1 and 2). Although some steps have been taken in this direction [6, 23, 14, 25], the huge number of Gaussians a scene can have, together with the specific formulation of an explicit collision measure, makes this problem especially hard.

To overcome these challenges, we propose FOCI, a trajectory optimization algorithm that leverages the overlap integral – the spatial integral over the multiplication of two functions – as a proxy measure for the collision between two Gaussians. By representing both the robot and the environment with 3D Gaussians, evaluating the full-body collision between them reduces to a sum of normal distribution evaluations. Furthermore, the resulting expression is fully differentiable, yielding expressive gradients in the optimization step.

papers.title: Large-deformation constitutive modeling of viscoelastic foams: Application to an open-cell foam material
papers.abstract: Open-cell elastomeric foams are widely utilized for impact protection and cushioning applications. These foams can demonstrate remarkable elastic compressibility and rate sensitivity over a wide range of force and acceleration protection levels. They often exhibit volumetric-distortional coupling in their mechanical response and potentially compaction banding when subjected to dynamic loads. Here, a phenomenological modeling framework, adopted previously for closed-cell foams, is specified using an experimental characterization-based approach for calibrating and validating the large-deformation, viscoelastic material model. Homogeneous simple compression and tension experiments were performed on isotropic, open-cell viscoelastic foam materials, and stress-strain and lateral-axial strain data were used for model calibration. Data were collected at decadal strain rates to inform the rate-sensitive aspects of the model. The modeling approach involved decomposing the total material response into an equilibrium hyperelastic contribution and several nonlinear, Maxwell-like contributions and utilized invariants of the logarithmic strain to account for large deformations and the strong volumetric-distortional coupling effect. The consistency between the measured responses from the validation experiments and the model predictions obtained from finite-element-based numerical simulations was largely within the experimental uncertainty bounds, demonstrating the predictive capability of the model.

Experiments over a wide range of strain rates have been conducted to attempt to capture time-dependencies in the material response of elastomeric foams. Elevated-rate experiments can largely be grouped into three categories on the basis of strain rate. First, low-rate “non-equilibrium” experiments, in which the response displays non-negligible hysteresis, often due to viscous effects in the matrix, typically span strain-rates of ϵ˙applied≈10−3​s−1\dot{\epsilon}_{\rm applied}\approx 10^{-3}\,\text{s}^{-1} or lower to 10010^{0} s-1 depending on the matrix material. Second, intermediate or impact-like rates, in which the response is hysteretic and other mechanisms, e.g., glassy transition of ligaments due to rate sensitivity (Yi et al., 2006) or microinertia (Calladine and English, 1984) may be active, occur over a typical strain-rate range of ϵ˙applied≈100​s−1\dot{\epsilon}_{\rm applied}\approx 10^{0}\,\text{s}^{-1} to 103​s−110^{3}\,\text{s}^{-1}. Third are high or ballistic-like rates, in which shock-front propagation mechanics dominate the overall response (Xi and Li, 2017; Sun et al., 2016), macroscopic force equilibrium no longer exists, and internal gas viscosity may play a role (Mills and Lyn, 2002). At high rates, the incident velocity, rather than an effective strain rate, is often used as the rate-defining metric since strain rate is highly nonuniform across a shock front. For sake of comparison, these rates roughly correspond to ϵ˙applied≈103​s−1\dot{\epsilon}_{\rm applied}\approx 10^{3}\,\text{s}^{-1} to 107​s−110^{7}\,\text{s}^{-1} and higher (Ma et al., 2009). Here, we focus on the low- and intermediate-rate, non-equilibrium response of three densities of a highly rate-sensitive, polyurethane-based impact protection foam. This follows upon our study of the quasistatic response of this material, in which we described a hyperelastic constitutive model that captures the nonlinear stress–strain and lateral–axial strain response in compression and tension that remains predictive under multi-modal loading states (Landauer et al., 2019), and upon our extension of this model to capture finite-strain viscoelasticity of a closed-cell foam (Li et al., 2022).

papers.title: Spectroscopic Signatures of Polaronic Density Wave Fluctuations in Superconducting Bismuthates
papers.abstract: The bismuthate high-temperature superconductors have been identified as potential bipolaron systems, where hole pairs are bound to local breathing distortions of the BiO$_6$ octahedra in their metallic phase. However, obtaining definitive evidence for these quasiparticles and their excitations remains challenging. Here, we report on periodic modulations of the spectral intensities and scattering rates of quasiparticles on the Fermi surfaces of doped bismuthates Ba$_{1-x}$K$_x$BiO$_3$ and BaPb$_{1-y}$Bi$_y$O$_3$, which are reminiscent of ``hot spot'' patterns that have been observed in cuprate superconductors. We show that these features can be well described by a model where electrons couple to fluctuating density wave modulations with short-range coherence along a $(\pi,\pi,\pi)$-oriented wavevector. The results are consistent with the existence of a two-component fluid where unpaired electrons interact with a fluctuating density wave created by residual bipolarons and their breathing distortions of the BiO$_6$ octahedra.

Unconventional forms of high-temperature (high-TcT_{\mathrm{c}}) superconductivity often arise in proximity to long-range ordered “parent” phases. For example, superconductivity emerges from doping an antiferromagnetic insulating state in the cuprates [23, 39, 17], doping a spin-density-wave state in the Fe-based superconductors [41, 39], and doping a charge-density-wave (CDW) in the bismuthates [40] and antimonates [20]. A key question for understanding the pairing mechanism in these materials is how the parent ordered phase relates to the resulting superconducting state. In particular, one needs to identify and quantify the strength of coupling to persistent fluctuations of the underlying parent order when the system is doped.

papers.title: Stochastic Optimization with Network Distribution Dynamics via Local Jacobian Approximation
papers.abstract: Network systems feature complex interactions among agents, whereby local decisions can influence the state distributions observed by other agents through coupled network dynamics. Such endogenous distribution shifts across large-scale networks pose significant challenges and call for distributed and adaptive decision-making pipelines. To address these challenges and collectively optimize a steady-state performance objective, we propose a distributed network-aware decision-response (D-NAD) gradient algorithm. This algorithm enables each agent to approximate network-response sensitivity using only local information (i.e., the Jacobians of local dynamics and objectives) and neighborhood communication. We establish a non-asymptotic closed-loop convergence guarantee and quantify the impact of the Jacobian approximation errors therein. Numerical experiments on a semi-synthetic networked electric-vehicle price--demand problem demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.

Such a feedback phenomenon arises in many practical scenarios, including strategic classification [3, 4], recommendation systems [5, 6], and dynamic pricing [7, 8], where players with market power impact the demand distribution through their pricing decisions. In these settings, decision-makers (a centralized entity or multiple interdependent agents) cause endogenous distribution shifts, which in turn affect future problems and subsequent decisions.

papers.title: A 3D Simulator for Passive SPAD Imaging
papers.abstract: Passive single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) cameras provide short-exposure observations for low-light perception, but collecting task annotations for these sensors remains difficult, and annotated datasets are scarce. We present a 3D simulation pipeline that generates realistic photon detections together with camera-motion and semantic labels, enabling perception models to be trained on synthetic SPAD observations and applied directly to real-world data. The pipeline couples controllable scene geometry and motion with a sensor-informed observation model that accounts for photon shot noise, dark counts, and spatial crosstalk. We evaluate the pipeline through calibrated photon-count comparisons and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer across three downstream perception tasks. We show that classifiers trained only on synthetic SPAD data achieve high accuracy on real low-light recordings at illumination levels less than 2 lux, without real-data fine-tuning. Similarly, we apply models trained entirely on simulated camera sweeps to real-world camera-rotation estimation and achieve mean absolute rotation errors of less than 1 degree on real 20-degree and 30-degree sweeps at 0.5 and 5.0 lux, when deployed zero-shot. We additionally train semantic segmentation models on synthetic data with automatically generated dense labels and perform direct inference on real-world low-light recordings; the results further demonstrate the usefulness of synthetic dense supervision for real low-light perception. Our simulator thus provides a practical source of annotated training data for real SPAD perception.

papers.title: Azimuthally Resolved Energy Dissipation Rates in the Impingement Zone of Equal Free Impinging Liquid Jets: A Three-Dimensional Model
papers.abstract: When two equal liquid jets collide, they form a thin sheet of liquid and lose some of their incoming kinetic energy (doi:10.1615/AtomizSpr.2025056396). Calculating the energy dissipation rate per unit mass requires estimating the volume of the region where the collision takes place. This paper develops a three-dimensional model of that region and uses it to calculate how the energy dissipation rate varies with angular position within the collision region. The model assumes that the thickness of the collision region varies linearly along each radial line from the stagnation point to its outer boundary. Combining the resulting volume with the kinetic energy lost during the collision provides equations for both the overall energy dissipation rate and the rate averaged over each narrow angular portion of the collision region (local energy dissipation rate). For equal jets with uniform inlet velocity profiles, the model predicts substantial differences in energy dissipation rate with angular position, even when the incoming jets and the resulting sheet have uniform mean velocities. The model also reproduces expected theoretical limits, including a cylindrical collision region for directly opposed jets. Preliminary micromixing results are consistent with the predicted variation, although independent validation of the assumed collision-region geometry and the location of energy dissipation is still needed.

papers.title: Superconductivity from a Cooper surface instability in a nodal Bose metal
papers.abstract: In underdoped cuprates, the superconducting gap is largest where low-energy electron spectral weight is already depleted above the transition. How can a weak attraction drive superconductivity when the one-electron density of states vanishes? In a momentum-space \(t\)--\(J\) model, the exactly solvable normal state is a nodal Bose metal with four one-electron nodes. Along two contours called Cooper surfaces, adding or removing a spin-singlet pair of electrons with opposite momenta costs no energy. The resulting logarithmic divergence of the pair susceptibility allows an arbitrarily weak pair-transfer attraction to stabilize a correlated nodal \(d\)-wave superconductor. Spin-resolved coincidence photoemission could test this pairing mechanism by resolving two zero-energy pair-removal ridges above the transition and a third along the underlying Luttinger surface below it.

How does a doped Mott insulator become a high-temperature superconductor when one-electron spectral weight is already depleted near the antinodes, where the gap below the superconducting (SC) transition is largest (1, 2)? In underdoped cuprates, angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) finds an antinodal pseudogap above the transition temperature TcT_{c}, leaving Fermi arcs of low-energy spectral weight near the nodes (3, 4, 5, 6, 7). Scanning tunneling microscopy (STM) indicates that the pseudogap evolves continuously into the SC gap on cooling through TcT_{c} (8). Local shot-noise measurements deep in the SC state find a pairing scale that tracks the pseudogap energy (9). Below TcT_{c}, ARPES and electronic Raman scattering distinguish a near-nodal pairing scale from an antinodal gap that can grow as TcT_{c} falls (10, 11, 12, 13). The SC coherence peak is weakest near the antinodes, where the pseudogap depletes the most spectral weight (14). Specific heat measurements reveal a loss of electronic entropy on entering the pseudogap regime (15). Can electrons with opposite momenta form a low-energy Cooper pair where exciting either electron costs finite energy?

papers.title: SentryWard: Formal Verification of Warp-Specialized GPU Kernels
papers.abstract:
Modern GPU kernels overlap asynchronous data movement, computation on general-purpose cores (e.g., CUDA cores), and computation on specialized cores (e.g., tensor cores) using warp specialization. These asynchronous-overlap optimizations introduce complex synchronization requirements, where incorrect ordering of asynchronous operations can lead to data races, premature resource reuse, and incorrect results. Testing alone cannot guarantee correctness because such errors are nondeterministic and may only manifest in rare execution schedules, and existing GPU formal verification techniques have limited support for warp-specialized kernels.
  We present SentryWard, a framework for formally verifying warp-specialized GPU kernels. SentryWard integrates synchronization verification, data-race and resource-lifetime analysis, and functional equivalence checking. The key idea is to establish that synchronization induces the same ordering constraints across all possible execution schedules. SentryWard extends this well-synchronization analysis to modern GPU barriers with asynchronous transaction tracking and derives a schedule-independent happens-before graph. It then uses this graph to verify memory safety and construct symbolic output expressions for functional equivalence checking. While SentryWard generally assumes tensor shapes and kernel launch configurations are given and unrolls loops, it uses compact representations of repeated structures across threads and tensor computations to improve scalability. SentryWard is publicly available at https://github.com/gpu-verifier/sentryward.

papers.title: X-Matte: VAE-Free Pixel-Space Flow Matching for Single-Step Image Matting
papers.abstract: Pre-trained generative models offer rich visual priors for image matting, but their adaptation often relies on variational autoencoders (VAEs), whose spatial compression can degrade fine alpha details and introduce additional inference overhead. To address these limitations, we propose X-Matte, a VAE-free pixel-space flow matching framework for single-step image matting. By eliminating latent compression, X-Matte formulates the RGB-to-alpha transition as a continuous flow directly in pixel space. We adopt trajectory-wide x-prediction with transition-aware alpha supervision, enabling the model to learn from intermediate states while directly predicting the target alpha matte in a single forward pass. This design avoids both VAE encoding and decoding and iterative sampling. Extensive experiments demonstrate performance competitive with state-of-the-art trimap-free matting methods on P3M benchmarks, together with promising zero-shot generalization to RWP-636 and AIM-500. Moreover, X-Matte achieves up to a 9.4x inference speedup over a constructed single-step latent counterpart at high resolution, demonstrating the effectiveness of VAE-free pixel-space modeling for accurate and efficient image matting.

papers.intro:
Image matting estimates the continuous per-pixel opacity of foreground objects, known as the alpha matte [14, 3, 15]. Unlike binary segmentation, matting requires accurate recovery of fine structures and semi-transparent boundaries, such as hair and fur, where small prediction errors can produce visible artifacts in image compositing [28, 5]. Recent discriminative methods, ranging from specialized CNNs to Vision Transformers (ViTs), commonly formulate matting as dense pixel-wise regression [45, 12, 6]. Despite their strong performance, generalization to unseen foreground objects and imaging conditions remains challenging [16, 46]. Pre-trained generative models offer a promising alternative by providing rich visual priors learned from large-scale image data. The key challenge is therefore how to adapt these priors to pixel-accurate alpha estimation without sacrificing fine structures or inference efficiency.

The key challenge is therefore how to adapt these priors to pixel-accurate alpha estimation without sacrificing fine structures or inference efficiency.

Existing generative matting methods, many of which build on Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) [31], largely fall into two paradigms. Iterative latent generation encodes alpha mattes into the latent space of a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) [8, 38] and commonly recovers them through iterative noise-to-alpha sampling [33, 38]. However, such VAEs are designed for natural RGB images rather than pixel-accurate alpha estimation, and their compression can discard spatial information to which fine structures and semi-transparent boundaries are particularly sensitive, while iterative sampling adds substantial overhead to what is ultimately a deterministic prediction. Fixed-timestep regression instead applies a pre-trained diffusion backbone at a fixed timestep for efficient dense prediction [42, 41, 34, 52], often with task-specific decoders that recover fine details from latent features [42, 41]. However, this paradigm still relies on compressed representations, incurs VAE overhead at high resolutions, and does not explicitly exploit supervision along a task-specific RGB-to-alpha trajectory. Both paradigms further face a resolution gap, as generative backbones are typically pre-trained at fixed resolutions far below those required for high-fidelity matting.

papers.title: End-to-End Image-Goal Navigation for Agile Quadrotors via Recurrent State Distillation
papers.abstract: Image-goal navigation asks a robot to reach the viewpoint of a target photograph without a map or goal pose. In three dimensions, this requires not only recognizing the goal but also estimating 3D displacement and generating continuous control actions to approach and settle at the target view. This is difficult because the same visual difference between current and goal image can require very different actions depending on the robot's velocity, yet monocular images alone reveal neither metric scale nor body motion. As a result, existing image-goal policies are limited to planar action spaces and rely on a state estimator for flight control. Policies that map directly from images to low-level control commands have been demonstrated for agile flight, but not toward goal images in unseen environments. We present the first image-goal navigation policy that directly commands thrust and angular rates for agile quadrotor flight in unseen 3D environments, without relying on state estimation (e.g., SLAM, VO, or SfM) or a separate velocity controller. We train a recurrent vision-based policy through a four-stage pipeline that combines geometric and motion supervision with privileged-teacher distillation and end-to-end reinforcement learning fine-tuning. On 1000 held-out flights in unseen environments, the policy achieves an 82.3% success rate with a mean terminal position error of 0.10m across successful flights. papers.title: The cost of being seen as AI in group bargaining
papers.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in collective decision-making, people's perceptions of AI may shape who reaches agreement and what they receive. We studied this in a repeated three-player majoritarian bargaining game with 2,234 participants. Players saw each opponent identified as Human or AI. The instructions described AI as acting either independently or on behalf of a human. Human participants made every decision. In mixed groups, players presented as AI received fewer points in opening offers, were included in fewer final agreements and earned about 18% less per round than those presented as Human. Smaller payoffs in agreements that included them accounted for most of the observed gap. Further analysis found a payoff gap even when all three players agreed. Social perceptions of AI may therefore shape who benefits from collective decisions, with potential costs for people represented by AI.

Proposers often secure a larger share, and a deal can leave some participants with nothing [5, 2]. As AI systems take on roles in these decisions, both as agents and as delegates, the way others perceive them may affect who gets included and what they receive. Whether a counterpart is taken to be human or AI can shape expectations about their behaviour, agency and standing in the group [33, 37].

In experimental games, people tend to be less prosocial towards AI counterparts [41]. Proposed explanations include greater self-interest, a willingness to exploit cooperative AI, and weaker reciprocity [25, 20, 38]. In some settings, describing the same behaviour as AI-generated reduces cooperation or trust and changes judgements of fairness [16, 11]. Fair behaviour, shared cooperative norms, and the information available about individual partners can lessen these differences [40, 26, 24]. People also judge similar offers differently depending on who made them and attribute different mental states to AI and human counterparts [10, 27, 23, 35, 32]. These studies point to several reasons why being seen as AI or represented by AI could matter in bargaining.

papers.title: Embodied Lower-limb Exoskeleton Assistance: Survey, Challenges, and Perspectives
papers.abstract: Over the past decade, artificial intelligence (AI) has enabled lower-limb exoskeletons to adapt to complex tasks and assist diverse users. Existing reviews, however, are organized around mechanical design, control strategies, or individual AI algorithms, and provide little systematic coverage of embodied lower-limb exoskeletons and their enabling technologies. This review defines embodied lower-limb exoskeletons and organizes the literature around four dimensions: structural self-adaptation, task adaptation, user-specific adaptation, and control self-regulation. In each dimension, state-of-the-art and representative studies are classified and discussed in terms of the associated challenges, including lightweight and compliant design, data acquisition and fusion, optimization of complex policies, and robust, compliant control. The review then identifies the principal limitations of current research and outlines future directions along these dimensions. From an embodied perspective, this review sets out the closed-loop relationship among mechanical structure, sensing, and control as a framework for analyzing lower-limb exoskeleton performance and for research on human-robot interaction. The directions it identifies point toward lightweight, comfortable, and practical physical assistance.
papers.intro:
Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have improved the ability of lower-limb exoskeletons to adapt to unstructured and dynamic environments, offering new opportunities to enhance walking ability in older adults and reduce the risk of joint injury [1, 2]. However, exoskeletons operate within tightly coupled human–robot–environment systems, where assistance strategies must continually adapt to changes in the wearer’s movement, assistance needs, and environmental conditions [3, 4]. These interdependencies make reliable and effective adaptive assistance challenging. To address these challenges, a growing body of research over the past five years has incorporated AI into exoskeleton systems to improve autonomous perception and decision-making, with the aim of improving the effectiveness of assistance [5, 6].

However, exoskeletons operate within tightly coupled human–robot–environment systems, where assistance strategies must continually adapt to changes in the wearer’s movement, assistance needs, and environmental conditions [3, 4]. These interdependencies make reliable and effective adaptive assistance challenging. To address these challenges, a growing body of research over the past five years has incorporated AI into exoskeleton systems to improve autonomous perception and decision-making, with the aim of improving the effectiveness of assistance [5, 6].

An embodied exoskeleton is a human-centered wearable intelligent agent capable of perception, decision-making, and adaptation to its operating context. In contrast to adaptive assistance, which adjusts the assistance strategy to the wearer, the task, or the environment, embodied assistance for lower-limb exoskeletons starts from the coupling among the human, the exoskeleton, and the environment. Mechanical structure, sensing, and control are brought into a single closed loop and act jointly: the exoskeleton integrates information about human–exoskeleton states, environmental conditions, and task requirements, and optimizes assistance torque profiles. The objective is efficient, comfortable movement assistance in dynamic environments [7, 5, 8]. Because these elements share one loop, that objective requires mechanical structure, sensing, and control to be addressed jointly. These same three elements are the perspectives from which exoskeletons are studied and performance is analyzed.

The objective is efficient, comfortable movement assistance in dynamic environments [7, 5, 8]. Because these elements share one loop, that objective requires mechanical structure, sensing, and control to be addressed jointly. These same three elements are the perspectives from which exoskeletons are studied and performance is analyzed.

Achieving the above assistance objective, however, presents four key challenges. First, the mechanical structure must be lightweight, conform to human anatomy, and accommodate complex lower-limb joint kinematics to minimize additional interaction constraints and ensure wearing comfort [9, 10]. Second, diverse assistance tasks and changing environments require assistance strategies that adapt to task demands and operating conditions [1, 3]. Third, differences in body morphology, physical capabilities, and gait characteristics necessitate assistance tailored to individual users [11, 8]. Finally, the bidirectional coupling between human and exoskeleton motion creates interdependencies between state perception and assistance control, requiring continuous optimization of assistance torques to balance assistance effectiveness and interaction comfort [4, 12]. Accordingly, the core challenges for embodied lower-limb exoskeletons can be categorized into four areas: structural self-adaptation, task adaptation, user-specific adaptation, and control self-regulation.

Accordingly, the core challenges for embodied lower-limb exoskeletons can be categorized into four areas: structural self-adaptation, task adaptation, user-specific adaptation, and control self-regulation.

To address these core challenges, existing research has pursued four complementary directions: joint self-alignment [10, 13] and compliant interaction [14, 9] to improve structural self-adaptation; multimodal information fusion [1, 5] and musculoskeletal-informed policy learning [3, 15] to support task adaptation; human-in-the-loop optimization [7, 11, 16] and cross-subject transfer learning [17, 8] to enable user-specific adaptation; and control compensation [18, 19] and human–exoskeleton control optimization [20, 4] to improve assistance control. From a system architecture perspective, structural self-adaptation primarily concerns the physical design of the exoskeleton, task adaptation and user-specific adaptation primarily concern the high-level controller, and control self-regulation primarily concerns the low-level controller. These components serve as the “body,” “brain,” and “cerebellum” of the embodied system, respectively [21]. Functionally, an embodied lower-limb exoskeleton forms a closed-loop system that integrates structural design, perception and representation, and control optimization. These interdependent elements work together to support efficient and comfortable movement assistance in complex, dynamic environments.

Existing reviews of lower-limb exoskeletons have established a systematic knowledge base covering mechanical design, perception and control, and the evaluation of assistive performance. For mechanical design, early reviews surveyed device evolution and key technologies, including actuation, sensing, power supply, and control [22, 23], and later reviews examined compliant mechanisms, attachment interfaces, bio-inspired structures, and human–robot interaction design [24, 25]. For perception and control, reviews of control and AI methods have addressed functional hierarchies, movement-intention recognition, user-specific parameter optimization, and reinforcement learning [26, 27, 28, 29], with increasing attention to gait planning that adapts to environmental conditions and to end-to-end, task-agnostic control [30, 2]. For evaluation, related reviews have broadened assistive outcomes to safety, embodiment, and physiological and clinical needs [31, 32, 33]. Together, these reviews provide a foundation for classifying technologies and understanding individual methods.

For mechanical design, early reviews surveyed device evolution and key technologies, including actuation, sensing, power supply, and control [22, 23], and later reviews examined compliant mechanisms, attachment interfaces, bio-inspired structures, and human–robot interaction design [24, 25]. For perception and control, reviews of control and AI methods have addressed functional hierarchies, movement-intention recognition, user-specific parameter optimization, and reinforcement learning [26, 27, 28, 29], with increasing attention to gait planning that adapts to environmental conditions and to end-to-end, task-agnostic control [30, 2]. For evaluation, related reviews have broadened assistive outcomes to safety, embodiment, and physiological and clinical needs [31, 32, 33]. Together, these reviews provide a foundation for classifying technologies and understanding individual methods.

However, this foundation has three limitations. First, because the reviews are organized by device type, functional module, or algorithm category, they offer limited analysis of how mechanical structure, sensing, algorithms, and control jointly support assistance through closed-loop interactions among the human, the exoskeleton, and the environment [2]. Second, reviews that adopt an embodied perspective on perception, interaction, and cognition remain focused on the functions of individual technical modules, so perception, interaction, and cognition are not connected through that loop [34, 35]. Third, the integration of AI into the loop has yet to be treated systematically, leaving the mechanisms for wearer comfort, changing task demands, individual differences, and the coupling between perception and control unclear. This review examines those mechanisms as four interrelated dimensions: structural self-adaptation, task adaptation, user-specific adaptation, and control self-regulation, together with their interdependencies and key challenges. In doing so, it provides a system-level perspective on personalized and comfortable assistance in complex, dynamic environments.

papers.title: Existence of odd-frequency free boundary points in the Signorini problem
papers.abstract: Up to a lower-dimensional set, the free boundary of the Signorini problem consists of points with frequency that is half-integer, even (at zero density points), or odd (at full density points). Surprisingly, despite extensive work on the structure and regularity of each of these sets, the existence of odd-frequency free boundary points has remained open. In this paper, we construct a solution with a free boundary point of frequency 3.

papers.intro:
The Signorini problem, also known as the thin (or boundary) obstacle problem, is a classical free boundary problem that goes back to the work of Signorini in linear elasticity [Sig33, Sig59]: it describes the equilibrium of an elastic body resting on a rigid frictionless surface, where the region of contact is not known beforehand; see also [KO88]. Its scalar version also arises in models of semipermeable membranes and boundary heat control [DL76] and, as the local formulation of the obstacle problem for the half-Laplacian [Sil07, CS07], in optimal stopping and option pricing [Mer76, CT04]. The regularity theory for the problem has been widely studied, with remarkable progress in recent years; see [Caf79, AC04, ACS08, GP09, PSU12, KPS15, DS16, FS18, CSV20, FJ21, FR21, SY22, FT23, FS24, EY24, CC24, FY25, Kit26] and references therein, as well as the survey [Fer22].

papers.title: Limit laws for Siegel theta sums
papers.abstract: Siegel theta sums are exponential sums over the integer lattice whose phases are determined by a quadratic form. For a random choice of quadratic form, we prove a limit law for the modulus of the normalised sum as the summation range tends to infinity. The limiting distribution depends on the space from which the quadratic form is sampled. We prove precise heavy-tail asymptotics for random sampling from (a) the full space of quadratic forms and (b) the space of diagonal forms. This study extends classic results by Jurkat and Van Horne for one-variable theta sums and by G\"otze and Gordin for theta series on Siegel half-spaces. Our approach uses the Shale--Weil representation of the metaplectic group and the ergodic theory of unipotent flows.

papers.title: WorldInteract: Controllable Streaming Video Generation for Multi-Material Interactions
papers.abstract: Video world models aim to create interactive physical worlds that capture how diverse materials move and interact. Yet material-dependent dynamics remain underexplored in controllable video generation, limiting reliable control in scenes with different materials. We present WorldInteract, a streaming video generation framework that decomposes cross-material interaction into material-dependent behavior generation and contact response computation. External pushes and contact impulses are expressed through a shared velocity-increment interface, allowing material behaviors learned from interaction-free videos to be reused in interacting scenes. A physics controller predicts contacts and computes velocity increments from estimated masses and restitution coefficients, while a causal generator executes these increments using learned material behaviors. This separation enables cross-material interaction without supervised contact videos spanning diverse material pairings and contact configurations. We train the generator on 30k simulated interaction-free videos spanning 22 material classes and introduce Material-Aware RL, using verifiable physical rewards to refine material behavior and control execution. WorldInteract substantially outperforms state-of-the-art methods on Physics-IQ and delivers more reliable push control on real-world images.

papers.intro:
Interactive video world models aim to respond to user actions with physically plausible outcomes, yet the same push can roll a ball, slide a box, or scatter a pile of sand. Mass and friction affect how far an object travels after a push; mass and restitution govern how contact changes the motion of both objects. Reliable control therefore requires modeling both material behavior, which describes how an object moves under an applied velocity change, and contact response, which determines how momentum is exchanged when objects collide. Their combination governs cross-material interactions. Ignoring either component makes control unreliable when materials or contact partners change.

Their combination governs cross-material interactions. Ignoring either component makes control unreliable when materials or contact partners change.

Recent work establishes important foundations for physical control. Recent work establishes important foundations for physical control. Force Prompting [10] and PhysCtrl [34] learn force control from simulated data, while Goal Force [11] extends video generation to goals involving object interactions. StreamForce [35] and PhysStream [7] support updated controls during streaming generation. However, systematic modeling of material behavior and cross-material interaction remains underexplored. Learning these behaviors directly from contact videos creates a coverage problem. Adding a material introduces new pairings with existing materials, even if its individual behavior is already represented. Each pairing can also appear under different contact configurations. papers.title: PersonaFactory: Stylistic User Prompt Augmentation with Synthetic Persona Bank
papers.abstract: Large language models increasingly replace real people in the AI development pipeline, as they are used to generate training dialogues at scale and to drive alignment and evaluation. However, out-of-the-box models produce monolingual and stylistically flat texts as synthetic user prompts, failing to replicate the real user-AI communication mechanics. We present PersonaFactory, an end-to-end pipeline that generates detailed user personas and uses them to augment existing user prompts from their point of view, producing a bank of over 740000 structured synthetic personas detailing their background and communication behaviors, and a corpus of roughly 1.24 million persona-styled synthetic conversations spanning 85 languages. We evaluate the effect of personal features on style adoption and intent preservation, using an LLM-judge and heuristic metrics to assess augmentation fidelity together with the downstream impact on assistant persona control through training data. Results show that our structured, attribute-based style representation enables per-axis control and better intent preservation at comparable style fidelity than free-text persona descriptions used in existing methods. A human expert evaluation found the augmented conversations plausible, with favorable ratings for intent preservation, style naturalness, and multilingual authenticity. Finally, PersonaFactory conversations achieve comparable performance to original training data on capability benchmarks, are preferred on real user prompts at equal reply length, and adapt their reply style more closely to users without explicit steering.
papers.intro:
Conversational datasets are integral to large language model development, shaping how models understand users’ intents and behave in diverse settings. Existing open-source datasets largely focus on LLM-generated synthetic setups because human-based data scaling is cost- and time-intensive. Therefore, AI is now used in all stages of training other models on real-life interaction with human users. This includes user questions and assistant responses, judging the quality of such QA pairs, and evaluating model effectiveness in chat interaction settings. However, this scalability comes at the cost of authenticity and diversity: the raw material for most simulated users is the same narrow band of text: instruction-tuning corpora written in a homogeneous, well-punctuated, standard-register “assistant/user” voice. The result is one averaged user who is monolingual, verbose and stylistically uniform, a narrow reflection of real users across cultures, languages and behaviors. Such datasets, widely used to train open models, lack non-native phrasing, code-switching, terse or lowercase typing, and dialectal variation, giving a narrow picture of how users actually communicate with AI in real-life conditions.

When simulating conversations, there are two common design pitfalls: (1) methods that simulate personalized conversations from scratch condition on short persona descriptions and underuse the background details that most shape content and style; (2) rewriting existing conversations preserves the original intent but changes little in how the text reads. Grounding conversations between a user and the AI assistant in a pre-generated persona presents an opportunity to address this, with related existing work on synthetic persona generation; however, persona descriptions are usually limited to a 2–5 short sentence summary or lack information about behavior in a chatbot setting. Compressing the user’s full background into a short description may change what the user is saying, but not how, as it does not focus on their writing style.

We present PersonaFactory, a pipeline to target these particular issues in synthetic persona and chat data generation (Figure 1). The key idea is to keep the original dialogue trajectory from an existing real or synthetic conversation, but re-simulate the user side under a structured synthetic persona: the request stays fixed, while the register, typing style, and language behavior match those of a simulated user drawn from a large, controllable population. The persona description covers not only basic information such as age, origin, occupation, and a short biography, but also writing style, linguistic quirks, digital fluency and AI stance, painting a much richer background on how the persona would interact with an AI model. Since the intervention is a constrained rewrite of existing user turns (real WildChat user logs and synthetic UltraChat and Nemotron seeds) rather than free generation, it keeps the original requests and dialogue trajectories while gaining the diversity and authenticity from the user’s side.

To improve the fidelity of user simulation, we introduce three components, which also represent the principal contributions of this paper:

1. A structured user-simulator profile schema and a bank of over 740000 profiles (Section 3). Each profile has a background layer (geography, occupation, education, age, native language, AI stance, digital fluency) and a style layer (capitalization, punctuation, emoji, typos, abbreviation habits, code-switching, quirks, and a verbatim example message). Profiles are grounded on a manually-curated country, sub-region, and occupation grid with region-decoupled occupations and sector-coherent fluency, generated by three open LLMs and screened by an independent judge. The pipeline can also extend existing persona banks with style axis information, improving the quality of downstream seeded data. 2. 1.2M persona-augmented conversations from a grounded simulation pipeline (Section 4) that (i) conservatively matches a language- and script-compatible persona to each log, refusing to assign a persona rather than risk a language mismatch; (ii) rewrites user turns to preserve the exact request, constraints, and language while adopting persona style; and (iii) regenerates assistant turns with next-turn continuity supervision, using the real follow-up user message as weak supervision that the simulated turn stays on-trajectory, followed by a six-class sanity gate. 3. An intrinsic evaluation of simulation fidelity (Section 5) separating style adoption from intent preservation, with position-bias and multi-judge controls, and complemented by judge-free corpus-scale metrics (embedding similarity, edit depth, and rule-based entity and style checks). Our headline finding is that a structured per-axis style representation is preferred over a free-text style description on style fidelity, while both preserve intent equally; at matched content and length, structure keeps the request more often and reads more naturally at comparable style (Appendix D).

papers.title: Pairing Powers of Pythagorean Pairs II
papers.abstract: Let $(a,b,c)$ be a pythagorean triple, i.e., $a^2+b^2=c^2$. Then $(c,a)$ and $(c,b)$ are hypotenuse-leg pairs (hl-pairs), i.e., pairs $(c,d)$ of positive integers such that $c^2-d^2$ is a non-zero square. An hl-pair $(c,d)$ is called a pythapotent hl-pair of degree $h$ if there is a pythagorean pair $(k,l)$, which is not a multiple of the pythagorean pair $(d,\sqrt{c^2-d^2})$, such that $(c^hk,d^hl)$ is again an hl-pair. To each hl-pair $(c,d)$ and each $h\geq 1$ we assign the elliptic curve $\Gamma_{c^h,d^h}: y^2=x^3+(c^{2h}-d^{2h})x^2-c^{2h}d^{2h}x$ and show that its torsion group is $\Bbb Z/2\Bbb Z\times\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$ and that $(c,d)$ is a pythapotent hl-pair of degree $h$ if and only if $\Gamma_{c^h,d^h}$ has positive rank over $\mathbb Q$. In this case there are infinitely many such pythagorean pairs $(k,l)$, not multiples of each other. Moreover, every hl-pair is a pythapotent hl-pair of degree $1$ and a pythapotent hl-pair of degree $3$, and we give sufficient conditions for degree $2$. The two cases $(c,a)$ and $(c,b)$, where $a=m^2-n^2$ and $b=2mn$, are worked out separately.

papers.title: MERLoc: Robust Robot Localization in Dynamic Environments with Pose-Based Retrieval over 3D Gaussian Splatting References
papers.abstract: Robots operating in previously mapped spaces must localize accurately despite moving people and rearranged objects. Most localization pipelines match the query against a sparse set of captured reference images retrieved by appearance, which is brittle under scene change and repeating structures. We present MERLoc, which turns a single metric 3D Gaussian Splatting scan into a dense Functional Reference Memory. Reference views are sampled over the navigable space for the robot's morphology and sensors at a target density and rendered offline. Pre-encoding them for the chosen off-the-shelf localizer removes the reference encoder from inference. A pose-based retrieval strategy then selects references by spatial proximity and viewing direction rather than appearance, sidestepping visual ambiguities whenever a prior exists. Across one classical and four learned localizers in simulated and real dynamic scenes, pose-based retrieval matches or outperforms appearance retrieval in most cases, even when the latter is gated by the same prior. On real data, it lowers position RMSE by 15-60 % in nine of ten backend/split combinations, and the rendered memory outperforms real-image caches posed by Structure-from-Motion. The system runs onboard a Jetson Orin NX at 5 Hz, enabling a navigation policy to successfully traverse a hallway with people roaming and rearranging objects.
papers.intro:
Robots deployed in homes, hospitals, and warehouses operate in spaces that are easy to scan but rarely remain identical to those scans over time. People walk through them, objects appear, and furniture moves. While structural elements provide reliable localization cues, these dynamic changes introduce distractors and ambiguities that degrade localization pipelines built for static scenes.

People walk through them, objects appear, and furniture moves. While structural elements provide reliable localization cues, these dynamic changes introduce distractors and ambiguities that degrade localization pipelines built for static scenes.

The dominant localization pipeline for previously mapped environments queries a sparse set of posed reference images [1]. References are posed offline by Structure-from-Motion (SfM) [2], retrieved online via appearance descriptors [3], and passed to a relative localizer. Frozen at mapping time, the reference set is limited to the captured viewpoints and can neither be densified nor adapted to a robot’s sensor suite. Furthermore, appearance-based retrieval is prone to visual aliasing, where distinct places look alike, such as repeated corridors or identical doors. Aliasing and scene changes since mapping both lead retrieval to return confidently wrong references that no relative localizer can recover from [4, 5, 6]. Recent feed-forward localizers replace the geometric solver but inherit both limitations; even when trained on dynamic scenes [7, 8, 9], most are, as we show, more sensitive than classical pipelines to aliased or changed references.

Given a pose prior, typically the previous estimate or odometry, we gate candidates within a radius and rank them by viewing-direction alignment and proximity, falling back to appearance-based matching only for initialization or recovery. papers.title: Tokenisation is not in APX
papers.abstract: In this paper, we prove that, unless P=NP, no polynomial-time algorithm can find a tokeniser whose objective is within any constant factor of the optimum, meaning that tokenisation is not in the APX complexity class. We prove this for direct and bottom-up tokenisation, under both a compression or unigram log-likelihood objectives, and for binary or larger alphabets. We further show that, even over unary alphabets, direct tokenisation is APX-hard, and thus admits no polynomial-time approximation scheme.

papers.intro:
Tokenisers are the “glasses” through which language models (LMs) see the world, converting raw text—made of bytes or characters—into sequences of tokens. They define an LM’s API costs, impact the models’ throughput, affect their performance, and directly shape output distributions (Zouhar et al., 2023; Lesci et al., 2025; Ahia et al., 2023). It is thus natural to pose the question: how should one choose a tokeniser? A recent line of research frames this question as an optimisation problem: define an objective function, and find a tokeniser that performs well on it. In fact, famous tokenisation algorithms can be seen as instantiations of this principle. BPE is a greedy algorithm for compression, iteratively merging the most frequent pair of adjacent tokens (Gage, 1994; Sennrich et al., 2016), while UnigramLM is an expectation-maximisation algorithm for log-likelihood (Kudo, 2018; Meister, 2026). Notably, these methods are purely heuristic, having no guarantees regarding their solutions’ quality.11 1 BPE, in particular, can have arbitrarily bad compression (Kozma and Voderholzer, 2026). See Yavuz et al. (2026) for an analysis of how these methods’ objective functions and optimisation algorithms interact when selecting a tokeniser.

papers.title: Enhancing Maritime Domain Awareness using Latent Space Representations
papers.abstract:
This work presents a novel application of Earth Observation (EO) embeddings for Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA) from the perspective of the geospatial foundation model TerraMind. By operating directly on compressed latent-space representations rather than on the original Sentinel-1 imagery, this approach directly addresses the data gravity bottleneck that increasingly constrains operational EO processing, in line with the objectives of the Embed2Scale project. In particular, linear and non-linear probing of compressed embeddings, latent space representations of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery, is used to detect, localise, and characterise vessels from Sentinel-1 GRD images. Vessel detection achieves a ROC-AUC of 0.95, while vessel localisation has a median error of around 300 m for vessels longer than 100 m, and vessel AIS type-code classification achieves 62% accuracy for the majority classes. The latter, however, is highly correlated with vessel length. These results reveal both the potential and current limitations of Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) when applied to fine-grained MDA understanding in real-world scenarios.
  Additionally, a new maritime remote sensing dataset is released, pairing about 2,000 Sentinel-1 images with temporally aligned AIS signals from commercial vessels. Through manual inspection, each candidate sample was verified for bounding-box quality and for consistency between the AIS-reported vessel length and the observed vessel extent, cross-checking vessel identity and location against publicly available vessel records and, where available, photographs. The dataset was made ready for use with the NeuCo-Bench neural compression benchmark framework, publicly available on HuggingFace through https://huggingface.co/datasets/embed2scale/S1-single-ship-downstream .

papers.intro:
The Copernicus programme generates over 22 terabytes of data per day [10], a volume that keeps growing and increasingly limits how quickly Earth Observation (EO) data can be transferred, stored, and processed. This bottleneck, often referred to as data gravity, is especially relevant for Maritime Domain Awareness (MDA), where the value of a detection depends on low-latency processing. Geospatial Foundation Models (GeoFMs) offer a potential way to ease this bottleneck by encoding EO imagery into compact latent-space representations that can be reused for downstream analysis. This study, developed within the Horizon Europe-funded Embed2Scale project, investigates whether core MDA tasks such as vessel detection, localisation, and characterisation can be performed directly from these representations, without sacrificing accuracy.

MDA has traditionally relied on the Automatic Identification System (AIS), which broadcasts vessel identity and position but is not mandatory for all vessels and can be deactivated or spoofed [2]. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) complements AIS by providing independent, all-weather, day-and-night observations, with Sentinel-1’s open access and short revisit time making it the standard source for operational ship detection [19]. Detection methods have evolved from statistical approaches such as Constant False Alarm Rate (CFAR) to deep learning-based object detectors, including YOLO-family architectures, which have improved both detection and classification accuracy [12, 20]; prior work applied YOLOv8 to an AIS-labelled Sentinel-1 dataset for this purpose [3]. More recently, GeoFMs such as TerraMind [15] have emerged as an alternative way to represent EO data, but their use in the maritime domain has so far been limited to feature extraction ahead of decoding or full-resolution processing. Whether MDA tasks can be performed directly within the compressed latent space itself remains largely unexplored, and is the gap this study addresses. Besides, a related limitation is the scarcity of high-quality, manually verified datasets pairing SAR imagery with AIS ground truth: existing AIS-SAR alignments are typically weakly supervised [14, 13] and rarely cross-checked against independent vessel records, which constrains both the training and the evaluation of vessel-related EO tasks. This study also addresses this gap by releasing a manually verified maritime benchmark dataset.

The vast scale and diversity of EO archives position them as a promising domain for foundation models [6]. These are well suited to settings where high-quality labelled data are scarce but large collections of unlabelled data are available. GeoFMs are therefore pretrained through self-supervision on large EO datasets to learn general representations from unlabelled imagery [26, 24, 23]. These representations can then support a wide range of downstream tasks using small labelled datasets and task-specific decoders [17, 25]. A common adaptation approach is end-to-end fine-tuning, where the backbone and a task-specific decoder are optimised jointly for each task. However, this requires repeated access to the raw imagery and repeated computation through the large backbone. A more efficient paradigm treats the GeoFM as a frozen feature extractor and reuses its intermediate latent-space representations as task-agnostic embeddings [16, 11, 8]. Each input scene is encoded once, after which lightweight models operate on the fixed representations. This reduces adaptation costs and enables compact representation stores, decentralised use, and similarity search at scale [21].

Probing provides a direct and low-cost way to assess this by training lightweight models on frozen representations [1, 4, 21]. Comparing linear and shallow non-linear probes further shows whether task-relevant information is directly accessible or requires a more expressive prediction model. In this work, latent-space representations generated by TerraMind from Sentinel-1 imagery [15] are probed to assess how well they capture vessel presence, type, size, and position.

papers.title: Predicting acute food crises and discovering actionable drivers with causal machine learning
papers.abstract: Acute food insecurity is driven by a compound of conflict, adverse climate events, displacement, and economic shocks. We enrich the open-access Harmonized Food Insecurity Dataset with driver variables (monthly, subnational, 80 countries, 2007--2024) and develop missing-data-resilient machine learning pipelines forecasting crisis occurrence at 3, 6, and 9-month lead times using both FEWS NET and, for the first time at scale, IPC/CH classifications. Pipelines, evaluated through nested cross-validation, outperform no-skill baselines by 15 to 50 percentage points in PR-AUC, with performance correlated with crisis prevalence rather than the classification system. TreeSHAP-based explainability reveals compound, geography-specific predictive signal profiles, with three recurrent forecasting archetypes. Comparing predictive importance against doubly robust causal estimates of actionable drivers, we find that acute conflict events, having the weakest predictive signals, emerge as primary causal drivers of crisis classification whilst agroclimatology is the sole dimension in which predictive importance and causal effect align.

papers.intro:
In 2025, 266 million people across 47 countries, nearly one in five of the analyzed population, faced high levels of acute food insecurity (AFI)[1]. Conflict, economic shocks, and climate extremes, frequently co-occurring and mutually reinforcing[1, 2], are the principal drivers, with impacts influenced by socioeconomic status, institutional resilience, and displacement[3, 4, 5]. These pressures are intensifying: conflicts are multiplying[6], global displacement has reached record levels[7], and climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events[8, 9]. Famines declared multiple times in Somalia, South Sudan, Sudan, and Gaza within the past fifteen years were ultimately products of political decisions — conflict, obstruction of aid, and governance failure — not environmental inevitability[10].

Tracking these dynamics requires timely, granular early warning that reflects the compound, multidimensional nature of the drivers themselves [11, 12]. Two compatible classification systems provide essential global monitoring: the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification/Cadre Harmonisé (IPC/CH) and the Famine Early Warning Systems Network (FEWS NET). Both use a comparable five-phase scale classification — from none or minimal food insecurity to famine — and deliver subnational assessments alongside short-term projections three to six months ahead. Yet, their methodologies differ: IPC/CH relies on a consensus-based convergence-of-evidence process, while FEWS NET draws on expert-driven scenario analysis[13, 14, 15, 16]. Global coverage remains uneven, with each system monitoring fewer than 60 countries with inconsistent frequency, limiting comparability across contexts and leaving critical gaps in early warning.

Machine learning (ML) offers a promising path toward more cost-effective, timely, and scalable food insecurity estimations[17, 18]. Recent studies span nowcasting and forecasting up to twelve months ahead at subnational level, leveraging conflict data, satellite-derived agroclimatic indicators, market prices, and food consumption surveys across multiple countries[17, 19, 20]. However, generalizability remains an ongoing challenge. Most studies are limited in geographic scope, covering only a handful to at most twenty countries, and focus exclusively on modeling the FEWS NET phases[17, 20]; IPC/CH phases, despite their centrality in humanitarian decision-making, have never been modeled at scale[19]. Furthermore, missing input data, including previous assessments, are rarely addressed, which limits these models where data are absent, delayed, or contested[21, 22, 23, 24, 25].

These limitations matter. Early warning linked to financing can trigger anticipatory action before crises escalate[26, 27, 28], yet funding for anticipatory action frameworks was only 1% of international humanitarian assistance in 2025 [29], and global humanitarian budgets are now contracting sharply[30, 31, 32, 33, 34, 35]. Two further gaps remain underaddressed. Existing ML models are rarely validated across both major classification systems simultaneously, leaving it unclear whether predictive skill is system-specific or genuinely transferable. And while explainability tools such as SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)[36] have made model predictions increasingly interpretable, translating feature importance into actionable prevention design requires causal evidence, something the food security literature has only begun to address[37, 38, 39]. Interpretability alone is also insufficient for responsible deployment[40]. Ethical early warning systems need continuous oversight, reproducibility, expert input, and risk mapping [41, 42, 43, 44]; the debate over Google’s flood model [45, 46] shows the cost of lacking them, especially in food security, where lives and billions in aid are at stake.

We address these gaps with a three-stage ML framework combining forecasting, explainability, and causal inference. By extending the Harmonized Food Insecurity Dataset (HFID) [16] with predictors across six dimensions (agroclimatology, conflict, economics, food security, disaster risk, and population exposure), we build the largest open-access food insecurity modeling dataset to date: monthly, subnational, and covering 80 countries over the period 2007–2024, with fully open code and data. In the first stage, we benchmark multiple ML pipelines — including missing-data-resilient ensemble and transformer models such as Histogram-based gradient boosting (HistXGBoost)[47, 48] and the Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN)[49] — to forecast monthly subnational AFI targets (crisis occurrence, emergency occurrence, crisis escalation) at three-, six-, and nine-month lead times under both IPC/CH and FEWS NET. This is the first study to model both systems in parallel at a global scale, evaluated through a rigorous nested cross-validation strategy combining multiple metrics, naive baseline comparisons, and statistical significance testing. In the second stage, we apply TreeSHAP-based explainability to a performance-weighted combination of both classification models, characterizing predictive signal profiles at the level of individual features and aggregated thematic dimensions, and tracking their spatial and temporal variation across countries and macro-regions. In the third stage, we estimate the Average Treatment Effect (ATE) of acute shocks on crisis probability and directly compare these causal estimates against SHAP-based feature importances. This disentangles what the model relies on for forecasting from the root causes relevant to structural intervention, a distinction with direct implications for intervention design, targeted policies and resource allocation.

papers.title: The Whitney sphere and tori as self-shrinkers
papers.abstract: We prove that the Whitney sphere in $\C^n$ is a self-shrinker for the Hamiltonian gradient flow of volume. We construct an explicit family of Lagrangian self-shrinking tori in $\C^2$ containing infinitely many pairwise noncongruent examples. We also characterize closed connected Lagrangian immersions whose Legendrian lifts lie in a Kor\'anyi sphere by showing that, up to scaling and a unitary transformation, they factor through the Whitney immersion via a diffeomorphism for $n\geq2$ and a finite covering for $n=1$.

papers.title: Evaluating Strategies for Multimodal Bidirectional Interactions between Pedestrians and AVs
papers.abstract: Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) share spaces with Vulnerable Road Users (VRUs) in encounters where driver cues are absent. This can leave people uncertain whether the vehicle has noticed them and understood their request. Existing research has studied how AVs communicate with pedestrians through external human-machine interfaces. This work investigates bidirectional multimodal VRU-AV interactions combining Augmented Reality (AR), speech, and gestures. The study follows four stages: literature synthesis of interactions, a survey with 124 participants, interaction loop implementation, and feasibility evaluation. Participants preferred AR cues that made vehicle motion or warnings explicit, high-level voice commands, and conventional gestures. Prototype measurements revealed a trade-off between faster local processing and more accurate infrastructure-assisted processing. The demonstration shows bidirectional interaction using AR wearables and vehicular communications, while leaving decision-making to the AV. Together, the results support treating AV-VRU interaction as a closed loop of intent expression, recognition, vehicle decision, and feedback.

This is particularly relevant for pedestrians, cyclists, and other vru, whose interactions with vehicles often rely on cues such as yielding behavior, driver eye contact, hand gestures, head movements, and speech [61, 67].

Most research has addressed explicit av-to-vru communication. \Acpehmi, projections, light bands, displays, and symbolic cues can communicate whether an av has detected a pedestrian, is yielding, or intends to continue moving [9, 52, 73]. These supplement implicit communication through vehicle speed, deceleration, and trajectory, which remains the most common way for road interaction. Explicit bidirectional communication becomes relevant when those cues are ambiguous or when either party needs to express a request or warning. Recent work shows that people may expect their own signals to be recognized and that pedestrian communication includes more than a binary crossing request [15, 78, 8]. A future av interaction system should, therefore, support vru-initiated input and report whether it was recognized and accepted.

papers.title: FEAST: Fair and Efficient Adaptive Sampling for Task-Free On-Policy Learning
papers.abstract: Language agents trained from self-generated experience must allocate a limited rollout budget across heterogeneous capabilities. A common strategy is to prioritize capabilities with strong current learning signals, but in on-policy learning these signals are endogenous: past allocation changes the policy and therefore the evidence available for future allocation. This can create a feedback loop in which under-trained capabilities receive increasingly fewer opportunities to improve. We formalize this effect through the Quota-Efficiency Law (QEL), which shows that allocation history can change learning efficiency even under matched capability-specific exposure. Motivated by this, we introduce FEAST, a task-free adaptive sampling framework that separates opportunity allocation from compute allocation. FEAST dynamically discovers capability clusters while preserving their learning histories, maintains continued sampling opportunities across clusters, and reserves a rollout budget for each selected cluster. Within each budget, it progressively concentrates computation on prompts with informative reward variation. Across GURU-18K and SMC, FEAST improves average performance over competitive adaptive sampling baselines under matched rollout budgets, while better preserving learning progress on weaker capabilities. Ablation studies further support the complementary roles of cross-cluster opportunity protection and within-cluster selective allocation. Code will be released upon acceptance.

papers.intro:
An agent that improves through reinforcement learning must decide where to spend its training experience. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) enables such self-evolution by allowing a language model to generate attempts, receive outcome feedback, and update its policy (Shao et al., 2024; Guo and others, 2025). As RLVR expands from mathematics to heterogeneous reasoning domains (Cheng et al., 2025; Ma et al., 2025; Akter et al., 2026), experience allocation becomes increasingly important: a fixed rollout budget must serve capabilities that differ in difficulty, current proficiency, and trainability. Moreover, predefined domain labels may not reflect the capabilities that matter to the current learner. The resulting challenge is to allocate experience where it is most needed without relying on a fixed task taxonomy.

Moreover, predefined domain labels may not reflect the capabilities that matter to the current learner. The resulting challenge is to allocate experience where it is most needed without relying on a fixed task taxonomy.

Adaptive curricula address this challenge by estimating learning utility and prioritizing promising data. Learning progress, policy advantages, and cross-domain transfer all provide useful guidance (Graves et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025; Yang et al., 2026). In on-policy learning, however, utility is not an intrinsic property of an example or capability: allocation decisions change the policy, which in turn changes the outcomes available for future learning. Recent work has begun to recognize this endogenous nonstationarity (McKenzie et al., 2026). As a result, a weak capability may show little immediate learning signal simply because it has received too few opportunities to improve. Prioritizing only the strongest observed signals can then create a feedback loop in which under-allocation produces weak evidence, and weak evidence justifies further under-allocation.

We formalize this phenomenon through the Quota–Efficiency Law (QEL), which compares allocation paths at matched exposure to a target capability. Consider two schedules that train the same capability at different frequencies. We allow the sparser schedule to run longer until both schedules have generated the same number of samples for that capability. Updates on other capabilities move the policy before later target-capability samples are collected, affecting both its current performance and the quality of its subsequent self-generated experience. QEL therefore captures a path-dependent change in learning efficiency, rather than the trivial effect of receiving fewer samples at the same training step. This observation motivates learning-opportunity fairness: weak current evidence should not permanently exclude a capability from future training. This notion does not require equal quotas. Instead, it requires continued opportunities to revisit allocation decisions as the learner evolves. At the same time, protecting a capability does not imply spending computation uniformly on all of its prompts. Some prompts are already saturated, some remain beyond the learner’s reach, and others exhibit informative variation in outcomes (Yu et al., 2025; Jiang et al., 2026). Effective allocation must therefore operate at two levels: deciding which capabilities receive learning opportunities and, within each, where additional computation is most useful.
