We introduce FEAST, a Fair and Efficient Adaptive Sampling framework for Task-free agent self-evolution. FEAST combines fairness across capability clusters with efficiency within each cluster. It discovers capability clusters from the learner’s representations and learning dynamics while maintaining fine-grained learning histories as those clusters evolve. It protects learning opportunities across evolving capability clusters and concentrates rollouts within each reserved budget, using persistent learning histories to guide both levels. • We demonstrate improvements over state-of-the-art sampling baselines under matched training and rollout budgets, both in aggregate performance and learning gains on initially weaker capabilities. Together, the ablations and observed training dynamics support protecting learning opportunities and using rollouts selectively within each cluster, confirming the contribution of each component.

papers.title: 3D CoCa v3: Contrastive Learners with Scene Graphs for Urban Scene Understanding
papers.abstract: Understanding large-scale 3D urban scenes requires representations that capture both multi-scale geometric structures and complex spatial relationships. However, existing 3D vision-language methods primarily emphasize global semantic alignment or object-level representations, leaving structured relational modeling underexplored within unified contrastive and generative frameworks. In this paper, we present 3D CoCa v3, a scene-graph-enhanced contrastive and generative framework for urban 3D scene understanding. Our framework features a Pyramid Vision Encoder for multi-scale geometric representation learning and a language-model-based decoder with question-guided caption retrieval and visual cross-attention. We further introduce MSG-based relational descriptions to enrich contrastive 3D-language alignment with structured spatial relationships. To support semantic and relational supervision, we construct City3D-9.6K, a multi-view urban vision-language dataset with aligned visual-geometric observations, scene captions, and scene graphs. Extensive experiments on City-3DQA demonstrate that 3D CoCa v3 achieves 88.35% and 64.79% overall top-1 accuracy on the sentence-wise and city-wise splits, surpassing 3D CoCa v2 by 20.88 and 3.57 percentage points, respectively. Furthermore, 3D CoCa v3 achieves the best performance on GeoEval3D, demonstrating its effectiveness in urban spatial reasoning and geometric understanding. Code is available at https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/3DCoCav3.

papers.intro:
Understanding large-scale 3D urban scenes is essential for spatial intelligence, with applications in 3D scene captioning [17], spatial reasoning [15, 18], and embodied navigation [14, 27, 13]. Compared with indoor environments, urban scenes exhibit complex geometric structures, diverse object categories, and intricate spatial relationships across multiple scales. Understanding such environments requires not only recognizing individual objects but also capturing their spatial configurations and semantic relationships. Recent advances in vision-language learning have enabled models to associate 3D observations with natural-language descriptions, supporting tasks such as question answering, visual grounding, and scene captioning. These developments underscore the importance of learning 3D representations that capture both geometric structures and spatial relationships in complex urban environments.

Existing 3D vision-language methods have evolved from task-specific understanding to unified representation learning and structured spatial reasoning. Early approaches, such as ScanQA [1], explored question answering over 3D scenes, while 3D-VLP [23] and 3D-VisTA [44] learned transferable representations through cross-modal alignment. Building upon contrastive and generative learning, 3D CoCa [16] jointly optimizes 3D-text alignment and caption generation, while 3D CoCa v2 [36] further enhances caption generalization through test-time search. Beyond semantic alignment, scene-graph-based methods [25, 42] incorporate explicit object relationships to facilitate structured spatial reasoning. Extending 3D understanding to urban environments, City-3DQA [34] introduces a city-scale question-answering benchmark and a scene-graph-enhanced reasoning framework, while 3DCity-LLM [8] explores coarse-to-fine representations for city-scale perception and understanding. Collectively, these advances establish important foundations for geometric representation learning, cross-modal alignment, and relational reasoning in 3D environments.

papers.title: MoS: Mixture-of-Modality Streaming for Low-Latency Online Video LLM Analytics over Dynamic Networks
papers.abstract: The serving model for next-generation video analytics systems is shifting from traditional task-specific vision models to general-purpose online video Large Language Models (LLMs). Online video LLMs enable flexible, contextual understanding of continuously arriving video content via natural language. However, their substantial resource requirements typically mandate cloud-based inference, making continuous video streaming from user devices necessary to keep the cloud model's context current for online interaction. This introduces significant challenges under existing dynamic and often harsh networks, degrading both accuracy and responsiveness in latency-sensitive applications. In this paper, we propose MoS, a new streaming system that adaptively streams a combination of visual and derived textual modalities over fluctuating networks to enable Pareto-optimal video LLM analytics. The key insight is to leverage the complementarity and interchangeability of different modalities, hidden in video LLM, to improve system performance. Concretely, MoS introduces adaptive anchor frame selection and incremental content tracking to enable low-latency text description generation at the device side. A joint profiler characterizes the accuracy and overhead of paired video and textual configurations, including caption input resolution and output-token budget. A stochastic optimization-based modality controller then selects modality combinations and configurations using this profile and the asynchronous latency of the two modalities to adapt to network conditions. Across 500 StreamingBench video-question pairs, 4G/5G uplink traces, and the VideoLLM-Online and DisPider backends, MoS reduces latency violations by up to 94.3% and improves accuracy by up to 60.4% relative to the evaluated streaming baselines.

papers.intro:
Driven by advancements in computer vision and the widespread adoption of networked cameras [37], real-time video analytics, which involves continuous inference over real-time video streams, is rapidly gaining traction. Traditionally, video analytics services rely on specialized vision models for fixed tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation [12, 43]. Recent general-purpose online video LLMs support diverse natural-language queries over multimodal inputs. While conventional video LLMs analyze a complete, prerecorded video before responding, online models continuously process incoming frames and maintain an evolving context [23, 5]. Some online video LLMs can further interact proactively, responding when an observed event warrants user attention rather than waiting for the video to end or for an explicit query [29]. This capability enables latency-sensitive applications such as wearable visual navigation, smart retail assistance, and robot-guided services, where responses must reflect the latest scene and arrive at the appropriate moment.

MoS targets the recurring operating regime shared by these deployments rather than every video workload: a battery-powered or embedded camera continuously observes a scene, queries arrive online, uplink capacity varies at sub-minute time scales, and a substantially larger cloud model provides the final answer. This regime also appears in remote inspection, body-worn assistance, and field robotics, where transmitting every high-quality frame is expensive but discarding the visual stream entirely is unsafe for fine-grained questions. Our claim is therefore scoped to interactive edge–cloud video LLM services with constrained uplinks; offline batch understanding and fixed-camera deployments with provisioned wired links are outside the intended scope.

This regime also appears in remote inspection, body-worn assistance, and field robotics, where transmitting every high-quality frame is expensive but discarding the visual stream entirely is unsafe for fine-grained questions. Our claim is therefore scoped to interactive edge–cloud video LLM services with constrained uplinks; offline batch understanding and fixed-camera deployments with provisioned wired links are outside the intended scope.

Due to the high computational demands of running video LLMs, these services are typically hosted on remote servers or rely on cloud APIs, such as OpenAI’s advanced voice and video platform, to infer results [26]. To maintain current visual context for online queries and proactive responses, video frames must be transmitted continuously to the cloud for processing, making end-to-end system performance highly sensitive to fluctuations in network bandwidth. As shown in Fig. 1 (a), when the network is constrained, maintaining high video quality to preserve analytics accuracy often results in significant latency. Conversely, reducing video quality to lower network latency via existing approaches such as adaptive streaming [43], region-aware encoding [34], and frame filtering [15] inevitably compromises accuracy.

From a system perspective, different modalities complement each other and offer distinct and synergistic benefits for accuracy. For example, the video modality provides rich, fine-grained visual context but incurs high computational overhead. In contrast, the text modality (e.g., compact summaries of objects and events) is faster to process and more focused, yet lacks global scene understanding. When combined, they can answer a broader range of queries more accurately and efficiently. On the other hand, different modalities demonstrate different resilience to network variations and offer partial interchangeability. When bandwidth is insufficient, textual descriptions can replace video to deliver certain semantic information, although fine-grained visual details may be lost.

This insight motivates us to propose a new streaming paradigm, named Mixture-of-Modality (MoM) streaming. As illustrated in Fig. 1(b), MoM streaming transmits a combination of visual and textual modalities over dynamic networks. It is a model-native design that aims at exploiting the complementary and interchangeable benefits across different modalities for better system design. While the vision is promising, its systematic realization still poses several non-trivial challenges. First, how to generate informative textual captions from video streams without incurring substantial latency on edge devices? While textual content is insensitive to network dynamics and incurs minimal transmission overhead, to enable MoM streaming, video frames have to be processed on live to generate a corresponding textual description, introducing extra captioning latency. Naively captioning every frame could lead to redundant descriptions with unnecessary computation and inference latency. Adopting existing contextual video captioning techniques either relies on resource-intensive models [46, 38] or performs dense captioning on offline videos [14, 39], making them unsuitable for low-latency online streaming scenarios. Furthermore, jointly adapting two asynchronous modalities on different timelines under a single end-to-end latency SLO makes online modality selection non-trivial.

papers.title: InstructTTS-OPD: On-Policy Distillation for Multi-Objective Instruction-Following TTS
papers.abstract: Instruction-following text-to-speech (Instruct-TTS) renders a target transcript in the manner described by a free-form natural-language instruction, and a good rendition must succeed on three fronts at once: following the instruction, pronouncing the transcript correctly, and sounding natural. Reinforcement learning has become the standard way to post-train such generative models toward human preferences, and TTS systems increasingly adopt it. When the three objectives are optimized together under a single scalar reward, typically with group relative policy optimization (GRPO), training tends to be unstable: the objectives compete, and the shared update drifts toward whichever one is easiest to improve, producing a seesaw among them. We instead adapt on-policy distillation (OPD), which fuses several single-objective teachers by matching their velocity fields on the student's own rollouts. Realizing this for Instruct-TTS first calls for a sound reward on each axis, which we analyze carefully: a distilled Qwen-Omni proxy for the costly Gemini judge, dialect-free data for the WER reward, and DNSMOS in place of the language-biased UTMOS. We then train three single-objective teachers with GRPO and fuse them with OPD, routing each rollout to the instruction-following or WER teacher by its data domain and letting every rollout additionally follow the MOS teacher for quality. This lets instruction following and intelligibility improve together without a trade-off, but the quality target conflicts with instruction following, so following it additively reintroduces the seesaw. We therefore propose conflict-aware velocity fusion, which projects the quality target off the direction that opposes the primary objective before fusing, and show that it markedly reduces the instruction-following/quality trade-off. The fused model improves over scalar-reward GRPO on all three objectives at once.

Text-to-speech (TTS) has advanced to the point where the synthesized voice is often hard to tell from a real recording (Anastassiou et al., 2024; Du et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2026a; Xu et al., 2026b; Liu et al., 2026c), and attention is shifting from merely reading a transcript to controlling how it is read (Li et al., 2026a; Yang et al., 2024). Instruction-following TTS (Instruct-TTS) captures this goal: given a target transcript together with a free-form natural-language instruction, such as “read this in a trembling, sobbing voice” or “speak the following line in Cantonese, sounding impatient,” the model must render the transcript in the manner described (Guo et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024). A good rendition has to succeed on three fronts at once: it must follow the instruction (instruction following, IF), pronounce the transcript correctly (intelligibility, measured by word or character error rate, WER/CER), and sound natural (quality, measured by mean opinion score, MOS). Among the three, instruction following is primary, as it distinguishes Instruct-TTS from ordinary TTS.

The result is the familiar seesaw among the three objectives, and reweighting the scalar only shifts the balance point rather than removing the tension.

papers.title: A Computational Model of Continuous Recognition Memory for Natural Images
papers.abstract: Recognizing an image we have seen before is a basic function of human visual memory. Understanding human continuous recognition memory (CRM) can help machine vision systems predict which images people are likely to remember and generate more memorable images. It can also inform the diagnosis of memory impairments and the development of interventions to improve memory. This paper proposes the first computational model for CRM. The model captures three key components of continuous recognition memory (CRM): image encoding, memory decay, and decision making. It encodes each image as a distinct random variable in a perceptual space. As the memory of an image fades, the distribution of its random variable drifts within that space. To decide whether the current image has been seen before, the observer retrieves samples from the distributions associated with previously encoded images and compares them with the current image. Our model predicts human observers' trial-by-trial responses in CRM tasks within the variability observed across human participants. Our model is parameter efficient, requiring only four shared parameters and two parameters per observer. It can accurately predict the memorability of an image no worse than prior methods that require millions of parameters.

Fundamentally, however, existing work has focused on memorability as a property of images, with less emphasis on the memory processes of human observers: the mechanisms underlying continuous recognition memory (CRM), a fundamental aspect of memory that allows us to recognize previously seen images as we encounter new ones, remain poorly understood. Understanding these mechanisms can improve predictions of image memorability and, more importantly, help identify deficits in how people encode, store, and retrieve visual information. Identifying where these deficits arise could inform the diagnosis of memory impairments and the development of targeted interventions [3].

papers.title: Structure Preserving Iterative Solution of Linear Systems Arising in Gauss Collocation for port-Hamiltonian DAEs
papers.abstract: This work presents structure-preserving computational techniques for the pencil Pad\'e approximation arising in the numerical integration of port-Hamiltonian differential-algebraic equations (pH-DAEs) via the Gauss-Legendre schemes. We first extend the concept of the diagonal Pad\'e approximation and introduce a generalized framework characterizing the $s$-stage Gauss method. We further examine its structural properties and the role of the full orthogonalization method (FOM) in approximating the discrete solution. Building on this, we analyze the iterative approximation of the pencil Pade approximation and establish conditions on the search space in Petrov-Galerkin-type approximations which guarantee that structure-induced properties, such as dissipativity or energy preservation, are inherited by the Petrov-Galerkin approximations. In particular, we show that FOM-based Krylov subspace methods preserve these properties iterate-wise. The presented results provide a new insight into the interplay between Krylov subspace methods and energy preservation in the numerical integration of pH-DAEs. Finally, we conclude with numerical examples illustrating the convergence and the conservation of the physical properties.

papers.intro:
Structure-preserving numerical integrators are essential for the reliable simulation of physical systems governed by ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and differential-algebraic equations (DAEs), particularly when such systems possess Hamiltonian or dissipative structures. A well-established example is the implicit midpoint rule, which is of second-order for ODEs as well as for index-1 DAEs [13]. The implicit midpoint rule is structure preserving in the sense that if the differential equation is linear and Hamiltonian or dissipative—implying that the exact solution preserves energy or decreases in energy over time, respectively—the approximations computed via the implicit midpoint rule feature the same behavior independently of the step size used [8]. This observation can be generalized to ss-stage Gauss-Legendre collocation methods of which the implicit midpoint rule corresponds to the case s=1s=1. These methods have order 2​s2s in the ODE case [9], and for ODEs as well as DAEs they all feature the same structure-preservation as the implicit midpoint rule [20].

Gauss-Legendre methods are implicit. For ODEs or DAEs with a large number of unknowns it might be costly to solve the resulting linear systems exactly using a factorization and one is led to use a numerical iterative linear solver instead. The iteration can, in principle, be stopped early, namely as soon as the iterate features an accuracy compatible with the order of the method. A crucial question is then whether the iterates produced by the linear solver are structure preserving, too. Otherwise, an early stopping of the iteration would compromise the structure preserving property of the integrator.

papers.title: ReMeDi: Single-Image PBR Material Estimation via Reparameterization between Metal and Dielectric Hypotheses
papers.abstract: Physically based rendering (PBR) material estimation facilitates relighting, material editing, and 3D content creation. As the reflectance of a surface heavily depends on whether it is a metal or a dielectric, producing any map that determines albedo involves a decision on metalness, which we call the "intended metalness" of the map. Rendering maps with mismatched intended metalness yields physically implausible or misinterpreted materials. The metallic--roughness workflow makes metalness explicit and thus encourages base color to match it, but does not enforce this match, especially for automated methods directly predicting each map. Therefore, we propose ReMeDi, which enforces the match through two components. First, we reparameterize base color as a metalness-weighted blend of its two variants, estimated under the all-metal and all-dielectric hypothesis, respectively. Second, as available supervision cannot teach a single network both hypotheses at every pixel, we restrict each of two separate networks to one hypothesis, so that each variant is ensured to follow its hypothesis. Besides enforcing the match, this also improves each estimated material map. Experiments show that ReMeDi outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both material accuracy and relighting fidelity.

The specular–glossiness (SG) workflow stores diffuse albedo 𝐃\mathbf{D} and specular albedo 𝐒\mathbf{S} directly, leaving 𝝁𝐃\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{D}} and 𝝁𝐒\boldsymbol{\mu}_{\mathbf{S}} implicit and unconstrained by each other (Tab. 1, SG). papers.title: When Skills Fail to Compose: Compatibility and Retention in Language Models
papers.abstract: Skill acquisition alone does not establish a reusable skill library: task proficiency does not specify a compositional interface. Motivated by agents that acquire and refine skills, we study independently learned soft-prompt skills on frozen language models, with skill identities and execution order supplied. Across four digit-task bases and three record-editing models, mean composition accuracy in one call is at most 7.6%, compared with 88.2% to 100% over two calls that add computation and an explicit intermediate output. Neutral-insertion training improves robustness but leaves substantial interference, which block length and per-token norm alone cannot explain on two of four digit bases. Blocks of the same operation need not be interchangeable: after training next to frozen learned partners, a post hoc test on two Qwen bases shows that replacing those partners with independently learned blocks of the same operations lowers median composition accuracy from 98.0% and 95.3% to 12.7% and 0.5%, although every replacement scores at least 90% alone. Repair can improve a composition while impairing the original skill, and rehearsal improves retention while transfer remains limited on Qwen2.5-0.5B. Internal interventions constrain explanations without identifying a shared failure mechanism. These findings motivate evaluating compatibility, retention and transfer alongside acquisition when building skill libraries for self-evolving agents. Code is available at https://github.com/YanLin-Quinne/SkillCompatibility.

papers.intro:
Language models can acquire new skills as small learned parameter blocks, such as soft prompts, prefixes, new token embeddings and adapters, while the base model stays frozen (Lester et al., 2021; Li and Liang, 2021; Hewitt et al., 2026). Recent agent systems store such blocks as reusable skills, including SkillSmith (Dery et al., 2026) and LatentSkill (Yu et al., 2026a), so that a library of them can be recombined and revised as an agent’s needs change. Realising this promise requires knowing which skills work together and which earlier behaviours survive revision, and successful acquisition alone establishes neither.

The explanatory challenge is that separately learned skills still act through a shared model. Their contributions may change when other skills enter the same context or when a skill is replaced by another learned implementation. Understanding reuse therefore requires examining the relationship between skill parameters, execution context and induced behaviour. We study these dependencies in a deliberately controlled setting: soft prompts, small blocks of learned input embeddings on a frozen language model (Lester et al., 2021), trained on synthetic digit transformations and record edits whose intermediate results can be checked. The setting trades realism for control, so it tests model-level requirements that a library of learned blocks inherits rather than agent behaviour. One thesis organises the results: task proficiency does not specify a compositional interface. Two blocks that each perform the same operation alone need not be interchangeable in composition, and compatibility may depend on the particular learned instance and on the skills it runs with.

papers.title: vSFT: Learning to Verbally Tune Agents at Test Time
papers.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly improved via agentic reinforcement learning, which can be on-policy but suffers from expensive rollouts and sparse rewards, limiting its application at test time. In this paper, we present a verbally Supervised Fine-Tuning (vSFT) framework that enables the conjunction of dense feedback in natural language and weight updates at test time. Specifically, our vSFT forms a closed loop between an agent and a supervisor via a hypernetwork, in which the supervisor generates verbal supervision from the agent's failed trajectories, and the hypernetwork converts that supervision into low-rank weight updates to tune the agent. We validate that this test-time in-parameter evolving process outperforms both its in-context counterparts and prevalent reinforcement learning methods. In particular, our vSFT using Qwen3-4B outperforms GRPO and Reflexion by 8.7% and 13.9% in success rate on ALFWorld, and by 4.8% and 18.2% on WebShop, respectively. We believe that learning how to adapt a model, rather than an adapted model, offers a promising path towards more capable agents that improve themselves.
papers.intro:
Modern autonomous agents use large language models (LLMs) as policies for interactive decision-making, enabling them to plan, act, call tools, and perceive the environment over multiple turns (Yao et al., 2023). Although pretrained LLMs possess strong general-purpose capabilities, they are not natively optimized for specific agent tasks, requiring to be further adapted via post-training methods for parameters updating (Jiang et al., 2025).

Modern autonomous agents use large language models (LLMs) as policies for interactive decision-making, enabling them to plan, act, call tools, and perceive the environment over multiple turns (Yao et al., 2023). Although pretrained LLMs possess strong general-purpose capabilities, they are not natively optimized for specific agent tasks, requiring to be further adapted via post-training methods for parameters updating (Jiang et al., 2025).

Recently, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) have been widely used for post-training LLM agents (Zhang et al., 2026a; Ji et al., 2026). In particular, on-policy distillation (OPD) becomes a promising paradigm (Wang et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026). Given golden trajectories, SFT is simple and data-efficient for forcing token-level imitation across positions in parallel, however, it is vulnerable to distribution shift on unseen trajectories due to the inherent off-policy nature (Nie, 2026). Moreover, it could also be problematic to collect golden trajectories for open-world agent tasks. In contrast, RL is on-policy, evolving the agent from its own rollouts rather than imitating from a fixed trajectory dataset. Nonetheless, RL often relies on sparse rewards at trajectory level and GRPO-style methods (Shao et al., 2024; Feng et al., 2025; Chu et al., 2026) which further increase the rollout costs due to multiple sampled trajectories.

As a lightweight alternative to RL fine-tuning, Shinn et al. (2023) introduced a verbal reinforcement learning (vRL), which reinforces agents at test time through in-context reflections. Unlike post-training methods that directly update weights and thereby improve the agents essentially, however, vRL relies on in-context learning, which incurs recurring context overhead and may become less effective in long-horizon tasks.11 1 Even LLMs that have undergone instruction fine-tuning can struggle to reliably satisfy constraints specified in context (Zhang et al., 2026d). For example, prompting alone does not guarantee that generated JSON is syntactically valid (Lu et al., 2025). Similar to prior work (Zhao et al., 2025; Geng et al., 2026), we observe that, regardless of whether the reflections could help complete the task, the agent often struggles to follow them, suggesting that in-context reflections cannot reliably steer the agent’s behavior (as shown in Fig. 2). This motivates us to develop an end-to-end trainable method that learns to internalize verbal feedback into model parameters to reduce context overhead and enable more reliable behavioral adaptation.

papers.title: Probing Visual Idiosyncrasies in Text-to-Image Models
papers.abstract: Text-to-Image (T2I) models turn short text descriptions into images, and the leading models now produce images of comparable visual quality. Whether their outputs still carry model-specific characteristics matters for attribution, for model comparison beyond aggregate quality, and for evaluations that assume anonymity. We ask whether images from frontier T2I models can still be classified by source, and which visual properties make this possible. Here we show that a standard ResNet-50 identifies the source of an image among HiDream-O1-Dev, FLUX.2-dev, HunyuanImage-3.0, and Qwen-Image-2512, the four highest-ranked open-source models on the Text-to-Image Arena, with 100.00% accuracy on held-out prompts. Human participants reach only 62.61% on the pairwise version of this task, so the distinguishing cues are not visually obvious. They are also not tied to a particular classifier and survive severe image corruptions and out-of-distribution prompts. We trace them to visual idiosyncrasies at three levels. Low-level texture statistics alone let a lightweight multi-layer perceptron match ResNet-50. Object layout, depth, and albedo estimated from the images each carry a source signal. Image captions reveal model-specific preferences in style and background that the prompts never specify. A one-sentence hint about these cues raises human accuracy by 9.03 percentage points. These idiosyncrasies make source classification a tool for measuring similarity between models and between real and generated images, and they caution against assuming anonymity in human preference evaluation of T2I models.

papers.intro:
As t2i (t2i) models rapidly advance and produce images of increasingly comparable visual quality (Arena 2026), whether their outputs still carry model-specific characteristics becomes a pressing question. Prior work has shown that generated images can be attributed to their source models (Girish et al. 2021; Bui et al. 2022; Corvi et al. 2023b; Guarnera et al. 2024), and most recently that frontier t2i sources remain distinguishable across models and generation settings (Xu et al. 2025). These studies, however, treat attribution as the end goal and leave open what makes the sources distinguishable: the visual properties that systematically characterize each model remain largely unexplored. Characterizing these properties reveals how models differ beyond aggregate quality, supports model comparison and real-synthetic similarity analysis, and bears on evaluation protocols that assume model identities are hidden.

papers.title: Sharp constant in 2D critical fermionic Hardy inequality
papers.abstract: We study the large-$N$ behavior of the optimal constant $\kappa_N$ in the two-dimensional fermionic many-particle Hardy inequality \[ \sum_{i=1}^N -\Delta_i \geq \kappa_N^{(2)}\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq N}\frac{1}{|x_i-x_j|^2}, \] understood as a quadratic-form inequality on antisymmetric wave functions. We prove that \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}(\log N)\kappa_N^{(2)}=4, \] thereby proving a conjecture of Frank, Hoffmann-Ostenhof, Laptev, and Solovej. The proof combines a dyadic Fefferman-de la Llave representation of the Coulomb kernel with separate estimates for squares of low and high particle occupation. A trace inequality controls the low-occupation regime, while sums of Neumann eigenvalues yield the sharp bound in the high-occupation regime.

papers.title: line racer: Rapid Calculation of Exoplanetary Radiative Opacities
papers.abstract: Detailed studies of exoplanet and brown dwarf atmospheres rely on precise knowledge of the spectral features of possible atmospheric species. These features are a result of the interaction of different molecules and atoms with the radiation of the host star or the intrinsic thermal radiation of the object. The interaction is described by the opacity of a species, which determines how much light is absorbed at a given wavelength. The strength and shape of these opacities are very dependent on the temperature and pressure of the atmosphere, which is why they have to be calculated for a wide range of conditions. line racer is a Python package that enables computing high-resolution opacities from large molecular and atomic line lists in an effective manner. It offers users a wide range of options to customize opacity calculations to their needs and available hardware. The code is designed for efficient parallelization on multi-core and multi-node systems and can produce outputs compatible with popular atmospheric modeling and retrieval tools.

papers.title: Reconstruction of Poisson Random Measures in the Variational Framework with Applications to Jump-Driven SPDEs
papers.abstract:
We establish a reconstruction principle for Poisson random measures arising in compactness arguments for jump-driven stochastic partial differential equations. A basic difficulty in such arguments is that, after a Skorokhod-type representation, almost sure convergence of the solution processes does not by itself identify the limiting stochastic integral, since integration with respect to a compensated Poisson random measure is not a pathwise continuous functional of the solution and the noise.
  We address this problem in the variational framework of a Gelfand triple $V\hookrightarrow H\equiv H^\ast\hookrightarrow V^\ast$ for equations with locally monotone drift. Starting from a tight sequence of approximating solutions in $D([0,T];H)\cap L^\alpha(0,T;V),$ we construct, on the represented probability space, a time-homogeneous Poisson random measure with the original L\'evy intensity and compensator, compatible with the limiting filtration, such that the limiting process solves the corresponding SPDE.
  The main ingredient is a noise bridge. Together with a shifted dyadic approximation of the solution, the increments of the solution path over dyadic time cells approximate the compensated noise increments; since the time integral of the drift is continuous in $H$, no regularisation of the drift is needed. The jumps are then recovered by a measurable registration procedure, while injectivity of the jump coefficient permits reconstruction of the corresponding marks through a Borel inverse obtained from the Lusin--Suslin theorem. The reconstruction is performed simultaneously at all truncation levels; consistency of the resulting finite jump measures and a monotone patching argument yield a Poisson random measure with the full L\'evy measure. Under the injectivity assumption, no enlargement of the represented probability space is required.

papers.title: Angular dependence of the Wigner time delay upon tunnel ionization of CO
papers.abstract: We report on Wigner time delays in the strong-field ionization of carbon monoxide. Using co-rotating two-color laser fields (395 and 790 nm), we retrieve time delays that depend on the electron emission direction in the molecular frame, with variations of up to $\pm70$ as. The measured angular dependence agrees with predictions from a simple model based on molecular Ammosov-Delone-Krainov (MO-ADK) theory. Our results demonstrate that the directional dependence of electron emission times in asymmetric molecular potentials can be experimentally accessed in the strong-field regime.

papers.title: Feasibility-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for O-CU and O-DU Mapping in 6G O-RAN
papers.abstract: This paper studies the mapping of the virtual network function components (VNFCs) of the O-RAN central unit (O-CU) and O-RAN distributed unit (O-DU) onto virtual machines (VMs) in sixth-generation (6G) open radio access networks (O-RAN). The problem is formulated as a feasibility-aware sequential decision process that maximizes the number of placed VNFCs and, secondarily, favors fewer active VMs and lower residual resource wastage. Although conventional optimization techniques can solve this problem, their computational cost becomes prohibitive for larger instances or when optimization must be repeated. To address this limitation, we explore two neural reinforcement learning (RL)-based methods: a deep $Q$-network (DQN) and a double deep $Q$-network (Double DQN). Whereas DQN uses the same target network to both select and evaluate the bootstrap action, Double DQN decouples these two operations to mitigate maximization-induced overestimation. We compare both methods against six baselines: random feasible placement, first-fit, first-fit decreasing, best-fit, a resource-wastage-aware heuristic, and a time-bounded mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) solver. We conduct a controlled experimental evaluation across four problem sizes with $30$ independent instances each, together with capacity-stress, distribution-shift, and reward-ablation experiments. For the $16 \times 8$ VNFC-to-VM scenario, DQN and Double DQN achieve mean placed-VNFC fractions of $0.990$ and $0.996$, respectively. However, first-fit decreasing and the resource-wastage-aware heuristic match this placement quality with lower efficiency cost and lower decision time, whereas the MILP attains the lowest efficiency cost at a much higher runtime. The results clarify the strengths and limitations of neural placement for this static problem, without establishing superiority over conventional methods.

The evolution toward 6G (6G) wireless networks is expected to enable highly dynamic, scalable, and intelligent communication systems that support heterogeneous service requirements, including ultra-low latency, massive connectivity, and ultra-high reliability [1]. These stringent and often conflicting requirements motivate a shift from rigid, monolithic network architectures toward flexible, software-driven designs. In this context, the O-RAN (O-RAN) architecture has emerged as a key enabler of flexibility and programmability [2]: it disaggregates traditional base stations into modular, interoperable components, namely the O-CU (O-CU), O-DU (O-DU), and O-RU (O-RU), which are connected through open interfaces [3]. This functional decomposition promotes multi-vendor interoperability, can reduce deployment costs, and enables fine-grained control over NF [4]. Furthermore, when combined with virtualization and cloud-native principles, this disaggregation allows NF to be implemented as VNF and deployed on geographically distributed O-Cloud (O-Cloud) infrastructure, thereby supporting dynamic resource allocation, network slicing, and on-demand service provisioning [5].

These stringent and often conflicting requirements motivate a shift from rigid, monolithic network architectures toward flexible, software-driven designs. In this context, the O-RAN (O-RAN) architecture has emerged as a key enabler of flexibility and programmability [2]: it disaggregates traditional base stations into modular, interoperable components, namely the O-CU (O-CU), O-DU (O-DU), and O-RU (O-RU), which are connected through open interfaces [3]. This functional decomposition promotes multi-vendor interoperability, can reduce deployment costs, and enables fine-grained control over NF [4]. Furthermore, when combined with virtualization and cloud-native principles, this disaggregation allows NF to be implemented as VNF and deployed on geographically distributed O-Cloud (O-Cloud) infrastructure, thereby supporting dynamic resource allocation, network slicing, and on-demand service provisioning [5].

However, the efficient mapping of the O-CU and O-DU, as VNF, onto available VM in O-Cloud sites remains a fundamental challenge [6]. This problem is inherently complex because of the tight coupling among computational, networking, and radio resources [5] and the need to satisfy diverse performance constraints such as latency, throughput, and reliability. The challenge is further exacerbated by O-RAN slicing, where multiple coexisting slices impose heterogeneous and often conflicting requirements on a shared wireless infrastructure [6]. Each slice may demand specific QoS (QoS) guarantees, isolation levels, and resource elasticity, turning the mapping problem into a multi-objective optimization task with stringent constraints. In such environments, suboptimal mapping decisions can lead to resource fragmentation, increased end-to-end latency, SLA (SLA) violations, and limited scalability of 6G networks [7]. Underlying all of these formulations is a common core problem: deciding, under storage and compute capacity constraints, which VM should host each VNF component. This paper focuses on that core research problem.

The VNF mapping problem has been extensively investigated across various network environments, including wireless and cloud-native infrastructures, using a wide range of conventional optimization and learning-based methodologies [5]. Because VNF placement is NP-hard and subject to strict constraints on latency, resource utilization, and energy efficiency, classical heuristic and metaheuristic methods have been widely adopted to obtain good solutions at acceptable computational cost [5]. For example, ACO (ACO) has been applied to joint VNF placement and routing in SFC (SFC) deployment [8]. In ACO, artificial ants construct candidate mappings probabilistically, guided by pheromone trails that are reinforced by high-quality solutions. Mao et al. [8] combine this mechanism with online learning to adapt deployment decisions over time while balancing objectives such as cost, service delay, and load balancing.

MILP (MILP) is one of the common approaches to the VNF mapping problem, since it can yield provably optimal solutions under resource and QoS constraints. Representative works include Moens and De Turck [9], who introduced an MILP-based model for NFV (NFV) resource allocation; Bari et al. [10], who investigated ILP (ILP)-based and heuristic orchestration methods; and Mehraghdam et al. [11], who formalized the placement of VNF chains as a mixed-integer quadratically constrained program. Martín-Pérez and Bernardos [12] extended the problem to multiple administrative domains, proposing scalable mapping algorithms that optimize inter-domain resource allocation under domain-level constraints and coordination overhead, which is particularly relevant for large-scale 5G (5G) and 6G networks spanning several operators. However, exact formulations become computationally intractable for large instances with complex constraints [13]. Decomposition techniques such as column generation, which split the original problem into a master problem and pricing subproblems, improve tractability while preserving good solution quality [14, 15].

It investigated four temporal-difference learning methods, namely the tabular and linear variants of SARSA (SARSA) and QQ-learning. The results demonstrated that RL can solve the VNFC mapping problem effectively, but they also exposed the limits of these representations: tabular methods require state-action values whose number grows with the problem size, whereas linear methods restrict the action-value function to a linear combination of hand-crafted features. Whether nonlinear function approximation, combined with experience replay and target networks, improves placement quality, efficiency, or learning stability in this setting therefore remained an open research question.

papers.title: Kelvin-invariant positive solutions for critical elliptic systems with repulsive interaction
papers.abstract: In this paper, we consider the following critical nonlinear elliptic system with repulsive interaction: \[ \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} -\Delta u_1 = \mu_1 u_1^3 - \beta(x) u_1 u_2^2 & \text{in } \mathbb{R}^4, \cr -\Delta u_2 = \mu_2 u_2^3 - \beta(x) u_1^2 u_2 & \text{in } \mathbb{R}^4, \cr u_1, u_2 \in \mathcal{D}^{1,2}(\mathbb{R}^4), & \end{array} \right. \] where $\mu_1, \mu_2 > 0$ and $\beta(x) \in C(\mathbb{R}^4,\mathbb{R})$ is a nonnegative function. Assuming that $\beta$ is invariant under the map $x \mapsto -\frac{x}{\vert{}x\vert{}^2}$, we establish the existence of positive solutions to $(\mathcal{P}_\beta)$ that are invariant under the Kelvin transform subject to suitable assumptions. This result provides a critical counterpart to the work of Sato [Y. Sato, Nonlinear Anal. 234 (2023), 113302], who established the existence of an even ground state for the corresponding subcritical problem. Furthermore, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of the obtained solutions as $\|\beta\|_\infty \to 0$.

Various existence results for critical elliptic systems with repulsive interaction have been obtained by imposing suitable symmetry conditions. Chen, Medina, and Pistoia [6] constructed nonradial solutions for a critical elliptic system with a small constant repulsive interaction by means of a Lyapunov–Schmidt reduction. Clapp and Pistoia [7] studied critical competitive elliptic systems in ℝN\mathbb{R}^{N} with constant coupling coefficients (also see [8]). In contrast to these works, we impose invariance only under the Kelvin transform, rather than under a larger group of conformal transformations. Although this weaker symmetry does not restore compactness of the critical Sobolev embedding, it allows us to analyze possible concentration bubbles by combining a profile decomposition argument with suitable energy estimates. Moreover, unlike the constant-coefficient settings considered in these works, we allow the coupling coefficient β⁡(x)\beta(x) to depend on xx, subject to the Kelvin-invariance condition (β​2)(\beta 2).

papers.title: Signals from the early Universe: primordial features from the full-shape analysis of BOSS galaxies and eBOSS quasars in combination with Planck
papers.abstract:
We search for primordial oscillatory features using cosmic microwave background (CMB) and large-scale structure (LSS) data, combining \textit{Planck} Public Release 4 (PR4) with galaxy clustering from the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (BOSS) and quasars from the extended Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey (eBOSS).
  For the LSS data we perform a full-shape analysis of the power spectrum multipoles with the one-loop effective field theory of large-scale structure, applying infrared resummation separately to each oscillatory component. We consider four templates: linearly and logarithmically oscillating features in Fourier space, with constant, localised, or power-law-decaying amplitudes, and fit them to the CMB and LSS data separately and jointly.
  We find no statistically significant evidence for primordial features in either dataset, individually or in combination. The best-fitting LSS features improve the fit by $\Delta\chi^2\simeq-6$ to $-10$, which corresponds to global significances of at most $1.6\,\sigma$ once the look-elsewhere effect is accounted for. In the CMB alone, the most significant feature is reduced to $\sim2.6\,\sigma$. Over the full frequency range, the LSS bounds on the feature amplitudes are weaker than those from \textit{Planck} by factors of $1.4$--$3$. Combining \textit{Planck} with \textit{BOSS+eBOSS} leaves the CMB constraints essentially unchanged, because the LSS data do not favour the frequencies preferred by the CMB.

papers.title: Will AI Replace Juniors? How Task Complexity Reduces Automation Risk
papers.abstract: How does task complexity shape firms' willingness to substitute entry-level labour with artificial intelligence (AI) tools? We study this question using a pre-registered survey experiment with managers from 1,435 German firms in the information economy and manufacturing industry. Managers are randomly assigned to consider a long lasting need for additional capacity involving either well-structured and standardised tasks, or more complex tasks that require professional judgement, contextual knowledge and independent problem-solving. Relative to standardised tasks, complex tasks reduce willingness to use AI rather than hire an entry-level employee by 0.54 points on a five-point scale and increase the importance attached to human oversight by 0.15 points. Further, pre-treatment responses indicate that managers expect the availability of AI applications to reduce hiring of both entry-level employees and experienced workers, but significantly more strongly for entry-level workers.

papers.intro:
The diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) and generative AI in particular has renewed concerns about technological displacement and employment. Yet, the emerging debate increasingly suggests that the consequences of the availability of AI applications are unlikely to be uniform across the workforce. Instead of only asking whether AI will destroy or create jobs, a more relevant question is which employees are the most vulnerable, i.e. most exposed to potential substitution, and why. One emerging concern is that AI might disproportionately affect workers at the beginning of their careers, i.e. entry-level employees.

The diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) and generative AI in particular has renewed concerns about technological displacement and employment. Yet, the emerging debate increasingly suggests that the consequences of the availability of AI applications are unlikely to be uniform across the workforce. Instead of only asking whether AI will destroy or create jobs, a more relevant question is which employees are the most vulnerable, i.e. most exposed to potential substitution, and why. One emerging concern is that AI might disproportionately affect workers at the beginning of their careers, i.e. entry-level employees.

Recent evidence provides some support for this idea, but remains contested. Hiring and employment have decreased among junior workers in several settings (Brynjolfsson et al., 2026; Lodefalk et al., 2026; Tucker, 2026). For instance, Brynjolfsson et al. (2026) report that employment among young workers (22–25 years old) in highly AI-exposed occupations has declined substantially compared to those in less AI-exposed occupations, while there is no comparable gap for experienced workers. However, other studies find less strong evidence for AI’s impact on junior workers. Lambert and Schindler (2026) show that AI exposure is strongly correlated with working from home (WFH) exposure and that the association between AI and the decline in junior hiring attenuates when WFH and AI are both considered. Fairlie and Wu (2026) find no significant relative increase in unemployment among recent US college graduates. Similarly, evidence from Germany, is less clear: Arntz et al. (2026) find a negative but statistically insignificant association between AI exposure and employment among young workers (aged 20–29) when accounting for WFH exposure and the current economic recession which they see as the main driver of this development.

There are several mechanisms that could create such an effect. AI might disproportionately increase the productivity of junior workers, which would allow firms to produce the same output with fewer employees (Brynjolfsson et al., 2025). Alternatively, AI might be especially capable of automating the type of tasks that is typically done by entry-level workers, consistent with task-based theories of technological change (Acemoglu and Restrepo, 2019; Autor, 2013; Hampole et al., 2025). Moreover, AI might lead to a "seniorisation" of entry-level work: When AI is used to automate simple activities, juniors might become responsible for tasks that require judgement, problem-solving and communication (Westby et al., 2026). Finally, AI applications might change organisational complementarities, allowing experienced employees to supervise AI tools instead of teams of entry-level workers. These mechanisms imply different transformations of entry-level work and career progression.

papers.title: Learning from Crowds with Unsupervised Item Response Models
papers.abstract: Item Response Theory (IRT) is the study of tests, including the properties of both test items and test takers. Crowdsourced labelling can be cast as an unsupervised IRT problem: annotators play the role of test takers with varying ability, and annotation tasks play the role of items with varying difficulty. We evaluate unsupervised variants of standard logistic IRT models for latent trait recovery and label inference on six datasets with crowdsourced labels and known ground truths. Unsupervised IRT models can recover annotator and item traits (e.g., ability, difficulty and discrimination) reliably across most datasets when compared to supervised variants trained on the ground truth. IRT models seem to be more stable in label inference compared to most baselines, but might not be the best possible choice depending on the dataset. We further propose to use IRT models to inform classifiers during training and compare against existing crowd-learning methods. We find that crowd-learning methods can improve F1 over majority-vote baselines, but no method significantly improves both F1 and calibration. IRT-informed curriculum methods seem to preserve calibration better than other crowd-learning methods, but are not at the frontier regarding F1, and the best crowd-learning methods in terms of F1 seem to be miscalibrated.

papers.intro:
Crowdsourcing is a common approach to annotating datasets in order to collect labels where they were previously unavailable. Recovering true labels from noisy annotations from annotators with different skills and reliabilities is called label inference (Zheng et al., 2017). Some work suggests that crowdsourced labels contain signal relevant for model training beyond an aggregation of the annotations as hard or soft labels (Uma et al., 2022; Plank, 2022). For example, without knowledge about the individual annotator behaviour, we cannot decide on their reliability regarding a task. Indeed, there are methods to explicitly train classifiers on the raw annotations without aggregation, such as (Rodrigues and Pereira, 2018; Chu et al., 2021; Herde et al., 2024b) and many more.

Item Response Theory (IRT) is the modern study of tests, which is used to compare the abilities of test takers, infer item properties such as difficulty, or even dynamically adapt test questions during test administration (Fox, 2010). This field appears closely related to crowdsourcing when we assume that the quality of labels heavily depends on the ability of the annotators and the difficulty of the examples. Research on Item Response Theory (IRT) dates back to at least the 1960s (Rasch, 1960; Birnbaum, 1968).

We argue that label inference is a natural application of unsupervised IRT, since it is like taking a test to which the correct answers are presently unknown. In this work, we investigate whether logistic IRT models can be used in an unsupervised manner for label inference, thus bridging the gap to well-established methodologies in test theory and recovering interpretable latent traits of items and annotators. We also explore whether the latent traits found by IRT models can be used to inform downstream model training.** * Code will be released upon peer-reviewed publication.

Trait recovery also seems to become more difficult as the number of traits increases. papers.title: EXPOSURE: Explaining Sources of Uncertainty in Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Shapley values in reinforcement learning are used to explain which observation features drive an agent's behavior and expected return, but not its certainty. Explaining certainty requires understanding how observation features influence different sources of return uncertainty, and Shapley values need the agent's prediction for every subset of visible features. We propose EXPOSURE, which uses one mask-aware belief network for both action selection and Shapley explanations. It explains the variance of the return, split into an observational part due to missing features and an inherent part due to the environment's own randomness, and the entropy of its belief over the masked features. In tic-tac-toe and Minesweeper, where exact Shapley values are computable, EXPOSURE gives more accurate explanations of expected return and its uncertainty, while uniquely explaining belief uncertainty.

papers.intro:
In a given state, two actions may have the same expected return, yet one may be risky while the other guarantees success. A reinforcement learning (RL) agent that explains only its expected return cannot tell them apart. In safety-critical applications such as healthcare, the agent’s uncertainty and its sources matter. Assessing an agent’s reliability requires understanding whether its uncertainty about expected return arises from observation features it does not see or from randomness inherent to the environment. It is also essential to know whether the observation features behind the agent’s certainty are plausible or just a shortcut. Shapley values [1] are commonly used to explain supervised models [2], including their predictive uncertainty [3]. In RL, they explain an agent’s decisions and outcomes [4, 5], but the sources of its uncertainty remain largely unexplored.

Every Shapley explanation requires a value for each coalition, i.e., each subset of visible features, and these values form a cooperative game. For each coalition, the uncertainty splits into an observational part, caused by the masked features, and an inherent part, which remains even when the agent sees all features, for example because the opponent plays randomly. Independent of the expected return, the agent also forms a belief, i.e., a probability distribution over the values of the masked features, and this belief can itself be uncertain. From experience, the agent learns which completions of a coalition are likely, and the entropy of its belief reflects how many remain plausible. Attributing each of these uncertainty targets answers its own question, namely which observation features make the agent less uncertain of the action’s value? (observational), which ones reveal that less uncertainty remains in the rest of the game? (inherent) and which ones narrow the agent’s belief about the masked features? (belief).

The common approach to obtain the coalition values is to train a separate surrogate network to predict the agent’s values from masked inputs [6], so the explanations describe the surrogate rather than the agent. We instead propose EXPOSURE, an agent built on a mask-aware belief network trained under random masks (Figure 1). The agent acts on its belief from the full observation, and the explanations use its belief from each coalition, so they come from the agent itself. We evaluate it in tic-tac-toe and Minesweeper 4×44\times 4, where exact Shapley values can be computed. We compare with the surrogate approach and with a mask-aware agent without a latent belief that maps masked inputs directly to expected return, which isolates the benefit of the belief. In both environments, EXPOSURE gives the most accurate explanations of every target it shares with the baselines, and it alone explains the belief uncertainty. In partially observable Minesweeper, it achieves a higher win rate than baselines, while being competitive in tic-tac-toe.

papers.title: Train-Only-Constrained LM for Synthetic Clinical Trajectories: Leak-Safe Calibration and Auditable Dynamics
papers.abstract: Simulating clinical time series necessitates temporal realism, calibration that preserves model integrity, and privacy transparency. We present a train-only, constrained language-model pipeline that factorizes generation. A compact GPT-style language model learns cross-biomarker co-occurrence through quantile tokens, and temporal directions are enforced by 3x3 per-biomarker Markov transitions fit on TRAIN, allowing dynamics to be audited. We fit a monotone quantile map (QMap) on TRAIN only (SYN(TRAIN) -> SIM(TRAIN)); no TEST statistics are used. The fixed map is then applied to SYN(TEST) severities. The constrained LM demonstrated improved distributional fidelity and co-occurrence in a 5,000-patient simulated testbed (parameters within published clinical ranges) compared to an empirical sampler, maintained near-chance detectability after a small lambda-sweep, and exhibits temporal adherence by construction. A classifier-based membership-inference audit results in an AUC of approximately 0.5; we make no differential-privacy claim. We present multi-seed results with paired 95% confidence intervals and quantify the severity of QMap's alignment (Delta W1 with confidence interval). This is a Stage-1 method result obtained on a controlled simulator; Stage-2 validation on real EHR cohorts with clinical endpoints is planned.
papers.intro:
Clinical time series are irregular, privacy-sensitive, and central to healthcare AI. Transformer language models (LMs) on coded EHR sequences (e.g., BEHRT, Med-BERT) learn strong representations (Li et al. 2020; Li et al. 2021), while generators such as TimeGAN and tabular diffusion aim to produce synthetic data (Yoon, Jarrett, and van der Schaar 2019; Kotelnikov et al. 2023). In practice, synthetic clinical generators repeatedly face: (i) temporal realism—unconstrained LMs invent implausible visit-to-visit dynamics; (ii) calibration drift—weak scales tuned post hoc using test statistics; and (iii) privacy opacity—memorization is hard to audit and can be probed via membership-inference attacks (MIA) (Shokri et al. 2017).

papers.title: Crystal-Symmetry-Dependent Field-Free Superconducting Diode Effect in CoPt/Nb Heterostructures
papers.abstract: Superconducting diodes convert nonreciprocal critical currents into current-polarity-selective switching between zero-resistance and resistive states. However, realizing the superconducting diode effect often requires complex device architectures and an external magnetic field to break spatial-inversion and time-reversal symmetry, substantially limiting its integration into cryogenic electronics and superconducting quantum circuits. Here, we demonstrate precise control of the field-free superconducting diode effect in epitaxial [111]-oriented A1-CoPt/Nb heterostructures. The critical-current asymmetry obeys the magnetic-point-group symmetry relation: it is finite along low-symmetry directions, suppressed along magnetic mirror axes, and reverses under either a 60{\deg} in-plane rotation or reversal of the CoPt magnetization. The same threefold symmetry dependence is observed in field-free current-induced magnetization switching in A1-CoPt films, indicating a common crystallographic origin for the superconducting and normal-state transport responses. Current- and temperature-dependent second-harmonic transport measurements are consistent with vortex-mediated nonreciprocity arising from an orientation-dependent interfacial edge landscape. We further exploit the magnetization-dependent diode polarity for proof-of-concept superconducting readout of electrically written magnetic states. These results establish crystallographic symmetry as an effective degree of freedom for engineering the superconducting diode effect, expanding the accessible materials space and providing a practical route toward field-free superconducting electronics.

papers.title: Nontrivial criticality and weakly first-order transitions in the frustrated spin-1 chain with single-ion anisotropy
papers.abstract: Frustrated spin chains host exotic phases beyond the Landau paradigm, yet weak first-order transitions and unconventional criticalities remain elusive. Combining large-scale density-matrix renormalization group with bosonization methods, we map the phase diagram of a spin-1 chain with next-nearest-neighbor (NNN) coupling and single-ion anisotropy (SIA). We pinpoint two topological phase transitions: a weakly first-order transition between the Haldane and NNN-Haldane phases with a tiny gap and a continuous transition from the Haldane phase to the large-$D$ phase located via level spectroscopy with Richardson extrapolation. For negative SIA, a spontaneous dimerized phase emerges between the N\'eel and NNN-N\'eel phases. Its transition into the N\'eel phase is a deconfined quantum critical point falling into the eight-vertex universality class, with central charge $c = 1$ and critical exponents varying continuously along the phase boundary. For positive SIA, we identify two vector-spin-chirality orders---an ordinary chiral phase and a narrow Haldane-chiral phase---with a weakly first-order transition between them, evidenced by a soft jump in the string order parameter. Our results reveal that frustration and anisotropy generate emergent orders and non-Landau criticalities, providing a platform for deconfined and topological phase transitions.

papers.intro:
In one-dimensional quantum spin chains [1, 2], the intricate interplay between competing interactions and magnetic anisotropies, notably the Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction [3], bond-directional exchanges [4, 5, 6, 7], and single-ion anisotropy (SIA) [8, 9, 10], stabilizes a variety of exotic quantum phenomena. These include the rank-2 vector chiral and spin-nematic phases [11, 12], the so-called “half fire, half ice” phases emerging in ferrimagnets [13], and the field-induced magnetization plateaus [14]. Substantial advances in understanding such unusual phases are driven by a synergistic combination of theoretical, computational, and experimental progress. On the one hand, the refinement of sophisticated analytical and numerical techniques has enabled the accurate detection and characterization of subtle quantum orders. On the other hand, the continuous discovery of pertinent material realizations provides essential experimental benchmarks and poses new challenges to theory [15, 16, 17]. One prominent example is the candidate spin-nematic phase in LiCuVO4, as evidenced by high-field magnetization and NMR experiments [15]; another is the chiral antiferromagnetic order recently uncovered in the S=1S=1 chain [Ni(pym)(H2O)4]SO4⋅{}_{4}\cdotH2O, where μ\muSR and neutron diffraction reveal a chiral modulation of the easy-axis anisotropy as the origin of chirality [17].

Spin-chain models serve as a fertile theoretical playground for exploring unconventional quantum phase transitions (QPTs) that lie beyond the conventional Landau-Ginzburg-Wilson (LGW) paradigm. Among these, two particularly prominent types have attracted sustained theoretical attention: topological QPTs involving non-Landau ordered phases, and Landau-forbidden continuous QPTs that separate two distinct symmetry-breaking orders. A paradigmatic example of the former is the transition into the Haldane phase [18] — a prototypical symmetry-protected topological (SPT) phase [19] characterized by a bulk gap, spin-1/21/2 edge modes, and a nonlocal string order parameter (SOP) originating from hidden ℤ2×ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}\times\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry breaking [20, 21]. The exactly solvable Affleck-Kennedy-Lieb-Tasaki (AKLT) model provides a crucial reference point for understanding its essential properties [22]. Beyond this well-known SPT example, topological QPTs have been identified in various other settings where conventional order parameters are absent, including spin-1/21/2 dimerized chains, spin-1 chains with SIA [8, 9, 10, 23], frustrated spin-1 J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg chains [24, 25, 26, 27], and spin-2 chains constructed from projection operators [28]. The second type—deconfined quantum criticality—is exemplified by continuous transitions between two conventionally ordered phases that would typically be separated by a first-order transition within the LGW framework [29, 30, 31, 32, 33]. Such deconfined quantum critical points (DQCPs) have been proposed, for instance, in certain frustrated ferromagnetic spin chains [34, 35, 36] and in Kitaev-type chains supplemented with multiple-spin interactions or SIA [37, 38], where the transition is driven by the condensation of fractionalized excitations.

Over the years, extensive research has been devoted to spin-1 chains with competing interactions and magnetic anisotropies in order to elucidate the nature of emergent phases and characterize the corresponding QPTs. These models include the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} chain with an XXZ-type exchange anisotropy [39] or multiple-spin interaction [40, 41, 42], the bilinear-biquadratic chain with SIA [43, 44] or Kitaev-type exchange anisotropy [45], the Heisenberg-Kitaev chain with SIA [46], and the inherently anisotropic Kitaev-Γ\Gamma chain [7, 47], where Kitaev and symmetric off-diagonal Γ\Gamma terms compete directly. While the frustrated J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} chain and the Heisenberg chain with SIA serve as two paradigmatic models for investigating competing exchange and local anisotropy separately, their synthesis—the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2}-DD chain—has only been explored in limited parameter regimes [48, 49]. It is therefore the objective of this work to present a comprehensive and high-precision phase diagram, characterizing every transition by its universality class and critical exponents, thereby providing a definitive reference for future studies on frustrated spin chains.

papers.title: Detector Operating Behavior Inference via Data-Space Sampling
papers.abstract: A detector scores candidate detections, but the recall and false alarms at a given confidence threshold depend on the input distribution. We introduce Detector Operating Behavior Inference (DOBI), a second-level inference task: estimating a fixed detector's threshold-dependent, distribution-level operating response from the internal evidence of a single unlabeled image. DOBI treats the detector's threshold response, i.e. recall, false positives, and precision across thresholds, as a latent behavioral state under the current data condition. Controlled data-space sampling probes this state space offline, and a lightweight monitor learns the inverse map from one image to this state, whose single functional output supports multiple operating policies. In a controlled proof of concept with a fixed YOLOv10-Nano person detector and COCO-derived degradations, predicted PR behavior reduces mean absolute deviation from 0.128 for an image-independent mean-behavior prior to 0.054, and predicted functional distances track empirical regime distances (Spearman 0.96). From one unlabeled image, the inferred behavior selects operating points as well as a non-deployable lookup that knows the true regime (macro-regime $F_1$ 0.6604 for both, versus 0.6407 under pristine calibration; oracle 0.6620). On this discrete benchmark, regime-supervised curve lookups are strong controls. Pre-specified continuous and compositional probing shows where functional inference matters: on unseen combinations, the functional decoder has a lower mean curve error than a template lookup, increasingly with distance from the training conditions, whereas the lookup is more accurate for interpolation. These results establish the feasibility of single-image inference of distribution-level detector behavior over the probed conditions. Source code is available at https://github.com/beckerio/dobi

An object detector assigns scores to candidate boxes, and a confidence threshold decides which detections are reported. Yet the same threshold yields different recall, precision, and false-alarm rates when the image distribution changes—for example, under blur, noise, or fog. Confidence scores tell us which predictions survive a threshold, not what operating trade-off that threshold achieves under the current conditions.

papers.title: From Telemetry to Intelligence: A Data-Centric Survey of O-RAN
papers.abstract: The Open Radio Access Network (O-RAN) has emerged as a new architecture for enabling programmability, intelligence, automation, and multi-vendor interoperability in the wireless domain of public telecommunications networks. Artificial Intelligence/Machine Learning (AI/ML), and more recently Agentic AI, are considered key enablers of automation and intelligentization in O-RAN. However, the effectiveness of such systems is constrained by the availability, quality, and structure of O-RAN data. In this survey, we present a data-centric perspective of O-RAN, focusing on how data support rule-based, AI/ML-driven, and emerging Agentic AI applications across various timescale control loops. We analyze O-RAN data along multiple dimensions, including source, accessibility, abstraction level, and application. We further identify key data challenges, and discuss their implications for intelligent control. The overarching objective of this work is to present the first comprehensive review of the data-centric perspective on intelligent applications in O-RAN. To this end, it introduces a unified framework for understanding the role of O-RAN data in enabling network intelligence and automation.

papers.intro:
The ORAN (ORAN) represents a shift in the design, operation and the deployment of next-generation mobile networks [1, 2]. It adopts four key principles: (i) disaggregation of network components; (ii) virtualization of network functions; (iii) openness of network interfaces; and (iv) intelligent control of network services. All those four principles provide the mobile network with flexibility, scalability, interoperability and intelligence [1].

It adopts four key principles: (i) disaggregation of network components; (ii) virtualization of network functions; (iii) openness of network interfaces; and (iv) intelligent control of network services. All those four principles provide the mobile network with flexibility, scalability, interoperability and intelligence [1].

Recent research on ORAN has focused primarily on three main directions. First, standardizing and implementing the ORAN concept, its architecture, open interfaces, and deployment strategies. The standardization efforts are mainly led by the ORAN Alliance [3] and 3GPP (3GPP) specifications [4]. The software-based implementations are led by different industrial and academic organizations, such as the open-source protocol stacks srsRAN [5] and OAI (OAI) [6]. A tutorial paper on ORAN deployment and implementation solutions provides more information in [7]. Second, investigating the security challenges introduced by this new, open, disaggregated and programmable RAN (RAN). These challenges include threats against open interfaces, RAN, controllers, as well as risks arising from malicious applications, data poisoning, misconfiguration, and unauthorized control actions [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13]. Third, proposing network management applications and deploying them on the ORAN architecture, following the app-store-like model where network functions can be extended through third-party software [14]. Examples of these applications include network slicing, traffic steering, interference mitigation, anomaly detection, and energy optimization, operating across different time scales ( RT (RT), NearRT (NearRT), and NonRT (NonRT)). In these applications, AIML (AIML) models are widely adopted, and recent work is also moving toward Agentic AI (AI), where LLM (LLM)-based or multi-agent systems can interpret intent and reason over ORAN data, call tools, and coordinate control actions. However, both intelligent and Agentic AI-based ORAN applications are fundamentally constrained by the data that are generated, exposed, and accessible across architectural components. While existing studies demonstrate the potential of AIML and Agentic AI in ORAN, they largely concentrate on algorithmic innovation (the methods) rather than examining the underlying data foundations that enable such intelligence. This paper addresses this gap by introducing a data-centric perspective of ORAN.

papers.title: DFLAT: Model-based Diffusion on Differentially Flat Spaces for Long-Horizon Trajectory Optimization
papers.abstract: Long-horizon diffusion-based planning for kinodynamically constrained systems requires both scalability and feasibility, yet existing diffusion planners typically sacrifice one for the other. We present DFLAT, a diffusion-based planning algorithm that operates directly on a differentially flat trajectory representation. Instead of diffusing over time-discretized controls, DFLAT denoises a compact set of Hermite curve parameters in the flat-output space, consisting of intermediate waypoints together with the endpoint tangents of each segment. Every denoised sample maps to a dynamically consistent trajectory, so feasibility holds by construction rather than being restored afterward. Experiments on challenging tractor-trailer planning benchmarks show that DFLAT matches or exceeds the success rates of existing baselines at consistently lower planning times, particularly on long-horizon problems requiring multiple forward-reverse maneuvers. In cases where kinodynamic RRT requires over 100 seconds, DFLAT plans in subsecond time, enabling practical deployment.
