papers.intro:
Planning motions that are both collision-free and dynamically feasible is a long-standing challenge in robotics, particularly for nonholonomic systems operating over long horizons [1]. Recent advances in generative modeling, including diffusion models and flow matching, have introduced powerful new approaches to robot policy learning and motion planning [2]. Diffusion-based planners, in particular, have demonstrated strong performance across a broad range of robotic planning tasks [3, 4].

Planning motions that are both collision-free and dynamically feasible is a long-standing challenge in robotics, particularly for nonholonomic systems operating over long horizons [1]. Recent advances in generative modeling, including diffusion models and flow matching, have introduced powerful new approaches to robot policy learning and motion planning [2]. Diffusion-based planners, in particular, have demonstrated strong performance across a broad range of robotic planning tasks [3, 4].

These results are harder to sustain once the dynamics are constrained and the horizon is long. Every candidate trajectory must remain dynamically consistent, yet the sample budget must not grow with the horizon, and existing representations trade one against the other. One route to feasibility is to diffuse over the control sequence rather than the state trajectory: samples are drawn from a distribution favoring low-cost controls and rolled forward through the known dynamics, so the resulting trajectories are dynamically feasible by construction [5, 6]. This representation scales poorly with the horizon: low-cost controls occupy a shrinking fraction of the sample space, so the sample budget must grow accordingly. An alternative is to diffuse over the trajectory directly [7, 4, 8], which avoids this conditioning problem, as obstacle and goal constraints act on the sampled variables themselves rather than through a long composition of dynamics steps. The resulting trajectory is no longer the rollout of any admissible control and is therefore not necessarily dynamically feasible, requiring projection or post-hoc refinement to recover a trackable solution [9, 10, 11, 12]. To the best of our knowledge, no existing diffusion-based planner is both feasible by construction and efficient as the horizon grows for such systems.

We resolve this tension through the choice of trajectory representation. A particular class of systems, called differentially flat, admits a set of outputs from which the states and inputs can be recovered [13]. In the flat-output space, a sufficiently smooth curve is therefore already a valid state and input trajectory, so feasibility follows from the representation rather than being restored after the fact. Our method diffuses over a compact parametrization of such a curve: a sequence of waypoints together with the in-segment parameters that join them into a smooth path. Because these parameters describe segments rather than time steps, the design space scales with the number of segments and the structure of the maneuver, not with the resolution of the discretization, and stays small as the horizon grows. Our method thus retains the dynamic consistency of control-sequence diffusion without the large sample budget it requires.

Model-based diffusion (MBD) uses the dynamics model to compute a training-free score function for trajectory optimization [5], and Safe Model Predictive Diffusion (Safe MPD) combines this with shielded rollouts to guarantee safety throughout sampling process [14]. Barrier-rate guided MPPI embeds barrier constraints into the sampling distribution for tractor–trailer maneuvers in narrow spaces [15]. These methods achieve kinodynamic feasibility by construction, but they operate on representations whose dimension grows with the planning horizon, causing sample efficiency to degrade on long-horizon problems. Recent work has also explored more compact parameterizations for diffusion planning. Guided Polynomial Diffusion (GPD) performs diffusion directly over Bernstein polynomial trajectory coefficients [8], and sparse control points with spline interpolation have been used to obtain smooth control trajectories from few samples in MPPI [16]. Hierarchical diffusion methods instead plan over temporally abstracted sub-goals [7, 4], and coupled hierarchical diffusion tightens the interaction between the two levels for long-horizon tasks [17]. Although these approaches improve horizon scalability, the sampled coefficients and sub-goals need not correspond to admissible motions. Feasibility is instead recovered afterward, for instance by filtering out samples that violate the constraints [18], or by projecting the sampled variables onto the constraint set [9, 11]. A representative instance related to our work diffuses over control points rather than over the trajectory itself, and recovers dynamic feasibility with a quadratic program [12], which is convex only when the relevant bounds are affine in the sampled variables and does not extend to nonholonomic models.

papers.title: Understanding Mode Collapse in Diffusion Models under Classifier-Free Guidance
papers.abstract: The use of classifier-free guidance in diffusion and flow models has proven critical to their empirical success, as it allows for the controllable generation of lower-temperature and higher-fidelity samples. Despite its widespread use, classifier-free guidance remains both empirically and theoretically poorly understood, owing to the difficulty of solving the associated transport equations for arbitrary normalizing flows. In this paper, we observe that the effects of classifier-free guidance arise from a mismatch between the representation capabilities of the conditional and unconditional distributions, wherein the conditional distribution exhibits higher complexity and fidelity. We propose an analytical model to capture this observation: the conditional distribution is a Gaussian mixture whose means lie on an ellipsoid, and the unconditional distribution is a single Gaussian approximating the mixture. The flows arising from this mixture are closed under scaling, enabling us to derive analytic closed-form solutions for the guided distribution at all noise scales and guidance levels. Our analytic solution shows that classifier-free guidance induces (a) a shift along a mean-axis direction and (b) a persistent skew toward, and concentration around, a singular point corresponding to the conditional sample starting from zero noise. We validate our theoretical predictions on pretrained, large-scale image diffusion models.

papers.title: ILMlip: fast and universal machine-learning interatomic potentials
papers.abstract: Large-scale pretrained machine-learned interatomic potentials keep growing more accurate as new models appear at a rapid pace, and more expensive: the current leader of Matbench Discovery as of November 2026 (F1 score 0.935) has $9.9\times10^7$ parameters and took 3.6 thousand GPU-hours to train. The ILMlip potentials presented here are optimised for speed as well as zero-shot accuracy. They are equivariant, conservative message-passing potentials in which every component is arranged for throughput: little work per pair of atoms and as much as needed per atom. Through ASE on one GPU, they run molecular dynamics up to about $10^3$ times faster than state-of-the-art message-passing potentials such as MACE (medium) and up to five times faster than NEP89 and DPA-4.1C. At the same time, six sizes with $1.4\times10^5$ to $2.8\times10^7$ parameters, pretrained on materials, molecules and solid acids, reach F1 scores of 0.75 to 0.91 on Matbench Discovery, placing the largest within 0.03 of the current leader. They therefore suit high-throughput, large or long simulations, and, being transferable, they are strong starting points for fine-tuning. Fine-tuned to six materials, the model of size S comes close to the ab initio force errors of a fine-tuned MACE, so it reaches reference-level accuracy at about 50 ns per atom and step (Cu fcc). Their components can be adopted separately, as a starting point for architectures with even better ratios of speed to accuracy. The ILMlip implementation is available at https://github.com/jhaens/ilmlip

papers.intro:
Machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) predict forces and energies close to the accuracy of the electronic-structure method they were trained on, at a cost that grows in principle linearly with the number of atoms [9, 3, 92, 20, 8, 4]. Large-scale pretrained MLIPs, so-called universal or foundation MLIPs (UMLIPs), trained on databases that cover most of the periodic table [44, 66, 19, 2, 75, 52, 46], offer such a potential to users who have no training set of their own [17, 19, 7, 67, 88, 73, 60, 27, 84, 62, 55]. Their accuracy has risen quickly, and mostly through size. On Matbench Discovery [74], where a model must decide which of about 250250 thousand hypothetical crystals are stable, the F1 score of this decision (11 is perfect) went from 0.570.57 to 0.940.94 within about three years. The current leader as of November 2026, DPA-4.1-Max-OAM-PFT [54], has 9.9×1079.9\times 10^{7} parameters and was trained for 3.63.6 thousand GPU-hours (Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition); PET-OAM-XL [12], another top-performing pretrained MLIP (7.2×1087.2\times 10^{8} parameters), was trained for over 2020 thousand GPU-hours (Nvidia H100). Their size is paid for again in every step of every simulation that uses them.

A high-throughput screening study, a simulation cell large enough to hold an interface or a trajectory long enough to show a rare event is limited by the number of force calls it can afford, and there a model that is nearly as accurate and far cheaper reaches further than the most accurate one for a fixed computational budget. Where a property must be trusted, a universal model applied as it is, zero-shot, is rarely the end point; the canonical route is to fine-tune it, that is, to train it further on a few hundred to a few thousand reference calculations of the system at hand [30, 35, 79, 33, 37]. In our own studies, foundation models of rather different architecture and size reached nearly the same error after fine-tuning [35]. What a fine-tuned model inherits unchanged from its foundation is the cost of a force call. Simulations limited by force calls and fine-tuned models thus ask for the same kind of model: one that balances zero-shot accuracy against speed rather than maximising the former.

Our fine-tuning studies [30, 35, 33, 37] make this the design principle of the present work: inference speed is as much a design target as zero-shot accuracy. The pretrained model must be accurate and transferable enough across the chemical space to be used as it is, for example to sample the configurations on which the reference calculations for a fine-tune are made [37]. At the same time, it must keep enough capacity to reach close to ab initio accuracy for a specific family of compounds after a short fine-tune. Benchmarks such as Matbench Discovery rank zero-shot accuracy, and most universal potentials have been developed towards it; how fast a model can be while meeting both requirements has received less attention.

Universal potentials designed for speed have emerged only recently, and they show that speed is a matter of design rather than of hardware. NEP89 [55] does without message passing, in which every atom receives learned features that its neighbours have computed from their own environments, so that its energy depends on atoms beyond its cut-off; it runs in its own engine, GPUMD [24]. DPA-4.1C [53] does without message passing as well and evaluates everything in one hand-written GPU kernel (Table 1). Both tie their speed to a dedicated engine or kernel. Much everyday work, however, runs in general-purpose tools: ASE [51], i-PI [57] and LAMMPS [78]. It is not the most accurate universal potential. Its six sizes, from XS with 1.4×1051.4\times 10^{5} parameters to XXL with 2.8×1072.8\times 10^{7}, reach F1 scores of 0.750.75 to 0.910.91 where the leader reaches 0.9350.935. What is gained depends on the comparison. Through ASE on one GPU, the small model S runs molecular dynamics (MD) of 10410^{4} atoms 920920 times faster than the established message-passing potential MACE-OMAT-0 [7] (medium, 9.19.1 million parameters), and three to five times faster than NEP89 (in its ASE implementation) and DPA-4.1C. XL and XXL are the accuracy end of the family: still 104104 and 4040 times faster than MACE-OMAT-0, but slower than NEP89 and DPA-4.1C. Almost every concept of ILMlip is known. The many-body products of the atomic cluster expansion [20, 23] and of MACE [4, 5] give it its body order; DPA-4.1C contributed pair-dependent modulations of the radial functions, fewer channels for higher angular momentum and a compact description of the last layer [53]; NEP89 the attitude that speed is a design goal from the first decision [55]. Our contribution is the combination of these parts into one model, under a single rule for where a fast model may spend its work, and the parts that are new: element-dependent cut-offs; one pair object per bond, shared by both layers; a message without the part that came from the receiving atom; Gram matrices of a learned projection; the removal of many-body products that are numerical multiples of others; two smooth bounds that keep the features finite at any density and leave the shortest distances to a screened nuclear repulsion [97]; and the evaluation of many independent simulations in one network call. Each of these parts can be adopted, replaced or extended on its own.

papers.title: Frequency Estimation from the Internal State of the Boyer-Moore Majority Vote Algorithm
papers.abstract: The Boyer-Moore Majority Vote algorithm identifies a majority candidate in a single pass over a data stream using constant memory O(1) and linear processing time O(n). While the classic algorithm identifies a candidate without directly estimating its frequency, its internal register states retain information about item occurrences during execution. This work investigates a frequency estimator derived directly from these internal counters. We establish the conditions under which the counter state enables exact recovery of the frequency of the majority element and characterize the estimation error when these conditions are not satisfied. In particular, we analyze the effect of stream ordering on the estimator and identify delayed-arrival configurations, such as Majority-Delayed sequences, that can lead to systematic estimation errors. We further derive the error behavior associated with late-arriving majority blocks and empirically evaluate the estimator across multiple stream topologies. The results demonstrate that the internal state of the Boyer-Moore algorithm can provide frequency information without increasing its O(1) space complexity. At the same time, its accuracy depends critically on the ordering of elements in the input stream.

Processing continuous data streams requires a careful balance between memory allocations and execution speed [4, 5, 6]. Many real-world systems, from network routing tables to distributed logging pipelines, must identify frequent items under strict hardware constraints [13, 14, 7]. Formally, when given an input sequence σ=⟨x1,x2,…,xn⟩\sigma=\langle x_{1},x_{2},\dots,x_{n}\rangle made of items from a universe 𝒰\mathcal{U}, the majority detection task looks for an item M∈𝒰M\in\mathcal{U} whose true frequency satisfies f⁡(M)>⌊n/2⌋f(M)>\lfloor n/2\rfloor. Storing full lookup tables to track every distinct key requires Ω⁡(|𝒰|)\Omega(|\mathcal{U}|) memory, which quickly becomes impractical on embedded devices or high-speed network switches [15, 12, 8].

Storing full lookup tables to track every distinct key requires Ω⁡(|𝒰|)\Omega(|\mathcal{U}|) memory, which quickly becomes impractical on embedded devices or high-speed network switches [15, 12, 8].

To operate within tight memory bounds, probabilistic synopses, sketch-based summaries, and approximate tracking schemes are widely used [16, 17, 9]. For instance, Lossy Counting by Manku and Motwani [4] offers ϵ\epsilon-deficient counts over continuous streams with small memory footprints, whereas modern counter-based surveys highlight trade-offs between update throughput and per-item estimation fidelity [7, 6]. Alongside these summary methods, the Boyer-Moore majority vote algorithm [1] remains a classic deterministic choice. Its generalization to kk-frequent items was formalized by Misra and Gries [2], its average-case step counts were modeled by Tsai using Markov chains [3], and Chassaing examined its optimal candidate tracking properties using martingales when elements arrive with unequal probabilities [10, 11]. Recent advances in space-efficient streaming emphasize minimizing counter updates to maximize hardware cache locality and processing speed [8, 9].

papers.title: Error estimates for a structure-preserving finite-element scheme of quasi-incompressible Navier-Stokes-Maxwell-Stefan systems
papers.abstract: A conforming finite-element scheme for quasi-incompressible Navier-Stokes-Maxwell-Stefan systems in a bounded domain with periodic boundary conditions is presented. The system consists of the Navier-Stokes equations, together with a quasi-incompressibility constraint, coupled with the cross-diffusion Maxwell--Stefan equations. The numerical scheme preserves the partial masses and the quasi-incompressibility constraint and dissipates the discrete energy. First-order error estimates in space and time are shown for a diffusion-augmented mobility matrix by using the relative energy method and suitable projection error estimates. Numerical experiments in two space dimensions illustrate the convergence of the scheme and indicate second-order convergence in space in the $L^2$ norm.

papers.intro:
The quasi-incompressible Navier–Stokes–Maxwell–Stefan equations provide a continuum-scale framework for modeling the coupled transport of mass and momentum in fluid mixtures. Assuming that the mixture is volume-additive, the fluid velocity satisfies an incompressibility constraint, but it is generally not divergence-free. The Maxwell–Stefan relations describe the multicomponent mass diffusion driven by concentration and pressure and capture cross-diffusion effects beyond the standard Fick law. The mass diffusion fluxes interact with the momentum balance, enabling the system to represent complex processes such as reactive flows, multiphase mixing, and transport in non-ideal mixtures.

The existence of weak solutions to this system was proved in [10], and a structure-preserving finite-element scheme was proposed in [7] without providing a convergence analysis. In this paper, we show the convergence of the scheme and, additionally, prove first-order error estimates for the particle densities, chemical potentials, fluid velocity, and pressure.

papers.title: How LLM Agents Reshape Financial Knowledge Graphs: A Survey
papers.abstract: Financial knowledge graphs (KGs) link information across sources to support risk assessment, investment research, asset recommendations, and forecasting. Large language models (LLMs) help build these graphs by extracting relationships from text and matching entities across records. Yet a workflow may still prescribe which sources to consult and which checks to run. If the chosen sources lack relevant evidence, even accurate extraction can leave a financial question unanswered. LLM agents can adapt the workflow as evidence emerges. They use the graph and earlier findings to decide where to look next, which claims to verify, and whether to update a record for later use. This is the first survey devoted to how LLM agents reshape the construction, maintenance, and use of financial KGs. Our taxonomy covers Knowledge Graph Construction, Temporal Evolution, Verification, Reconciliation, and Admission, Adaptive Acquisition, and Knowledge Graph Usage. We examine how studies evaluate graph quality, agents' use of evidence, financial task outcomes, and reliability over time. These evaluations show that agents can recover evidence missed in an initial search and revise records as new information arrives. Three questions remain unresolved. How can an agent tell whether it has enough evidence for a financial decision? After a record is corrected, how can the agent identify which earlier conclusions need to change? Which relationships and rules can it reuse in a new graph or domain?

papers.title: Sports Agent: A Self-Evolving System for Conversational Data Analytics
papers.abstract:
Conversational sports analytics requires accurate, evidence-based responses with low latency. Changes in query distributions, data resources, and model behavior can degrade static agent configurations, motivating controlled evolution guided by runtime evidence.
  We present Sports Agent, a self-evolving framework integrating an Agentic SQL Model for structured-data reasoning, a harness for planning and tool orchestration, and a unified Feedback Engine connecting online execution with offline evolution. The engine assesses responses and execution trajectories, verifies factual claims, diagnoses failures, and generates evolution signals. Model evolution combines SQL-to-Question Scaling for coverage expansion with Graph-Guided Scaling for error-targeted synthesis. Generated questions undergo trajectory distillation and quality filtering for iterative supervised fine-tuning, followed by a separate Post-RL stage. Harness evolution translates recurrent failures into bounded prompt and skill updates, validated through independent audits, execution replay, and regression testing. Performance-tolerance checks guard against unacceptable degradation during simplification.
  The resulting Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-based model outperforms Qwen3.8-Max on sports question answering and analysis while achieving approximately three times the inference efficiency. Across 30 harness-evolution rounds, the aggregate performance score improves by 10.8 points. In a live sports analytics product, the evolved system improves factual correctness by 10.5 points and average response length, a proxy for answer richness, by 158.1%, while reducing average latency by 41.3% relative to the baseline.

papers.intro:
Sports Agent targets factual retrieval and analytical reasoning over heterogeneous sports data. Unlike LLM-based chatbots that rely primarily on parametric knowledge (Singh and others, 2025), a production-grade sports agent must select appropriate data sources and specialized tools, retrieve evidence from the external environment, and ground its responses in the retrieved evidence.

Sports Agent targets factual retrieval and analytical reasoning over heterogeneous sports data. Unlike LLM-based chatbots that rely primarily on parametric knowledge (Singh and others, 2025), a production-grade sports agent must select appropriate data sources and specialized tools, retrieve evidence from the external environment, and ground its responses in the retrieved evidence.

Conversational sports analytics draws on diverse and evolving data sources, including structured databases, knowledge bases and real-time web search (Xia et al., 2024; Zheman, 2026). Structured databases support precise queries over schedules, player profiles, game records, and statistics; knowledge bases and FAQs provide rules, terminology, and historical context; web search delivers the latest news, injury reports, and roster updates (Hui et al., 2026; Qin et al., 2025). Differences in data structure, update frequency, and access mechanisms require the system to select appropriate sources and tools for each request. Simple factual questions may require a single lookup, while statistical analysis demands a precise understanding of metric definitions and aggregation logic. Questions involving real-time information or multiple aspects of a topic often require coordinated tool use and evidence synthesis across sources. A sports agent must therefore support an end-to-end workflow encompassing intent understanding, tool selection, evidence verification, and response generation based on the retrieved evidence. Conversational sports analytics is also highly interactive. Users expect accurate, timely, and verifiable responses with low latency (Martinez et al., 2025). Although multi-step planning, iterative tool invocation, and cross-source evidence verification can enhance factual reliability, they introduce additional retrieval and inference overhead. Maintaining factual accuracy while minimizing response latency under evolving data and database schemas therefore remains a central challenge for production-grade sports agents.

Conversational sports analytics integrates information from multiple sources to support a broad range of applications, including professional sports analysis, live-event engagement, and sports information services (Xu et al., 2026b). StatMuse translates natural-language questions into structured sports-statistics queries, returning textual answers alongside the underlying results (StatMuse, ). Wimbledon Match Chat integrates live match data with generative AI to support in-match statistical queries and performance analysis (IBM, 2025; Baughman et al., 2025). AthleteGPT, deployed at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games, used retrieval-augmented generation to provide approximately 11,000 athletes with guidance on venues, rules, and event information (Intel Corporation, 2024). Collectively, these applications illustrate the growing role of conversational sports analytics as an interface to official databases, live-event data, and domain knowledge. However, integrating these resources does not, by itself, ensure sustained performance as data sources, tool interfaces, and model capabilities evolve. Maintaining reliable operation under such changes remains an open challenge.

Most existing agent systems follow an “offline development–deployment–manual maintenance” paradigm (Zhai et al., 2025). During development, the foundation model, prompts, skills, tool descriptions, and routing policies are configured for a target task distribution and operating environment, with system performance validated through offline evaluation. The effectiveness of this approach depends on the deployment conditions remaining broadly consistent with those used during development and evaluation. In sports applications, however, evolving user requirements, data resources, and model capabilities can progressively widen the gap between static system configurations and operational demands (Gao and others, 2025; Liu et al., 2026a).

Query Distribution Shift. User interests shift substantially across the competition calendar. During the regular season and playoffs, queries primarily concern game results, player and team statistics, and standings; during the offseason, attention shifts toward trades, the draft, and roster changes. Conversely, stronger models may render some harness components redundant. Model changes therefore require a reassessment of the surrounding harness configuration.

papers.title: MUSE: Multi-Task Uncertainty-Aware Self-Supervised Encoder for mmWave ISAC
papers.abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) allows a wireless system to use the same waveform for communication and environment sensing. At mmWave frequency bands, ISAC enables diverse human sensing tasks, such as localization, gesture recognition, and pose estimation, with high precision. However, each task requires training a dedicated model, typically from scratch on a task-specific dataset, with no mechanism to flag unreliable predictions. This hurts the scalability, transferability, and reliability of mmWave ISAC models. In this work, we propose MUSE (Multi-task Uncertainty-aware Self-supervised Encoder), a unified framework for mmWave human sensing. MUSE leverages a self-supervised transformer model with per-dataset tokenization and is trained via masked autoencoding across five datasets. During fine-tuning, MUSE uses evidential classification heads that enable uncertainty quantification. MUSE replaces N separate encoders with a single shared transformer encoder, an N-times backbone parameter reduction, while achieving a 9.7 percentage points improvement in classification performance compared to the task-specific model, showing that learning jointly across tasks improves per-task generalization. Across four classification tasks, MUSE produces reliable uncertainty estimates that enable selective prediction, improving accuracy by abstaining on the least confident 20% of predictions. We further improve the reliability of the model's confidence estimates using temperature scaling and conformal prediction. Finally, MUSE's uncertainty signal remains reliable even under cross-user deployment, assigning higher uncertainty to wrong predictions than to correct ones 78% of the time, and recovering 9.2 percentage points of accuracy through selective prediction, with no additional retraining on the unseen user.

Millimeter-wave frequency bands (24-100 GHz) [1, 2] offer high bandwidth that can support data rates of several gigabits per second to enable advanced 5G and 6G communication services. At the same time, the high range and spatial resolution associated with mmWave signals can be exploited for high-precision environmental sensing. These characteristics make mmWave ISAC (ISAC) a key enabler for emerging applications such as XR (XR) and autonomous driving. In these applications, mmWave ISAC can provide advanced sensing functionalities, including device-free gesture recognition, pose estimation, environment mapping of indoor and outdoor environments, and obstacle detection

Recent works have shown significant progress in such applications, particularly for human sensing [3, 4, 5, 6]. However, each task is typically solved in isolation using a dedicated deep learning model trained from scratch on a single task with no mechanism to learn shared representations across related tasks [5, 7, 3, 8, 9, 10, 11]. This isolated-task paradigm creates a number of challenges. First, every task requires collecting and annotating a dataset and recruiting participants, which becomes particularly expensive and time-consuming. Further, there is a lack of research hardware platforms at mmWave frequency bands that enable access to signal features as CSI (CSI) [5]. As a result, most of the existing mmWave datasets have a small amount of labeled data, compared to vision or text-based applications, where the dataset collection is comparatively cheaper. Because of smaller datasets, task-specific models learn task-specific representations, resulting in poor generalization. Further, most of the works on ISAC do not indicate the model’s reliability score i.e., a confidence score reflecting how likely a prediction is to be correct. However, deep learning models are often poorly calibrated [12], outputting overconfident predictions even on unseen or out-of-distribution (OOD) inputs. In critical applications such as autonomous driving, there should be a mechanism to flag unreliable predictions to prevent erroneous decisions. Moreover, in ISAC sensing systems, deploying N independent models for N tasks adds to the computational, storage, energy, and maintenance costs. Each model is typically trained from scratch and requires its own dedicated training pipeline, hyperparameter tuning, and retraining on new tasks, resulting in significant engineering and deployment overhead that limits scalability.

Although different mmWave sensing tasks, such as gesture recognition and pose estimation, differ in objectives, they operate on a common physical phenomenon, i.e., mmWave signals reflecting from a human body. This shared signal structure suggests that common representations could be learned across tasks rather than training separate task-specific models. Self-supervised learning (SSL) [13], such as masked autoencoding (MAE) [14], has shown that unlabeled data can be used to derive powerful representations by masking portions of the input and forcing the model to reconstruct missing portions. This is done without requiring any actual labels. Then, these representations are used for diverse visual or language tasks. Can the same approach be applied to ISAC data? The major challenge with ISAC data is the heterogeneity in the input data, such as in shape, signal features (CSI, beam SNR, PPBP (PPBP), and micro-doppler), sampling frequencies, and underlying hardware imperfections. Further, these inputs may be gathered from diverse sensing geometries. This heterogeneity is significantly greater in wireless signals compared to vision SSL, where images have a standard input resolution. Consequently, applying SSL to ISAC data is significantly more challenging, since SSL methods often rely on consistent input structures and assumptions about data regularity to learn meaningful shared representations.

To address the above-mentioned limitations, we propose MUSE (Multi-task uncertainty-aware self-supervised encoder), a framework for ISAC-based human sensing. MUSE leverages MAE for SSL pretraining across five real-world heterogeneous datasets, enabling the learning of transferable representations from unlabeled ISAC data. We evaluate the proposed framework on multiple heterogeneous ISAC datasets covering localization, gesture recognition, pose estimation, and person identification tasks. MUSE relies on a two-phase training strategy (cf., Figure 1). During SSL pretraining, MUSE uses masked reconstruction as a learning objective across all five datasets simultaneously. Instead of random masking of input patches, which may omit or underemphasize regions that carry critical motion and reflection information, we propose a novel saliency-based masking approach: we mask the most informative patches based on signal variability and energy. This encourages the encoder to learn the most informative regions in the signal from incomplete observations, capturing the underlying physics of the mmWave signals. These learned representations are subsequently used for uncertainty-aware prediction during fine-tuning.

papers.title: Diagnosing internal leakage currents through magnetometry of lithium-ion cells
papers.abstract: Internal leakage currents are difficult to detect and to localize through measurements at the terminals of lithium-ion cells. We measured the magnetic fields of pouch cells non-invasively with a magnetometer while a battery cycler set the current and recorded the voltage. A three-axis magnetoresistive sensor remains fixed inside a three-layer magnetic shield, and two linear stages move the cell in two dimensions relative to the sensor to acquire a map of the magnetic field above the cell. The field of an intact cell was linear in current from 10 to 420 mA, and its maps were symmetric between charge and discharge. To create internal leakage currents, two 600 mAh cells were damaged by mechanical indentation. Both cells developed a magnetic field at zero applied current that decayed over hours, while the cell voltage showed a loss of charge by self-discharge. This field breaks the symmetry between the charge and discharge maps, which allows leakage to be detected while the cell is being cycled. At rest, the setup detects leakage currents down to about 1--3 mA. The results highlight opportunities for battery diagnostics and safety, and may help in designing techniques for characterizing soft shorts.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the field around a cell maps the susceptibility of the electrode materials, and with it the state of charge and mechanical defects 23, 29. Direct magnetometry dispenses with the magnet. We then indent cells in place and follow the field of the resulting internal leak at open circuit, without an applied magnetic field, starting minutes after the damage. papers.title: geo-eval-harness: An Evaluation Harness for Geospatial Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Geospatial foundation model (GFM) research papers are plagued by inconsistent evaluation settings (e.g., different pre-processing and probes), making it difficult to separate performance from evaluation choices. We propose geo-eval-harness}, an open-source framework for controlled model comparisons. We use this harness to evaluate 100 GFMs and general vision models on 6 classification and 14 segmentation datasets, using multiple probes on frozen or low-rank-adapted encoders. We show that under controlled evaluation, general vision backbones are competitive on RGB classification and high-resolution segmentation, but GFMs shine on multispectral tasks. When we compare any two of the top-ten classification models on a single dataset, their 95% confidence intervals overlap 73% of the time. We show that bigger models are not always better: inference FLOPs correlate weakly with segmentation performance. Moreover, translating inference compute into large-area mapping workloads shows how small accuracy differences have outsized deployment cost differences: with frozen encoders on SpaceNet2, a 0.9-point mIoU difference corresponds to 5.9x the compute and days of additional projected GPU time. Our findings stress the importance of comparing models under explicit and fixed settings, and reporting uncertainty and deployment compute alongside accuracy. Our geo-eval-harness makes controlled experiments easy, fast, and fully reproducible. We release the code, configurations, and results at https://github.com/torchgeo/geo-eval-harness.

papers.intro:
Geospatial foundation models (GFMs) are developed to learn representations that transfer across Earth observation (EO) tasks, from agricultural monitoring and land-cover mapping to disaster response [53, 37]. These models differ in their pretraining methods and in their pretraining data, which varies in modality (optical, radar, hyperspectral), sensor (e.g., Sentinel-2 or aerial RGB), and spatial resolution (sub-meter to 30 m) [53, 66]. As the range of available models grows, assessing their usefulness in downstream tasks requires a practical way to compare new candidates under controlled conditions.

However, published results do not always provide a reliable starting point for such comparisons. In an audit of 152 GFM papers, Corley et al. [15] identified 47 cases in which the scores reported for the same model, benchmark, and protocol differed by at least five points across papers, including 18 that differed by at least ten points. The same audit found that 39% of papers released no model weights and that papers making up 19% of the corpus provided a public code repository but no released model [15]. These findings mirror broader concerns about the reproducibility of empirical results in machine learning [60] and motivate developing a shared evaluation harness for GFMs. Language-model evaluation offers established precedents for this approach: HELM combines standardized evaluation conditions with public results and a reusable toolkit [46], while lm-evaluation-harness provides a unified framework for evaluating language models across diverse benchmarks with consistent metrics and protocols [74]. Marin extends this transparency to model development and publicly documents training and evaluation pipelines as well as logs for successful and failed experiments [27].

Within EO, GEO-Bench [43], PANGAEA [56], and GEO-Bench-2 [71] have established common tasks and evaluation recipes for GFMs. However, building on these resources requires making their evaluation procedures easy to reuse as new models become available. Even when studies adopt the same datasets and protocols, evaluation pipelines that are built independently can differ enough to prevent direct comparison. One cause is the preprocessing needed to handle the sensor and spatial characteristics of EO data [66]. Freezing a model’s weights still leaves choices about image resizing, normalization, spectral-band selection and ordering, feature pooling, optimization, and hyperparameter search, and these choices can change the measured quality of a representation. Corley et al. [14], for example, report accuracy gains of 11 points on EuroSAT and 32 points on So2Sat from image resizing and normalization alone.

We present geo-eval-harness, an open-source harness for controlled comparisons between GFMs, to address this gap. Our contributions are: 1. A shared evaluation harness and comprehensive benchmark results for GFMs. Most GFM papers evaluate with their own code, and the same model on the same dataset has been reported with scores ten or more points apart [15]. Our shared harness is easily extensible – a model or dataset is added by writing a small wrapper and we use it to evaluate 100 models on six classification and 14 segmentation datasets. 2. A study of evaluation sensitivity and uncertainty. We show several common evaluation choices change benchmark scores. Switching from a kkNN to a linear probe raises scores by 15.3 points on average and reorders the models (Kendall’s τ=0.60\tau=0.60), and normalizing inputs with a model’s pretraining statistics instead of the dataset’s changes scores by up to 37.5 points. Any two of the ten best classification models also have overlapping 95% confidence intervals on a single dataset 73% of the time. 3. A controlled comparison of model accuracy and cost. We find that inference compute is only weakly related to segmentation rank (Spearman ρ=−0.11\rho=-0.11), however this matters for downstream applications. On SpaceNet2, the best frozen model needs 5.9×5.9\times the compute of ConvNeXt-T DINOv3 to map 1,000,000 km2, for a 0.9-point gain in mIoU.

papers.title: Weak-strong stability and uniqueness of measure-valued solutions to (nonlocal) pressureless Euler-type systems
papers.abstract: We consider the pressureless Euler equation possibly coupled with non-local forces like the Poisson and alignment interactions. We overcome the lack of strict convexity in the relative entropy inequality that arises from the lack of pressure. The key to this result is the appropriate framework of the solution scheme utilizing the generalized Young measure which yields extra structural properties for the oscillation and concentration parts of the measure-valued solution. We overcome the problem of density mismatch via two complementary techniques. The first takes advantage of a Figalli--Kang-type transport inequality. The second involves establishing a generation lemma for the generalized Young measure which simultaneously establishes $L^2$-based control in flat metric between the measure-valued density and the density generating sequence.

[2, 16]) motivates the study of weak–strong uniqueness principles. Such results assert that a suitably defined weak solution coincides with a strong solution emanating from the same initial data, as long as the latter exists. For the pressureless Euler system, this question is particularly subtle due to the possibility of oscillation and concentration effects and the lack of regularizing mechanisms from e.g. the pressure. Moreover, lack of pressure means that the standard relative entropy considerations fail in capturing the distance between the strong and weak density.

Measure-valued solutions provide a natural framework for capturing oscillations and concentrations in nonlinear PDEs, particularly in regimes where classical or even weak solutions fail to be well-posed. This approach was first systematically introduced by DiPerna [30] and further developed with Majda [29], who showed that weak limits of bounded sequences of approximate solutions can be described by parametrized probability measures encoding oscillatory behavior, together with concentration effects. Their framework was later refined by Alibert and Bouchitté [1] through the introduction of generalized Young measures, which incorporate an additional concentration measure and recession function to fully describe nonlinear limits. This added structure is essential in problems such as the pressureless Euler system, where solutions naturally develop concentrations (e.g., delta-shocks) and classical notions of weak convergence are insufficient.

A key conceptual advance, advocated in the framework of [10] and subsequently adopted in the compressible setting [34, 35], is to define measure-valued solutions intrinsically, as objects independent of any generating sequence, rather than as limits of particular approximations. This approach is essential for the logical structure of weak-strong uniqueness. If the solution concept depended on the choice of approximating sequence, then uniqueness would be a statement about a specific approximation scheme rather than a property of the solution itself. Indeed, in the compressible Euler case it has been shown that not every measure-valued solution can be approximated by a sequence of weak solutions [22]. Further, we provide Example 2.4 of a measure-valued solution to (1) which cannot be generated by an approximating sequence of bounded weak solutions, further justifying our motivation for obtaining weak-strong uniqueness and stability properties which do not rely on approximating sequences of weak solutions.

papers.title: Generalized oriented chromatic numbers and directed generalized coloring numbers of graphs
papers.abstract: For a graph $G$ and a positive integer $q$, we bound the $q$-transitive oriented chromatic number $\chi_o^q(G)$ in terms of the directed weak coloring number $\overrightarrow{wcol}_{2q}(G)$. For orientations with no directed cycle of length at most $2q$, we compare $q$-transitive oriented colorings with $\vec P_{2q}$-preserving oriented colorings. We also show that the directed strong coloring number at radius $2k-1$ bounds the density of every depth-$(k-1)$ shallow topological minor of $G$. These results characterize bounded expansion in terms of directed coloring numbers, oriented colorings, and homomorphisms of acyclic orientations.

papers.intro:
Graph theory and combinatorics contain a wealth of problems and results concerning colorings and partitions. Motivated by earlier work on the oriented chromatic number [6, 4, 5, 15, 24, 28], we introduce and study various generalizations of this concepts, which are called directed path preserving coloring, qq-transitive oriented chromatic number. The first requires a homomorphism to map the ends of each short directed path to an arc. The second requires the homomorphism to be injective on each such path. We compare the resulting chromatic numbers and bound them in terms of directed generalized coloring numbers. We then use these bounds to characterize graph classes of bounded expansion.

papers.title: Structure-preserving finite element method for the 2D MHD-$\alpha$ turbulence system
papers.abstract: We propose a structure-preserving finite element method for the two-dimensional MHD-$\alpha$ turbulence model, which filters the transport velocity at a length $\alpha$ while retaining the ideal invariants of the original MHD equations, with the energy replaced by an $\alpha$-dependent energy. The scheme preserves mass conservation and the magnetic Gauss law pointwise and satisfies discrete dissipation laws for the energy, the cross helicity and the mean square magnetic potential, which reduce to exact conservation in the ideal limit. The discrete systems are solved by an augmented Lagrangian preconditioner with monolithic geometric multigrid, observed to be robust with respect to the filter width $\alpha$ and the Reynolds numbers, and to the mesh size for small time steps. The scheme converges at the optimal rates and agrees with a Fourier pseudo-spectral direct simulation of the original MHD equations at the large scales. In under-resolved flows, the unfiltered scheme has no numerical dissipation and accumulates energy at the grid scale. Filtering relieves this accumulation and a larger $\alpha$ gives a more compact spectrum. Long-time simulations reproduce selective decay, including relaxation toward the Arnold-type bound and the inverse cascade of the mean square potential.

In a turbulent flow, energy cascades from the large scales toward ever smaller scales until it is removed by viscosity at the dissipation scale according to Kolmogorov’s 1941 theory [31]. A direct numerical simulation (DNS) resolves all scales down to this dissipation scale, so its cost grows rapidly with the Reynolds number and becomes prohibitive [42]. Large eddy simulation (LES) instead resolves only the large scales and models the effect of the unresolved small scales on them [46]. The fundamental requirement is to truncate the scales to those representable on a computationally feasible mesh without substantially altering the large flow structures [34].

For long-time turbulence simulations to be reliable, the numerical method should respect the invariants and their dissipation laws, which calls for structure-preserving discretizations. A structure-preserving scheme, however, introduces no numerical dissipation. While the flow is resolved, this is an asset; but in long-time turbulent computations the energy it conserves cannot be removed there and accumulates at the smallest resolved scales, thus polluting the simulation. Conventional turbulence codes address under-resolution at the level of the scheme, through numerical or eddy viscosity, which, however, changes the dissipation rates of the ideal invariants. This highlights an interesting tension between structure-preserving schemes and the need for dissipation in under-resolved turbulence simulations. To address this issue, we seek to suppress the accumulation of energy at the smallest resolved scales without introducing additional dissipation, while retaining the cross helicity and the mean square potential (2) of the original MHD system, together with a modified energy, so that long-time computations remain reliable. This can be achieved with the regularized α\alpha-model [36, 20], which we now review from the perspective of the ideal MHD invariants.

papers.title: Aligned Machine: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Embedding Similarity via Human Comparative Judgements
papers.abstract: Embedding models increasingly inform how people search, recommend, and retrieve information, yet we lack credible ways to test whether these similarity judgments reflect how humans understand meaning. Existing benchmarks typically rely on static, expert-labeled pairs with coarse Likert-style annotations, limiting scalability and making it difficult to obtain consistent, high-confidence annotations. We introduce Aligned Machine, an interactive, public-facing platform that transforms broad participation into a continuously growing Human-Aligned Similarity Benchmark (HASB) for evaluating semantic alignment in embedding-based systems. Participants complete a cognitively-natural, forced-choice task, comparing two pairs of items (text or images) and selecting which pair is more similar. This comparative design is accessible to non-experts, yields clean preference data, and supports robust aggregation. We report results from an initial deployment with 115 participants contributing 2,875 total labeled pairs and 872 unique pairs. Using HASB, we evaluated 12 widely used embedding models and found only partial alignment between embedding similarity and human judgments. Text-only models consistently achieve higher overall agreement than multimodal models, while multimodal performance varies systematically by task type: alignment is strongest for image-image comparisons, weaker for image-text comparisons, and lowest for text-text comparisons. Aligned Machine is designed to evolve over time as participation grows, supporting longitudinal analysis, domain-specific studies, bias detection, and measurement of concept drift across model versions. By combining accessible public participation with rigorous comparative evaluation, HASB provides a scalable and accountable framework for auditing semantic alignment in embedding models.

Embedding models play a central role in decision-making, as their representations of semantic similarity drive retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), AI search, and recommendation systems. Rather than directly determining downstream decisions, embeddings serve as foundational components in retrieval and ranking pipelines, where similarity estimation shapes system behavior. Yet the similarity scores produced by these models often do not align with human intuition (Vulić et al., 2020). As a result, misalignment at this representational layer exposes alignment gaps in systems that rely on embeddings.

Embedding models play a central role in decision-making, as their representations of semantic similarity drive retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), AI search, and recommendation systems. Rather than directly determining downstream decisions, embeddings serve as foundational components in retrieval and ranking pipelines, where similarity estimation shapes system behavior. Yet the similarity scores produced by these models often do not align with human intuition (Vulić et al., 2020). As a result, misalignment at this representational layer exposes alignment gaps in systems that rely on embeddings.

Prior studies have shown that similarity relations learned by embedding models often differ from how humans judge meaning, especially across languages, domains, and cultural contexts (Vulić et al., 2020; Aroyo and Welty, 2015). This mismatch reflects broader concerns that embedding-based representations often prioritize statistical regularities in training data over semantic distinctions grounded in human interpretation (Bender et al., 2021; Faruqui et al., 2016). There exists a gap in current evaluation practice: performance on end-user tasks or static similarity datasets does not reveal whether embedding representations align with human semantic judgments.

This mismatch reflects broader concerns that embedding-based representations often prioritize statistical regularities in training data over semantic distinctions grounded in human interpretation (Bender et al., 2021; Faruqui et al., 2016). There exists a gap in current evaluation practice: performance on end-user tasks or static similarity datasets does not reveal whether embedding representations align with human semantic judgments.

Despite growing recognition that embedding representations often diverge from human semantic understanding, existing evaluation practices provide limited ways to examine this misalignment directly. Existing datasets such as STS-B (Cer et al., 2017) and SimLex-999 (Hill et al., 2015) rely on static, often expert-labeled pairs with coarse Likert-style annotations. These approaches are limited in scope and vulnerable to inter-annotator inconsistencies (Agirre et al., 2015). Moreover, these benchmarks typically rely on small groups of expert annotators, implicitly treating expert consensus as a proxy for human semantic understanding. This design limits the diversity of perspectives captured in evaluation and obscures how non-expert users interpret meaning across social, cultural, and contextual differences. As a result, dominant or expert-aligned interpretations are often overrepresented, while alternative or minority understandings remain largely invisible. These constraints make it difficult to examine whether embedding models capture the semantic distinctions that matter in public-facing contexts, where judgments are inherently comparative and situated.

This design limits the diversity of perspectives captured in evaluation and obscures how non-expert users interpret meaning across social, cultural, and contextual differences. As a result, dominant or expert-aligned interpretations are often overrepresented, while alternative or minority understandings remain largely invisible. These constraints make it difficult to examine whether embedding models capture the semantic distinctions that matter in public-facing contexts, where judgments are inherently comparative and situated.

To address this gap, we introduce the Aligned Machine, an interactive, public-facing platform that turns broad participation into a benchmark for evaluating semantic alignment in embedding-based systems. Inspired by participatory studies such as Moral Machine (Awad et al., 2018), the platform invites people to complete simple comparative tasks in which they are shown two pairs of items, either text–text (TT), image–image (II) or mixed image–text (IT) pairs, and asked to select which pair appears more semantically similar (e.g., “Is (A, B) more similar than (C, D)?”). Using a binary, forced-choice format, our platform captures comparative judgments that are intuitive for non-experts and yield structured preference data for evaluation. These judgments allow model-induced similarity relations to be compared directly with aggregated human judgments, making alignment observable at the level of embedding representations. Collected at scale, these comparisons form the basis of a continuously evolving dataset, the Human-Aligned Similarity Benchmark (HASB), designed to support rigorous model evaluation alongside meaningful public engagement. HASB v1 introduces an evaluation paradigm intended to expand methodological approaches to embedding assessment, serving as an initial release of this framework. By focusing on similarity relations rather than task-specific outcomes, HASB enables alignment to be examined directly within embedding representations, without relying on application performance or assuming a single, fixed notion of semantic correctness.

papers.title: Schr\"odinger's Legacy: The Wave Function and Quantum Reality
papers.abstract: The article discusses how Schr\"odinger arrived at the formulation of wave mechanics and his legacy on the philosophy of quantum mechanics, focusing in particular on the metaphysics of the wave function. Schr\"odinger's interpretation of the wave function as electron charge density is generally dismissed or presented only as a curious historical example in the literature. On a closer look, however, while this interpretation was eventually abandoned in favor of Born's statistical interpretation, Schr\"odinger's idea survived in modern realist approaches to the wave function, such as the mass-density approach and the multi-field interpretation. It also proved to be of great utility in modern techniques and approximations in quantum chemistry to compute the shape of atoms and molecules. Overall, Schr\"odinger's interpretation of the wave function and his realist understanding of quantum mechanics paved the way to modern attempts to define a clear ontology of the microscopic world, a tradition that survived the Copenhagen interpretation of Bohr and Heisenberg and that is still present today.

papers.intro:
Erwin Schrödinger is one of the founding fathers of quantum mechanics. From his early works on quantum theory, he attempted to find an alternative formulation with respect to the matrix mechanics developed by Heisenberg, Born and Jordan in 1925.11 1 Heisenberg (1925); Born and Jordan (1925); Born, Heisenberg and Jordan (1926). Schrödinger’s motivation for such an attempt was to search for a theory in continuity with classical mechanics, a theory describing continuous processes in space and that did not force us to abandon entirely the ontology of the microscopic world. He developed such an alternative formulation, known as wave mechanics, in four papers in 1926. In these works, he derived the central dynamical equation of quantum mechanics, i.e. the Schrödinger equation, and the wave function as the mathematical representation of a quantum system. Right from the beginning, Schrödinger realized that the newly developed wave mechanics was not as intuitive as he sought, certainly not as intuitive as wave optics or classical mechanics. The main difference with previous classical theories was the nature of the wave function: this new entity was mathematically defined in the system’s configuration space and, for a many-particle system (described by a nn-particle entangled state), could not be factorized without losing information on the system state. In other words, even if wave mechanics looked like a theory of real waves, there were no waves in three-dimensional space, or at least no classical waves. The wave function was something new in the ontology of physics. Still, Schrödinger believed that the wave function had to be part of the ontology of physics, or (in more modern terms) he was a realist on the wave function. To this end, he proposed to regard the absolute square of the wave function multiplied by the charge of the electron22 2 Schrödinger considers the charge as a property and the electron as a specific particle. Probably this was just an initial case study to see whether the interpretation was feasible. In the letter of June 6 to Lorentz he explicitly states to consider “a certain property of the particle”. This suggests he had in mind to generalize this definition.: −e​|ψ|2-e|\psi|^{2} (1) as the electron charge density or equivalently the density of electricity. Both for one particle and many particle systems, the electron charge density was defined in three-dimensional space, and taken to be the ontology associated with the wave function (the latter being just a formal tool to compute the real charge density). This kind of interpretation was abandoned however in favor of the statistical interpretation proposed by Born, which became part of the postulates of quantum mechanics (intertwined with the collapse postulate). Nevertheless, the “battle for the ontology” was not lost, or not entirely: Schrödinger’s idea to connect the wave function to a physical entity in three-dimensional space survived and in recent times has been used in various occasions, such as the notion of mass-density introduced by Ghirardi et al. (1995) in the spontaneous collapse models or the multi-field interpretation in Bohm’s theory (Forrest 1988; Belot 2012; Hubert & Romano 2018).

papers.title: Tipping the scales in Blue Jay: Dust energy balance overpredicts IR luminosity in galaxies at $z\sim2$
papers.abstract: The spectral energy distribution (SED) of a galaxy encodes vital information about its chemical composition, stellar populations, and dust content. To model the infrared emission, many modern SED-fitting codes rely on dust energy balance, which assumes that all energy absorbed by dust in the UV-optical is equal to the energy emitted by dust in the infrared regime. However, few studies have been carried out to test the validity of this assumption at high redshift, where direct infrared observations are sparse. In this work, we perform aperture photometry in 111 galaxies from the Blue Jay survey ($1.7 < z < 3.5$) using public JWST/MIRI observations from the PRIMER, COSMOS-Web and COSMOS-3D surveys. Focusing on a subsample of 89 star-forming galaxies, we reconstruct best-fit SED model spectra from Prospector using only HST and NIRCam photometry and compare the predicted mid-infrared fluxes to the measured MIRI photometry. We find that mid-infrared fluxes are systematically overpredicted by about 10% at 7.7$\mu$m up to a factor of $\sim3$ at 21$\mu$m. The discrepancy increases with inferred dust attenuation, indicating that dust energy balance suffers from line-of-sight effects in systems with complex dust geometries. We find that adding NIRSpec spectroscopy to the fits breaks parameter degeneracies and strongly reduces the overprediction. When fitting the measured MIRI photometry together with the HST and NIRCam data, the best-fit model spectra of dusty galaxies ($A_V\gtrsim1$) result in significantly lower infrared luminosities by -0.6 dex compared to best-fit spectra obtained without MIRI, consistent with steeper, SMC-like attenuation curves or complex star-dust geometries. Our study highlights the limitations of dust energy balance at high redshift and underlines the importance of direct observations for accurately recovering the ISM and dust properties of galaxies at cosmic noon.

papers.intro:
In recent decades, a large number of surveys have found that galaxies evolve rapidly at 1<z<31<z<3, with about half of all stellar mass formed by z∼1z\sim 1 (Dickinson et al., 2003; Fontana et al., 2003; Rudnick et al., 2003; Bundy et al., 2005; Drory et al., 2005, e.g.). This crucial phase, commonly referred to as cosmic noon, is marked by the peak of the cosmic star-formation rate density and dust-obscured star formation (Casey et al., 2018; Casey et al., 2021), as well as a vast diversity of galaxy morphologies and colours (Bundy et al., 2005; Shapley, 2011; Madau & Dickinson, 2014, e.g.).

This crucial phase, commonly referred to as cosmic noon, is marked by the peak of the cosmic star-formation rate density and dust-obscured star formation (Casey et al., 2018; Casey et al., 2021), as well as a vast diversity of galaxy morphologies and colours (Bundy et al., 2005; Shapley, 2011; Madau & Dickinson, 2014, e.g.).

Our primary source of information about the physical properties of galaxies at low and high redshift is their integrated spectral energy distribution (SED), which is predominantly shaped by the stellar emission and its reprocessing by dust. Dust grains absorb and scatter stellar radiation in the UV-optical regime and re-emit this energy through a modified blackbody in the infrared (Draine, 2003; da Cunha et al., 2010; Orellana et al., 2017), especially in the most massive systems (Whitaker et al., 2017). Furthermore, the reddening of the UV continuum slope of galaxy spectra suffers from a strong degeneracy between dust attenuation, stellar age and metallicity (Papovich et al., 2001; Gallazzi et al., 2005). To extract the wealth of information encoded in the SEDs of galaxies and connect observations to inferred physical properties, sophisticated models are needed. Since full multi-wavelength sampling of galaxy SEDs is rare, SED models are constantly facing the task of extrapolating galaxy properties based on the limited information available (see reviews by Walcher et al., 2011, Conroy, 2013, and Salim & Narayanan, 2020).

Early efforts to model the reprocessing of stellar light by dust relied on solving the radiative transfer equation for idealised distributions of stars and dust (Rowan-Robinson, 1980; Efstathiou & Rowan-Robinson, 1990; Popescu et al., 2000; Gordon et al., 2001). More sophisticated approaches incorporated the evolutionary histories of stellar populations alongside dust, providing more realistic predictions of galaxy SEDs (Silva et al., 1998). While these models are highly effective at interpreting the detailed emission of individual galaxies, their computational complexity makes them poorly suited for deriving statistical constraints from large galaxy samples (da Cunha et al., 2008). Instead, many recent SED libraries and fitting frameworks such as Cigale (Noll et al., 2009; Boquien et al., 2019), Magphys (da Cunha et al., 2008; da Cunha & Charlot, 2011), and Prospector (Johnson et al., 2021) rely on dust energy balance, which assumes that the energy absorbed in the rest-frame UV-optical regime is equal to the energy re-emitted by dust in the infrared. Hence, in principle, this approach allows constraining the infrared luminosity (LIRL_{\mathrm{IR}}) by fitting the rest-frame UV-NIR regime alone. This is especially important as a precise estimate of LIRL_{\mathrm{IR}} is necessary to accurately infer the star formation history (SFH) and dust content of a galaxy (Leja et al., 2017). However, while providing an efficient framework for modelling galaxy SEDs, this approach comes with some key limitations. Crucially, measuring the starlight attenuation along a specific line of sight does not reliably constrain the global, isotropic distribution of dust emission, particularly in structurally asymmetric or highly inclined systems (Chevallard et al., 2013). Furthermore, galaxies exhibit a variety of dust geometries and grain size distributions which are difficult to generalise for large samples (Zhang et al., 2023, e.g.).

By fitting the rest-frame UV-to-near-infrared SED using only HST and JWST/NIRCam data, the mid-infrared dust emission is purely extrapolated from the inferred dust attenuation. This setup provides a powerful test of the energy balance assumption, allowing us to evaluate its predictive accuracy and identify potential limitations in current models describing the interplay between stellar populations, gas, and dust. papers.title: From random intersection to spatial graphs: a unified asymptotic framework
papers.abstract: Random intersection graphs and spatial random graphs provide different mechanisms for generating edges and clustering. We investigate their interplay through geometric random intersection graphs, where vertices are adjacent whenever they share a spatially located group. First, a Poisson decomposition by attachment sets yields exact subgraph probabilities and laws of large numbers for connected subgraph densities. It distinguishes triangles supported by a common group from those requiring three distinct groups. Second, explicit representations of global and average local clustering reveal their different dependence on model parameters and the role of shared groups in edge correlations. Finally, by varying the strength and spatial range of group memberships, we establish convergence to random connection, random geometric, random intersection, Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi, and complete graphs. We characterize the corresponding clustering limits and show that clustering need not converge to that of the limiting graph, highlighting the distinction between spatially local convergence and global graph statistics.

papers.title: Compute-Aware Submodular Online Learning in Open Multi-Agent Systems
papers.abstract: This paper studies policy learning for cooperative task allocation in open multi-agent systems, where submodular utilities model diminishing marginal returns due to overlapping agent contributions. While standard methods evaluate every candidate action to update the policy, this may incur an excessive computational cost online. Hence, we impose a budget on these evaluations and analytically study the effect of query budget on online learning. Our algorithm samples a prescribed number of agent-action pairs and applies inverse-probability weighting to their marginal gains, yielding an unbiased gradient estimate of the expected stage utility for a Kullback-Leibler (KL) mirror-ascent update. We derive a $1/2$-approximate regret bound that elegantly splits into a tracking error between optimal and learned policies, quantified by their KL divergence, and a query-dependent feedback term. Experiments on cooperative information coverage show that our approach retains high performance with significantly less computation online.

papers.intro:
Multi-agent task allocation refers to the problem where cooperative autonomous agents are dispatched to engage with given tasks. Sub-additive agent contributions give rise to so-called diminishing returns: each agent’s individual (or marginal) contribution to global performance decreases when more agents engage with a target. This is common in robotics where diminishing returns model, e.g., overlapping camera fields-of-view in cooperative coverage (Tzoumas et al., 2016). Submodularity offers an elegant framework to formally capture such overlaps and derive provable suboptimality gaps if the feasible set has added structure in the form of a matroid, which includes common cardinality and partition constraints (Nemhauser et al., 1978; Calinescu et al., 2011).

However, this assumption may fail in online learning; if the physical learning device (e.g., a mobile robot or smart sensor) carries limited compute, it cannot timely evaluate all marginal gains corresponding to a large number of actions or agents, introducing a latency bottleneck for real-time operation. Moreover, open systems, where agents may join or leave during operation (Deplano et al., 2026), exacerbate this issue; each agent must select its action while accounting for possible changes in the team.

papers.title: GeoCAM: Self-Supervised Sonar-Optical Representation Learning via Geographic Overlap Supervision
papers.abstract: Cross-modal self-supervised learning for paired side-scan sonar and underwater optical imagery is a promising direction for benthic habitat understanding, but it remains underexplored because existing methods do not fully exploit the one-to-many correspondences and geographic metadata available in real opti-acoustic surveys. This limits the ability to learn representations that are both semantically meaningful and geometrically consistent from abundant unlabeled marine data. To address this problem, we present GeoCAM, a geography-guided framework that learns a shared embedding space for sonar tiles and their associated optical views without semantic annotations. GeoCAM achieves its goal by combining three components: (i) a Set Attention Aggregator that adaptively summarizes multiple optical observations into a single tile-level representation; (ii) a geometry-weighted InfoNCE objective that converts GPS-derived footprint overlap into soft positive supervision; and (iii) an optional cross-modal masked reconstruction branch that encourages physically grounded cross-modal alignment. Experiments on the BenthiCat SSS-CAM dataset show that GeoCAM can be effectively exploited to learn which sonar and camera samples describe the same seabed patch, improving cross-modal retrieval and alignment over strong contrastive baselines. Code is available at https://github.com/FadiZidiDz/GeoCAM.

papers.intro:
Despite covering more than 70% of Earth’s surface, the ocean floor remains one of the least understood environments on the planet. Benthic habitat maps, which describe the spatial distribution of seafloor substrates such as sand, mud, rock, Posidonia oceanica, and corals, are essential for marine biodiversity monitoring, conservation planning, and sustainable resource management [8]. In practice, these maps are often produced from Side-Scan Sonar (SSS) surveys collected by oceanographic vessels or Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs). SSS offers wide-area coverage and performs well under poor visibility conditions [9], but it also exhibits a low signal-to-noise ratio, inter-class ambiguity between substrates with similar backscatter patterns, and a lack of color and texture cues that are useful for fine-grained interpretation. As a result, reliable benthic classification from SSS alone remains difficult, even for trained experts [1].

Recent deep learning methods have improved dense seafloor segmentation in SSS imagery [11] and have also explored hybrid convolutional and recurrent transformer-based architectures for the same task [10]. However, these approaches remain constrained by the need for large amounts of manual annotation, which is particularly costly in marine environments because it requires extensive survey time, expert interpretation, and ground-truth validation. This label bottleneck has limited the scale and diversity of public SSS benchmarks, and it remains one of the main obstacles to progress in benthic habitat understanding.

Self-supervised learning offers a natural way to reduce this dependence on manual labels. Contrastive learning and related representation learning methods have shown that semantically useful embeddings can be learned without annotation [2]. In the marine setting, this becomes particularly attractive because opti-acoustic surveys—which combine SSS with co-registered underwater cameras—provide a complementary modality: optical imagery captures color, texture, and fine-scale morphology that are often absent from SSS, while remaining georeferenced through the same survey metadata. The central challenge is therefore not the lack of signal, but how to exploit the signal already encoded in survey geometry. In this context, the BenthiCat (SSS-CAM) benchmark provides a promising yet challenging resource consisting of SSS tiles geo-referenced with matched optical imagery. Although the BenthiCat dataset includes semantic annotations and segmentation masks for seabed classes, avoiding the use of such labels offers an opportunity to investigate learning strategies that reduce dependence on manual annotation, motivating the development of self-supervised cross-modal approaches.

In addition, the GPS-derived overlap between sonar and optical footprints provides a continuous measure of correspondence strength, but standard contrastive losses reduce this signal to a binary positive or negative label. This discards useful geometric information that could guide learning more precisely and leaves a gap between the structure available in BenthiCat SSS-CAM and the structure exploited by current representation learning methods [7].

papers.title: Energy-Aware Distributed Task Allocation via Local Submodular Maximization
papers.abstract: This paper studies distributed task allocation under time-varying agent sets, task sets, and communication graphs. At each decision epoch, the stage allocation problem is formulated as monotone submodular maximization over a time-varying, energy-filtered admissible ground set subject to a partition-matroid constraint. We develop a Distributed Adaptive Greedy Bidding Algorithm (DAGBA) that combines local admissible-set construction, conditional marginal bidding, and neighbor-based conflict resolution under limited communication. We prove that DAGBA guarantees per-epoch feasibility, finite-round convergence, and residual-energy safety. Theoretically, we identify a sequential-greedy regime where DAGBA recovers the classical $1/2$-approximation guarantee. For general executions with partial information, we derive a local-information-factor approximation bound and conservative bounds computable from the execution trace that quantify the degradation caused by local estimates and parallel fixing. Simulations on cooperative observation missions demonstrate that DAGBA achieves task-completion progress and utility close to centralized and complete-communication references, while improving communication efficiency and maintaining strict energy feasibility.

papers.intro:
The rapid deployment of autonomous agents in open environments, such as swarms of unmanned aerial vehicles, mobile sensor networks, and robotic search-and-rescue teams, has stimulated extensive research on adaptive and scalable task allocation strategies [1, 2, 3, 4]. In these applications, agents must repeatedly coordinate to accomplish spatially and temporally evolving tasks, including target tracking, area coverage, and information gathering. In practice, the participating agent set, the active task set, and the communication topology may all change over time due to mobility, failures, energy depletion, and asynchronous task arrivals and completions [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12]. These time-varying features challenge the assumptions underlying many classical distributed coordination methods, which typically require fixed agent teams, stable communication networks, and sufficient time for bidding or consensus to stabilize [13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20].
