Recent studies on dynamic multi-agent coordination have made important progress in distributed optimization, online resource allocation, and open multi-agent systems (OMAS) [5, 11, 8, 9, 10, 12, 6, 7]. However, these works primarily address continuous-valued optimization problems with convex or linear objectives. The task allocation problem studied in this paper is combinatorial in nature. Its admissible decisions are discrete agent-task pairs, the utility is nonadditive due to cooperative sensing effects, and feasibility is coupled with local motion constraints and residual energy budgets. In particular, assigning additional agents to the same task often improves observation or tracking performance but with diminishing marginal benefit, a structure naturally formalized by monotone submodularity [21, 22, 23].

However, these works primarily address continuous-valued optimization problems with convex or linear objectives. The task allocation problem studied in this paper is combinatorial in nature. Its admissible decisions are discrete agent-task pairs, the utility is nonadditive due to cooperative sensing effects, and feasibility is coupled with local motion constraints and residual energy budgets. In particular, assigning additional agents to the same task often improves observation or tracking performance but with diminishing marginal benefit, a structure naturally formalized by monotone submodularity [21, 22, 23].

The present problem introduces several difficulties that are not simultaneously captured by existing distributed submodular maximization frameworks. First, the admissible ground set is time-varying: at each decision epoch, candidate agent-task pairs depend on the currently active agents, active tasks, residual energies, and motion-feasibility conditions. Second, each agent carries a finite onboard energy reserve over the mission horizon. Energy consumed at the current epoch reduces the residual energy available at subsequent epochs and may therefore restrict future admissible ground sets. Third, the communication graph determines which bidding and confirmed-assignment information is locally visible to each agent. Under neighbor-limited communication, different agents may maintain different estimates of the accepted assignment, so the exact centralized greedy sequence used in classical matroid-constrained submodular maximization cannot in general be enforced. Online optimization methods such as regret minimization, bandit allocation, and budgeted utility maximization [24, 25, 26] address submodular objectives in isolation, but they are not designed for this communication-limited, multi-agent setting with cross-epoch energy coupling. Existing distributed submodular maximization frameworks face the same limitation from a different angle: consensus-based bundle methods [17, 20] and distributed sequential greedy algorithms [21, 27, 28] typically assume a static agent set or a stable communication structure, while continuous-relaxation methods attaining the tight (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-approximation of the multilinear extension [29, 30] rely on oracle access and multiple rounds of gradient-consensus iterations per decision epoch, rendering them computationally prohibitive for per-epoch deployment in time-critical missions.

Motivated by these observations, this paper studies distributed task allocation under time-varying feasibility, residual-energy constraints, and local communication. At each decision epoch, the currently available information defines a stage allocation problem formulated as monotone submodular maximization over an energy-filtered admissible ground set subject to a partition-matroid constraint. Since future agent arrivals, task completions, and communication changes are unknown at decision time, we evaluate the proposed algorithm against the offline optimum of the same-epoch problem, which provides a natural and tractable per-epoch benchmark. To solve the stage problem, we develop the Distributed Adaptive Greedy Bidding Algorithm (DAGBA). Even against this per-epoch benchmark, establishing an approximation guarantee is nontrivial. Under neighbor-limited communication, each agent maintains only a local estimate of the accepted assignment and multiple pairs may be fixed in parallel, deviating from the exact sequential greedy order required by the classical 1/21/2-approximation [31]. Our contributions are as follows: 1. We formulate distributed task allocation in OMAS with time-varying agent sets, task sets, and communication graphs as a sequence of stagewise monotone submodular maximization problems over time-varying, energy-filtered admissible ground sets subject to partition-matroid constraints. Unlike recent dynamic multi-agent optimization methods that address continuous-valued convex objectives [9, 8, 10, 12], this formulation simultaneously captures the combinatorial decision structure, cooperative diminishing returns, neighbor-limited communication, and cross-epoch coupling through residual energy constraints. 2. We propose DAGBA, a distributed greedy coordination algorithm based on local admissible-set construction, conditional marginal bidding, and neighbor-based conflict resolution. The central design challenge is to realize the greedy marginal-selection principle without a global coordinator: because the marginal gain of each candidate depends on which agents have already been assigned, every agent must bid against a locally maintained assignment estimate that is generally neither identical to nor synchronized with those of other agents. Unlike consensus-based bundle methods [17, 20] that require a stable agent set for bidding to converge, DAGBA accommodates time-varying agent and task sets by reconstructing local admissible subsets and local assignment estimates at each decision epoch, without requiring global consensus. 3. In a sequential-greedy regime, DAGBA recovers the classical 1/21/2-approximation with a curvature-dependent refinement. For general local-information executions, we derive a local-information-factor approximation bound and conservative bounds computable at runtime that quantify the degradation caused by stale local estimates and parallel fixing. The analysis is nontrivial because, under sparse communication, different agents evaluate marginal bids with respect to different local estimates and multiple pairs may be fixed in parallel, deviating from the exact sequential greedy order assumed by classical matroid-constrained submodular maximization analysis [31]. The proof requires a new charging argument that verifies local estimates are subsets of the final assignment, establishes the submodular charging inequality for arbitrary, not necessarily nested, pairs of assignments, and exploits the partition-matroid structure to prevent double-charging.

papers.title: Galaxy cluster thermodynamic profiles beyond self-similarity
papers.abstract: Galaxy cluster formation is a self-similar and scale-free process of gravitational collapse. However, the thermodynamic properties of the intracluster medium often deviate from self-similar predictions. We investigate these deviations using a sample of 92 galaxy clusters selected through their Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect signal, spanning a mass range of $M_{500c}=[0.5-20] \times 10^{14}{M}_{\odot}$, and with redshifts $0.08 < z < 1.13$. Adopting a flexible framework that allows for radial variations in both redshift and mass scaling, we characterise the behaviour of scaled density, temperature, pressure, and entropy profiles, while simultaneously constraining their intrinsic scatter. We detect significant radial deviations from self-similar expectations in both redshift and mass scalings in all profiles. These deviations are strongest in the core regions, but remain measurable out to large radii ($\sim R_{500c}$), indicating that cluster outer regions are not fully described by purely gravitational evolution. We investigate the impact of an offset, a mass-dependence, and increased scatter between the mass proxy and the true mass on the radial mass scaling, finding that while its shape remains stable, its normalisation depends on the latter two effects. The pressure is the only thermodynamic quantity that exhibits approximately self-similar behaviour: outside the core it evolves self-similarly, with no dependence on mass. The entropy exhibits the strongest deviations from self-similarity as a function of radius. The intrinsic scatter peaks in the central regions and reaches a minimum at intermediate radii ($\lesssim 20 \%$ at $\sim 0.2$-$0.8 \ R_{500c}$), making this range optimal to reduce scatter in scaling relations. We conclude that the thermodynamic distributions exhibit non-self similar, mass-dependent scaling extending well beyond the core regime.

papers.intro:
In the Λ\Lambda cold dark matter scenario (Λ\LambdaCDM), the hierarchical gravitational collapse of dark matter halos drives the structure formation from the last massive to galaxy clusters. The rarefied gas of the intra-cluster medium (ICM) follows this collapse, heating through shocks and compression to temperatures up to 107−10810^{7}-10^{8} K, becoming a fully ionised plasma, emitting in the X-ray band through bremsstrahlung radiation and line emissions. Photons from the cosmic microwave background (CMB) interact with the hot ICM plasma through inverse Compton scattering, producing a spectral shift of the CMB emission in the direction of clusters, the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect (Sunyaev and Zeldovich 1972, SZE;).

Photons from the cosmic microwave background (CMB) interact with the hot ICM plasma through inverse Compton scattering, producing a spectral shift of the CMB emission in the direction of clusters, the Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect (Sunyaev and Zeldovich 1972, SZE;).

If the hierarchical collapse model is completely driven by gravity, the process is self-similar and scale-free (Kaiser 1986; Bryan and Norman 1998). With the additional assumption of a constant gas mass fraction, the various integrated properties of the ICM display power-law relationships as a function of the total cluster mass. Deviations from this ideal power-law scaling arise essentially from non-gravitational processes - primarily feedback from active galactic nucleus (AGN), star formation, stellar feedback, and radiative cooling of the gas – and have been predicted (Voit 2005; Planelles et al. 2014; Ettori and Eckert 2023, e.g.) and observed both in integrated thermodynamic properties (Maughan 2007; Croston et al. 2008; Pratt et al. 2009; Giodini et al. 2013; Mantz et al. 2018; Bulbul et al. 2019; Lovisari and Maughan 2022, e.g.) and in the associated radial profiles (Arnaud et al. 2010; Pratt et al. 2010; Maughan et al. 2012; Mantz et al. 2016; McDonald et al. 2017; Pratt et al. 2022; Sotira et al. 2025; Oppenheimer et al. 2025, e.g.).

The advent of SZE surveys (Hasselfield et al. 2013; Bleem et al. 2015; Planck Collaboration XXVII 2016; Bocquet et al. 2019; Zubeldia et al. 2025; Chérouvrier et al. 2025) has allowed us to explore the galaxy cluster population at high redshift, and to study how this population changes over time. Due to the differing degrees of correlation between the X-ray and SZE signal properties and the underlying cluster mass, SZE and X-ray selections sample the underlying population in distinct ways. It is likely that SZE selected clusters, which tend to be less X-ray luminous at a given mass than X-ray selected clusters, exhibit a somewhat different distribution of dynamical states than X-ray selected systems (Planck Collaboration XXIX 2014; Rossetti et al. 2016; Bartalucci et al. 2019, e.g.). Indeed, the dynamical state may be thought of as the third fundamental cluster property, after the mass and the redshift.

Deviations from self-similarity can give important clues about the effects of non-gravitational processes on the thermodynamic properties of the cluster population. In this paper, we use radial profiles of the gas density and temperature of 92 objects selected via their SZE signal to examine how scaled cluster properties deviate from self-similarity in concentric radial shells. Quantifying the radial dependence of the mass and redshift scaling factors across the sample, we find the strongest deviations from self-similar behaviour in the core regions, where the effects of non-gravitational processes are the most pronounced: unsurprisingly, cluster cores do not evolve in a self-similar fashion. We show that these deviations can persist up to a large radius and that this persistence is mass-dependent. We then derive the universal scaled thermodynamic profiles of the sample and the associated intrinsic scatter, using the posterior distributions of the radial dependence of the mass and redshift scaling factors as additional priors. We compare the resulting intrinsic scatter profiles to those from previous work (Ghirardini et al. 2019; Pratt et al. 2022; Riva et al. 2024; Muñoz-Echeverría et al. 2025), finding that our intrinsic scatter is generally somewhat smaller outside the core regions. We investigate the extent to which a different cluster selection (X-ray, SZE) or dynamical state (relaxed, disturbed) affects our results. Finally, we quantify the impact of the absolute mass scale and the scatter about the various mass proxy relations on our results.

We then derive the universal scaled thermodynamic profiles of the sample and the associated intrinsic scatter, using the posterior distributions of the radial dependence of the mass and redshift scaling factors as additional priors. We compare the resulting intrinsic scatter profiles to those from previous work (Ghirardini et al. 2019; Pratt et al. 2022; Riva et al. 2024; Muñoz-Echeverría et al. 2025), finding that our intrinsic scatter is generally somewhat smaller outside the core regions. We investigate the extent to which a different cluster selection (X-ray, SZE) or dynamical state (relaxed, disturbed) affects our results. Finally, we quantify the impact of the absolute mass scale and the scatter about the various mass proxy relations on our results.

We assume a flat Λ\LambdaCDM cosmology with Ωm=0.3\Omega_{m}=0.3, ΩΛ=0.7\Omega_{\Lambda}=0.7, and H0=70H_{0}=70 km s-1 Mpc-1. papers.title: SkySearcher: High-Altitude Onboard VLM Reasoning for Aerial Semantic Search
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have improved semantic and visual reasoning, enabling UAVs to search for open-vocabulary queries in unstructured environments at high altitude. However, existing systems mainly follow low-altitude strategies, focusing on close-range iterative exploration, requiring storage-intensive dense 3D metric-semantic reconstructions or relying on large cloud-serviced VLMs assuming constant internet access. We propose SkySearcher, an aerial semantic search navigation method designed for large outdoor scenes. SkySearcher integrates onboard VLM reasoning with a lightweight probabilistic representation that guides an information-driven exploration. The VLM extracts semantic information at high altitude about the target or cues informing about its location. This information is projected to the ground using the camera frustum instead of limited-depth sensors, actively exploiting the expansive field of view offered by elevated sensing. The information regarding the presence or absence of semantic cues is then integrated into a probabilistic map by modeling the spatial belief of the query, maintaining a task-driven memory for the mission and guiding the exploration towards semantically promising regions. Extensive simulations for Aerial Object Goal Navigation on public benchmarks demonstrate that SkySearcher significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in success rate, flight time, and navigation precision, while a deployment of SkySercher running fully onboard a drone demonstrates the applicability of our approach.

papers.title: Height function covariance and point-to-line coalescence in the directed landscape
papers.abstract: We prove an integration-by-parts formula for the KPZ fixed point with a deterministic $C_b^1$ terminal reward. For flat data, let $C(x)$ denote the spatial height covariance at time one. For almost every $x>0$, we show that $-C'(x)$ is the probability that the point-to-line geodesics started at $0$ and $x$ coalesce by time one. The proof uses Gaussian integration by parts for the O'Connell--Yor polymer, followed by the zero-temperature and directed-landscape limits.

papers.title: SysBio-SR: Benchmarking Symbolic Regression for Trajectory Fidelity and Mechanism Recovery in Systems Biology
papers.abstract: Symbolic regression seeks to discover interpretable governing equations for dynamical systems from data. In systems biology, however, accurately reproducing system trajectories does not necessarily imply recovery of the underlying reaction mechanisms. Existing benchmarks evaluate numerical accuracy, expression complexity, or equation-level similarity, but not agreement between recovered reactions and reference mechanisms in biological systems. We introduce SysBio-SR, a benchmark of 198 literature-based biological ODE systems with reaction annotations spanning mass action, Michaelis--Menten, Hill, and complex kinetics. Trajectory fidelity is evaluated across all systems under in-distribution reconstruction and out-of-distribution (OOD) extrapolation, while mechanism recovery is assessed on the subset of 161 systems. We evaluate trajectory fidelity across 11 symbolic-discovery methods and assess mechanism recovery for three reaction-based methods. Joint analysis across systems highlights how severely trajectory-based evaluation overestimates true mechanism recovery. Motivated by these findings, we develop KineSelect, a framework that searches candidate reaction topologies under biologically grounded kinetic laws to select optimal mechanisms that balance trajectory fidelity with structural parsimony. Compared with the strongest baseline, KineSelect improves aggregate OOD extrapolation \(R^2\) by 19.2\% and overall reaction F1 score by 14.3\%.

papers.intro:
Biological systems evolve through interacting processes such as production, degradation, and regulation (Kholodenko, 2006; Fell and Cornish-Bowden, 1997; Aldridge et al., 2006), which are classically modeled using ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Traditionally, constructing these mathematical models relies on labor-intensive manual curation from domain literature and expert intuition. Symbolic regression (SR) offers a promising data-driven alternative to automate this workflow by inferring interpretable governing equations directly from time series measurements (Koza, 1994; Schmidt and Lipson, 2009; Brunton et al., 2016). Unlike black-box neural approximations, SR discovers explicit functional forms to expedite model development and uncover novel regulatory rules.

Biological systems evolve through interacting processes such as production, degradation, and regulation (Kholodenko, 2006; Fell and Cornish-Bowden, 1997; Aldridge et al., 2006), which are classically modeled using ordinary differential equations (ODEs). Unlike black-box neural approximations, SR discovers explicit functional forms to expedite model development and uncover novel regulatory rules.

In systems biology, a mechanism comprises both the reaction network topology and its governing kinetic rate laws. However, existing symbolic regression benchmarks evaluate models primarily on numerical trajectory accuracy, expression complexity, or simple equation matching (La Cava et al., 2021; Matsubara et al., 2022; d’Ascoli et al., 2023; Bideh et al., 2026). Moreover, these suites focus heavily on physics-inspired scalar expressions (Udrescu and Tegmark, 2020; La Cava et al., 2021) or generic dynamical systems (d’Ascoli et al., 2023; Bideh et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025), leaving mechanism recovery in coupled biological ODEs unexamined. This creates a critical evaluation gap: because distinct reaction pathways can produce virtually similar trajectory curves (Szederkényi et al., 2011), high trajectory fidelity does not imply biological correctness. On the Munz2009 system (Munz et al., 2009), multiple baselines achieve near-perfect trajectory fidelity R2≈1.0R^{2}\approx 1.0 but symbolic-term F1 of 0–0.67 (Figure 1(c)). For this example, we compute symbolic-term F1 by manually matching predicted and reference ODE terms. Terms must agree in symbolic form and sign, while parameter values may differ. LLM-SRBench (Shojaee et al., 2025) evaluates whole-expression symbolic accuracy using GPT-4o to judge mathematical equivalence between predicted and reference equations after replacing constants with parameter placeholders.

papers.title: DoseSteer: Steering diffusion-based dose prediction models towards clinical targets via Dual-Response Guidance
papers.abstract: AI dose-prediction models generate patient-specific 3D dose distributions from patient anatomy. Yet these predictions can still miss structure-level clinical dose targets. Once deployed, most existing predictors offer no direct mechanism to correct such deviations, deferring target enforcement to downstream plan optimization. We introduce DoseSteer, an inference-time framework that steers frozen diffusion-based dose prediction models towards specified clinical targets without retraining. To meet clinical targets while preserving overall dose prediction quality, we propose Dual-Response Guidance (DRG), a structure-centric algorithm that probes the model's responses to perturbations in each structure's noisy dose and context and jointly solves for per-structure steering strengths. Across five dataset-model configurations spanning three diffusion architectures and three datasets, DRG outperforms 12 training-free baselines under identical reference-derived target proxies, removing at least 97% of the target error, reducing the official dose error by 7.8% on average, and improving dose fidelity outside the steered structures. DoseSteer reconciles learned anatomical dose priors with explicit structure-level targets at test time, establishing a principled, training-free mechanism to refine AI dose predictions prior to plan optimization. Code is available at https://github.com/csp2002/DoseSteer.

In automated radiotherapy workflows, deep learning models predict patient-specific 3D dose distributions from patient anatomy [2, 54]. Despite advances in average accuracy [29, 39, 30, 18, 55], AI-predicted dose can still miss structure-level clinical targets, such as exceeding an organ-at-risk (OAR) mean-dose limit or under-covering a planning target volume (PTV) (Fig. 1). Since deployed predictors typically act as fixed black boxes, resolving these discrepancies is typically deferred to downstream plan optimization [1, 3, 36, 63, 7, 61]. We therefore explore a direction orthogonal to training a better model for higher raw prediction accuracy: use structure-level clinical targets to steer a trained dose predictor at inference, thereby incorporating clinical targets directly into the AI prediction stage.

Recent conditional diffusion predictors [64, 17, 14, 9, 57] offer a natural handle for inference-time steering because their multi-step sampling trajectory allows progressive correction. At each denoising step, these networks refine a noisy 3D dose estimate conditioned on the planning image (CT or MRI) stacked with multi-channel anatomical representations such as structure masks and signed distance maps. While training-free guidance has flourished in natural image restoration and text-to-image synthesis, directly applying existing methods off the shelf overlooks the structure-centric nature of radiotherapy: clinicians specify treatment goals through discrete, structure-level dose objectives (e.g., OAR mean dose or PTV coverage), making individual anatomical structures the natural units of control. Existing guidance methods struggle to align with this structure-centric nature in two ways [12, 59]. First, most methods manipulate only the noisy state (or clean estimate), treating the structure context as a static background. Second, they typically rely on a global guidance scale across all targets rather than solving for structure-specific strengths, making it difficult to coordinate multiple structures.

To address this, we introduce DoseSteer, an inference-time steering framework and its core algorithm, Dual-Response Guidance (DRG). Designed around anatomical structures as the natural unit of control, DRG steers through both the noisy state and the structure context of a frozen diffusion predictor and coordinates corrections across structures by jointly solving for per-structure steering strengths. Specifically, at each steering step, DRG probes the model to extract two complementary directions for each target structure: the noise response (by perturbing the structure’s noisy dose) and the context response (by switching off its conditioning channels, analogous to structure-wise classifier-free guidance [23]). Rather than tuning step sizes by hand, DRG combines both responses across all target structures and jointly solves for all steering strengths in a single regularized least-squares step, adaptively balancing both levers across predictors and denoising steps.

papers.title: A Causal Energy Prior for Learning Directed Acyclic Graphs
papers.abstract: Bayesian learning of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) has long relied on non- or weakly informative priors, on the assumption that the information needed for an informative one is rarely available. In genetics and systems biology, annotation databases now make it possible to assemble a prior DAG before learning from data. Existing informative priors are local: they score a DAG arc by arc and cannot encode how interventions propagate along its paths. Thus, we propose the local-global energy prior (LGE), a Gibbs distribution over DAGs whose energy combines a local divergence from the prior DAG, the Structural Hamming Distance, and a causal one, the Structural Intervention Distance. We derive rules to calibrate its decay and the weight of the two divergences from the prior DAG alone. We quantify how much prior mass stays on the true DAG, and how much data overturn the prior, when the prior DAG is partially incorrect. In simulations, LGE improves both the structural accuracy of maximum a posteriori DAGs and the fit of the corresponding Bayesian networks to the true distribution over non- and weakly informative priors, even when half of the arcs of the prior DAG are wrong. We also showcase LGE on a gene regulatory network learned from single-cell kidney data.
papers.intro:
Directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) are an integral part of foundational models in statistics and machine learning. In Bayesian networks (Lauritzen, 1996, BNs;), they encode patterns of conditional independence between the variables of a multivariate distribution via graphical separation; in causal networks (Pearl, 2009), they encode the cause-effect relationships between the parts of a data generating process. Both have been widely applied in the life and clinical sciences, from sequencing (Carapito et al., 2022) and molecular data (Brown et al., 2023) to epidemiology (Petersen et al., 2023), electronic health records (Papanastasiou et al., 2025) and clinical conditions (Balordi et al., 2025; Delucchi et al., 2022; Lim et al., 2022; Belyaeva et al., 2021).

This interest has in turn motivated progress in posterior DAG learning for BNs: maximum a posteriori (MAP) search has improved in accuracy and scalability (Nazaret and Blei, 2024; Huang and Suzuki, 2026), marginal likelihoods are available for increasingly complex data (Kratzer et al., 2023; Azzimonti et al., 2021), and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) samplers over DAGs (Kuipers and Moffa, 2017; Nikzad et al., 2026; Grzegorczyk, 2025) have evolved to explore the enormous search space (Harary and Palmer, 1973).

In contrast, graphical prior specification has been less explored. Classical BN literature assumes a non-informative, uniform prior over the space of DAGs for both computational and mathematical simplicity (Friedman and Koller, 2003). Later proposals switched to weakly informative priors that control sparsity either by modelling node in-degrees (Eggeling et al., 2019) or by setting a uniform prior on the inclusion and direction of individual arcs (Scutari, 2016). These works assume that specifying granular, informative priors over DAGs is unfeasible because of the intrinsic limits of eliciting priors from experts and formalising them mathematically. When otherwise feasible, Castelo and Siebes (2000) defined prior inclusion probabilities for a subset of relevant arcs, while Mukherjee and Speed (2008) proposed a systematic way to put priors on a small set of more complex graphical features using energy-based priors.

Estimating the effects of interventions is a key use of both BNs and causal networks: in systems biology, network models rank candidate treatment targets, and only a model that reflects the effects of pharmacological interventions can do so reliably (Carapito et al., 2022; Klinke et al., 2022). In clinical studies, separating the direct and indirect effects of an intervention requires an accurate map of the causal pathways involved (Glocker et al., 2021). Those effects spread along the paths in the DAG, so two DAGs that differ by a single arc may agree on every causal effect or disagree on many of them. A prior defined over individual arcs cannot tell which is the case, regardless of how much prior information is available.

Structural divergences give formal ways to measure how two DAGs differ, and have progressively moved from local to causal criteria. Older divergences from the BN literature, such as the Structural Hamming Distance (Tsamardinos et al., 2006, SHD;), are local: they compare two DAGs at the level of individual arcs, regardless of where those arcs appear. Causal divergences such as the Structural Intervention Distance (Peters and Bühlmann, 2015, SID;) instead count the pairs of nodes for which two DAGs disagree on how the effects of interventions propagate along the paths connecting them. However, they have not been used to inform DAG learning: the causal discovery literature relies on identifiability through distributional assumptions and maximum likelihood estimation rather than on Bayesian learning. To our knowledge, the prior we propose is the first to incorporate a causal divergence and to encode prior information on the interventional behaviour of a DAG.

papers.title: Computing hydration free energies and crystalline solubility of drug-like molecules with MACE
papers.abstract: Accurate prediction of thermodynamic solubility is critical in drug discovery, where it influences oral bioavailability and drives decisions in formulation chemistry. First-principles calculations of intrinsic solubility offer the potential to achieve superior generalization to existing direct, data-driven predictors, which often suffer significant performance degradation outside of their training distribution. Whilst free energy perturbation calculations provide a rigorous framework to estimate these quantities, their accuracy is typically limited by the quality of the empirical force field used. In this work, we present a computational workflow driven by the MACE family of machine learning interatomic potentials to compute the solubility of neutral drug-like molecules. We introduce $\lambda$-MACE, a potential optimised for condensed-phase free energy calculations, which enables hydration free energy calculations at experimental accuracy on an evaluation set of 70 compounds from the FreeSolv database selected for their relevance to medicinal chemistry. We further combine these hydration free energy calculations with sublimation free energy calculations to predict crystalline solubility given a known experimental crystal structure, on an additional set of 10 compounds. We achieve state-of-the-art performance for each leg of the calculation, with experimental accuracy for the hydration leg, and accuracy competitive with industry-standard DFT for the sublimation leg. However, the overall errors after combining both legs lead to accuracy of 1.53 log units. This is significantly above the experimental accuracy (0.17-0.6 log units). Closing this gap will require substantially tighter accuracy in each leg, on the order of half of chemical accuracy (0.5 kcal/mol), with crystalline thermodynamics the hardest remaining challenge.

papers.intro:
In drug discovery, solubility is a fundamental physicochemical property. For oral dosing, the solubility of a drug determines the maximum concentration that will be available for absorption through the gastrointestinal tract, in turn limiting the maximum systemic exposure that is achievable [7, 26]. Poorly soluble compounds may also show increased variability in exposure between patients if dosed close to the limit of their solubility. Its importance to oral bioavailability is reflected in solubility being one of the two parameters (along with gastrointestinal permeability) that form the widely used Biopharmaceutics Classification System [1]. While poor drug solubility (for both oral and IV dosing) can sometimes be mitigated via alternative formulations, this can be costly and time-consuming to investigate.

Poor solubility also presents problems at early stages of drug discovery, where compounds are typically less efficacious and need to be tested at higher concentrations [16]. For example, in the case of fragment-based drug discovery (FBDD) it is not unusual to test early compounds in biophysical or biochemical assays at millimolar concentrations. Inadequate solubility in these experiments can lead to incomplete or even misleading concentration response curves, which makes interpretation of the results (and hence optimisation of molecules) significantly more challenging.

However, these models suffer from poor generalisation outside of the training distribution and systematic improvement is hampered by the limited availability of high quality data [6].

Free energy perturbation (FEP) calculations provide a rigorous approach to computationally estimating thermodynamic properties, like solubility or binding free energy. Its use has become commonplace in pharmaceutical R&D, where they see broad application in structure-based drug discovery programs, augmenting rational design approaches [37, 31].

Its use has become commonplace in pharmaceutical R&D, where they see broad application in structure-based drug discovery programs, augmenting rational design approaches [37, 31].

Among free energy methods, alchemical transformations are perhaps the most popular approach for constructing sample-efficient estimators of free energies. These methods integrate the free energy difference along a non-physical path that connects the physical end-states of interest. For thermodynamic solubility, the end states correspond to the molecule of interest in solid phase, and the same molecule in aqueous solution. The alchemical pathway connecting these end-states combines calculation of both hydration and sublimation free energy.

FEP relies on Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations to sample the conformational phase space of the molecular systems under consideration. Thus, the accuracy of free energy calculations depends crucially on the force field being used. Empirical force fields, e.g. the General Amber force field (GAFF) [42] or OpenFF [4], typically have their nonbonded parameters fitted to experimental condensed phase data. This often includes measurements of density, hydration and transfer free energies, and heats of vaporisation, covering commonly occurring functional groups. Directly fitting to experimental data raises the concern that the force field may reproduce the fitted observables without adequately capturing the underlying interactions in a transferable manner. Consequently, applying the resulting nonbonded parameters to functional group interactions, or combinations thereof, not represented in the fitting data may lead to large errors in free energy calculations.

Considerable work has gone into using machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIP) to ameliorate the deficiencies of empirical force fields [41]. MLIPs are typically trained to predict energies and forces using datasets of quantum mechanical calculations, most commonly Density Functional Theory (DFT). This avoids the risk of relying on cancellation of errors to accurately estimate observables. As a result, it is hypothesized that MLIPs may more accurately capture nonbonded interactions. Of particular relevance to this paper is the MACE organic force field (MACE-OFF)[25]. This MLIP is trained on a subset of the SPICE dataset, consisting of energies and forces for 1.1 million neutral organic molecules and peptides, computed at the ωB97M-D3 level of theory [8].

This MLIP is trained on a subset of the SPICE dataset, consisting of energies and forces for 1.1 million neutral organic molecules and peptides, computed at the ωB97M-D3 level of theory [8].

Although MLIPs are fast compared to DFT, they are significantly slower than classical mechanical force fields. Thus, MLIPs are often applied to model only intramolecular ligand energetics, while remaining interactions are treated with an empirical force field. Whilst there is limited evidence that such a corrective scheme improves performance [36], a growing consensus suggests that embedding MLIPs within classical force fields can introduce inconsistencies between the modified and retained interaction terms, making it difficult to achieve accuracy gains across a broad range of molecular systems [23]. The alternative setting, and the one considered in this work, is to use an MLIP to model the full molecular systems under consideration. Examples of this include Moore et al. [30], where the authors use MACE to compute hydration free energies on a limited set of organic molecules, and Nam and Gómez-Bombarelli [32] who use the same force field to compute the free energy of vacancy formation and element changes in crystals.

This is due to their relatively smaller sampling requirement compared to other free energy calculations, e.g. protein-ligand binding free energies. To this end, the FreeSolv database [28] provides a collection of around 600 experimental hydration free energy measurements against which to compare computational predictions. These values have been manually curated from the existing literature, and compounds are typically closer to fragment-like, rather than drug-like chemical space, but it nonetheless provides a more exhaustive benchmark of what has been offered in Moore et al. papers.title: Weak monotonicity, Critical exponents, and Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequalities on weighted graphs
papers.abstract: We study weak monotonicity of heat kernel and ball averaged functionals on weighted graphs, and the associated critical exponents. Under sub-Gaussian heat kernel estimates, weak Bakry-\'Emery estimates for the semigroup are proved, with explicit values of the H\"older regularity exponent in the strongly recurrent case. Applications of the theory include Gagliardo-Nirenberg, Sobolev, Nash and isoperimetric inequalities on strongly recurrent graphs and their products.

papers.title: PineIR: 3D molecular structures from an infrared spectrum alone
papers.abstract: Computing the infrared (IR) spectrum of a molecule from its structure is routine. The inverse problem is not. In practice, IR spectra are used to identify the functional groups present in a molecule, while the determination of its complete structure requires additional measurements. Machine-learning models that return 3D structures from IR spectra exist, but all of them need extra input, such as Raman, ultraviolet or nuclear magnetic resonance spectra, the molecular formula, or the number of atoms. In this work we present PineIR, a generative model that returns 3D molecular structures from the IR spectrum alone. PineIR builds the molecule atom by atom, and each atom is associated with its contribution to the IR spectrum. This contribution is subtracted from the input spectrum before the next atom is generated. To train it, we computed with a machine-learned interatomic potential the IR spectra of 4.6 million structures of 3.1 million molecules, including conformer ensembles. On computed spectra of held-out molecules, the best-ranked of fifty candidates has the correct connectivity in 43% of the cases, and the generated geometries reproduce the conformer and the diastereomer that produced the input spectrum. After fine-tuning on 161k spectra calculated with the hybrid functional B3LYP, the model can also be applied to spectra at this level of theory.

Infrared (IR) spectroscopy is one of the most widely used tools to characterise molecules. It is cheap, fast and non-destructive, it works in the gas, liquid and solid phase, and its bands carry information on the molecular structure [1]. However, the analysis of an IR spectrum is still mostly limited to the identification of functional groups [2]. Experts do not determine a complete structure from IR spectroscopy alone, but combine it with nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), mass spectrometry and chemical intuition [14].

It is cheap, fast and non-destructive, it works in the gas, liquid and solid phase, and its bands carry information on the molecular structure [1]. However, the analysis of an IR spectrum is still mostly limited to the identification of functional groups [2]. Experts do not determine a complete structure from IR spectroscopy alone, but combine it with nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), mass spectrometry and chemical intuition [14].

The difficulty is that the inverse problem is ill-posed [4]. Different molecules can have nearly identical spectra [5], while the spectra of different conformers of the same molecule usually differ moderately, and for some flexible molecules even strongly [6]. Structure elucidation from IR spectra should therefore be treated as a problem of statistical inference, and not of regression. A useful model must return several candidate structures and rank them.

Three machine-learning approaches have been proposed for this problem. Retrieval methods compare the spectrum with a reference library [7, 8, 9, 12] and can only find molecules that the library contains. 2D generative models predict molecular graphs, or their representation as strings in the simplified molecular-input line-entry system (SMILES), directly from the spectrum [42, 10, 13, 14, 15, 16], and some of them no longer need the molecular formula [10, 17, 15, 16]. SMEN and SECS link retrieval and generation through a learned joint embedding of spectra and molecules: SMEN decodes SMILES strings from it [12], and SECS uses it to score structures evolved by a genetic algorithm from the closest library molecules [14]. None of these methods returns the 3D geometry. Finally, 3D generative models, built on equivariant and latent diffusion [27, 35, 20, 21], have recently been conditioned on spectra. DiffSpectra generates 2D and 3D structures with a diffusion model [6]. MAST (motif-augmented diffusion with search tree) extends this approach with a prior on molecular substructures and a tree search over the denoising steps [23]. IR-GeoDiff generates 3D geometries from IR spectra with a latent diffusion model [7]. In all of them the number of atoms is fixed before generation, and in IR-GeoDiff also the complete molecular formula [7].

The formula can usually be measured, but supplying it changes the problem. With a fixed composition, structure elucidation reduces to the ranking of isomers, and a second measurement becomes necessary to interpret an IR spectrum. A second obstacle is the lack of training data. Quantum-chemical IR spectra are expensive to calculate, and the available datasets are limited to molecules of the QM9 database, which contains small organic molecules with up to nine heavy atoms (C, N, O and F) [28, 4, 12], or to a few hundred thousand molecules [5, 8, 10]. The key is the simple observation that the IR spectrum of a molecule can be written exactly as a sum of atomic contributions. Our model, PineIR, builds a molecule one atom at a time, and the contribution of each new atom to the spectrum is known. To our knowledge, this is the largest dataset of calculated IR spectra, and the first that contains conformer ensembles. Note that all results below are obtained on computed spectra. The application to experimental spectra is discussed at the end of the paper.

papers.title: Speckle renewal, not bandwidth alone, mitigates kinetic Raman scattering at moderate bandwidth
papers.abstract: Broadband lasers are expected to mitigate laser--plasma instabilities by shortening the coherence time. Using two-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations of kinetic Raman scattering, we compare two broadband beams with identical power spectra but different speckle dynamics. At 2% bandwidth, where Brillouin scattering is negligible, induced spatial incoherence (ISI) gives 34% less Raman backscatter than a broadband beam focused through a random phase plate (RPP+BB), an ordering that persists with immobile ions. The two fields differ in their finite-time speckle contrast.

papers.title: MonoQPM: Splitting Features into Concepts for Inherent Interpretability and Predictive Performance
papers.abstract: Alongside superposition, polysemanticity is one of the primary obstacles to achieving interpretable deep neural networks. While these phenomena are typically intrinsically linked, the Quadratic Programming Enhanced Model (QPM) naturally decouples them. By representing classes with a sparse binary assignment of very few features, QPM prevents superposition by design on its final features but still exhibits polysemanticity. However, measuring polysemanticity is an open problem. This work proposes a utility-focused approach to measuring polysemanticity by quantifying the decrease in interference-induced activation errors, which yields the practical utility of tighter prediction sets using Conformal Prediction (CP). We explicitly disentangle the polysemantic features of QPM into monosemantic concepts to create the Monosemantic QPM (MonoQPM). Because its features are disentangled, MonoQPM acts as a significantly more efficient Conformal Predictor. Additionally, we introduce CUBCars, a dataset providing ground truth information about shared concepts. Using this and other datasets, we demonstrate that polysemanticity emerges in QPM across all tested architectures, but is effectively alleviated by MonoQPM. For instance, MonoQPM guarantees 88% coverage using Adaptive Prediction Sets on ImageNet with just 66% of the frozen QPM's set size.

papers.intro:
As deep neural networks become increasingly capable, aligning them with human values is essential to mitigate potential risks (Wang et al., 2026). Towards that goal, there is an increasing need for mechanistic interpretability, understanding individual neurons to uncover what the model has actually learned. This contrasts with relying solely on the outputs of specific test samples, as models can learn to conceal misalignment (Hubinger et al., 2024). However, two intertwined phenomena, superposition and polysemanticity, pose a significant hurdle to understanding individual neurons (Elhage et al., 2022). The core idea is measuring whether explicitly splitting up features into their concepts (Fig. 1(a)) removes false residual activations on irrelevant classes, a phenomenon known as interference (Kong et al., 2025). papers.title: Bayesian Calibration of Effective Material Parameters in Electric Machine Stators
papers.abstract: Efficiency-driven faster switching by wide-bandgap semiconductor devices increases electromagnetic interference (EMI) in electric vehicles (EVs). Mitigating this EMI becomes more complex as system components grow. Therefore, electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) is assessed early via system-level simulation of the EV powertrain. A key EMC-critical quantity is the impedance of the electric drive machine, forming a major part of the EMI propagation path. Finite element (FE) simulations are typically used but are computationally expensive and limited by insufficient material property knowledge. We present a surrogate model based Bayesian calibration framework for 3D full-wave FE simulation of an externally excited synchronous motor (EESM) stator. Effective material parameters (EMPs) are calibrated to match broadband differential mode (DM) impedance measurements up to 30 MHz. A multi-output surrogate model replaces the demanding FE simulation, while an orthogonal surrogate model compliant discrepancy term assesses material modeling completeness. Using Hamiltonian Markov Chain Monte Carlo, we construct posterior distributions of the EMPs for three calibration scenarios with different parameter ranges. Two of three scenarios achieve good agreement with measurements. However, accurate calibration requires "datasheet-deviating" EMPs, while "datasheet-aligned" ones yield deficient results, indicating material models do not fully capture the underlying physics. The proposed methodology enables estimating unknown material properties from impedance measurements and evaluates the sufficiency of chosen material models. Although identified EMPs may differ from datasheet values, they reliably estimate frequency-dependent DM impedance. This work focuses on EMPs influencing the stator's DM impedance; complete machine calibration, including rotor and common-mode impedance, is the scope of future research.

papers.intro:
Since the mid-2010s, automotive industry has been constantly shifting towards sustainable, electric passenger transport, with 25% of cars sold in 2025 being electric (International Energy Agency (IEA), 2026, p. 15). This trend drives power electronics (PE) in electric vehicle (EV) powertrains to be more efficient and power-dense. This is realized through wide bandgap (WBG) semiconductor devices with higher switching frequencies and faster transient slopes (Zhang and Wang, 2020). However, the rise in switching frequencies and transient slopes increase electromagnetic interference (EMI) which is a significant concern in EV powertrains. Mitigating this unwanted EMI requires understanding its source, propagation path, and sink. While this was traditionally done through measurement-based prototyping, electromagnetic compatibility (EMC) has been assessed early in the design phase by simulation since the mid-2000s (Lai et al., 2006). This is particularly true at the system level involving entire EV powertrains (Spadacini et al., 2016; Hillenbrand et al., 2017; Gsoels et al., 2026; Bohl et al., 2026; Gruenwald et al., 2026).

A typical EV powertrain consists of power electronics, control units, cabling, housings, and electrical drive machines, forming a complex electromagnetic environment (Gsoels et al., 2026). Within this environment, the EMI propagation path is crucial for the quality of EMI models in the MHz range and above (Ran et al., 1998). A key EMC-critical quantity along this propagation path is the impedance of an electric drive machine, which needs to be accurately modeled (Spadacini et al., 2016).

Model calibration adjusts the parameters of a parametric model such that the model best fits an observed quantity of interest (QoI), such as an impedance measurement. Calibration methods fall into two groups: optimization-based methods that yield parameter point-estimates, such as least-squares (LSQ), maximum likelihood (ML), or maximum a posteriori (MAP) (Kay, 1993), and sampling-based methods that yield the full distribution of the unknown parameters, such as Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) (Brooks et al., 2011). While the former focus on estimating single parameter values, the latter aim for both parameter estimation and an accurate representation of the QoI, especially when the model is imperfect (Sung and Tuo, 2024). Consequently, MCMC is nowadays increasingly applied in electrical engineering (Neumayer et al., 2019; Badeli et al., 2021; Fan et al., 2026).

All of these approaches use a surrogate model or model order reduction scheme to reduce the computational cost of the forward simulations. This is because MCMC-based parameter inference requires repeated forward model evaluations, typically reaching several thousands (Paun and Husmeier, 2021, pp. 1, 2), which becomes computationally expensive for intensive simulations (Brooks et al., 2011, pp. 172, 407). However, none of them accounts for model discrepancies arising from a chosen modeling approach. This work presents a Bayesian calibration of the effective material parameters (EMPs) (σi​j\sigma_{ij}, εi​j\varepsilon_{ij} and μi​j\mu_{ij}) of a 3D FE simulation of an externally excited synchronous motor (EESM) stator. The calibration follows the Kennedy and O’Hagan (2001) formulation and is solved via Hamiltonian Markov Chain Monte Carlo (HMCMC). A multi-output Gaussian process regression (MOGPR) surrogate model replaces the computationally expensive simulation. papers.title: EGQCA Code: automated high-throughput thermodynamic modeling of solid solutions
papers.abstract: Modeling disordered systems from first principles across the full composition range is a long-standing computational challenge. We present a code package implementing the extended generalized quasichemical approximation (EGQCA), which describes solid solutions through the statistics of a finite set of clusters and enables their thermodynamic modeling at arbitrary compositions and temperatures. The package automates the complete workflow and interfaces with both DFT codes and universal machine-learned interatomic potentials (uMLIPs). We show that replacing DFT with uMLIPs reduces the cost of the cluster calculations by up to five orders of magnitude while preserving the thermodynamic predictions. To make computationally demanding properties tractable, we additionally introduce a cluster-selection algorithm that identifies the most relevant configurations. Together, these developments establish EGQCA as a fast and accurate framework for the thermodynamic modeling of solid solutions and a practical route toward high-throughput screening of disordered materials.

Alloys are indispensable to a wide range of modern technologies, from the automotive [124, 14, 29] and aerospace industries [88, 27] to biomedical implants [125, 82, 89], the energy sector [90, 114], and fusion reactors [55, 51, 117, 119]. By combining different elements, their properties can be systematically tailored for specific applications, motivating extensive efforts to design new alloys with technological impact [3, 64]. Traditionally, alloy design has focused on a few base elements, with small amounts of solutes introduced to modify their properties. More recently, the focus has shifted to alloys containing several principal elements, commonly referred to as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [47, 100, 121, 20], greatly expanding the space of accessible compositions and material properties.

Traditionally, alloy design has focused on a few base elements, with small amounts of solutes introduced to modify their properties. More recently, the focus has shifted to alloys containing several principal elements, commonly referred to as high-entropy alloys (HEAs) [47, 100, 121, 20], greatly expanding the space of accessible compositions and material properties.

Navigating the vast compositional space of alloys remains tractable as long as the atomic arrangement is ordered. In such cases, standard density functional theory (DFT) calculations based on small unit cells enable efficient in-silico materials design. In disordered alloys, however, the constituents randomly occupy the lattice sites, and a faithful description requires large supercells, increasing the computational cost of first-principles predictions significantly. Developing efficient methods that treat disorder more realistically therefore remains an active field of research, with multiple existing approaches.

In disordered alloys, however, the constituents randomly occupy the lattice sites, and a faithful description requires large supercells, increasing the computational cost of first-principles predictions significantly. Developing efficient methods that treat disorder more realistically therefore remains an active field of research, with multiple existing approaches.

Effective-medium theories, such as the coherent potential approximation (CPA) [122, 113, 108, 105] and the virtual crystal approximation (VCA) [28, 9], replace the random alloy by a single effective medium and thus treat the system within a mean-field picture, neglecting any ordering arising from local correlations. Capturing these microscopic effects requires structural approaches that retain the actual atomic interactions. Among these, cluster-expansion techniques combined with Monte Carlo sampling [96, 22, 36] rely on fitting an effective Hamiltonian to describe the configurational energetics, while the special quasirandom structures (SQS) method [126, 115] improves upon random supercell generation by constructing a single cell whose correlation functions reproduce those of the true random alloy at one composition as closely as possible.

The generalized quasichemical approximation (GQCA) [103] offers an alternative route to describing alloy thermodynamics across the full solubility range. The GQCA is based on representing the crystal as a set of symmetry-inequivalent clusters of fixed size, whose occurrence probabilities are determined by minimizing the free energy of the system, accounting for both mixing enthalpy and configurational entropy. The framework was later extended to incorporate vibrational contributions, leading to the extended GQCA (EGQCA) [39]. To evaluate the cluster probabilities, only the ground-state energy of each cluster and, optionally, its volume and phonon density of states are required. Once these probabilities are determined, thermodynamic and physical properties can be readily obtained as cluster-weighted averages at any composition, temperature and pressure, with negligible additional computational cost. This provides an efficient framework for capturing the thermodynamic behavior and phase stability [98, 53, 109, 54] of disordered alloys and predicting their properties, such as bandgaps [54, 81, 75, 5], optical absorption [54, 13, 57], superconducting TcT_{\text{c}} [39], transport properties [13], or bulk moduli [98, 109], across the full composition range. The method has already been successfully applied to a wide range of materials, including semiconductors [16, 53, 13], topological insulators [81], superconductors [39, 101, 74, 40], and strongly correlated materials [116].

With this work, we aim to make the EGQCA method widely available by introducing an open-source, easy-to-use code package that automates the thermodynamic assessment of solid solutions and predicts how their properties evolve with composition. Beyond these core functionalities, we extend the method to interface with state-of-the-art machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) [24, 8, 110, 7, 31, 123, 106, 120, 6, 11] to reduce the computational cost of ground-state energy and phonon calculations. The paper is organized as follows. Section II introduces the EGQCA formalism for quasi-binary systems. We state the assumptions underlying the approach, derive the governing expressions, and detail the procedure by which the equilibrium cluster probabilities are determined. Section III gives a brief overview of the implementation. In Sec. IV the implementation is benchmarked against a chemically diverse set of materials and we show how MLIPs can be used to accelerate the workflow. We then describe how thermodynamic functions and the composition dependence of physical properties are obtained within the framework, apply the method to calculate the miscibility gap, and conclude by discussing the role of phonons in the EGQCA description. We summarize our findings in Sec. V and discuss the computational details in Sec. VI.

papers.title: The oxygen cold trap in protoplanetary discs
papers.abstract: The diffusive transport of oxygen in protoplanetary discs followed by sequestration into ice in the midplane, a process known as the cold trap, can substantially alter the chemical environment where planets form. This paper presents a new time-dependent modelling framework that allows us to consistently simulate kinetic gas-phase chemistry, ice growth and desorption, turbulent diffusive mixing, and gravitational settling of icy particles with a changing particle size distribution over million-year timescales in one-dimensional vertical columns. Applying our model to a T Tauri disc across radii from 1 to 100 au reveals that vertical cold trapping becomes an effective mechanism once the diffusion-to-settling timescale ratio exceeds unity, simultaneously driving the gas-phase C/O up toward unity, and the gas-phase C/H down, by up to two orders of magnitude at large distances. All models feature the development of an upward counter-flux due to the turbulent up-whirling of icy particles followed by ice sublimation above the horizontal icelines, which brings the cold trapping to a halt and eventually establishes a relaxed vertical structure after about $10^4$ to $10^6$ yr, depending on the radial distance. The ice formation leads to a strongly peaked size distribution around 1 mic, which contains the majority of the condensed mass in the disc after ice formation, and changes the dynamical behaviour of the grains substantially. We conclude that the vertical cold trap can provide an important part of the explanation why evolved discs observed with ALMA often show high C/O ratios as inferred from strong emissions from hydrocarbon molecules in the outer disc, such as C2H and c-C3H2. However, in none of our models does the C/O ratio exceed unity, which is a consequence of CO-blocking, a chemical process where water molecules naturally stop forming once C/O approaches unity.

The transport of water ice is key to establishing the chemical gradients that define the planet-forming environment.

Protoplanetary discs are not vertically homogeneous. The upper layers are exposed to intense stellar UV radiation, creating a warm photodissociation region (PDR) where molecules are broken down into atoms. Outside of just a few au, gaseous water is only found in trace concentrations in discs as shown by both thermo-chemical models Aikawa2002; Woitke2009; Walsh2010 and observations; for a review see vanDishoeck2021. Herschel/HIFI observations, for example by Bergin2010, Hogerheijde2011 and Du2017 yielded one detection (TW Hya) but mostly upper limits far below model predictions, which was interpreted as water ice locked in grown, settled grains. Instead, oxygen is predominantly present in form of CO and oxygen atoms. Water ice is not stable in the upper layers as either the small grains residing there are too warm, or UV photo-dissociation destroys the water ice. In stark contrast, the dense and cold midplane is shielded from this radiation, providing a quiescent environment where volatiles can freeze onto the surfaces of dust grains. Water ice has been detected in the outer disc of HD 142527 (Min2016) and in absorption in edge-on discs with JWST (Sturm2023). In these deeper regions, gaseous water molecules would be stable against photo-dissociation, but the cold temperatures cause them to freeze out almost instantaneously. Even the younger Class I discs show little water vapour (Harsono2020). This vertical dichotomy presents a fundamental puzzle: since the direct gas-phase formation of gaseous H2​O\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O} lacks an effective neutral-neutral pathway at temperatures T<200T\!<\!200\,K (Woitke2009b), oxygen must be transported from the atomic reservoir in the upper layers to the midplane to form water ice. Many dynamical models for water ice formation and transport, however, have ignored this crucial chemical step. Previous models have explored various aspects of this problem. For instance, detailed chemical networks have successfully predicted the vertical stratification of key species in static disc models (Woitke2009; Fogel2011; Bruderer2012, e.g.). Oberg2011 developed a clear model based on the simple but powerful idea of sequential freeze-out along the midplane, resulting in gaseous C/O≈1\rm C/O\!\approx\!1 between the CO2\text{CO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}} and CO icelines, a concept that is challenged, however, by the vertical dichotomy. Separately, the vertical transport through turbulent diffusion and gravitational settling has been extensively studied by e.g. Dullemond2004 and Riols2018, and it has been shown that icy grains can be constantly mixed over the horizontal snowline (Woitke2022) releasing water molecules locally. Without such a model, the long-term efficiency of sequestering atmospheric oxygen into midplane water ice – a process we term the cold trap – cannot be robustly quantified.

papers.title: Decentralized Clustered Federated Learning for Cellular Traffic Forecasting over LEO Constellations
papers.abstract: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite constellations are positioned to act as orbital edge-compute nodes in emerging 6G non-terrestrial networks, supporting forecasting and control tasks for ground cellular infrastructure. However, training such models is challenged by heterogeneous ground-cell traffic patterns, intermittent links to ground stations, and the satellites' own orbital motion, which continuously shifts the data each satellite observes. In this work, we extend Decentralized Federated Clustering (DFCA) to the LEO setting and apply it to cellular internet-traffic forecasting on the Telecom Italia Milan+Trentino dataset. Satellites cooperate exclusively through $k$-nearest inter-satellite gossip with no ground-side aggregator, while zero-shot head selection lets each satellite specialize to the latent traffic regime of the ground cell currently beneath it. Averaged over $K{=}20$ post-training orbital snapshots, our extension reduces forecasting Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) by $15.3\%$ over a decentralized FedAvg baseline of equivalent capacity, with cluster recovery accuracy of $85.3\%$. The results indicate that clustered specialization yields measurable gains under the structural heterogeneity inherent to realistic cellular-over-LEO scenarios.

Cellular traffic forecasting is a long-standing problem in mobile network management, used to drive resource allocation, slicing, and capacity planning. With the standardization of non-terrestrial networks (NTN) in 3GPP Release 17 and the trajectory toward 6G satellite mobile edge computing (MEC) integration Lin et al. (2019) Pachler et al. (2021), an emerging research direction places forecasting tasks directly on Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellites that observe ground cells as part of their orbital footprint. This shifts the problem from a centralized terrestrial setting to one with three distinguishing properties.

1. No persistent ground link: Satellites cannot rely on a ground-based parameter server for synchronous aggregation. Ground-station visibility is intermittent and bandwidth-limited Razmi et al. (2022) Yang et al. (2024). Decentralized federated learning over inter-satellite links (ISLs) is therefore the natural fit. 2. Orbital motion induces continuous data shift: The ground cell under a given satellite changes as the satellite orbits, so each satellite’s effective training distribution is time-varying. This distinguishes the LEO setting from static decentralized federated learning, where each client’s data is fixed. 3. Structural inter-regional heterogeneity: Cellular traffic patterns differ qualitatively across regions, with dense urban cells exhibiting smooth, sustained internet-data peaks, while rural cells display sparse, bursty patterns Pavlidis et al. (2024). These are not merely magnitude differences but differences in temporal shape that a single shared model cannot resolve without internal capacity waste.

papers.title: Bringing Singles to $GW$: A Coupled-Cluster Perspective on Orbital Relaxation
papers.abstract: The one-shot $G_0W_0$ approximation suffers from a pronounced dependence on the underlying mean-field starting point. Here, we explore an alternative to conventional self-consistent $GW$ schemes by introducing single excitations within the recently established connection between $GW$ and extended coupled-cluster (ECC) theory. Starting from the equivalence between $G_0W_0$ and ionization-potential/electron-affinity equation-of-motion direct-ring extended coupled-cluster doubles (IP/EA-EOM-drECCD), we extend the formalism to include right-hand single-excitation and left-hand single-deexcitation cluster amplitudes coupled to the direct-ring doubles amplitudes. The resulting approximation, denoted singles-$G_0W_0$ (s$G_0W_0$), incorporates orbital-relaxation effects without explicitly introducing self-consistency in the Green's function. We assess the performance of s$G_0W_0$ for molecular valence and core ionization potentials using Hartree-Fock and Kohn-Sham starting points. For both types of ionizations, the inclusion of singles largely suppresses the starting-point dependence observed in conventional $G_0W_0$, yielding quasiparticle energies close to those obtained from the Hartree-Fock reference, irrespective of the initial mean-field description. Although this does not necessarily translate into improved absolute accuracy, it demonstrates that singles provide an effective route to reducing the starting-point dependence of $GW$-like approximations without resorting to self-consistency.

The G​WGW approximation has become one of the most widely used approaches to the calculation of charged electronic excitations in molecules and extended systems.[55, 6, 95, 110, 86, 47, 79, 56] Originally introduced by Hedin as an approximation to the electronic self-energy, it describes the propagation of an electron or hole in terms of the one-body Green’s function GG and the dynamically screened Coulomb interaction WW.[55, 54, 128, 58] Screening is usually evaluated within the random-phase approximation (RPA), [12, 13, 94, 100, 112, 27] which resums an infinite series of polarization diagrams — the so-called ring or bubble diagrams — and thereby captures an essential part of the electronic response in the weakly-correlated regime.[88, 45] Efficient stochastic, low-scaling, and auxiliary-space algorithms have further broadened the range of systems accessible to G​WGW.[93, 50, 142, 148, 40, 34, 138] The combination of G​WGW quasiparticle energies with the Bethe-Salpeter equation also provides an established framework for optical excitations.[129, 95, 86, 11, 10] The resulting compromise between physical content and computational cost has made G​WGW particularly attractive for ionization potentials (IPs), electron affinities (EAs), quasiparticle band structures, and fundamental gaps.[59, 46, 35, 21, 85, 141, 23, 109, 18, 47, 92, 96, 77]

This starting-point dependence can, to some extent, be turned into an advantage. A suitable KS reference, often obtained from a hybrid functional, can yield significantly more accurate G0​W0G_{0}W_{0} quasiparticle energies than a semilocal KS or HF reference.[85, 66, 18, 44, 65, 89] In particular, changing the fraction of exact exchange modifies the starting-point gap and therefore both the poles of G0G_{0} and the amount of screening entering W0W_{0}. Global and range-separated hybrids, including nonempirically tuned functionals, have consequently been used to improve the description of molecular IPs and EAs.[44, 65, 14, 90, 125, 32] Such choices preserve the simplicity of a one-shot calculation but leave open the question of which starting point is best suited to a given system. A more systematic way to reduce this dependence is to introduce self-consistency. In eigenvalue-self-consistent G​WGW (evG​WGW), the energies entering the Green’s function and screened interaction are updated while the orbitals are kept fixed. This often reduces the sensitivity to the initial spectrum, although the dependence on the reference orbitals remains.[47, 65, 23, 72, 74, 91] Quasiparticle-self-consistent G​WGW (qsG​WGW) additionally updates the orbitals through an effective static, Hermitian approximation to the G​WGW self-energy.[36, 140, 67, 63, 41, 81, 77] This eliminates starting-point dependence, provided that the iterations converge to the same self-consistent solution. However, the Green’s function retains an independent-particle form with unit quasiparticle weights and no satellite contributions. Fully self-consistent G​WGW (scG​WGW) removes this last restriction by iterating Dyson’s equation for the interacting GG and updating WW accordingly.[24, 20, 124, 126, 119, 25, 23, 149, 53, 145, 147] This treatment is formally independent of the initial reference once a particular self-consistent solution has been reached, but it is substantially more demanding. The frequency dependence of the Green’s function must be retained, and many implementations exploit imaginary-time and Matsubara-frequency representations, frequently at finite temperature.[149, 1, 101, 102, 60, 103] The nonlinear equations may also display slow convergence or multiple solutions, even for relatively small systems.[105, 104, 106] Importantly, self-consistency alone does not restore the missing vertex corrections, which has motivated many approaches that improve the screening or the self-energy beyond G​WGW.[33, 120, 117, 51, 78, 144, 17, 39, 42] Its effect on accuracy is therefore property- and system-dependent: improvements have been documented in rigorous molecular comparisons, notably in recent work by Zgid and coworkers,[23, 53, 145, 146, 39] whereas other benchmarks and model studies have identified cases where a carefully chosen one-shot or partially self-consistent calculation is competitive or superior.[65, 32, 74, 143] Thus, removing the reference dependence is not, by itself, a guarantee of better quasiparticle energies. papers.title: EgoMyo: Physical Hand State Estimation from Egocentric Video and Wrist Electromyography
papers.abstract: Physical hand interaction depends on configuration, contact, and force, yet nearly identical appearances can conceal different contact states and exerted forces. We therefore formulate physical hand state estimation from egocentric video and wrist surface electromyography (sEMG), combining visual geometry with neuromuscular evidence to jointly recover these coupled components. To support this task, we introduce EgoMyo, a benchmark spanning 5.75M video frames, 50 participants, 34 contact configurations, and repeated donnings, synchronizing these inputs with 3D hand pose and with contact and normal force registered onto the hand surface from bare-hand pressure. Controlled analysis reveals that vision resolves spatial structure while sEMG better estimates force magnitude, that sEMG's gains concentrate in regions where vision is least reliable, and that contact localization limits force accuracy. Guided by these findings, we propose MyoBridge, which makes the hand region the unit of vision-sEMG fusion, lets each region gate its own share of sEMG, and distributes regional force magnitudes only over predicted contact vertices at inference. On held-out trials, MyoBridge reduces pose and force error by 39.8% and 18.5% over the strongest baseline and achieves the lowest pose error on unseen sessions and subjects.

papers.intro:
Hand sensing supports applications from augmented and virtual reality [22, 11, 60, 61] to human–computer interaction [30, 13], teleoperation [38, 16], and dexterous manipulation [12, 2, 19]. Many of these applications depend on hand motion and interaction with the environment [16, 2], yet nearly identical configurations can correspond to no contact, light touch, or firm pressing [10]. We therefore define the physical hand state by three coupled components. Kinematics describe hand configuration, contact specifies where the hand touches its environment, and interaction force captures how strongly it acts. Egocentric vision naturally observes the hand and its interaction scene from the user’s viewpoint [11, 4]. However, kinematics can often be inferred from appearance, whereas contact and force are weakly observable and easily obscured by occlusion.

papers.title: Infinite Hyper-Order of Entire Solutions of a First-Order Differential Equation
papers.abstract:
Let $\varphi$ be a transcendental entire function of finite order. We prove that every entire solution of $$g'=e^\varphi g+1$$
  has infinite hyper-order. Then we prove the Br\"uck's conjecture.

papers.title: The THESAN-ZOOM project: interpreting candidate Population III-enriched absorption line systems during reionization
papers.abstract: With JWST, metal absorption lines are now being detected at increasingly high redshift, where signatures of the first generation of stars (Population III) may be observable. Interpreting observations of possible Pop III-enriched gas is challenging, as metals released by stars inevitably mix with pristine gas accreting onto galaxies and recycled gas from different episodes of star formation. Inference of Pop III enrichment from low-ionisation absorption lines requires placing stellar nucleosynthesis yields within the broader context of galaxy evolution. With THESAN-ZOOM, a set of high-resolution radiation hydrodynamical zoom-in simulations of galaxies, we investigate the metal abundance patterns observable in absorption. As our fiducial simulations do not include Pop III enrichment channels, our primary goal is to test how galaxy formation processes can shape observed abundance ratios. Our results indicate that a single abundance ratio plane, such as the commonly used [Si/O] vs. [C/O], cannot conclusively distinguish Pop III enrichment from enrichment by subsequent populations of stars. Robust detections instead require characterising multiple abundance ratios. In our simulations, a larger dispersion in abundance ratio distributions (often interpreted as possible evidence of pollution from the first stellar populations) naturally arises with increasing redshift, when the metallicity and dust content are lower. However, this alone does not reproduce all the observed results. By running an additional simulation with an updated THESAN-ZOOM model containing Pop III stars, we show that this has a large impact on the simulated abundance ratios, pushing them closer to those observed in potential Pop III-enriched gas.
