papers.title: $99.99\%$ of cubic surfaces have a rational point
papers.abstract: When cubic surfaces in $\mathbb{P}^3$ over $\mathbb{Q}$ are ordered by height, we prove that almost every such surface satisfies the Hasse principle. This extends work of Browning, Le Boudec and Sawin and completes the proof of the conjecture of Poonen and Voloch for Fano hypersurfaces. We also obtain an upper bound for the least height of a rational point on almost all everywhere locally soluble cubic surfaces and we give an upper bound for the number of cubic surfaces with a Brauer--Manin obstruction to the Hasse principle. Finally, once combined with a calculation of Beneish and Keyes about the density of everywhere locally soluble cubic surfaces, this establishes the explicit proportion of cubic surfaces that have a rational point.

The Hasse principle asks whether the existence of points over every completion of ℚ\mathbb{Q} guarantees the existence of a rational point. For quadrics this is the Hasse–Minkowski theorem, whereas cubic surfaces can fail the Hasse principle. Poonen and Voloch [11] proposed a statistical formulation for hypersurfaces: in the Fano range, almost every hypersurface of a fixed degree and dimension should satisfy the Hasse principle when ordered by the size of its coefficients. Browning, Le Boudec and Sawin [3, Theorem 1.1] proved this prediction in every case except cubic surfaces. Our purpose is to establish the remaining case.

papers.title: Integrable nearest neighbor interaction Hamiltonians and the rigidity of the Toda Lattice
papers.abstract: We consider mechanical Hamiltonian systems, where the potentials describe a nearest-neighbor interaction law. In this setting, a non trivial example of an integrable system is the celebrated Toda lattice. We study deformations of this potential (for three particles), and show that some classes of analytic deformations of the potential break its integrability, without assuming anything about the form of the integrals. This result is reminiscent of local rigidity of ellipses in billiards. The proof relies on the fact that high energy orbits for the Toda lattice approximate billiard orbits in some polytopes.

papers.title: The Weak Negotiation Function
papers.abstract:
Subgame-perfect equilibria (SPEs) constitute a refinement of Nash equilibria, where the players are not allowed to resort to non-credible threats to discourage deviations. In graph games equipped with a broad class of objectives, SPEs are captured by a tool called the negotiation function.
  After giving a quick overview of what has already been achieved using this tool, we define a variant of it: the weak negotiation function. We show that weak SPEs, a standard relaxation of SPEs, can be captured by the weak negotiation function exactly like SPEs are captured by the negotiation function. This characterisation yields a new computational result: deciding whether a given game contains a weak SPE where each player's payoff lies in a given interval is an NP-complete problem if the game has mean-payoff objectives. We also provide a new proof that the same problem in B\"uchi games is in P. The proofs reuse many arguments from their SPE counterpart, demonstrating the robustness of the tool.
  We also use the weak negotiation function to present a new proof, significantly shorter than the known one, of the existence of weak SPEs in mean-payoff games. We argue that those new techniques should be reusable in other settings, in particular to prove an open conjecture about the existence of randomised $\epsilon$-SPEs in mean-payoff games.

papers.intro:
A Nash equilibrium (NE) is a strategy profile from which no player can deviate profitably, given the strategies of the others. As a fundamental solution concept in game theory, NEs are widely used to model rational behaviors of multiple agents, or to prescribe a collective behavior that comes with the guarantee that no agent is tempted to deviate from it.

A Nash equilibrium (NE) is a strategy profile from which no player can deviate profitably, given the strategies of the others. As a fundamental solution concept in game theory, NEs are widely used to model rational behaviors of multiple agents, or to prescribe a collective behavior that comes with the guarantee that no agent is tempted to deviate from it.

Unfortunately, in sequential games, NEs suffer from the problem of non-credible threats [19, Chapter 5.5]: some players may be discouraged to deviate only because other players threaten them with actions that are not rational, with regard to their own interests. To avoid such dynamics, the stronger concept of subgame-perfect equilibrium (SPE) is often preferred: those are defined as profile of strategies where, after any possible history, the strategies that the players plan to follow afterwards still form an NE. Then, SPEs ensure rationality not only in players’ effective actions, but also in their planned responses to alternative scenarios.

papers.title: Turing instability for periodic reaction-diffusion systems
papers.abstract: This paper is devoted to the study of Turing instability of spatially homogeneous periodic solutions for time-periodic reaction--diffusion systems with Neumann boundary conditions. We first identify three classes of such periodic systems for which the Turing instability does not occur. Then we analyze a class of periodic Riccati equations and give a complete classification of their global dynamics. This result enables us to establish a new criterion for Turing instability in periodic reaction-diffusion systems of predator-prey type. A further comparison with the autonomous case shows that our Turing instability criterion is equivalent to the classical one for spatially homogeneous equilibria, while it is complementary to a criterion for the Hopf-Turing instability.

papers.intro:
Since Turing’s pioneering work [28], there have been extensive investigations of diffusion-driven instability (i.e., Turing instability) in reaction–diffusion systems, see, e.g., [3, 21, 19, 16, 17, 22, 34] and the references therein. This phenomenon occurs when a spatially homogeneous state is stable for the kinetic system but becomes unstable after diffusion is introduced. It provides a mechanism for the emergence of spatial patterns in biological and chemical systems [15]. Thus, diffusion can promote rather than merely suppress spatial heterogeneity.

Since Turing’s pioneering work [28], there have been extensive investigations of diffusion-driven instability (i.e., Turing instability) in reaction–diffusion systems, see, e.g., [3, 21, 19, 16, 17, 22, 34] and the references therein. This phenomenon occurs when a spatially homogeneous state is stable for the kinetic system but becomes unstable after diffusion is introduced. It provides a mechanism for the emergence of spatial patterns in biological and chemical systems [15]. Thus, diffusion can promote rather than merely suppress spatial heterogeneity.

Much of the existing literature concerns autonomous reaction–diffusion systems. For spatially homogeneous equilibria, the classical theory reduces the stability problem to an algebraic eigenvalue problem [15]. Casten and Holland [3] rigorously reduced the linear stability of spatially homogeneous equilibria under Neumann boundary conditions to a family of finite-dimensional eigenvalue problems associated with the Neumann Laplacian. Extensions to multicomponent systems and cross-diffusion were studied in [19, 22]. Beyond equilibria, Maginu [13] obtained a sufficient condition for the instability of spatially homogeneous periodic solutions in terms of the variation of their period under an auxiliary perturbation. Building on Maginu’s approach, Yi [34] derived sufficient conditions for the Turing instability of stable periodic solutions arising from a Hopf bifurcation, with extensions to reaction–diffusion systems with cross-diffusion and related patch models. Turing instability near Hopf bifurcation has also been investigated in a number of general and model-specific settings [5, 35, 17, 11, 32, 31].

Building on Maginu’s approach, Yi [34] derived sufficient conditions for the Turing instability of stable periodic solutions arising from a Hopf bifurcation, with extensions to reaction–diffusion systems with cross-diffusion and related patch models. Turing instability near Hopf bifurcation has also been investigated in a number of general and model-specific settings [5, 35, 17, 11, 32, 31].

However, Turing instability in time-periodic reaction–diffusion systems has received comparatively less attention. Timm and Okubo [27] investigated a plankton predator–prey model with periodically varying diffusivity. Dancer [4] constructed a periodic predator-prey reaction–diffusion system of Lotka-Volterra type for which the Turing instability occurs. papers.title: Dynamics of Collective Diversity in Human-AI Co-Creation for Creative Tasks
papers.abstract: Generative AI systems are increasingly deployed at scale to support human users in creative tasks across a variety of domains. However, as more users adopt the same AI agent, the resulting artifacts may become increasingly homogeneous, leading to a collapse in collective diversity. Prior work has documented this risk, but lacks a systematic framework for understanding how collective diversity changes as AI adoption scales across co-creation settings. In this work, we conduct a large-scale crowdsourcing study to understand and model the dynamics of collective diversity, quality, and effort in human-AI co-creation across two creative domains: Creative Hypothesis Generation and Creative Story Writing. We find that current AI agents used in co-creation can improve artifact quality and reduce effort, but at the cost of declining collective diversity as adoption increases. We further show that more fine-grained human-AI interaction, along with more diverse agent policies, can mitigate this collapse. Finally, we fit predictive models that quantify how collective diversity scales with adoption across co-creation settings, providing insights for designing AI agents that aim to preserve collective diversity.

papers.intro:
Generative AI systems are increasingly deployed at scale to support creative work across domains such as design, science, and education [1, 2, 3, 4]. In many such settings, large populations of users interact with the same AI agent (e.g., ChatGPT) to co-create artifacts such as written content, product designs, and scientific ideas [5]. While adopting AI agents can improve artifact quality and reduce effort for individual users [6, 7, 8], widespread adoption of the same agent may also make independently produced artifacts more homogeneous at the population level, limiting the breadth of ideas and solutions generated by the population [9, 10]. This motivates our central research question: How does collective diversity scale as AI agents are adopted across a population, and how can human-AI co-creation systems be designed to preserve collective diversity?

This motivates our central research question: How does collective diversity scale as AI agents are adopted across a population, and how can human-AI co-creation systems be designed to preserve collective diversity?

Recent work has begun to document the risk of diversity collapse, showing that generative AI can improve individual outputs while making outputs across users more similar [9, 11]. Follow-up studies have characterized related effects, such as slower diversity growth [10] and persistent homogenization after AI assistance is withdrawn [12]. However, these studies typically examine a limited number of configurations of agents, tasks, and user populations. As a result, it remains a challenge to have a good understanding of how collective diversity changes as AI adoption increases across a population, how agent design choices can mitigate diversity collapse, and how to predict the dynamics of collective diversity for new deployment settings, such as a different agent policy or interaction mode.

papers.abstract: We point out substantial shortcomings in the main theorems and their proofs in Hansen (2026). We also question the interpretation Hansen (2026) gives to his results.

Substantial problems with the main theorems and their proofs in Hansen (2026), henceforth abbreviated as (H), are discussed. We also question the interpretation (H) gives to his results. The main points we make are the following:

• Several of the main theorems in (H) are plagued by problems, ranging from being incorrect as stated to containing ill-defined quantities. • Substantial errors in the proofs of Theorems 1-5 in (H) are documented. It is shown how Theorems 1 and 4 have to be amended in order to become correct. Furthermore, it is shown how the error in the proof of Theorem 3 can be repaired. A number of more minor errors are also pointed out along the way.11 1 The list of errors we point out may not be complete. In particular, we have not checked Sections 6, 7, and 9 in (H) as well as the section on asymptotic theory in the supplementary material for correctness. • In the important special case where all clusters have size one (i.e., in a heteroskedastic linear regression), it turns out that under (H)’s Assumption 3, which underlies most of his theorems, his proposed variance estimator ν^52\hat{\nu}_{5}^{2} coincides with the classical HC3-variance estimator, even if there are noninvertible clusters. • (H)’s interpretation of his results, that they would establish an advantage of his proposal over existing procedures, loses much of its relevance once one allows for choices of critical values cc that can depend on the observed design matrix XX (and on the cluster structure), which is the natural thing to do. Interestingly, the choice of cc recommended in (H) based on a Satterthwaite approximation itself depends on XX (and on the cluster structure). • The simulation study in (H) does not show a noteworthy advantage of his proposal over Bell-McCaffrey, except – at first glance – in the situation of Table 3 in (H). In the scenario leading to Table 3, we show that (H)’s proposed confidence interval is uninformative, explaining the findings in Table 3. We also point to some substantial limitations in the simulation study. • In light of the above, neither the theory nor the simulation experiment in (H) seem to justify the claim of superiority in (H) of his inference procedure over all the competing procedures.

papers.title: Do Not Let the Prior Heal the Anomaly: Selective Anchoring for Detection from Incomplete Measurements
papers.abstract: Generative priors can recover anatomical detail from incomplete medical measurements, but may erase the very lesions that imaging aims to detect, even when the measurements contain evidence of them. We introduce selective anchoring that protects reliably measured image components from prior-driven changes, while allowing expressive generative models to reconstruct unresolved structure. Acquisition uncertainty in the protected components is either added deterministically to the downstream test or carried by the ensemble through stochastic perturbations of the readings. We implement this principle as a wrapper for pretrained diffusion and flow samplers and as AnchoredFM, a fast constrained flow model. Under a linear-Gaussian measurement model, the protected coefficients are unbiased in expectation and achieve nominal interval coverage across repeated acquisitions, independently of the learned prior. Across sparse-view CT, accelerated brain MRI, and photoacoustic tomography, selective anchoring improves lesion contrast preservation and uncertainty reliability, and can reduce reconstruction error within lesions. For tumor detection in accelerated MRI, with a healthy reference estimated from the measurements alone, deterministic anchoring raises mean AUROC across eight samplers from 78.4% to 84.6% and lesion sensitivity at 0.25 false-positive marks per slice from 38.8% to 47.5%, with gains in all four predefined tumor-size groups. At thresholds frozen on healthy validation data, mean sensitivity rises from 20.2% to 44.1% (37.6% with stochastic anchoring). These findings show how expressive generative priors can reconstruct unresolved anatomy without healing away the abnormalities that the measurements support.

Incomplete measurements do not constrain every part of an image equally. Some image components can be estimated reliably from the observations, while others are weakly measured or entirely unobserved. Existing generative methods were designed for image quality, not for anomaly preservation and detection. Samplers that guide or condition on the measurements [1, 3, 8] let the prior alter reliably measured components, which can weaken an anomaly and cause missed lesions. Samplers that enforce the measurements exactly [9, 10, 11] give every sample the same measured values, so a downstream test reads their agreement as certainty although the readings are noisy, causing false alarms. A reconstruction meant for detection should therefore take both the evidence and its noise from the measurements, and leave to the prior only what they do not resolve.

papers.title: Memory as the Backbone: A Dual-Store Associative Memory Architecture for Visual Recognition
papers.abstract: We investigate whether explicit memory can serve as the organizing principle of a general-purpose visual backbone. Inspired by the interaction between working and long-term memory in human cognition, we introduce DuSAM (Dual-Store Associative Memory), a hierarchical memory-native visual backbone coupling image-local working memory (WM) with a fixed-capacity persistent semantic memory (PM). WM organizes local visual evidence into compact, spatially anchored states that are updated and transported across stages, then read back to refine dense features. PM consolidates semantic evidence from training images and annotated regions into prototypes, whose retrieved content enriches the same working states. With these memory operations in place of self-attention or state-space blocks, DuSAM achieves competitive performance relative to representative, similarly sized backbones on ImageNet-1K classification, ADE20K semantic segmentation, and COCO object detection and instance segmentation. Ablations show contributions from both stores, with PM particularly benefiting class groups with fewer annotated training pixels. At $2048\times2048$, the complete DuSAM-based UPerNet segmentor achieves $2.36\times$ the throughput of the evaluated DeiT-S/16 counterpart while using $59.5\%$ less GPU memory, and $1.24\times$ the throughput of the linear-complexity VMamba-T. Memory analyses reveal spatially selective WM access and semantic associations between retrieved prototypes and training regions. Class-targeted removal and restoration further demonstrate that category-specific experience can be replenished through state updates without changing network parameters. These results establish explicit memory as a viable organizing principle for visual backbones and provide a foundation for jointly designing contextual computation and addressable semantic memory.

papers.intro:
Visual backbones have evolved around different ways of exchanging information. Convolutional networks build context through local, weight-shared operations (He et al., 2016). Vision Transformers organize interactions through token-based self-attention (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021), while hierarchical variants extend these interactions to multi-scale representations and dense prediction (Liu et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021). More recently, visual state-space models use selective scans and state recurrence to propagate information (Zhu et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2024). In this work, we ask: can a general-purpose visual backbone be built around explicit memory, using memory writes and reads to organize the exchange of visual information?

Explicit memory organizes information as addressable states that can be stored, updated, and retrieved. Existing approaches have used memory to extend language-model context (Wu et al., 2022), supply cross-image reference features for contrastive learning (Alonso et al., 2021), and preserve evidence over long video sequences (Cheng and Schwing, 2022). For a backbone built around memory, both access and state organization matter. Associative retrieval provides content-based access to stored representations, with modern Hopfield formulations making this operation differentiable (Ramsauer et al., 2021). Such a retrieval rule alone, however, does not determine what to retain or how these states should support a spatial hierarchy.

papers.title: Analytic sc$GW$ nuclear gradients with the resolution-of-identity approximation
papers.abstract: We present the first fully analytic derivation and implementation of nuclear gradients for the finite-temperature sc$GW$ method. The derivation is formulated within the $\Phi$-derivable framework of sc$GW$, using a Lagrangian formulation to obtain the analytic gradients. With the resolution-of-identity approximation, the computational cost of evaluating the gradients scales as $O(N_{\tau}N_\text{aux}^{2}N_\text{AO}^{2})$, exhibiting the same asymptotic scaling as the parent sc$GW$ method. Using the newly implemented analytic gradients, we perform geometry optimizations for several molecular systems and benchmark the resulting structures against those obtained with Hartree--Fock, $G_{0}W_{0}$, MP2, CCSD, and CCSD(T). We find that sc$GW$ generally yields reasonable molecular geometries, with its performance being comparable to that of CCSD for several systems. Overall, these results demonstrate the potential of analytic sc$GW$ gradients for reliable geometry optimizations for molecular systems while retaining the favorable $O(N_{\tau}N_\text{aux}^{2}N_\text{AO}^2)$ scaling of the underlying method.

papers.title: Milk-removal feedback shapes lactation sustainability and daily output in a model of human lactation
papers.abstract: Milk production during lactation is dynamically regulated by milk removal, yet quantitative models linking feeding or pumping schedules to subsequent production remain scarce. We develop a minimal model describing milk accumulation and production between removal sessions, and the stimulation of subsequent production through milk removal. We compare different assumptions about how stimulation depends on the amount of milk removed or the duration of removal, and consider two removal protocols: prescribing either the removed amount or the removal duration. When stimulation depends on the removed amount, declining production can reduce subsequent stimulation and reinforce the decline. This leads to a critical wait interval beyond which no repeated constant schedule can sustain lactation. If stimulation is inefficient for small removal amounts but more efficient at intermediate amounts, the model can exhibit bistability: depending on the initial conditions, milk production either persists or ceases. In contrast, duration-dependent stimulation does not permit a zero-production state under continued removal, but can generate non-constant long-term dynamics under certain conditions. We further show that maximizing milk removal per session need not maximize daily output, because increased removal competes with session frequency. The framework provides a basis for testing alternative feedback hypotheses against longitudinal data and for optimizing feeding and pumping schedules.

papers.intro:
Human lactation affects a large proportion of mothers and infants, yet difficulties in establishing or maintaining an adequate milk supply are common and are a frequent source of concern during breastfeeding and pumping (Gatti 2008). Human milk provides appropriate nutrition as well as immune and other bioactive components to the infant, making the successful establishment and maintenance of lactation clinically and practically important. This is especially true for prematurely born babies (Haiden and Ziegler 2016). At the same time, the regulation of milk production is inherently dynamic: milk removal alters subsequent production, but much of the practical guidance available to mothers remains qualitative. A quantitative mechanistic framework could therefore help translate general principles such as frequent and effective milk removal into more precise predictions about how feeding or pumping schedules influence milk supply. Ultimately, such models could be used to address practical questions including how lactation is best established, how supply can be maintained or increased under time and scheduling constraints, how pumping schedules can be optimized, and how lactation can be reduced or stopped in a controlled manner. Before making such predictions, however, it is important to understand which qualitative behaviours arise robustly from the underlying feedback structure and how they depend on specific assumptions about how milk removal stimulates subsequent production.

Human milk is synthesized and secreted by mammary epithelial cells lining the alveoli of the lactating breast. During breastfeeding or pumping, milk is transported from the alveoli through the ductal system and removed from the breast. Once lactation is established, milk production is strongly regulated by milk removal, allowing supply to adapt to demand (Truchet and Honvo-Houéto 2017; Kent et al. 2012). In particular, short-term measurements in lactating women indicate that the subsequent rate of milk synthesis is associated with the degree to which the breast is emptied during milk removal (Daly et al. 1996). Several mechanisms have been implicated in this local feedback, including mechanical stretching of the mammary epithelium or local biochemical feedback signals within the breast (Weaver and Hernandez 2016; Truchet and Honvo-Houéto 2017; Peaker and Wilde 1996). If milk is not removed for sufficiently long periods, milk synthesis declines and the mammary gland eventually enters involution (Truchet and Honvo-Houéto 2017), the process by which the lactating mammary gland returns toward its non-lactating state.

If milk is not removed for sufficiently long periods, milk synthesis declines and the mammary gland eventually enters involution (Truchet and Honvo-Houéto 2017), the process by which the lactating mammary gland returns toward its non-lactating state.

In addition to the local feedback, milk removal also stimulates lactation through neuroendocrine pathways, whereby nipple stimulation triggers neural signals that induce the release of hormones including oxytocin and prolactin (McNeilly et al. 1983). Oxytocin induces contraction of myoepithelial cells surrounding the alveoli and thereby drives milk ejection, whereas prolactin supports milk synthesis and secretory activity of mammary epithelial cells (Truchet and Honvo-Houéto 2017). However, the relationship between stimulation and subsequent milk production is not straightforward: for example, although prolactin is released in response to nipple stimulation, circulating prolactin concentrations during established lactation are not directly correlated with the short-term rate of milk synthesis (Cox et al. 1996). Thus, the physiological feedback from a milk-removal event to subsequent production likely combines neuroendocrine stimulation with local effects associated with the amount of milk removed. In our model we therefore describe this feedback phenomenologically and consider separately stimulation that depends on the duration of milk removal and stimulation that depends on the amount removed.

Despite extensive experimental work on human lactation, its dynamic regulation has received relatively little attention from mathematical modelling. Mechanistic models of the human lactating breast have primarily focused on the biomechanics and fluid dynamics of milk removal, including transport through the mammary ductal system and the mechanical processes involved in milk removal by the infant (Mortazavi et al. 2015; Mortazavi et al. 2017; Azarnoosh and Hassanipour 2020). A notable exception is the MSc thesis of Faulkner (2019), which developed ordinary differential equation models coupling milk production and removal with hormonal, neural and local regulatory mechanisms, and used them to investigate the effect of feeding frequency. In other mammalian systems, particularly dairy cattle, mechanistic modelling has a longer history, ranging from models of mammary metabolism and secretory-cell dynamics to models explicitly linking udder filling and milking frequency to milk yield and mammary regression (Dijkstra et al. 1997; Vetharaniam et al. 2003). More recently, data-driven approaches have also been applied to human lactation, for example to predict breastfeeding outcomes or identify low milk supply from milk composition and maternal and infant characteristics (Agudelo-Pérez et al. 2024; Jin et al. 2025). However, these approaches do not describe the dynamic feedback between individual milk-removal events and subsequent milk production.

papers.title: Ground Your Steps: Optimizing Sampling Schedules in Flow Matching Robot Policies
papers.abstract: Flow matching robot policies generate action chunks by integrating a learned velocity field at inference. However, under a fixed budget of neural function evaluations (NFEs), the integration result depends on the sampling schedule. This motivates optimizing the schedule to bring the generated action distribution closer to the demonstrations and improve task success. We propose Ground Your Steps (GYS), a training-free method that optimizes the sampling schedule by matching the generated and demonstrated chunk distributions at each observation. GYS applies truncated fractional differencing along each arm joint's action sequence and compares two types of pairwise differences between action chunks at each observation: differences of a generated chunk against a demonstration, and differences of two independent generated chunks against each other. After fractional differencing, these two pairwise-difference distributions coincide exactly when the distributions of generated and demonstrated action chunks match. GYS minimizes the energy distance between these distributions to obtain an improved schedule for each task and NFE budget. Compared with the uniform grid, GYS brings the generated chunk distribution closer to the demonstrated distribution and raises the success rate through the sampling schedule alone. On RoboTwin 2.0 benchmarks, GYS improves success rates at nearly every budget, with gains of 2.8 percentage points for both $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7. The gains also transfer to three real-world manipulation tasks, reaching up to 3.3 percentage points. Code is available at https://github.com/D-Robotics-AI-Lab/GroundYourSteps.

papers.intro:
Vision–language–action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions (Ma et al., 2026b; Kawaharazuka et al., 2025). Flow-based VLAs couple pretrained vision–language backbones with action experts (Black et al., 2025b). Recent models use flow matching (Black et al., 2025a; NVIDIA et al., 2025) to generate these actions in chunks (Zhao et al., 2023). During training, the action expert predicts the velocities of straight paths from Gaussian noise to demonstrated action chunks. Under squared loss, the optimal prediction is the conditional average of these velocities at a given state, flow time, and observation, called the marginal velocity field (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023). Exact integration of this field transports Gaussian noise to the demonstrated action distribution (Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023). In practice, however, the policy integrates a learned approximation to the marginal field with finite neural function evaluations (NFEs), so the generated action distribution can deviate from the demonstrated distribution.

Vision–language–action (VLA) models translate visual observations and language instructions into robot actions (Ma et al., 2026b; Kawaharazuka et al., 2025). Flow-based VLAs couple pretrained vision–language backbones with action experts (Black et al., 2025b). Recent models use flow matching (Black et al., 2025a; NVIDIA et al., 2025) to generate these actions in chunks (Zhao et al., 2023). During training, the action expert predicts the velocities of straight paths from Gaussian noise to demonstrated action chunks. Under squared loss, the optimal prediction is the conditional average of these velocities at a given state, flow time, and observation, called the marginal velocity field (Lipman et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2023). Exact integration of this field transports Gaussian noise to the demonstrated action distribution (Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden, 2023). In practice, however, the policy integrates a learned approximation to the marginal field with finite neural function evaluations (NFEs), so the generated action distribution can deviate from the demonstrated distribution.

Two mechanisms shape the generated action distribution under this finite-step integration. (i) Trajectory curvature—averaging differently directed path velocities can produce curved marginal trajectories, which coarse integration steps may fail to resolve (Ma et al., 2026a; Kornilov et al., 2024). (ii) Lipschitz window—near the action endpoint, the marginal field can become highly sensitive to the action state, allowing small deviations from the marginal flow to be amplified (Gao et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026b) (Section A.3). Since curvature and the amplification of small deviations vary along flow time, evaluations at different times need not influence the endpoint distribution equally. Choosing these evaluation times, the sampling schedule, therefore provides a way to change the generated distribution. Our goal is to optimize the sampling schedule to bring the generated distribution into agreement with the demonstrations and improve task success for each fixed budget BB.

To see whether these distributional effects matter in closed loop, we vary the NFE budget and sampling schedule for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and GR00T N1.7 across 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks (, panel (a)). Under uniform sampling, success peaks at B=4B=4 for π0.5\pi_{0.5} and B=6B=6 for GR00T N1.7, then falls at larger budgets. At fixed B=5B=5, a moderate bias toward the noise endpoint outperforms the uniform grid, whereas concentrating nodes near either endpoint lowers success. The non-monotonic budget trend and fixed-budget schedule sensitivity are consistent with the combined effects of trajectory curvature and late-time amplification. Taken with the mechanisms above, these observations identify the sampling schedule as a lever on both the generated action distribution and task success. They motivate a demonstration-grounded criterion for selecting evaluation times at each fixed budget.

We propose Ground Your Steps (GYS), a training-free method that grounds the sampling schedule in the demonstrations, motivated by Drifting (Deng et al., 2026), which trains a generator by driving its generated distribution into agreement with the data distribution. GYS’s target is that the chunks the frozen policy generates be distributed as the demonstrated ones at each observation. GYS compares candidate sampling schedules using a truncated fractional-difference operator: it applies finite differences of a calibrated, possibly non-integer order along each arm joint’s action sequence. This generalizes first-order differences between consecutive actions and second-order differences between those changes, using a fixed window of action steps. One demonstrated chunk per observation still cannot estimate the demonstrated distribution, so GYS instead compares two types of pairwise differences: generated–demonstrated differences and generated–generated differences, formed at the same observation using independent noise draws. Both are transformed by the fractional-difference operator. Under the stated identifiability assumptions, their distributions coincide exactly when the transformed action distributions match, so driving them into agreement realizes this target (Section 4.2). GYS optimizes the sampling schedule offline for each task by minimizing an energy distance between the two transformed pairwise-difference distributions (, panel (c)), and the optimized schedule replaces the uniform one. At the same budget, GYS brings the generated distribution closer to the demonstrated one and raises the task success rate.

papers.title: SimFusion: Multi-Fidelity Simulation-based Testing of Automated Driving Systems
papers.abstract: Simulation is the primary means of validating automated driving systems (ADS). Testing typically relies on a single simulator, forcing a trade-off between the speed of low-fidelity (LoFi) simulation and the realism of computationally expensive high-fidelity (HiFi) simulation. We present SimFusion, a multi-fidelity search-based testing framework that decides, for every candidate scenario, which simulator should execute it. Rather than approximating the ADS or its fitness, SimFusion learns whether LoFi and HiFi simulators are likely to agree on a scenario's outcome: scenarios predicted to agree run in the fast LoFi simulator, while all others are conservatively run in HiFi. We evaluate SimFusion on two ADS stacks, three driving scenarios, and four simulators, against LoFi-only, HiFi-only, and surrogate-assisted testing. Across six runs per configuration, SimFusion finds on average 2.1x more HiFi-validated failures than HiFi-only testing and 1.6x more than surrogate-assisted testing, up to 3x and 1.7x faster per failure, while executing 31% fewer HiFi simulations than HiFi-only testing. SimFusion also achieves the highest failure coverage in all three scenarios. An ablation with random simulator selection shows that the gains stem from the learned agreement model rather than from combining two simulators alone. These results suggest that predicting cross-simulator agreement is an effective alternative to surrogate modeling, as simulation fidelity can serve as an optimization dimension in ADS testing.

papers.title: A Bayesian Approach to Prioritizing the Follow-Up of Near-Earth Objects
papers.abstract:
We present pneo, a Bayesian classifier that computes the probability that a single-night tracklet belongs to a near-Earth object (NEO), using only its sky position, angular motion, and apparent magnitude. A tracklet does not determine the object's distance or radial velocity, so pneo integrates a model of the Solar System's small-body populations over all bound orbits consistent with it. The result is the exact posterior probability under that model, with no tuned scores or separately chosen priors: its classifications are optimal for the adopted model, and its probabilities are calibrated.
  On real discovery tracklets from the NEO Confirmation Page, the classifier is well calibrated and its selection is 1.14 times purer than that of digest2, the classifier now in use, at the same completeness. The advantage grows at Rubin's depth, where the faint background of main-belt and more distant objects is still largely undiscovered. On simulated tracklets to that depth, its selection is 2 times purer than that of digest2 (96% against 48%). On the Rubin alert stream and Rubin Data Preview 2 its selection is 1.4-1.7 times purer than that of digest2, and its predicted NEO counts are close to those observed. By raising the fraction of follow-up targets that are NEOs, pneo could potentially double the effective capacity of NEO follow-up in the Rubin era.

papers.intro:
Near-Earth Objects (NEOs)—asteroids and comets with orbits that bring them within 1.3 AU of the Sun—are typically discovered by wide-field sky surveys that detect new moving objects by taking a sequence of two to four images within a single night. Detections that cannot be matched to any known body are reported to the Minor Planet Center (MPC) as a tracklet. Candidates consistent with an NEO orbit are identified and posted to the MPC’s NEO Confirmation Page [22, 36, NEOCP;]. A candidate remains there until follow-up astrometry either secures its orbit—earning it a designation—or identifies it as a main-belt asteroid or other non-NEO. In this way, the NEOCP serves as the central community clearinghouse for collecting NEO candidates and prioritizing their follow-up.

A candidate remains there until follow-up astrometry either secures its orbit—earning it a designation—or identifies it as a main-belt asteroid or other non-NEO. In this way, the NEOCP serves as the central community clearinghouse for collecting NEO candidates and prioritizing their follow-up.

The Vera C. Rubin Observatory’s Legacy Survey of Space and Time [17, LSST;] will make this prioritization much harder. Today, roughly 5–27 candidates are added to the NEOCP each night, depending on lunar phase [43]. But simulating the first year of LSST under the current posting criterion, a digest2 score of at least 65, Wagg et al. [43] estimated that Rubin alone could submit about 129 candidates per night, around eight times the present rate, with only 8.3% of the candidates being NEOs. Most of the remainder are faint, previously undiscovered main-belt asteroids. Even removing candidates that Rubin is likely to recover on its own reduces the list only to about 64 per night, with the NEO fraction still below 10%.

papers.title: Cosmological rigidity in $3$ spacetime dimensions
papers.abstract: We establish rigidity theorems for cosmological spacetimes in $3$ spacetime dimensions. In the setting of the Bartnik Splitting Conjecture, under the additional assumptions of null geodesic completeness and the dominant energy condition, we show that the spatial topology is either spherical or the spacetime splits as a product. Our methods rely on the theory of marginally outer trapped surfaces, known rigidity results in the presence of a timelike or null line, and more recent rigidity results in the context of Penrose's singularity theorem due to the first two authors, from which the existence of a foliation by totally geodesic null hypersurfaces can be concluded. Our second main result closes the argument by establishing a splitting theorem for cosmological and null geodesically complete $3$-dimensional spacetimes which satisfy the dominant energy condition and which admit a foliation of the aforementioned type. In its proof, we make use of the local Kundt structure of the metric and construct a global parallel generator for the null foliation.

papers.title: Anti-AI in the Wild: From Toxic Discourse to Action
papers.abstract: Online discussion of generative AI has become increasingly contentious, and communities devoted to supporting, opposing, or debating AI have emerged on social media. Some of these communities take anti-AI actions, such as deploying crawler tarpits and data-poisoning services to interfere with data collection and model training. Yet, the scope of these actions and their relationship to online discourse remain poorly understood. In this paper, we present the first measurement study of online conflict over generative AI, from toxic discourse to anti-AI actions. We collect 931,640 posts from 25 Reddit communities, label them with a large language model detector validated against human labels, identify 3,312 anti-AI actions, and trace the output of three deployed anti-AI tools. Our analysis reveals that 30.0% of posts in communities devoted to this conflict are toxic, compared to 4.4% in general AI communities. Anti-AI actions in these communities mainly target AI crawling or model training data, such as image cloaking and data poisoning. We further examine the implications of these anti-AI actions for AI training, by analyzing the text and code generated from deployed tools. Notably, 66.5% of the code samples generated by a data-poisoning service contain fabricated facts, misused APIs, or broken logic, yet 93.6% passes a public code-curation pipeline, close to the rate for real source code (95.0%). For crawler tarpit output, adding a period to the end of each paragraph increases the curation survival rate from 16.4% to 91.9%. We also find that crawler tarpit and data-poisoning output has already entered Common Crawl, a widely used public web archive, and that crawler tarpit output has also entered FineWeb, a released pretraining dataset. We hope our study can facilitate a better understanding of online conflict over generative AI and its implications for content moderation and AI training.

papers.title: Dancing dervishes, spinning skirts and whirling waves
papers.abstract: Inspired by the patterns seen in the tunic of a whirling dervish or the long skirt of a Kathak dancer, we study the dynamics of a \emph{soft} heavy circular sheet spinning steadily around its axis. Using experiments, we show that the initially draped sheet can pass through three archetypal states as it rotates: a gravity-dominated draped rotation state, a flat state, and finally a whirling state marked by retrograde rotation of wavy patterns relative to the rotating frame. We map out these various configurations in a three-dimensional phase diagram, analyze the transitions using a minimal model, and derive scaling laws to describe the phase boundaries which we confirm using experiments.

papers.title: PAC Learning to Sample: On Computational Aspects of Language Generation
papers.abstract:
The success of language models has motivated theoretical work on learning to sample from distributions on discrete domains. A prominent abstraction is the model of language generation in the limit, introduced by Kleinberg and Mullainathan (NeurIPS 2024), in which the algorithm must generate from the target language after some finite but unspecified number of positive examples. While its positive results are surprisingly general, most guarantees are qualitative. In this work, we seek quantitative guarantees on sample and time complexity, inspired by statistical and computational learning theory.
  To this end, we study a PAC model of language generation, proposed (in a different context) by De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio (SODA 2015), in which a Boolean concept class $C$ over $\{-1,1\}^n$ defines the target languages: given uniformly random positive examples of an unknown concept $f \in C$, the learner must output a sampler whose output distribution (conditioned on the training data) is close in total variation to the uniform distribution over $f^{-1}(1)$. Their work implicitly gives an efficient algorithm for PAC learning to sample $C$, given three primitives for $C$: an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and an SQ learner.
  We ask whether these ingredients, in particular online learnability, are necessary. First, we construct a Boolean concept class $C$ for which online learning is cryptographically hard, yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient. Then, we develop new algorithms that use offline ERM oracles instead of online learners, together with approximate sampling/counting oracles for intersections of concepts in $C$ and an SQ learner for $C$. We view our results, together with the work of De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio, as a first step towards understanding the computational complexity of language generation.

papers.title: Unsupervised and explainable authorization of change point in multivariate industrial data for trustworthy system and process monitoring
papers.abstract: The paper introduces a Change point Hypothesis Assessment for Significance in Multivariate data (CHASM) - a novel non-parametric approach for evaluating the significance of change points detected in multivariate data, especially relevant for a trustworthy autonomous industrial system. The method is highly scalable, doesn't require data labeling, and allows for customizable evaluation criteria, such as inter-component relationships. Its non-parametric nature broadens applicability to non-Gaussian distributed data. CHASM incorporates robust auxiliary statistics that maintain reliability even in the presence of outliers, enabling accurate assessment of change point significance for complex data. Beyond statistical significance testing, CHASM also facilitates root-cause analysis of detected changes. It offers a solution expected by practitioners for validating change points identified by segmentation-based algorithms, particularly those lacking rigorous statistical foundations. To support situation aware decision making, a {trustworthy factor} is introduced and its performance demonstrated for simulated and real-world data recorded in machine monitoring system. Using MAPE, it was evidenced that the two-stage procedure - identification of the change point and authorization of the change point - significantly outperforms (23-fold in the reported experiment) the one-stage scheme. All these are essential in real-world applications, where overfitting and false alarms can lead to loss of trust in technical solutions.

papers.title: Data-driven framework for invariant manifold identification in multiscale systems
papers.abstract: Multiscale dynamical systems often exhibit fast transient behavior followed by slow evolution on a low-dimensional attracting manifold, on which their long-term dynamics unfold. Identifying this structure directly from data remains challenging when the governing equations, Jacobians, and fast-slow variable partitions are unknown. In this work, we propose a fully data-driven framework for timescale decomposition, slow invariant manifold (SIM) approximation, and reduced-order model identification. A sparse-regression surrogate of the vector field is reconstructed from the data, and its Jacobian, estimated with a matrix-free Krylov method, is analysed with Computational Singular Perturbation diagnostics. The resulting fast-slow partition guides the learning of explicit SIM algebraic representations through regression, and the reduced model follows by restricting the dynamics to it. For a linear stochastic system, this regression agrees with the Mori-Zwanzig projection at leading order in the timescale ratio. We demonstrate the validity of the framework on an illustrative linear system, the Michaelis-Menten model, a biofilm growth model, and a five-dimensional target-mediated drug disposition (TMDD) model. The method accurately identifies fast variables, reconstructs slow invariant manifolds, and generates accurate reduced models. Furthermore, we map the performance boundaries of the framework under sparse sampling and measurement noise, showing robust recovery for low-dimensional systems and highlighting data-requirement limits in higher dimensions. These results demonstrate that interpretable multiscale reduction can be achieved directly from time-series data, without requiring explicit prior knowledge of the underlying fast/slow timescale separation.

papers.title: Spin-Orbit Coupling in Symmetry-Forbidden Reactions: A Selection Rule Tested on the Chalcogen Trimers
papers.abstract: A reaction is forbidden by orbital symmetry when an occupied and an empty orbital of different symmetry change places along its path. With spin-orbit coupling orbitals become spinors, and those of two such orbitals can mix only if the orbitals differ by the symmetry of a rotation; the operator component of that symmetry couples ground state and diradical triplet. We test this rule on the ring opening of the chalcogen trimers O3 to Po3, where an in-plane and an out-of-plane orbital cross ($C_{2v}$ surfaces; NEVPT2, spin-orbit configuration interaction), by letting the operator components act separately. In Se3 and Te3 the component named by the rule alone lowers the barrier by 2.2 and 5.1 kcal/mol (complete operator: 2.2 and 5.2), the other two by 0.2 and 1.3 kcal/mol; in Po3 they contribute in second order. The triplet crosses the ground state 6.5 to 9.0 kcal/mol below the forbidden saddle. Spin-orbit coupling makes this crossing passable in O3 and S3 and, from Se3 on, merges the two states into one surface whose saddle lies 2.6, 5.5, and 13.1 kcal/mol lower. Molecular rotation obeys the same rule but is 6 to $2.8\times 10^{3}$ times weaker, which bears on the lifetime predicted for cyclic ozone.

papers.title: Distractor-Robust Reinforcement Learning via Variational Bisimulation
papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) promises data efficiency and generalization, but typical reconstruction-based objectives encourage models to waste representational capacity on task-irrelevant distractors. We introduce VIBES (Variational Inference for Bisimulation-based Encoded States), a new objective that replaces pixel reconstruction with an adversarial term, which enforces that latent states suffice to predict both rewards and the next latent state. We show that this objective measures how far the encoder is from reward and dynamics sufficiency, and that whenever exact sufficiency is attainable, its global optima induce bisimulation relations on histories. Combined with a fixed-capacity latent bottleneck, this encourages latent states to retain task-relevant information while discarding irrelevant variation. Our method serves as a drop-in replacement for Dreamer's model-learning component, achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Distracting Control Suite, and extends to visually complex manipulation in Realistic ManiSkill. Unlike prior approaches, it does not rely on image-specific augmentations and applies equally well to high-dimensional vector-state tasks, demonstrated on a 100-link swimmer robot. Finally, latent-space analyses (UMAP embeddings and nearest-neighbor probes) confirm that the learned representations are sensitive to task-relevant structure while invariant to distractors.

papers.title: Generic bi-stochastic semigroups are flows
papers.abstract: We demonstrate genericity wrt. the weak polynomial topology of the space $\mathrm{Aut}(X, \mu)$ of invertible measure-preserving transformations within the space of bi-stochastic operators over $L^{2}(X, \mu)$ for standard probability spaces $(X, \mu)$. This improves upon the approximation and residuality results established by Brown [4] and Kim [26] (cf. also [16]). We make crucial use of a reformulation of the Birkhoff--von Neumann theorem [2, 43] due to Kim for bi-stochastic operators over infinite dimensional Hilbert spaces. This enables the construction of stochastic processes, via which dilations and thereby $\mathrm{PW}$-approximations may be obtained. In a similar fashion, we demonstrate the weak-genericity of weakly-continuous measure-preserving flows on $(X, \mu)$ within the space of $\mathcal{C}_{0}$-semigroups of bi-stochastic operators on $L^{2}(X, \mu)$. To achieve this, we make use of random measures (viz. Poisson point processes) and build on our discrete-time result. This complements recent advances in ergodic theory due to Furlong on the genericity of measure-preserving flows in the space of measure-preserving semi-flows.

papers.title: Is Chaotic Dynamics Enhancing Particle Swarm Optimization? An Anytime Performance Assessment
papers.abstract: The search dynamics of particle swarm optimization (PSO) can be driven by random or chaotic values. We study if there are performance differences between random and chaos if distributional equivalence of the used sequences is observed. Therefore, we consider an anytime performance assessment which quantifies the fraction of runs reaching a given target value within a specified numerical budget. Furthermore, we connect quantifiers of the chaotic dynamics to performance metrics of the anytime analysis. The results show that once the underlying distributions are controlled, deterministic chaotic sequences yield no general or consistent advantage over random sequences. Performance differences arise most prominently from the underlying distribution, but also from search-space dimensions, benchmark targets, and numerical budgets. We also find potential budget-dependent advantages under specific parametrization of chaotic maps and distribution settings.

papers.title: You Only Look Multiple Times: YoloMT, a Real-Time Streaming Model on a T4
papers.abstract: We introduce a new model for real-time streaming captioning on a single GPU. YoloMT is a 449.8M-parameter streaming captioner that provides Pareto-frontier performance among generative vision models in its class. Distilled from a 27B teacher by SFT and GRPO, it leads every model under 1B parameters on OVO-Bench, MVBench, StreamingBench and Video-MME, answered from its captions, and beats LFM2.5-VL-1.6B and SmolVLM2-2.2B. YoloMT is designed to read more frames cheaply and make them informative, encoding each frame once and caching it as 16 tokens. This allows the model to incorporate and infer from past frames without additional vision passes, making it efficient and effective. We also provide a detailed recipe for training YoloMT, with its stages and data, as well as ablations that demonstrate the contribution of each component.

papers.title: Time-resolved Polarimetry of the Type Ibn Supernova 2025kzr Suggests a Possible Ejecta-CSM Misalignment
papers.abstract: Type Ibn supernovae (SNe) are rare interacting transients. The dense, helium-rich circumstellar material (CSM) surrounding these events provides insight into the final stages of massive-star evolution. The geometries of the ejecta and CSM provide complementary constraints on the explosion and pre-SN mass loss, yet their temporal evolution has remained largely unexplored by spectropolarimetry. Here we present the first spectropolarimetric time series spanning the interaction-to-ejecta transition of the Type Ibn SN\,2025kzr. Three epochs of Very Large Telescope observations, combined with two epochs of published $V$-band imaging polarimetry, span 5--34 days after explosion. Continuum polarization is low at the earliest epoch, then rises to $\sim$0.6\% by day\,11 as the SN ejecta sweep up the dense CSM. This rise, together with a rotating polarization position angle, indicates a significant change in the geometry of the emitting region. The polarization subsequently falls below our detection limit as the photosphere recedes into the ejecta. Radiation-hydrodynamic and Monte Carlo polarization models illustrate that this evolution can be reproduced by an oblate CSM and prolate ejecta, with the symmetry axis of the cold dense shell tilted relative to that of the CSM. Binary mass transfer can produce an equatorially enhanced CSM, although the polarization data alone cannot identify the progenitor's formation channel. Similar polarization signatures in other supernovae suggest that misaligned ejecta and CSM may be common, making time-resolved spectropolarimetry a powerful probe of the link between pre-explosion mass loss and explosion geometry.

authors.name: Xudong Wen
authors.institution: Chengdu University of Traditional Chinese Medicine

papers.title: Stochastic extinction: convergence in distribution
papers.abstract: We develop a general framework to show the convergence in distribution of non-irreducible Markov processes to invariant distributions supported on lower-dimensional subsets of the state space. In applications, these singular supports signal the emergence of distinctive long-time behaviours, such as the extinction of species in ecology and the concentration on laminar states in fluid dynamics. The proposed approach is made widely applicable by tailoring its assumptions so that they can be verified using the theory of stochastic persistence/extinction. We illustrate the framework by applying it to stochastic perturbations of the Lorenz and Rosenzweig-MacArthur models and to a general two-dimensional Kolmogorov system.

authors.name: Leo Hahn
authors.institution: Amsterdam UMC Location University of Amsterdam

papers.title: Is Sara Omar the true author of D{\o}devaskeren (The Dead Washer)? Authorship attribution in Danish literature
papers.abstract: The bestseller D{\o}devaskeren (The Dead Washer) was published in 2017 under the name Sara Omar. A Danish colleague has suggested that the novel may have been written by another author, possibly Mads Peder Nordbo. To investigate this authorship question, four authorship attribution methods were applied, namely Delta, intertextual distance, Nearest Shrunken Centroids (NSC), and na\"ive Bayes. Using various parameter settings, these approaches consistently identify Nordbo's writing style in the doubtful novel, although the results do not provide conclusive evidence that he authored the novel in its entirety. In a second step, the novel was divided into non-overlapping segments of 5,000 tokens. Once again, Nordbo's style was identified in the majority of the segments. However, a small number of passages do not clearly support this conclusion and instead suggest the possible involvement of another, as yet unidentified, author, possibly Sara Omar herself.

papers.title: How resampling method can help us: Improving the Delta model
papers.abstract: Delta has been successfully employed as an authorship attribution method in various contexts, although its effectiveness is not always perfect. Since it is based on the most frequent words, its results can be readily interpreted and explained in plain English. In this study, we propose improving its performance by applying a resampling method to the selected stylistic features. The results show that this approach increases the accuracy of the model while preserving the interpretability of its outcomes. However, the main drawback of the proposed technique is the additional computational time required to obtain more accurate results.

papers.title: Using waveform types, discrete Sobolev distances, and trend compatibility to cluster short time series of clinical data
papers.abstract: Clinical tests, such as the oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), perturb a physiological system at rest and record its excursion over a fixed protocol window as a short, undersampled time series. Such curves rarely allow parameter identification at the individual level, yet their trends carry physiological information that emerges at the population level as recurrent response patterns. Standard clustering methods aggregate differences globally and average out those trends, losing precisely the information about how the system regains control after the perturbation; identifying response patterns requires a method that preserves them. We present a nonparametric framework that factorizes each curve into unit waveforms, sorts them with a symbolic trend-compatibility filter, and compares compatible shapes using discrete Sobolev-type distances on finite differences up to order $k$. The number of clusters, i.e., distinct response types, equals the number of realizable trend patterns the cohort populates, validated by resampling. Applied to 1283 five-point OGTTs, the method identifies 7 glycemia and 8 insulinemia types. The count holds across a threefold range of resolution. In benchmarks against six classical clustering methods, ours alone never mixes opposite trends, with comparable reconstruction error and stability. Clinical normality, assessed after clustering, is graded, overlapping, and distributed unevenly across response types ($h=0.14$--$0.48$). Overall, our method distinguishes response types among curves too short for alignment-based methods yet too informative for reduction to summary values. It applies to any protocol recording a system's response to a standardized perturbation on a short grid.

papers.title: RR Lyrae stars as distance indicators I. Sample selection and characterisation
papers.abstract: RR Lyrae stars (RRL) are well-established Population II distance indicators, with period-metallicity-luminosity (PLZ) relations linking pulsational properties to absolute luminosity. Gaia parallaxes now allow these relations to be anchored to geometric distances with unprecedented precision, offering an independent route to the extragalactic distance scale. We present the first paper in a series aimed at deriving new empirical PLZ and metallicity-luminosity relations for RRL in the optical and near-infrared. We describe the selection and characterisation of a sample of bright nearby field RRL, with distances anchored to reliable Gaia DR3 parallaxes. We conducted a multi-band photometric campaign of 172 RRL: 101 in Johnson-Cousins UBVRI with the IAC80 telescope and 130 in JHKs with the IRSF telescope, with 59 stars in common. The iron abundances come from the Spectroscopic Rome RRL Catalog catalogue, mostly from high-resolution spectroscopy. The light curves were modelled with GLOESS (optical) and near-infrared templates, and the mean magnitudes, amplitudes, and Fourier parameters were derived via a bootstrap Monte Carlo method. The linear relations were fitted with a Bayesian Markov Chain Monte Carlo method. The sample spans -3.4 to 0.2 dex in [Fe/H]. We found tight relations between the Fourier parameter $\phi_{31}$ in each optical and Gaia band and its V-band value for RRab stars (scatter below 0.06). The near-infrared amplitude ratios with respect to V or G increase continuously with period, without the break reported in globular clusters. We provide a homogeneous calibration of the colour at minimum light across all filter combinations from U-B to H-Ks, revealing significant period and metallicity dependences, and we use it to derive reddening estimates for 15 stars outside current 3D extinction maps.

papers.title: Grey-Box Experimental Identification of Reduced-Order Models for Grid-Forming Converters
papers.abstract: This paper proposes a grey-box system identification for identifying and validating reduced-order models (ROMs) of grid-forming (GFM) converters. Three reduced-order modeling techniques are compared within a common identification procedure: singular perturbation with frequency cutoff and participation factors (SP-PF), singular perturbation with energy residuals (SP-Energy), and balanced truncation (BT). Testing is on experimental data with real-life components. Results show that BT achieves the highest time-domain fit, followed by SP-Energy and SP-PF; SP-Energy better preserves key properties of the identified full-order model; BT places the dominant mode closest to the stability boundary and exhibits the highest sensitivity to parameter variations; SP-Energy outperforms SP-PF in both fit quality and consistency of modal preservation. Findings suggest that the model with the best time-domain fit does not always provide the most reliable representation of the modal properties for small-signal stability, with SP-Energy offering the best compromise between accuracy, physical interpretability, and modal preservation for the considered case study.

papers.title: A singular Lawson cone minimizing the fractional perimeter in dimension seven
papers.abstract: We prove that the nonlocal Lawson cone constructed by Davila, del Pino, and Wei (J. Differential Geom. 2018) in $N=7$ minimizes the fractional perimeter for all sufficiently small orders $s$. Thus nonlocal minimal surfaces can have singularities already in dimension $7$. This contrasts both with the classical theory, where the first singular example occurs in dimension $8$ (Bombieri-De Giorgi-Giusti, Invent. Math. 1969), and with the fractional theory for orders $s$ close to $1$ (Caffarelli-Valdinoci, Adv. Math. 2013).

papers.title: Make the Adversary Spend More: Stateful Deception as a Cost-Exchange Primitive for AI-Era Cyber Defense
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are transforming the economics of intrusion by reducing the attacker's cost to scan and adapt, while tempting defenders into unbounded compute. We argue that cyber deception should be judged by the cost exchange it imposes, not by realism or detection, and that the primitive making that exchange favorable is adversary-specific persistent state. Rather than a honeypot that resets or merges sessions, each recognized adversary re-enters the world it believes it has compromised, kept coherent with its own past actions and isolated from every other adversary, while the language model acts only as a constrained renderer of explicit state, never as its store. We formalize the trade-off as a Deception Exchange Rate (DER), relating mission-weighted adversary effort burned to defender resources spent, and instantiate it in an SSH honeypot pairing Cowrie with a local LLM. In this paper, we focus on the defender-side evaluation of that exchange, while specifying, but not yet measuring, per-adversary state and the adversary side of the DER. Across five open-weight models, deterministic-layer and prompt optimizations cut per-session defender cost by around 63% against a naive all-LLM decoy.

authors.name: Alessandro Cantelli-Forti
authors.institution: Consorzio Nazionale Interuniversitario per le Telecomunicazioni

papers.title: Bar Kinematics in Paired and Isolated Galaxies: Slow Bars Are More Likely Found in Paired Galaxies
papers.abstract: Bars are common structures in disk galaxies that can strongly influence the evolution of their hosts. Simulations predict that bars formed through tidal interactions tend to rotate slower than bars formed in isolation. We test this prediction observationally by studying the kinematics of 314 bars in galaxies between $0.016<z<0.130$. We use estimates of the bar pattern speed ($\Omega_p$) and the rotation rate ($\mathcal{R}$) obtained from four studies using IFU data from the MaNGA survey. We cross-match the host galaxies of the bars to the Galaxy Zoo DESI catalogue in order to study their environment and classify each galaxy as paired or isolated. We find that bars that are slower in terms of $\mathcal{R}$ are more likely to be found in paired galaxies. The fraction of bars in paired galaxies increases from $5^{+6}_{-2}\%$ for $0<\mathcal{R}<1.0$ to $31^{+15}_{-9}\%$ for $3.0<\mathcal{R}<4.0$. Our results also suggest a possible difference in the distribution of $\mathcal{R}$ between paired (mean $\mathcal{R}=2.1 \pm 0.2$) and isolated (mean $\mathcal{R}=1.75 \pm 0.07$) galaxies (p-value=0.037; 2.09$\sigma$). On the other hand, our analysis reveals no noticeable trend between the fraction of paired galaxies and the bar pattern speed, which indicates that the pattern speed is not correlated with the likelihood of a galaxy being paired. We also find no difference in the distribution of $\Omega_p$ between paired and isolated galaxies (p-value$>$0.250; $<$1.15$\sigma$).

papers.title: How Well Do Vision-Language Scene Graphs Serve as Memory for Embodied Question Answering?
papers.abstract: Embodied QA needs memory, but answer accuracy mixes retained evidence, reading errors and question priors. For a simulated multi-room scene-graph pipeline we define answerability: the fraction of questions a fixed rule-based reader answers correctly from the graph alone. The baseline recovers 24.1% of visible object types and its room labels flicker. Four targeted repairs double recall, raise answerability from 27.2% to 37.4%, and improve retrained QA from 71.4% to 75.9%, yet better object F1 can lower answerability. A question-type prior beats this reader on every predicted graph. In one real-video test, graph memory lowers accuracy. These exploratory findings favour scoring retained evidence alongside accuracy.

authors.name: Niyati Rawal
authors.institution: University of Modena and Reggio Emilia

papers.title: Probabilistic Monocular Biomechanical Reconstruction via Guided Flow Matching
papers.abstract: Reconstructing 3D joint kinematics from a single video is ill-posed due to depth and stature ambiguity, limb occlusion, and missing uncertainty estimates. We introduce the Biomechanical Flow Model (BFM), a continuous-time flow-matching prior over subject anthropometry, anatomical joint-angle trajectories, and virtual markers, trained on multi-camera clinical recordings from 565 participants and steered toward monocular 2D keypoints at test time without paired video training. In a head-to-head comparison on the same clinical trials against a state-of-the-art deterministic trajectory optimizer fitting the identical skeleton, BFM achieves comparable joint-angle accuracy across walking and timed-up-and-go (TUG). Across held-out control, prosthetic, and neurologic participants, BFM reaches 3.91 deg and 4.97 deg mean absolute joint-angle error on walking and TUG while providing credible intervals that bridge temporal and whole-limb occlusions. Where keypoints are hidden, the intervals widen with the error and keep their coverage near nominal. Supplying individual anthropometric calibration removes most monocular pelvis depth error, whereas testing on out-of-distribution pediatric crouch gait produces biased, overconfident extension predictions, highlighting the need for pathologically diverse movement priors.

papers.title: Horizontal velocity eigenfunctions of solar inertial modes using local correlation tracking of magnetic features
papers.abstract: Solar inertial modes enable probes of the bulk of the convection zone over a broad latitude range. A proper study of high-latitude modes requires near-surface horizontal flow maps above 65 deg latitude at a cadence of at least one day. Previous observations have utilised ring-diagram analysis (RDA) of acoustic modes and local correlation tracking (LCT) of granules, but these methods do not have the capacity to access higher latitudes without compromising the signal-to-noise ratio (S/N). We measured flows associated with solar inertial modes using local correlation tracking of small magnetic features in SDO/HMI magnetograms separated by 1 h (LCTMag). This non-helioseismic method extracts horizontal near-surface flows with a good S/N up to 85 deg latitude. To carry out a comparison below 65 deg, we also measured flows using LCT of granulation features in continuum intensity images separated by 45 s (LCTGran). We constructed longitude-latitude maps of horizontal flows at a cadence of 6 h from LCTMag and LCTGran using overlapping 5 deg tiles. We additionally applied the RDA pipeline to HMI Dopplergrams over the same period to obtain flow maps at a cadence of 9 h. After removing large-scale systematics and long-term variations, we applied spectral analysis to identify modes in the inertial frequency range and extracted their spatial shapes via singular value decomposition. Mode shapes are consistent between LCTMag and LCTGran below 65 deg, but granulation tracking performs poorly at higher latitudes due to insufficient granule resolution. LCTMag provides higher-latitude access than both RDA and LCTGran with better S/N values, resulting in reduced spectral leakage from the window function. We also report a new retrograde inertial mode in the LCTMag dataset at frequency -192 nHz in the Carrington frame with a longitudinal wavenumber m = 3.

papers.title: Source Detection in Complex Networks: Observability, Identifiability, and Inference Frameworks
papers.abstract: Tracing diffusion to its origin is a central inverse problem in complex networks, with applications ranging from epidemic investigation and information spreading to cyber incidents and disruptions in interconnected systems. Although source-detection methods have advanced along diverse methodological lines, their capabilities cannot be assessed independently of the evidence on which they operate. Network structure and diffusion dynamics determine which propagation histories are possible, while the observation mechanism determines which traces of those histories are retained. This review develops an information-centric and identifiability-aware perspective that connects these elements to source inference. We organize existing research around three overlapping observation settings: complete state snapshots, incomplete or noisy observations, and sensor-based observation and design. Within this organization, we examine structural, probabilistic, message-passing, simulation-based, and learning-based methods, comparing their required inputs, underlying assumptions, inference mechanisms, and computational demands. System-theoretic observability, statistical identifiability, and information-theoretic constraints provide complementary ways to examine what the available observations can reveal, while separating limitations of the evidence from those of estimation. Drawing on applications across epidemiological, information, biological, neural, and socioeconomic systems, we identify challenges in uncertainty assessment, model robustness, transfer across networks, and the acquisition of informative observations. This synthesis clarifies the conditions under which diffusion sources can be identified and how inference methods should be selected according to the available observations.
