authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Robust large-scale approximate solutions of the constrained Kemeny aggregation ranking problem
papers.abstract: The Kemeny aggregation ranking problem consists of computing the consensus rankings of an election with respect to the well-known Kemeny-Young voting method. These consensus rankings satisfy many fundamental properties and are the geometric medians of the votes in the election under the Kendall-tau distance which counts the number of pairwise disagreements. While having various applications in computational social choice, machine learning, operations research, and biology, the problem of computing the consensus rankings is NP-hard and encounters a severe bottleneck in practice. In this paper, we consider the more general Kemeny aggregation ranking problem under immutable input pairwise constraints and propose robust and scalable approximate methods with provable guarantees. We thus provide an algorithmic solution to the more general constrained problem of incorporating a posteriori immutable pairwise constraints into past rankings (e.g., historical voter ballots or legacy laboratory assays) without incurring the cost of generating new data. Our base algorithm $\Gamma$-XCC provides a source of rankings with a bounded constant approximation factor. $\Gamma$-XCC generalizes the Copeland ranking method and satisfies the constrained Condorcet consistency property, an extension of the Condorcet winner criterion for elections with immutable pairwise constraints. Thereby, our methods provide large-scale solutions that address the reliability and explainability issues. Our algorithms are also applicable to weighted tournaments with input pairwise constraints and satisfy similar properties in this larger context.

papers.title: Computing Normal-Form Correlated Equilibria in Extensive-Form Games is in PPAD
papers.abstract: We study the computational complexity of finding any normal-form correlated equilibria (NFCE for short) in the succinct games of extensive-form with perfect recall, which is considered as a major open problem in algorithmic game theory. Our main results place this problem in PPAD for an arbitrary numbers of players. Our second result establishes PPAD-hardness of computing such an NFCE with support size of at most quadratic in the size of the game, even for two-player games. The posed restriction on the support size in PPAD-hardness construction is motivated by our PPAD algorithm, which constructs an NFCE with support size quadratic in the size of the input extensive-form game.

authors.name: Florian Horn
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

authors.name: Mahsa Shirmohammadi
authors.institution: Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique

papers.title: Diffusion Effects on a Stochastic Amplifier Driven by the Square of a Gaussian Field: Discontinuous Transition to Intermittency
papers.abstract: We study the effects of diffusion on the transition to intermittency in stochastic amplification driven by the square of a Gaussian field. The transition is characterized by an order parameter quantifying the spatial uniformity of the amplification. We consider a model in which the diffusion-amplification process is embedded in a random lattice of point absorbers in such a way that the Feynman-Kac formula is restricted to Brownian paths with a range not exceeding a finite cut-off. In this setting, with the Gaussian driving field in a wide class of physical interest, we show that diffusion-induced damping of the amplification is sufficiently strong to change the nature of the transition: from continuous in the absence of diffusion, to discontinuous in the presence of diffusion.

papers.title: SoK: When FL Clients Cannot Train -- Delegated Federated Learning for IoT
papers.abstract: Federated learning (FL) assumes that a client can perform the computation required to produce its own contribution. This assumption is often unrealistic for resource-constrained Internet of Things (IoT) devices, motivating designs that delegate some or all client-side training to more capable parties. We systematize this setting as delegated federated learning (Delegated FL), where data ownership and execution of owner-attributed learning are separated. We develop a framework that examines three dimensions over the same delegated transition: delegate-view privacy, delegated attribution, and constrained-owner feasibility. Our audit of 29 systems reveals a recurring composition gap. Privacy mechanisms protect selected artifacts without necessarily characterizing the accumulated view. Attribution mechanisms establish individual execution relations without necessarily binding the complete delegated transition. Furthermore, computational offloading does not establish whether the remaining workload fits the owner's resource budget. Two controlled studies on Raspberry Pi devices illustrate these gaps. We show that encrypted inputs can coexist with information leakage through an exposed residual and that locally retained labels remain inferable from split-learning gradients. We also show that message authentication can reject tampering without establishing that the executor performed the prescribed computation. Our findings demonstrate why individually established guarantees do not necessarily support the same end-to-end claim and motivate evaluating privacy, attribution, and residual owner cost over the same delegated transition.

papers.title: Nonlocal approximation of stable minimal surfaces with prescribed number of connected components
papers.abstract:
We show that every strictly stable classical minimal hypersurface in a Euclidean ball can be approximated, for $s$ sufficiently close to $1$, by a stable $s$-minimal surface in a smaller ball. We also give an explicit lower bound on the size of the interval of admissible values of $s$.
  As a consequence, we construct stable nonlocal minimal surfaces with an arbitrarily large number $k$ of connected components in a bounded region, under the quantitative condition $k \leq \frac{C}{\sqrt{1-s}}$, attaining an optimal result (at least in dimensions $2$ and $3$).
  As part of the proof of our main result, we obtain an auxiliary result of independent interest, providing quantitative estimates for foliations of constant mean curvature embedded hypersurfaces near a stable minimal surface. The resulting foliation supplies nonlocal barriers thanks to known results of uniform convergence of the nonlocal mean curvature to the classical one when $s \to 1$.

papers.title: Casper: A Projection-Based Neurosymbolic Layer for Scalable & Guaranteed Constraint Satisfaction
papers.abstract: Many real-world problems demand exact constraint satisfaction to be meaningfully solved, yet existing neurosymbolic methods face a stark trade-off: those that guarantee satisfaction fail to scale, while those that scale must resort to approximation. Meanwhile, traditional deep learning approaches offer no satisfaction guarantees at all. In this paper, we propose Casper, a neurosymbolic layer that simultaneously (i) guarantees constraint satisfaction, (ii) scales at inference time, (iii) is fully automated, requiring no problem-specific engineering, and (iv) is fully differentiable, making it composable with any neural predictor both at training and at inference time. Casper casts constraint satisfaction as a closed-form Euclidean projection onto the constraint-feasible region, computable in a single forward pass. Experiments across MNIST arithmetic (up to 1024 digits), Sudoku solving, and Warcraft pathfinding show that Casper is the only method that produces guaranteed-valid outputs at scale: on $30\times30$ Warcraft grids, exact baselines time out and approximate ones produce valid paths less than 7% of the time, while Casper produces them 100% of the time.

papers.title: Global solutions of the planar plasma equation with infinite $p$-mass
papers.abstract: We study entire solutions of $-\Delta u=u_+^p$ in the plane for $p>1$. A solution which is nondecreasing in one direction is invariant in that direction, and for each nonconstant solution in this class the plasma region $\{x:u(x)>0\}$ is a strip, the transverse profile has affine tails, and the Morse index is infinite. The stable solutions are the nonpositive constants, and the nonconstant solutions with finite Morse index are precisely the translated and scaled radial profiles of finite $p$-mass, each of which has Morse index one. We also construct a continuous branch of solutions which are periodic in one variable, depend on both variables and have infinite Morse index.

authors.name: Ruijun Wu
authors.institution: Qingdao University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Letting Models Manage Their Own Context: Where We Stand
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses today manage context on the model's behalf: when the window fills, the harness triggers a compaction that summarizes the history. We study the alternative, \emph{model-driven} context management, in which the model itself decides when and what to compact through a context API. We gave models control over their own context in \nooa, NVIDIA's open source agent harness, and compared the two strategies on document research and machine learning engineering across context budgets from 8K to 512K tokens. Models that use the context API effectively reach higher accuracy, often with fewer input tokens, especially at tight budgets: \textbf{GPT 6.1 nearly triples its score at a 32K budget} on OfficeQA Pro v2 (21\%~$\rightarrow$~56\%), and \textbf{Kimi gains with up to 41\% fewer input tokens}. Models differ widely, however, in how often they use the API, how aggressively they compact, and when they start compacting, and prompt changes shift that timing. Finally, we show that \textbf{inference engines can make model-driven edits cheaper}: by reusing the KV cache of the unchanged suffix after an edit, \textbf{we cut prefill compute by up to 15\% per request with no measurable change in accuracy}. Together, these results point to a new co-design frontier: models trained to manage their own context, served by inference engines that support KV cache editing.

papers.title: Rank-size analysis of optimal portfolio weights with a reverse-engineering application
papers.abstract: This paper investigates the shape of optimal portfolio weights using rank-size analysis. We consider four portfolio selection models: Global Minimum-Variance (GMV), minimum-CVaR, Risk Parity (RP), and the Most Diversified Portfolio (MDP). For each model, we fit seven rank-size specifications to the sorted portfolio weights generated over rolling windows. To compare the fitted specifications, we combine standard goodness-of-fit measures with Cumulative Second-order $\varepsilon$-Stochastic Dominance, an $\varepsilon$-parameterized generalization of Second-order Stochastic Dominance that quantifies the extent to which the exact dominance conditions are satisfied or violated. Empirically applied to major equity indices, this approach provides a systematic criterion for identifying the optimal functional form across diverse market compositions. Furthermore, we address the inverse problem of identifying the generating model from the observed weight structure. We use the calibrated rank-size parameters as inputs to a Random Forest classifier, evaluated by a blocked cross-validation that accounts for the overlap between estimation windows. The parameters separate minimum-risk from risk-diversification strategies and identify the RP and MDP portfolios, whereas the GMV and minimum-CVaR portfolios are difficult to distinguish. These results indicate that rank-size parameters provide a compact and informative description of portfolio allocation geometries.

papers.title: Platform-Induced Coordination
papers.abstract: This paper studies a platform that influences collective action by selecting which posts each user observes. Each user would like to take an action close to those of the others and to an ideal action determined by her private type and an aggregate state. Posts are non-strategic but correlated with the types of their authors, so each post carries information about the state and its author. We characterise the unique Bayes-Nash equilibrium in closed form. Two explicit networks give the minimum and maximum collective action the platform can induce. Moreover, collective action depends on the network only through the numbers of readers. Hence, many networks induce the same collective action, but they can induce different individual actions. These networks may differ for a regulator, and we compare them by welfare, polarisation and cross-type exposure. In particular, the complete network need not maximise welfare, and the segregated network need not maximise polarisation.

authors.name: Julian Chitiva
authors.institution: Libera Università Internazionale degli Studi Sociali Guido Carli

papers.title: Solitons as conversion events in quadratic crystals
papers.abstract: In a $\chi^{(2)}$ crystal with temporal walk-off and negligible dispersion, signal, idler and pump pulses obey the integrable three-wave interaction. For a pump of intermediate group velocity we describe each soliton as a conversion event: the fusion of a signal--idler pair into a pump pulse, or the decay of a pump pulse, at a definite depth in the crystal. The asymptotic $\mathrm{sech}$ pulses, usually treated with three separate $2\times2$ scattering problems, are the legs of the event, a single pole of the $3\times3$ problem. For one event we give the conversion curve in closed form and the minimum crystal length; for several events, the rule by which they displace each other. A pump pulse is unstable, and its growing mode is the tail of a decay event: a seed carrying a fraction $\varepsilon$ of the photons along this mode makes the pulse decay after $\Gamma^{-1}\ln(c_+/\varepsilon)$, with $\Gamma$ the conversion rate and $c_+$ of order one. Unmatched signal and idler pulses form the resonance of Kaup, Reiman and Bers; we show that it is a fusion followed by a decay, each within a conversion length, and give its pump photon number in closed form. Since the delay between the input pulses sets the depth of the vertex, these quantities can be read on the output face of a single crystal; we give the scales for periodically poled KTiOPO$_4$.

papers.title: Same Seed, Different Top Prediction: Cross-Platform Reproducibility of AlphaFold 3 Inference on TPUs, GPUs, and CPUs
papers.abstract: AlphaFold 3 returns the highest-ranked of several sampled structures and computes each prediction on one device. Computing centers may schedule them on different GPU types or CPU nodes. Floating-point results can differ between devices, so the same input and seed may return another structure. Neither AlphaFold 3's documentation nor its outputs warn of this. We measure how often the device changes the returned structure, and tell users what to report and how to make devices agree. We used identical inputs, weights, seeds, and settings on two Google tensor processing unit (TPU) generations (v5e, v6e), three NVIDIA GPUs (L4, A100, H100), and an Intel Xeon CPU. On 60 protein-ligand complexes, with five seeds each, switching TPU generations changed the top-ranked sample in 18.0% of 300 predictions. Recompiling never changed it on either TPU, but did so in 7.3% on the L4 GPU. Yet the structures barely moved. The top-ranked pose switched between correct and incorrect in 3.3% to 3.7% of predictions, against about 10% for a new seed. These switches nearly always came from one validity check, with the ligand within 2 angstroms. Follow-ups found the effect again on 72 new targets and between the TPUs and the CPU. Between the A100 and H100 it exceeded recompilation, although AlphaFold 3's developers verified its numerical accuracy on both. An exploratory analysis links the changes to near-tied candidates. We recommend reporting the device and every near-tied sample. A float32 trunk with full-precision matrix products made all five accelerators agree on nearly every prediction.

authors.name: Lorenzo Pazienza
authors.institution: Libera Università Internazionale degli Studi Sociali Guido Carli

papers.title: Higher-Dimensional Automata in Geometric Logic
papers.abstract: What does the topos of a higher-dimensional automaton know about its infinite behaviour that its language does not? We write partial HDAs with an infinite run as models of a geometric theory over an intuitionistic metatheory with no choice. The topos of a machine is that of sheaves on its prefixes. The label word of a prefix records the shape and acceptance bit of each cell with the ipomset of each step. Under unique choice these words give a geometric morphism to the label topos of sheaves on label words, which thus records the shapes and acceptance bits that the B\"uchi language forgets. Machines sharing their B\"uchi language and their frames can differ over the label topos. The bouquet of two squares shares its frame and its B\"uchi language with the interleaved square; each accepted run of either reads the two events in parallel forever. Only the interleaved square has runs through cells of shape a, and the geometric sequent excluding such runs separates the two over the label topos. Over alphabets with decidable equality, finite rigid machines are unambiguous exactly when their label maps are inclusions of locales, and their equivalence over the label topos is decided whenever either is unambiguous. Equivalences of frames over the label topos transport points with their labels, and the invariants of fibres and of the language of points follow from this transport. On finite partial HDAs over alphabets with decidable equality, Muller and B\"uchi acceptance coincide exactly under a weak form of excluded middle.

papers.title: Necessary conditions for the boundedness of directional maximal operators
papers.abstract: Given a set of directions $\Omega$, we investigate whether the associated directional maximal operator $M\_\Omega$ is bounded on $L^p(\RR^2)$, for $p>1$. One can associate to $\Omega$ a numerical quantity called its \textit{Perron capacity}. If the latter is finite, then $M\_\Omega$ is unbounded on $L^p(\RR^2)$ for $p \geq 1$. In this paper, we generalize a method introduced by D'Aniello, Gauvan and Moonens to compute the Perron capacity of oscillatory sets of directions such as \[ \Omega\_{\mathrm{cos}} = \left \{\frac{\cos (n)}{n}\,: n \in \NN^*\right \}. \] In a second part, using geometric arguments, we show that if the Minkowski dimension of $\Omega$ is positive, then $M\_\Omega$ is unbounded on $L^p(\RR^2)$ for a small range of $p>1$.

papers.title: Semisimple-Unipotent Decomposition and the Exact Order of a Linear Cellular Automaton over F_2
papers.abstract: We study the linear cellular automaton on the cyclic graph $C_n$ over $\mathbb{F}_2$ defined by the local rule $v_i(t+1)=v_{i-1}(t)\oplus v_i(t)\oplus v_{i+1}(t)$ (Wolfram's Rule 150 under periodic boundary conditions). Identifying the configuration space $V_n=\mathbb{F}_2^n$ with $R_n = \mathbb{F}_2[x] / \langle x^n - 1 \rangle$, the evolution operator corresponds to multiplication by $G(x)=1+x+x^{n-1}$. We re-derive the invertibility criterion $3\nmid n$, classify periodic and transient behaviour, and prove that Hamming weight is non-monotone for every $n\ge3$. We then factor $x^n-1$ via the Chinese Remainder Theorem and separate semisimple contributions governed by finite-field multiplicative orders from unipotent contributions governed by Frobenius squaring. We determine the exact local unipotent orders and obtain a closed-form global order $r(A)$: $r(A)=2^{m-1}$ for $n=2^m$ with $m\ge2$, while for $n=2^m q$, $q>1$ odd and $3\nmid n$, $r(A)=2^m\operatorname{lcm}(m_2,\ldots,m_r)$. The theory is illustrated by $n=5,7,8,16$ and computationally verified for small dimensions.

papers.title: The hitting time index: bounds, a sharp threshold, the proof of a conjecture and the disproof of another conjecture
papers.abstract: We prove some new upper and lower bounds for the hitting time index ($HT$ index) of an $n$-vertex graph, showing along the way that the largest order of the index is $n^5$ and the smallest is $n^3$. More specifically, we prove the conjecture that the smallest value of the index is $\frac{n(n-1)^2}{2}$, which is attained by the complete graph. We also find a sharp threshold for the minimal degree $\delta$ so that the $HT$ index goes from an $n^4$ order to an $n^3$ order if the threshold is surpassed. We disprove the conjecture that the largest value of the index is attained by the $n$-path, and look at the lollipop graphs, some of which attain the $n^5$ order, and seem to be the natural candidates among which the largest value of the index should be attained.

papers.title: Benchmarking Segmentation Models for Scalable Mangrove Mapping with Sentinel-1/2 Imagery
papers.abstract: Mangroves are dynamic coastal ecosystems that contribute to carbon storage, coastal protection and biodiversity conservation, but are vulnerable to climate change. Very-high-resolution imagery such as Pl\'eiades enables detailed mangrove mapping but it is costly and have a low revisit rate. Large-scale monitoring requires free and regularly available data such as Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 but their spatial resolution poses challenges for detailed mangrove mapping. In this work, we benchmark deep learning approaches for mangrove mapping from Sentinel-1 radar and Sentinel-2 optical imagery using reference maps derived from very-high-resolution Pl\'eiades imagery. We compare four segmentation configurations based on CROMA and BigEarthNet-pretrained ResNet50 representations with different segmentation decoders. We construct a mangrove mapping dataset covering French Guiana, Suriname, and Amap\'a. CROMA + UPerNet achieves the best performance, with an F1-score of 0.9218 and an IoU of 0.8549. These results highlight the potential of pretrained multimodal Earth observation representations and open Sentinel data to support mangrove resilience through scalable monitoring.

papers.title: PROVE: Mitigating Long-Horizon LLM Collusion with Reinforcement Learning from Verified Evidence
papers.abstract: When LLM agents verify each other's work over a long interaction, they drift into collusion: they come to accept work without the evidence that the verification protocol requires. Collusion is absent at the start and builds up episode by episode, which we trace to accurate feedback accumulating in memory. An agent that follows the rule is told that its verdict was wrong whenever its peer was right, so breaking the rule is the reward-maximizing choice, and agents talk themselves into it in their private reflections. Existing mitigations leave the agents unchanged; we train the behavior out. PROVE (Protocol Reinforcement from Verified Evidence) is a multi-agent reinforcement learning method that rewards verdicts by the evidence behind them rather than by their outcome, and credits every call an agent makes, including the calls that solve its own task, with the outcome that call controls. On Qwen3.6-27B, a LoRA adapter trained on six-episode interactions takes the collusion rate on held-out task sequences at the original ten-episode horizon from 65.0% to 1.0%, with no detectable change in task success. Collusion that converged in every interaction now converges in none, and the gain holds four episodes beyond the longest interaction seen in training. The trained 27B model colludes less than every model evaluated in the original study, closed-weight frontier models included. Code is available at https://github.com/Haochen-Luo/PROVE.

papers.title: Normalized ground states for the nonlinear Born--Infeld problem with Sobolev-critical and supercritical growth
papers.abstract:
We study normalized solutions to the nonlinear Born--Infeld problem
  \begin{equation*}
  -{\rm div}\left(\frac{\nabla u}{\sqrt{1-|\nabla u|^2}}\right)
  +\mu u=f(u)
  \quad\hbox{in }\mathbb{R}^N,\qquad \int_{\mathbb{R}^N}|u|^2\,dx=2m^2,
  \end{equation*} where $N\ge3$, the mass is prescribed, the frequency $\mu>0$ is unknown, and $f$ has Sobolev-critical or supercritical growth at the origin, with no upper growth bound at infinity. We find three thresholds $c_*\le\rho_0<\widetilde r_e$ for $m^2$. Normalized action ground states exist for $m^2>c_*$ and do not exist for $m^2<c_*$. Least energy normalized solutions exist for $m^2>\rho_0$, and the energy attains its minimum on the mass sphere if and only if $m^2\ge\widetilde r_e$. In dimensions $3\le N\le6$, we prove that $c_*<\rho_0$ and that the first two existence results hold also for $m^2=c_*$ and $m^2=\rho_0$, respectively. The Lagrange multiplier of the energy minimizers is obtained from an abstract multiplier rule for constrained local minima of functionals with a convex nonsmooth part.

papers.title: A Sweedler dual seen as a terminal object in a category of bialgebras
papers.abstract: We study the Sweedler dual of the polynomial algebra $\mathbb{K}[X]$ equipped with the multiplicative coproduct $\delta(X) = X \otimes X$, and show that the resulting bialgebra $\mathbb{K}[X]^\star$ is the terminal object in the category of pairs $(B, \lambda)$, where $B$ is a bialgebra and $\lambda$ is a character of $B$. This generalizes a result of Aguiar, Bergeron, and Sottile on combinatorial Hopf algebras in the graded and connected setting. We describe the subcoalgebras and subbialgebras of $\mathbb{K}[X]^\star$, which lead to the introduction of the spectrum of a bialgebra. We also study the particular cases double bialgebras (bialgebras equipped with two compatible coproducts), firstly examining their connection to unital near-semirings or near-rings. Introducing a subbialgebra of $\mathbb{K}[X]^\star$ obtained from the intersection with another Sweedler dual, we prove it is the terminal object in the category of double bialgebras. As a consequence, we show that the spectrum of any double Hopf algebra is a subgroup of the group of roots of unity. This imply that not any bialgebra can become double. We finally apply this framework to a bialgebra of graphs with a coproduct given by contraction and deletion of edges, relating its invariants to Bergman colorations of edges arising from graphical matroids.

papers.title: A fake quadric that is not a bidisk quotient
papers.abstract: Fake quadrics are minimal complex surfaces of general type with $b_1=0$ and $e=4$. The paper gives a construction of a fake quadric $S$ that is a $32$-fold branched cover of $\mathbf{CP}^1\times\mathbf{CP}^1$ along nine curves. This configuration is given by four horizontal lines, four vertical lines and the diagonal. We show that $S$ is not aspherical. As a corollary the universal cover of $S$ is not the bidisk $\mathbf{H}\times\mathbf{H}$.

papers.title: Plausible Is Not Proven: Testing Failure Explanations in Monocular Depth Estimation
papers.abstract: Failure analyses of monocular depth models often name a cause for each error, such as an occluding boundary, a thin object or a reflective surface, but such labels are rarely tested. We present the Vision Error Observatory (VEO), an audit that finds regions failing the $\delta_1$ criterion on sensor-measured pixels, labels each with a likely cause or abstains, and then subjects the labels to four tests: agreement with object annotations on data the label model never saw, agreement with blinded human raters, response to targeted image edits, and value as a training signal. We apply it to eight models on NYU Depth V2, DIODE and iBims-1, with labels also checked on Hypersim, and fix most decision rules before their results. The occluding-boundary label agrees with annotations (AUROC 0.85 on NYU, 0.81 on Hypersim, 0.69 on iBims-1), but a single depth-edge cue does as well, and most boundary failures of the strongest model vanish under a 2-pixel tolerance. The reflection label does not transfer to synthetic data, the textureless label is near chance against annotations, and only one of four edit tests, an exploratory one, supports its label. Evaluated against five blinded raters, VEO's labels matched the human consensus only at chance level (Cohen's $\kappa$ = 0.05). In addition, an increase in the weight on the diagnosed regions during fine-tuning led to an increase in the error on targeted pixels at every weight tested. The architecture-specific failure fingerprint claimed by an earlier version of this project also failed to replicate across the datasets. Plausible failure explanations, in short, need to be tested before they are trusted; we release the protocol, code, ratings and every result file.

papers.title: Equivariant cohomology of stacky Lie group actions
papers.abstract: In this work we introduce equivariant cohomology for Lie groupoids and differentiable stacks. For Lie groupoids equipped with a strict action of a Lie 2-group, we define the corresponding equivariant cohomology via the Borel model and establish its Morita invariance. We also construct a simplicial Cartan model and prove that, under standard compactness assumptions, it recovers the equivariant cohomology defined via the Borel model. In the framework of stacky Lie group actions, we show that if a connected and \'etale stacky Lie group acts on a differentiable stack admitting an equivariant atlas, then the stacky action admits a strict presentation by a Lie 2-group action. Furthermore, we prove that different choices of equivariant atlases yield equivariantly Morita equivalent presenting actions, giving rise to a well-defined notion of equivariant cohomology for differentiable stacks. As an application, we compute the equivariant cohomology of toric symplectic stacks.

papers.title: Linear images of graphs of vector-valued affine fractal interpolation functions
papers.abstract: We determine the Hausdorff and box dimensions of every linear image of the graph of a vector-valued affine fractal interpolation function with positive vertical factors. The same formula holds for signed factors under a rank condition on the active branches. Outside an explicit finite union of hyperplanes in the space of vertical factors it holds simultaneously for all choices of interpolation knots and all linear images. The dimension is determined by the branch contractions, the rank of the projected deviations from the endpoint line, and the affine dimension of the projected knots. The proof gives uniform entropy estimates over bounded slopes for tilted projections of homogeneous triangular systems. Permutations of words with prescribed symbol frequencies then transfer the dimension estimates to unequal branch contractions. For the homogeneous systems covered by the entropy estimate, we also compute the exact dimensions of Bernoulli measures and their tilted projections. Examples with exceptional factors exhibit distinct Hausdorff and box dimensions.

papers.title: Constraining the Inner Accretion Geometry of GX 9+9 with Broadband Spectral and Timing Studies
papers.abstract: We present a broadband spectral and timing study of the bright atoll neutron star low-mass X-ray binary GX~9+9, using simultaneous NICER, NuSTAR, and MAXI observations from 2019 and 2022. The broadband spectra are well described by a combination of multicolor disk emission, thermal Comptonization of blackbody seed photons from the neutron star surface or boundary layer, and associated disk reflection. We report a clear detection of reflection features in this source, including a moderately broad Fe K$\alpha$ complex and a reflection hump, confirming an earlier detection from a different observation. These features likely arise from the illumination of the moderately ionized disk by thermally Comptonized emission from the boundary layer or warm corona. While the source remained in the soft spectral state during both observations, the 2022 observation exhibits a relatively larger thermal contribution, together with a steeper Comptonized component and lower coronal optical depth. Both reflection and disk-continuum modeling favor a truncated disk, with the latter indicating a smaller inner disk radius in 2022. The inferred radial extent of the boundary layer of $\sim8~r_{\rm g}$ may play a role in the observed disk truncation. Assuming that the disk is truncated at the magnetospheric radius, we obtain an upper limit on the magnetic field strength of $\lesssim3\times10^{10}$ G. Timing analysis reveals a relatively stable disk component and a highly variable Comptonized component, consistent with the typical characteristics of the soft state.

papers.title: Gradient Optical Diffraction Tomography Using Deep Learning-Assisted Amplitude Estimation
papers.abstract: Gradient Optical Diffraction Tomography (GODT) enables the non-invasive reconstruction of a spatial derivative of the 3D sample's refractive index distribution, providing enhanced sensitivity to subtle refractive index variations through gradient-based contrast. Implemented using lateral shearing interferometry (LSI), GODT benefits from a common-path architecture that provides environmental stability and high signal-to-noise ratio measurements. Unlike conventional optical diffraction tomography (ODT), which requires numerical integration of LSI-derived phase gradients to recover the object phase, GODT enables direct tomographic reconstruction from the LSI data. Notably, GODT requires derivatives of both the phase and amplitude of the object fields as input. While the phase derivative can be readily extracted from LSI data, the amplitude gradient cannot be directly retrieved. Thus, in the original GODT formulation, the amplitude gradient was assumed to be negligible, limiting the accuracy of the resulting 3D reconstruction. In this work, we introduce amplitude-informed GODT (AI-GODT), which employs physics-informed supervised deep learning to estimate the missing amplitude gradient based on accessible LSI data, specifically the fringe modulation. The proposed approach, applying a ResNet architecture and training on computer-generated data, is validated through numerical simulation and experimental measurements of both a well-characterized test object and primary neuronal cell culture, demonstrating the network's ability to generalize to diverse samples. We show that incorporation of the recovered amplitude gradient into the GODT reconstruction pipeline improves the 3D reconstruction quality, especially in its out-of-focus regions. The software and datasets are openly available to facilitate reproducibility and further development.

papers.title: Frustration in system with intercalated and bilayer smectic structure
papers.abstract: The dimeric mesogens exhibit an unusual variety of mesophases - nematic and smectic, with distinctly different packing schemes. The relation between molecular and mesophase structure was studied for homologue series of non-symmetric bent dimers CBO6.Om, obtained by serial Pd- and Pt-catalyzed cross-coupling chemical reactions. The shorter homologues of the series form smectics with an intercalated structure, and longer homologues form bilayer smectics with broken up-down symmetry of molecular orientation within the layers, for intermediate homologues frustration leads to a nematic gap. The additional structure complexity arises from the tendency of bent dimers to form twisted structures, in which the azimuthal angle of tilted molecules forms both short- and long-pitch helices. Here we confirm, through resonant X-ray diffraction, that longer homologues form a helical four-layer structure of SmCTB-SH phase, along with a more complex one in which, in addition to the basic four-layer unit, an extra helix is superimposed, SmCTB-DH phase. This additional helix has a periodicity that is strongly temperature-dependent; upon cooling, it changes from 100 nm to 40 nm.

papers.title: Norm groups of orders and the algebraic unknotting number
papers.abstract: We use number-theoretic tools to find an explicit and effective obstruction for a knot to have algebraic unknotting number equal to $1$. As an example, we show that the connected sum of $T(2,5)$ (the cinquefoil) and $-T(2,3)$ (the negative trefoil) has algebraic unknotting number $1$, even though $T(2,5)$ has algebraic unknotting number $2$.

papers.title: Measurable equidecomposability and the Banach--Ruziewicz problem over locally compact non-Archimedean valued fields
papers.abstract: We prove a measurable analogue of the Banach--Tarski paradox over locally compact non-Archimedean valued fields. Let $\mathbb K$ be the completion of a number field at a non-Archimedean place (e.g., $\mathbb K=\mathbb Q_p$) and $n\ge 2$. Then any two bounded Haar measurable subsets of $\mathbb K^n$ with nonempty interior and equal Haar measure can be cut into finitely many Haar measurable pieces and rearranged into each other by elements of a certain countable group $\Gamma$ of affine isometries. We also show that the Haar measure is, up to a constant factor, the unique nonzero finitely additive $\Gamma$-invariant measure on the bounded Haar measurable subsets of $\mathbb K^n$, which solves a $p$-adic version of the Banach--Ruziewicz problem. Both results follow from the fact that the action of $\Gamma$ on $\mathbb K^n$ is expanding, a property closely related to the spectral gap. For $n=1$ and arbitrary characteristic, we obtain analogous results when the residue field is not prime, using a countable group of isometries that are not necessarily affine.

papers.title: An Exact Branch-Price-and-Cut Algorithm for the Vehicle Routing Problem with Floating Targets
papers.abstract: The Vehicle Routing Problem with Floating Targets (VRPFT) is a generalization of the capacitated vehicle routing problem where targets may actively move to locations ''convenient'' for the vehicles. In particular, each target may leave its home location at a bounded speed. A solution to the VRPFT is a sequence of targets for each vehicle to visit and a meeting point in space-time for each target. In this paper, we solve the VRPFT exactly with a branch-price-and-cut algorithm. Our key contribution is a dominance criterion for the pricing labeling algorithm that utilizes closed-form lower and upper bounds on a vehicle's trajectory cost given a fixed sequence of targets. We prove that the criterion preserves optimality, and the algorithm has smaller computation time than the exact dynamic program of prior work on identical hardware. We also provide a relaxed criterion that prunes more aggressively; the resulting heuristic is faster than our exact algorithm and matched every certified optimum on the benchmark.

papers.title: Calibration of Neuromusculoskeletal Models Using Differentiable Physics: Recommendations for Improving Model Accuracy
papers.abstract: Differentiable physics has shown potential to usher in a new paradigm in human neuromusculoskeletal (NMS) model calibration. Early results from pioneering works have demonstrated that auto-differentiable NMS models can greatly reduce NMS model calibration time while achieving comparable accuracy compared to traditional calibration methods. The efficient gradient-based optimizers have enabled calibration of increasingly sophisticated human models with a large number of parameters, which seek to narrow the gap between simulation and reality. Several modules have been evaluated separately in different studies, but have never been directly compared within the same study. In this work, these modules are compared on the same differentiable upper limb model with a 3-DoF shoulder, a 2-DoF elbow, and 11 superficial and 5 deep muscles in the calibration to find an optimal pipeline for improving model accuracy. The considered modules include muscle synergy, learnable bone parameters, optimizable geometry of wrap objects, and constraint torque of the differentiable arm model. To evaluate the effect and interplay between the modules on calibration accuracy, one or more modules were used in each of 16 calibration configurations, which were compared in terms of the error between two joint torques calculated by the forward and inverse dynamics with the calibrated model on 9 distinctive testing movements across 4 subjects. Results showed that torque loss was reduced by 23.6% on average using muscle synergy extrapolation to estimate deep muscle activities, and by 10.9% on average through bone dynamic parameter optimization, which are both recommended to be incorporated in the calibration.

papers.title: Last-Iterate Equilibrium Learning in Symmetric Congestion Games under Semi-Bandit Feedback
papers.abstract: We study last-iterate learning of mixed Nash equilibria in atomic symmetric congestion games under resource semi-bandit feedback, where players observe both the costs and the loads of their selected resources. For strictly increasing latency functions, the restriction of the potential function to symmetric marginal profiles is strongly convex. However, players' independent stochastic updates need not preserve this symmetry without explicit synchronization. We show that a quadratic consensus penalty makes the potential globally strongly convex while making the symmetric equilibrium the unique minimizer of the transformed potential. We propose a variant of online projected gradient descent that achieves $O(t^{-2/3})$ squared distance to equilibrium and $O(t^{-1/3})$ maximum deviation gain in expectation, for every $t\geq 1$ and for any initialization. The played profile also converges to equilibrium almost surely.

authors.name: Dimitris Fotakis
authors.institution: Athena Research and Innovation Center In Information Communication & Knowledge Technologies

papers.title: The smallest vertex triangle in a fixed polygon
papers.abstract: Among the triangles determined by $n$ points in convex position in the unit square, one has area at most $32/n^3$. Equality is possible exactly when $4$ divides $n$, and then the maximizing point set is unique. We prove a fixed-container theorem for a class of convex $s$-gons that includes affinely regular polygons and a one-parameter family of pairwise affinely inequivalent hexagons without a centre of symmetry. If the container has equal ears of area $a$ and the tips of its directed side vectors are in convex position, the sharp bound at $n=sk$ is $a/k^3$. Its equality conditions determine every side vector of the maximizing polygon. The proof uses the area enclosed by the normalized side directions. We compare the result with the area-normalized smallest-ear theorem of Gronchi and Longinetti and give consequences for unrestricted Heilbronn configurations with 13 and 15 points.

papers.title: Cartesian product of $\psi$-badly approximable sets
papers.abstract: In this note, we study the Cartesian products of sets in $\mathbb R^{d}$ that are $\psi$-approximable but not $c\psi$-approximable for arbitrarily small $c>0$, often denoted $\mathbf{Bad}_{d}(\psi)$. Setting $d=\sum_{i=1}^{N}d_i\in\mathbb N$ and $\psi_i(q)=q^{-\tau_i}$ with $\tau_i\geq 1/d_i$, $i=1,\ldots,N$, we calculate \[ \dim_{\mathrm H}\prod_{i=1}^{N}\mathbf{Bad}_{d_i}(\psi_i) =\min_{1\leq i\leq N}\left\{\frac{d_i+1}{\tau_i+1}+(d-d_i)\right\}=d- \max_{1\leq i\leq N}\left\{ d_i-\frac{d_i+1}{\tau_i+1} \right\}, \] for $\dim_{\mathrm H}$ denoting the Hausdorff dimension. The lower bound is obtained by combining the delayed-pruning construction of Koivusalo-Levesley-Ward-Zhang (IMRN, 2024) with the product Cantor-set method of Wang-Wu (TAMS, 2024).

papers.title: Development of a GPU-accelerated numerical simulation model for liver infection in realistic domains
papers.abstract: Viral hepatitis reduces the functionality of the liver and constitutes a major global health concern because it oftentimes evolves to chronic inflammation leading to long term liver damage. Mathematical models on a mesoscopic scale abstract from only partly known cell-scale processes while providing an in-silico tool for understanding tissue-scale development of the disease. In this work, we investigate the interactions between virus and immune cells in a realistic three-dimensional liver geometries by using a reaction-diffusion model that reproduces infection courses with cure and with chronic developments. A GPU-based finite-difference implementation, released as an open-source Python library, achieves speedups greater than x30 for realistic mesh sizes, making three-dimensional simulations on realistic geometries computationally tractable. This provides a basis for future in-silico studies of treatment strategies, such as testing antiviral or immunomodulatory therapies, and for patient-specific simulations based on individual liver geometries, paving the way towards personalized healthcare.

papers.title: FokasNets: Completing missing boundary data in Physics-Informed Neural Networks and Operators via the Global Relation
papers.abstract: We introduce FokasNets, a framework that combines Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) and operators (PINOs) with the Global Relation (GR) formulation of the Fokas method (also referred to as the Unified Transform), for mixed boundary problems. The general framework considers lifted representations of the neural network models, where the Dirichlet boundary conditions are imposed by construction and the neural network learns the interior correction. The Global Relation is used as an additional solve during training that provides the missing boundary conditions to the lifted neural network, making training more efficient and accurate in the interior and on the boundary. We develop the construction of FokasNets for elliptic and evolution PDEs (Fokas-PINNs), and the corresponding PDE solution operator problems (Fokas Operator Networks - FONets), using the Global Relation formulations for these PDE classes. Furthermore, we develop the necessary theoretical framework for FokasNets, including error and stability analysis and show that FokasNets are universal approximators. We provide comprehensive numerical experiments, using examples with manufactured solutions and literature benchmarks. Compared to standard PINNs and Physics-Informed DeepONets and their lifted versions, FokasNets achieve significant improvements in solution accuracy in the interior and boundaries, both for single PDEs and particularly for solution operators, where the improvement reaches multiple orders of magnitude and fixed threshold errors are reached faster during training.

papers.title: A new method of Ecological Inference based on the Cressie--Read power divergence
papers.abstract: Ecological inference aims to estimate the bivariate association structure between a pair of variables from the row and column totals of a set of contingency tables. The paper introduces a new approach based on minimizing the Cressie--Read power divergence, applied to the estimation of vote transitions between two elections. It also outlines a Fisher scoring algorithm and derives the asymptotic distribution of the estimator.

papers.title: OSIRIS-REx Lessons Learned Report: Insights from the Journey to Bennu and Back
papers.abstract: OSIRIS-REx, NASA's third New Frontiers mission, was the first U.S. mission to return a sample from an asteroid. Proposed in 2010 for an \$811 million lifecycle cost, the mission was completed for \$828 million, returned more than \$52 million of Headquarters reserves unused, and delivered at least 121.6 g of pristine material from near-Earth asteroid (101955) Bennu in September 2023, more than twice the Level-1 requirement. It did so despite a surface far more rugged than predicted, the discovery of particle ejection, sampling in a regolith much weaker than expected, operations during the COVID-19 pandemic, and an off-nominal parachute sequence on Earth return. This report sets out the lessons learned by the mission's leadership across six areas: leadership and governance; cost, schedule and risk management; systems engineering; mission operations; sample return, curation and analysis; and data archiving. Recurring themes are that a PI-led structure integrating science, engineering and project management gives the discipline to make fast, informed decisions; that reserves and schedule margin spent early to retire risk, such as funding Natural Feature Tracking as a backup navigation system, buy the flexibility to absorb discovery; that heritage hardware reduces risk only when its verification and engineering knowledge are preserved; and that contamination knowledge, sample science and data stewardship are mission-long responsibilities, not post-flight tasks. Each section pairs background with specific recommendations for future sample-return and small-body missions.

papers.title: What, Who, and When: Structured Harm Assessment for Mental Health Safety via Short Reasoning
papers.abstract: The growing use of large language models (LLMs) for mental health support raises important safety concerns. Existing guard models primarily identify categories of harmful content, often overlooking the context needed to determine an appropriate response. We introduce a clinically grounded taxonomy that characterizes harm along three dimensions: what the harm is, who is involved, and when it occurs. It further separates harm characterization from intervention decisions, thus enabling safety policies to be specified outside the model weights through explicit, clinician-curated instructions that can be updated and audited. We validate the taxonomy with expert clinicians and validate a panel of LLM judges to scale annotation. Relabeling public benchmarks in this taxonomy shows that they rarely contain harm directed at the user, which accounts for nearly half of the harm in real conversations. We then train MindGuard2, a 35B-A3B reasoning-based guard model using supervised fine-tuning on short reasoning traces followed by reinforcement learning with a reasoning-length penalty, to minimize inference overhead while preserving the benefits of reasoning. On two public benchmarks and real-world conversations, MindGuard2 achieves balanced accuracy comparable to the substantially larger GLM-5.3 at approximately 10x lower median latency, advancing the accuracy-latency Pareto frontier. Furthermore, it achieves low false-positive rates at high recall, helping balance the need to detect unsafe situations against the risk of unnecessary interventions that may disrupt support and undermine user trust. We release a safety guardrail model with SOTA performance trained on synthetic data, together with synthetic conversations and annotations of public benchmarks in our taxonomy.

papers.title: Photometric Uncertainty Correction for Time-Domain Surveys: Vera C. Rubin Data Preview 2 Case Study
papers.abstract: Time-domain science, from variability detection to supernova cosmology, relies on accurate photometric uncertainties. We present a data-driven, catalog-level method to validate and improve the photometric uncertainties reported by time-domain surveys. The analysis is based on transforming light curves of non-variable objects into mean-variance whitened signals. We then estimate a correction to the uncertainties by matching the distribution of the whitened signals of all objects to the standard normal distribution, which they ought to follow when the uncertainties are correct. The correction can be modeled as a function of each measurement's flux, reported uncertainty, and available observational metadata, and can be applied to measurements of both non-variable and variable objects. Applied to the Rubin Observatory Data Preview 2 (DP2), the method shows that the uncertainties of bright sources are underestimated by up to a factor of five. The inferred corrections correspond to a magnitude error floor of about 10 mmag for both direct-image and difference-image photometry, decreasing to about 6 mmag in deeper fields. We provide the corrected uncertainties as part of the Rubin DP2 HATS catalogs.

authors.name: Sean McGuire
authors.institution: The University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center

papers.title: LiveRelight: Sub-Second Global Illumination Editing for Gaussian Interiors
papers.abstract: Relighting reconstructed 3D scenes remains challenging due to the complex nature of light transport: slow or approximate visual feedback restricts the editor's ability to fine-tune the results to satisfaction. We present a hybrid relighting approach that enables interactive, high-fidelity updates of direct and indirect indoor illumination without per-edit optimization. Our approach permits the editor to make a wide range of relighting edits at room-scale, with near-instant feedback. Our key insight is to precompute geometric light exchange rather than illumination responses, retaining an inexpensive transport solve that accommodates changes in emission and surface reflectance. We evaluate direct illumination on reconstructed 2D Gaussians using visibility-aware sampling of one-sided emitters, while propagating diffuse interreflection through sparse radiosity on a triangle proxy. A sparse projection fitted through Gaussian alpha compositing transfers the proxy solution to the reconstruction. Our formulation further supports fast fixture transformations and emitter insertion by recomputing light source injection. Across eight relighting conditions of our synthetic test suite, our sub-second edits improve relighting fidelity over prior path-traced editing by an average of 5\,dB PSNR, while reducing editing latency by up to three orders of magnitude. Qualitative results further demonstrate realistic, interactive relighting of real-world captures.

papers.title: Passive Fault-Tolerant Antenna Stabilisation for Ship-to-Shore Communication
papers.abstract: Directional ship-to-shore radio links require continuous antenna alignment with the shore station, while vessel heave induces variations in antenna height above the sea surface, thereby altering the multipath interference governing the received power. In conventional stabilised gimbals, attitude compensation is provided, whereas fault tolerance is rarely considered. To address these limitations, a passive fault-tolerant control scheme is proposed, whereby the antenna is mounted on a ship-mounted six-degree-of-freedom manipulator, enabling simultaneous regulation alignment and antenna height. Through feedback linearisation, the manipulator dynamics are decoupled into perturbed integrators, each controlled by a multi-barrier adaptive super-twisting sliding-mode controller. The nested barriers are associated with the performance regions of fault-tolerant control, such that inter-sample barrier crossings under discrete-time implementation lead to graceful performance degradation rather than loss of confinement. Under simulated conditions, superior pointing and heave accuracy is achieved compared with single-barrier designs, for which either precision or confinement is compromised.

papers.title: Most of the Way There: Turning a Strong Video Prior into an Action-Conditioned World Model
papers.abstract: Modern video generators excel at producing visually plausible futures guided by text and image prompts. Yet their emphasis on semantic plausibility does not guarantee fidelity to the physical consequences of specific actions. Action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), in contrast, aim to simulate how the world responds to robot actions, enabling scalable policy evaluation and improvement without costly real-world rollouts. The challenge is not merely to generate a plausible future, but to predict what follows from a specific physical action. As video priors grow stronger, we ask how little adaptation is truly needed to bridge this gap. We introduce Dianjing, a minimal recipe that preserves and unlocks the capabilities of strong video priors through unified physical action conditioning, training concentrated at the high noise levels where motion and layout, and thus the consequences of actions, are decided, and native history conditioning. Built upon MiniMax H3, a 33B video foundation model, Dianjing freezes the pretrained backbone and trains only 0.34% of its parameters using approximately 65 hours of robot video across two embodiments, without additional robot-specific pretraining or camera calibration. Controlled ablations show that where training is allocated across noise levels matters more than how actions enter the network. On WorldOracle, which evaluates predictions against paired real-world executions, Dianjing achieves the best scores on four of the five evaluation tracks and ranks second on AgiBot-Long. Our findings suggest that strong video priors already bring us most of the way to world modeling; lightweight physical action grounding can unlock their potential for real-world prediction.

authors.name: Xianglong Guo
authors.institution: Harbin University of Science and Technology

papers.title: Probing Dynamical Dark Energy with Hyper Suprime-Cam Year 3 Cosmic Shear
papers.abstract: Recent measurements of baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) and Type Ia Supernovae (SNe) have revealed a preference for a time-evolving dark energy equation of state. Because such dynamical behavior alters both the cosmic expansion history and the late-time growth of structure, weak gravitational lensing measurements can be used to test these extended models. We present an extended analysis of the real-space cosmic shear two-point correlation functions (2PCFs) from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Year 3 (HSC-Y3) survey. Using over 25 million galaxies across 416 deg$^2$, divided into four tomographic redshift bins ($0.3 < z \le 1.5$), we constrain both a constant ($w$CDM) and a time-varying ($w_0w_a$CDM) dark energy equation of state. To break the geometric degeneracies inherent in cosmic shear, we combine the HSC-Y3 data with a CMB-independent suite of background distance probes: DESI DR2 BAO, the recalibrated DES five-year SN sample (DOVEKIE), and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis (BBN) priors. In the $w$CDM paradigm, our joint analysis yields $w =-0.936^{+0.074}_{-0.067}$, consistent with a cosmological constant. Within the $w_0w_a$CDM framework, we find $w_0 =-0.832^{+0.071}_{-0.059}$ and $w_a = -1.23^{+0.66}_{-0.44}$, representing a $2.4\sigma$ preference for dynamical dark energy. Although the unconstrained dark energy parameters reduce the cosmic shear-only $S_8$ constraints to smaller values, our joint multi-probe analysis agrees with the baseline HSC-Y3 $\Lambda$CDM structure growth amplitude. We obtain $S_8 = 0.774^{+0.027}_{-0.034}$ for $w$CDM and $S_8 = 0.772^{+0.031}_{-0.030}$ for $w_0w_a$CDM. Our results demonstrate that the weak lensing amplitude is robust to extended dark energy parameterizations, and that the dynamical dark energy signal is currently driven primarily by the geometric distance ladders, a critical consistency test for next-generation Stage-IV cosmological surveys.

authors.name: Surhud More
authors.institution: Inter-University Centre for Astronomy and Astrophysics

papers.title: Measuring the flavor composition of high-energy neutrinos from the Milky Way
papers.abstract: The origin of the Milky Way's high-energy neutrinos is debated. Their flavor composition reflects how they are made and could help settle it, but remains to be measured. We show that IceCube and KM3NeT, which see the inner Galaxy in complementary ways from opposite hemispheres, could start resolving its flavor composition in about a decade. With upcoming telescopes, they would infer the $\nu_e$ fraction at the sources to within 27%. A first comparison of Galactic and extragalactic flavor compositions could reveal strong magnetic fields in extragalactic sources or neutrino decay.

papers.title: Provably Efficient Offline Discounted Reinforcement Learning under Recursive Entropic Risk
papers.abstract: We study risk-sensitive reinforcement learning in finite discounted infinite-horizon Markov Decision Processes with recursive entropic risk measures (ERM), parameterized by $\beta\neq 0$. We consider both risk-averse ($\beta>0$) and risk-seeking ($\beta<0$) settings. We consider the offline RL setting, where the agent is provided with a fixed dataset and wishes to learn a near-optimal policy using this dataset. We introduce a model-based algorithm, called ERM Value Iteration Lower Confidence Bound (ERM-VI-LCB) and derive a PAC-type bound on its sample complexity. We also establish a corresponding lower bound, demonstrating that exponential dependence on $|\beta|/(1-\gamma)$ asserted by the upper bound is unavoidable in the worst case. The presented bounds provide the first rigorous sample complexity guarantees for offline RL under recursive ERM across both risk-averse and risk-seeking regimes.

papers.title: Under the Influence -- of What? A Controlled Evaluation of Influence Functions
papers.abstract: Influence functions are a promising way to identify which training examples are responsible for a model's output. However, so far empirical evaluations on LLM pretraining level only assumed that they work as intended. This is the first work to systematically evaluate whether the 'influential' examples actually have properties relevant to a language model output, based on re-training with controlled data splits. We investigate three prominent Hessian approximation methods (GradSim, TrackStar, K-FAC) in two settings (linguistic phenomena and factual knowledge) in GPT-2 type models (68M-5.6B training tokens). We find that on average, the `influential' examples are indeed relevant, but they do not always bear the target properties directly, and the ratio and kind of relevance varies by setting.

papers.title: Genus one mirror symmetry and surfaces with trivial first Chern class
papers.abstract:
The main goal of this paper is to study the extension of genus-one BCOV type mirror symmetry for smooth projective varieties with vanishing $c_1(X)$. We show that the naive generalization of the expectation that one can encode genus one Gromov-Witten invariants in the BCOV invariant of the mirror family cannot hold in this setup. We show this by completing the study of these invariants for surfaces. Progress had been made recently by Oberdieck's proof of the Klemm-Mari\~no conjecture for Enriques surfaces, which can be combined with computations of equivariant analytic torsion by Yoshikawa. We also perform the analogous study for bielliptic surfaces.
  Both of these cases present a sign issue not present in the known trivial canonical bundle cases, which we show implies that the mirror symmetry predictions cannot hold for varieties with torsion canonical bundle, even up to sign.

authors.name: Dennis Eriksson
authors.institution: Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, Alnarp

papers.title: Who Attributes a Mind to Whom? Mutual Theory of Mind in Simulated User-Assistant Conversation
papers.abstract: When users assume that an AI chatbot has mental states, they are more likely to develop over-reliance, emotional dependence, and in extreme cases, psychological harm or self-harm. However, how these mind attributions arise in conversations and how human or AI factors influence this is still unknown. We study how users attribute minds using a minimal framework: a simulated user with different characteristics chats with assistants that differ in social style and memory. We also introduce a message-level measure of who attributes a mind to whom in four directions, checked with trained coders and applied by a fine-tuned encoder that reproduces an LLM judge. Our results show that, on average, nine out of thirteen characteristics raised simulated users' attribution to the assistant. We found that relational needs such as attachment anxiety raised it as theory predicts, some general personality traits raised it as well, and AI-specific characteristics the least. By contrast, the assistant's social style barely changed simulated users' mind attribution. Instead, sycophantic instructions raised the assistant's attribution to itself. Memory raised users' attribution only with some user models. The model playing the user changed overall attribution and the effects of characteristics, style, and memory. Our framework measures how persona descriptions affect mind attribution in simulation. It gives concrete hypotheses for human studies and shows the need for more consistent user simulators.

papers.title: Counter-DECEIVR: Counterfactual Explanations for Deepfake Detectors using Detector-Guided Rectified Flow Inversion
papers.abstract: Deep-learning-generated media are increasingly passed off as real, driving an arms race between image generators and deepfake detectors. Trust in the latter is limited by their often black-box nature; and, while region-based explanations can sometimes be extracted, these become less useful as generation quality improves. Counterfactual examples, which show the minimal change that flips a detector's decision, reveal what evidence drives a verdict, helping analysts decide whether to trust it. This work introduces Counter-DECEIVR (DEtector-guided reCtifiEd flow InVeRsion for counterfactuals), a novel training-free framework that generates counterfactual examples. Counter-DECEIVR steers latents in the velocity field of a rectified flow model using gradients from off-the-shelf deepfake detectors, without training a generator or adapting the detector; unlike prior methods, it requires no per-instance or per-detector fitting and no diffusion training on the target data. It also leverages the detector's explanation maps to concentrate editing to salient regions, turning low-level feature importance into localised counterfactual edits. A single parameter controls the strength of the edits. Across two deepfake detectors and two widely used forensics datasets, Counter-DECEIVR outperforms prior counterfactual generation methods, including training-based ones. Code will be made available upon acceptance.

papers.title: Voltage-Enhanced Photorefractive Hysteresis in Thin-Film Lithium Niobate Photonic-Crystal Cavities
papers.abstract: We observe voltage-enhanced photorefractive hysteresis in thin-film lithium niobate nanocavities, causing the resonance to appear at different wavelengths during increasing- and decreasing-wavelength laser scans. Their separation grows with bias magnitude and optical power, but depends weakly on scan speed over 1-200 nm/s. A quasi-static surface-trap model links voltage-biased carrier transport to asymmetric trapping, whose space-charge field shifts the resonance through the Pockels effect. The model captures this hysteresis across three cavities through switching between stable steady states. Space-charge feedback opposes further carrier separation, limiting the hysteresis gap. The model informs photorefractive mitigation and resonance control in integrated electro-optic devices.

authors.name: Dashiell L. P. Vitullo
authors.institution: United States Army Combat Capabilities Development Command

papers.title: Crucible: Evaluating LLM Agents in Executable Chemistry Research Environments
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on chemistry knowledge benchmarks, which mainly assess question answering and isolated tasks. Chemical research, however, requires using specialized tools and interpreting their outputs to obtain chemically valid results. To address this gap, we introduce Crucible Bench to evaluate this ability across all four stages of the design-make-test-analyze (DMTA) cycle. The benchmark contains 1,078 tasks in 12 task families curated from 18 published datasets, covering molecular design, synthesis planning, experimental execution, closed-loop optimization, simulation, and analytical characterization. Agents access 75 domain-specific tools through the Model Context Protocol in seven isolated environments. Sandboxed graders verify the resulting synthesis routes, experimental protocols, and other outputs. Laboratory tasks use robotic simulators or previously measured experimental data. We evaluate 14 LLMs as agents and find that the best achieves an overall score of 0.545, with synthesis planning and closed-loop optimization emerging as the hardest domains. Overall performance does not predict optimization performance well: the model ranked twelfth overall achieves the highest score in closed-loop optimization. Error analysis also shows that agents often submit chemically invalid results despite running their tools successfully. Stronger models benefit more from tool access, but reliable use of chemical software remains a challenge that Crucible Bench can track as models improve.

authors.name: Xiuying Chen
authors.institution: Children's Hospital of Chongqing Medical University

papers.title: First Order Real Resonant Digital Filters and A Novel Orthogonal State Generator
papers.abstract: We describe FOREST, a real, first order digital resonant filter and orthogonal state generator. We show that in spite of the imaginary nature of the roots of the transfer function of a resonator, appropriate interpretation of this transfer function nonetheless leads to a practical first order filter with real coefficients. We use a discrete state space model of FOREST to predict the resonator properties, and implement the filter in digital signal processing slices on a digital signal processing platform. Applications are in real time digital signal processing, engineering fields such as mains electricity monitoring and motor control, any application requiring a phase locked loop, and physics applications utilising high-quality-factor resonators.

authors.name: Edward J. Daw
authors.institution: École Nationale Supérieure d'Ingénieurs de Caen

papers.title: Variational Principles and Machine Learning: a Numerical Analysis and PDE perspective
papers.abstract: Variational principles have played a fundamental role in the development of modern mathematics, physics, and scientific computing. From the principles of least action in mechanics to the calculus of variations and the variational formulation of partial differential equations, they have provided a powerful framework for understanding complex problems and designing reliable numerical methods. In recent years, Machine Learning has introduced a new computational paradigm, in which highly expressive nonlinear function spaces and large-scale minimisation problems play a central role. In these notes, we explore the connection between these two frameworks. We develop a variational and numerical-analysis perspective on Machine Learning algorithms, focusing in particular on their formulation as nonlinear minimisation problems. We investigate how classical concepts such as stability, consistency, approximability, and compactness acquire new interpretations in this setting, and how the variational structure of the underlying continuous problem can govern the behaviour of neural-network approximations. This perspective provides a mathematical framework for understanding existing ML algorithms while also suggesting new approaches to their design. In particular, alternative and strongly coercive variational principles can lead to more stable, reliable, and potentially more efficient computational methods.

papers.title: On the Hardness of Optimal CNOT Circuits
papers.abstract: This note revisits the computational problem of optimal CNOT synthesis: given an invertible binary matrix $A\in \mathsf{GL}(d,2)$ over the field of two elements and a budget $K$, decide if $A$ can be implemented with $\leq K$ CNOT gates. The $\mathsf{NP}$-completeness of this problem was recently published independently by Acuaviva, Acuaviva, and Acuaviva (arXiv:2608.03825) and by Li and Guan (arXiv:2609.04160). This note gives a new proof, with three features. First, $\mathsf{NP}$-completeness holds even over linear oracles, i.e., matrices of the form $(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})\mapsto(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}+F\mathbf{x})$, which are the standard reversible embedding of a linear function $F$. These are involutions, and seemingly simpler than the families of the two previous works, which both have order four. Second, hardness persists when SWAP gates are free and qubits may be permuted (and this holds under any connected topology). Third, the exposition is arguably simpler to follow. Along the way, it gives a proof of the XOR-circuit lower bound of Boyar, Matthews, and Peralta [J. Cryptology 26 (2013)] that is, perhaps, simpler than existing ones.

papers.title: Critical exponents and near-critical limits for random matrix products
papers.abstract: We study the approach to the zero-Lyapunov-exponent transition for products of independent, identically distributed invertible matrices. The matrix laws are supported in a common compact subset of $GL(d,\mathbb{R})$ and converge in total variation to a strongly irreducible and proximal law with zero top Lyapunov exponent. We establish a near-critical renewal theorem for the occupation measure and a functional diffusion limit for the logarithmic cocycle as well as exact asymptotics and scaling limits for three observables describing the transient dynamics. The expected number of escapes from the unit ball and the expected number of visits to a fixed annulus diverge as the inverse absolute Lyapunov exponent, and both counts have exponential limits after normalization. The time spent on the side opposite to the asymptotic drift has critical exponent two and converges, after rescaling, to the positive occupation time of Brownian motion with negative drift.

papers.title: Frozen Phonons on Dense $\mathbf{q}$-Grids Using Set Covers
papers.abstract: Phonon dynamics determine a vast number of properties in the solid state, such as the heat capacity, thermal expansion, and thermal conductivity. Phonons are obtained through the dynamical matrix, which, in the frozen phonon approach, is calculated as a finite difference derivative of the analytical Hellmann-Feynman force. This approach unfortunately typically suffers from requiring very large supercells, even for modest $\mathbf{q}$-grids. The non-diagonal supercell method remedies this issue by determining the smallest supercell commensurate with a given $\mathbf{q}$-point, drastically reducing the supercell size, but in turn requiring a new supercell for each $\mathbf{q}$-point on the grid. This introduces redundancy, however, since a single non-diagonal supercell may be commensurate with several $\mathbf{q}$-points. In this work I present a method to determine a minimal set of supercells, such that every $\mathbf{q}$-point on the grid is commensurate with at least one supercell. I present an algorithm to solve the problem and prove that it yields the optimal solution, before summarizing the algorithm using pseudocode. The scaling of the number of supercells with the density of the grid is discussed. Numerical results on a variety of systems show the significant computational advantage of the method, which increases with the density of the grid.

The energy range of a typical phonon causes it to be populated at room temperature, implying that thermal properties are often governed by phonons. This includes heat capacity [1], thermal expansion [2], and thermal conductivity [3], among others. Phonons are furthermore experimentally observable, for example through neutron diffraction techniques [4] or Raman [5] and infrared [6] spectroscopy.

This facilitates the calculation of dynamical matrices on dense 𝐪\mathbf{q}-grids. Despite the success of DFPT, its availability is limited by difficulty of implementation, in stark contrast to the simplicity of the frozen phonon approach. Being agnostic to the employed electronic structure calculation, frozen phonons are often used for more advanced electronic treatments such as hybrid functionals [10, 11] or the GW approach for electron correlation [12, 13]. Modern approaches to anharmonic vibrational effects also tend to stray from linear response approaches such as DFPT [14, 15, 16], even though higher-order force constants (third and fourth) have been obtainable using linear response for decades [17, 18, 19]. The frozen phonon approach is therefore still relevant, motivating the search for ways to increase its efficiency.
