papers.title: Graded Monoidal Categories and Internalization
papers.abstract: In stable homotopy theory, there are a variety of ways to construct a point-set level smash product of spectra, each with its own advantages and limitations. These constructions often involve internalizing some graded external product. In this paper, we aim to formalize this process through a general categorical framework, providing a common language for these constructions. We propose a general theory for internalizing a graded monoidal product, investigate its 2-categorical properties, and use this framework to recover both Day convolution and the smash product of $S$-modules.
papers.intro:
In homotopy theory one is often concerned only with objects of interest up to homotopy. However, when possible, one may wish to lift a homotopical phenomenon to the point-set level to be studied prior to passing to the homotopy category. For instance, one might desire a well-behaved smash product of spectra that lifts the symmetric monoidal structure of the stable homotopy category. However, in [10], it is shown that no such lift can exist without surrendering at least one property desirable of this product.

In homotopy theory one is often concerned only with objects of interest up to homotopy. However, when possible, one may wish to lift a homotopical phenomenon to the point-set level to be studied prior to passing to the homotopy category. For instance, one might desire a well-behaved smash product of spectra that lifts the symmetric monoidal structure of the stable homotopy category. However, in [10], it is shown that no such lift can exist without surrendering at least one property desirable of this product.

In fact, many weaker smash products of spectra exist, varying in which of these properties are compromised and what point-set model of spectra is favored. For example, one can construct a smash product of symmetric or orthogonal spectra using Day convolution [12, 14, 7]. Alternatively, if one wishes to use the coordinate-free spectra of [1] then restricting to SS-modules yields another smash product. Both of these constructions entail some external graded product being pulled into a single degree to yield the desired internal smash product. In this paper, we propose a general categorical axiomatization of this procedure of internalizing a graded product: we define an additional structure on graded monoidal categories which permits an internalization, show that the resulting product is monoidal, and recover the constructions of several classical smash products of spectra using this framework.

We make the following contributions. – The structure of an internalization on a graded monoidal category, forming what we call an internalized category (Definition 2.19). – A framework for constructing an ordinary monoidal product on the degree one component of an internalized category, which can be equipped with additional structure allowing for the recovery of standard properties like symmetry and closure (Theorem 2.26, Corollary 2.30, Corollary 2.35). – A 2-categorical theory of graded monoidal categories and internalization, including the corresponding notions of functors and natural transformations between them (Section 3). – An outline of free-forgetful adjunction between graded monoidal categories and internalized categories, as well as the coreflective relationship between ordinary categories and graded monoidal categories, and between monoidal categories and internalized categories (Corollary 3.9, Theorem 3.21, Theorem 3.23). – Derivations of Day convolution and the smash product of SS-modules within the framework of internalization, providing a common language across both constructions using their graded monoidal structure (Proposition 4.7, Theorem 4.24).

papers.title: A Stackelberg strategy for the semi-linear heat equation with boundary controls
papers.abstract: This work continues the results presented in \cite{calsavara2022new} where a hierarchical control problem is solved. Our first goal is the case of both controls acting on the boundary. The follower control solves a null controllability problem, and the leader minimizes a $L^2$ cost functional. Additionally, we solve the case where one control acts on the boundary and the other on an open subset of the domain. More precisely, we prove the existence and uniqueness of a leader-follower couple and give some techniques to solve the problem.

papers.title: SAT-Driven Exact Treewidth via Safe Separators and Structure-Aware Encodings
papers.abstract: Treewidth is a standard measure of graph structure, but computing it exactly is NP-hard. SAT- and MaxSAT-based approaches provide a uniform way to solve treewidth by encoding it in conjunctive normal form and delegating the search to modern Boolean solvers, thus directly benefiting from continued progress in SAT technology. This report studies how to strengthen such SAT-driven solvers with structural reasoning and low-overhead guidance, both at the meta-algorithmic level and within the encoding itself. Starting from a baseline SAT/MaxSAT formulation, we investigate structure-based simplifications that reduce solver effort while preserving exactness, and we evaluate practical heuristic enhancements (fast upper/lower bounds and solver guidance) within iterative SAT and MaxSAT workflows. Experiments show consistent speedups on instances with exploitable structure, and clarify where SAT-based approaches remain limited.

papers.title: Murmurations in Short Intervals for Elliptic Curves Ordered by Height
papers.abstract: Murmurations are the phenomenon, first observed by He, Lee, Oliver, and Pozdnyakov (2025), that the average value of $\epsilon(E) a_p(E)$, the $p$-th $L$-function coefficient weighted by the root number, over elliptic curves of conductor in some range $N(E) \in [N_1, N_2]$ seem to approximate a continuous, oscillating function. While murmurations have been proven for other families of $L$-functions (notably by Zubrilina (2025) for weight $k$ modular forms), the only unconditional murmuration formula for elliptic curves is a partial result by Sawin and Sutherland (2025) ordering by naive height instead of conductor. In this setting, murmurations appear by first averaging $\epsilon(E) a_p(E)$ for a single curve over $p \in (C_1, C_2)$ and then average over elliptic curves of bounded height. However, Sawin and Sutherland's results average $\epsilon(E) a_n(E)$ over all of $\mathbb{N}$ instead of a small interval $(C_1, C_2).$ In this work, we prove how small the interval $(C_1, C_2)$ can be taken while preserving the conclusion of Sawin and Sutherland's first murmuration formula (Proposition 7).

Murmurations are a statistical phenomenon, first observed by He, Lee, Oliver, and Pozdnyakov for elliptic curves in [10]. Specifically, they concern oscillations in the averages of LL-function coefficients apa_{p} (for fixed prime pp) over curves with similar conductor. These oscillations, which are dependent on the rank of the averaged curves, appear to approximate a continuous function. Recent work has demonstrated that the phenomenon holds more generally for LL-functions of families of modular forms.

papers.title: Parallel sums of nilpotent elements: exact realization and structured eigenvalue splitting
papers.abstract: We prove that, over every infinite field and for $m\ge2$, the parallel sums $N(N+C)^{-1}C$ of nilpotent $m\times m$ inputs with invertible sum are exactly the matrices of nullity at least two. Every positive split of the target nullity between the input kernels is realizable. Over $\mathbb{C}$, we determine the paired derivative image and characterize universal full matrix cancellation at nonzero residues. For analytic input paths, nilpotence is required only at the base. An adjugate identity forces the last two characteristic coefficients to be $O(\varepsilon^2)$, yielding sharp bounds $O(|\varepsilon|^{2/3})$ at nonzero three-dimensional nilpotent residues and $O(|\varepsilon|^{1/(m-2)})$ at nilpotent residues for $m\ge4$. At every base with residue of type $[m-1,1]$, $m\ge4$, we prove a generic splitting law, also with fixed input sum. For $m\ge5$, it has $m-2$ roots on the scale $|\varepsilon|^{1/(m-2)}$ and two on the scale $|\varepsilon|^{1/2}$, separating the largest-root and spectral-gap scales. A separate sharpness family keeps both inputs nilpotent and two roots zero. At the nonzero nilpotent three-dimensional boundary, a finite coefficient criterion computes the splitting orders for each exceptional affine fixed-sum direction. For each such path, the punctured spectral gap is at least $c|\varepsilon|^3$ near zero for some $c>0$, and the exponent is optimal over this class. Over a nonzero unital ring with $2$ invertible, we construct two $3\times3$ matrix inputs, each of nilpotency index exactly three, with invertible sum. In the complex unital Banach case, the residue has spectrum ${0}\cup\tfrac12\sigma(Q)$ for every coefficient $Q$. With the common core allowed to vary, a complex matrix is a finite-Drazin Hua output if and only if its nullity is not one.

papers.abstract: Standard Transformers allocate independent dense weight matrices to every feed-forward network (FFN) layer, coupling parameters linearly with depth (O(L)) and discarding prior compute when scaling capacity. Conversely, weight-tied Looped Transformers decouple depth from parameters (O(1)) but enforce time-homogeneous updates. We formulate the L-layer FFN stack as a 3D Tensor Cuboid and introduce QuatTucker-ZigZagGPT, unifying: (1) 4D Quaternion Hamilton GEMMs in bfloat16 (4x FFN compression), (2) 64x64 Block-Diagonal Tucker SwiGLU Cores for depth-specific rotations over a shared basis, (3) Braided ZigZag Diamond Routing (L0 -> L2 -> L1 -> L3) for zero-FLOP top-down refinement, and (4) Exact 2D Zero-Loss Continual Scaling in both width and depth. We also introduce Annealed Gated Bounce-Back Scaffolding (GatedBounce), which self-distills to 0.0% inference overhead. Across algorithmic tasks (8-bit Parity, 56-seed routing ablations, Mod-53 Grokking) and language modeling (TinyStories, FineWeb-Edu), our model outperforms standard Transformers at 2x-7.6x compression. On A100, QuatTucker-ZigZagGPT-12 (39.0M backbone) beats StandardGPT-12 (85.0M backbone) at 5/5 controlled checkpoints. Continually scaling one lineage across 6.00B tokens via zero-loss width growth (rank 6144 -> 8192), two bit-exact depth expansions (L = 12 -> 16 -> 20, 70.9M backbone, max_diff = 0.000000), and WSD cooldown reaches 3.3582 FineWeb-Edu loss (28.74 PPL) and 44.75% full-split zero-shot accuracy across 16,955 questions (ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, WinoGrande, BoolQ), matching GPT-3 Small (125M, 300B tokens) at 50x fewer tokens.

papers.title: Geometric realization of the local Langlands and local Jacquet-Langlands correspondences for $\mathrm{GL}_n$ in a partially ramified case
papers.abstract: We construct a new family of algebraic varieties over a finite field, realizing the local Langlands and local Jacquet-Langlands correspondences for $\mathrm{GL}_n$ in their compactly supported \'etale cohomology. The resulting representations have $L$-parameters which are induced from characters of a partially ramified field extension.

Let KK be a non-archimedean local field with residue field 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} of characteristic pp, and let WKW_{K} be its Weil group. Let n≥1n\geq 1 be an integer, and let DD be the central division algebra over KK of invariant 1/n1/n. The local Langlands correspondence for GLn⁡(K)\GL_{n}(K) gives a bijection between irreducible supercuspidal representations of GLn⁡(K)\GL_{n}(K) and irreducible nn-dimensional representations of WKW_{K}, while the local Jacquet-Langlands correspondence gives a bijection between irreducible essentially square-integrable representations of GLn⁡(K)\GL_{n}(K) and irreducible smooth representations of D×D^{\times}. We distinguish the unramified, totally ramified, and partially ramified cases according to the ramification of L/KL/K.

However, this realization relies on global methods and does not by itself provide an explicit description of the correspondences. Beginning with the work of Yoshida [17], it has become clear that such explicit descriptions can be obtained by studying the reductions of suitable formal models of Lubin-Tate spaces. In particular, Yoshida showed that a Deligne-Lusztig variety appears in the reduction of a semistable model at the first level, reflecting the realization of depth-zero supercuspidal representations.

papers.title: Data Centers: The Error of Generalizing Environmental and Socioeconomic Impacts. The Need for a Contextualized Assessment of Computing Infrastructure in Brazil and Worldwide
papers.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud computing has intensified debates about the environmental and socioeconomic impacts of data centers, including electricity and water consumption, noise, land use, and employment. A recurring methodological problem in these debates is the use of global data, or of evidence produced in a particular country, to draw conclusions about facilities located in very different settings. This paper argues that the impacts of a data center depend on the geographic, climatic, energy, technological, economic, and regulatory conditions of the territory where it operates, and must therefore be assessed at the appropriate territorial and technological scale. Using Brazil as a case, we discuss the country's predominantly renewable electricity mix and the curtailment of renewable generation, the reported prevalence of closed-loop cooling, national and municipal noise regulations, the water-efficiency requirement of the new Redata tax regime, and the ongoing litigation over the Pec{\'e}m data center in the state of Cear{\'a}. We also examine a recent study of data centers in Northern Virginia, showing the limits of its external validity and of its noise measurements. We propose a multiscale assessment framework and conclude that international evidence should inform which questions are asked, not predetermine the answers -- a principle that applies equally to claims of harm and to claims of safety.
papers.intro:
The expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud computing has driven a significant increase in demand for computing infrastructure. In parallel, discussions about the environmental and socioeconomic impacts of data centers have intensified, particularly regarding water consumption, energy demand, noise pollution, land occupation, and job creation. However, there is a recurring problem in how these arguments are constructed: global data, or studies conducted in particular countries, are used to support conclusions about facilities located in entirely different settings.

The expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud computing has driven a significant increase in demand for computing infrastructure. In parallel, discussions about the environmental and socioeconomic impacts of data centers have intensified, particularly regarding water consumption, energy demand, noise pollution, land occupation, and job creation. However, there is a recurring problem in how these arguments are constructed: global data, or studies conducted in particular countries, are used to support conclusions about facilities located in entirely different settings.

A data center is not an infrastructure independent of the environment in which it is embedded. Its operation depends on the geographic, climatic, energy, technological, economic, and regulatory characteristics of the territory where it is built. Therefore, we cannot use the environmental impacts identified in U.S. facilities as sufficient evidence of the impacts a Brazilian facility will produce. Likewise, we cannot indiscriminately use data from São Paulo to assess a project located in Ceará, since, even within a single country, there are significant differences among regions, states, and municipalities.

This does not mean disregarding international research, but rather understanding the limits of its external validity. Global data are important for characterizing trends, while regional studies make it possible to identify specific phenomena. Neither, however, replaces an assessment of the concrete conditions under which a given project will be installed.

papers.title: Counting Classical Fullerenes I: Exact Enumeration and Generic Achiral Symmetry
papers.abstract: We give an exact arithmetic formula for the number of classical fullerenes on $2m$ vertices. The oriented count is known; the new contribution counts achiral fullerenes, those admitting an orientation-reversing symmetry. We transport these symmetries to a lattice, classify eleven types, and express their contribution as seven weighted orbit counts. The complete formula is printed here, together with an exact algorithm producing all counts through index $M$ in quasilinear bit time with fast integer multiplication. We also prove that the proportion of achiral fullerenes with a unique orientation-reversing symmetry tends to one as the size increases. That symmetry is either a reflection or a fixed-point-free involution, with cumulative proportions $527/529$ and $2/529$. Among all fullerenes on $2m$ vertices, the achiral proportion has order $m^{-5}$; the same order holds cumulatively. The exceptional achiral classes with nontrivial orientation-preserving symmetry number $O(m^2)$.

papers.title: Counting Classical Fullerenes VII: Arithmetic Unranking of Fullerene Isomers
papers.abstract: Given a vertex number $2m$ and a rank, we construct the corresponding ordinary fullerene as a planar adjacency list. Choosing the rank uniformly therefore samples ordinary isomorphism classes exactly from the vertex number alone. We select an integral period by counting lattice points on a quadratic level in polytopes with fixed facet directions. For a fixed positive semidefinite integral form on a box of radius $H$, with a linear term of coefficients $O(H)$, the algorithm computes all level counts simultaneously in $O(H^2\operatorname{polylog}(2m))$ bit operations when $H=O(\sqrt m)$ and the facet offsets have $O(\log(2m))$ bits. A signed decomposition into orthogonal simplices gives this bound. For fullerenes we use deterministic $O(m^2\operatorname{polylog}(2m))$ bit work to construct an index of $O(m\log(2m))$ bits. With this index a rank costs $O(m\operatorname{polylog}(2m))$ bit work, uniformly in the rank. Two families of recuts let energy descent escape self-contacts in the slit polygon. The decoder then writes the graph from its selected period in $O(m)$ arithmetic word operations.

papers.title: Auditing Identity and Timing Signals in Operational Logs
papers.abstract: Models that predict events from operational logs, such as sepsis in ICU records or failures in hard drives, can score well by recognizing which patient or drive a record came from, or when it was recorded, instead of predicting the event. I introduce two simple audits that measure how much of this information a dataset carries before any event-prediction model is trained, and apply them to seven public datasets in six domains. One asks whether a classifier can tell that two records came from the same unit; the other asks which of two records from the same unit came later. Under the stated nulls, both have expected AUC 0.5. In ICU data, the identity audit flags a common preprocessing step: carrying the last measurement forward raises identity AUC from 0.916 to 0.993. On a 12-hour sepsis forecasting task, carrying forward makes a model look 0.163 AUC better than raw values when a patient's hours are split between training and test, but only 0.046 better when patients are held out. The exaggeration under patient overlap also appears in a second ICU dataset with mortality as the outcome. On the sepsis task, a chronological control with complete follow-up, in which training sees only a patient's earlier, resolved hours, shows no positive mean overlap gap. Timing is a strong predictor: with complete follow-up, hour of stay and measurement counts alone, with no clinical value, score 0.761 on held-out patients, and adding the raw clinical values changes that by +0.018. Outside the ICU, 95% of drives and 75% of loans have records on both sides of a calendar cut, and the overlap gap persists under a calendar split. The audits show which features and preprocessing choices to check; the evaluation protocol decides the consequences. I release the code, a library that runs the audits on any table with a unit column and a time column, and a guide to using the audits.
papers.intro:
An event-prediction model may recognize the patient, loan or drive that produced a record, or infer where that record falls in time. When labels are correlated within units, recognizing a unit seen in training can improve test scores without improving predictions for new units. Prior work documents these evaluation failures (Kaufman et al., 2012; Kapoor and Narayanan, 2023; Tampu et al., 2022; Chaibub Neto et al., 2019). The appropriate split follows from deployment: new units require unit-disjoint evaluation, while predictions for known units require training information available before prediction. An audit score does not change those requirements.

I introduce two audits, both run on units with no recorded event (Figure 1A). The identity test distinguishes same-unit from different-unit pairs matched on time and offset. The temporal test distinguishes earlier from later records within a unit. Using established classification and verification methods (Lopez-Paz and Oquab, 2017; Jain et al., 2004), I measure unit identity and temporal ordering as dataset properties, without fitting a downstream event-prediction model and with expected held-out AUC 0.5 under the stated nulls. To my knowledge, no earlier work measures both signals together on the same panels across domains. Controlled downstream comparisons then examine how their consequences depend on preprocessing and evaluation design.

What the audit adds is a measurement of which features and preprocessing choices make records recognizable, and that measurement points at real problems. In ICU data, carry-forward imputation makes records from the same patient much easier to match (identity AUC 0.916 to 0.993), and it exaggerates its own benefit more than threefold when a patient’s hours are randomly split across training and test (0.163 against 0.046). The overlap effect also appears in a second ICU dataset with mortality as the outcome. On the sepsis task, a within-patient chronological control with complete follow-up shows no positive mean overlap gap, so a recognizable patient does not produce an inflated score under every protocol. Timing works the same way: the audit locates timing signal in ICU measurement counts, and on the sepsis task evaluated here hour of stay plus those counts, with no clinical value, scores 0.761 on held-out patients. Adding the raw clinical values raises that to 0.779 (complete follow-up). A calendar split does not remove the unit: 95% of drives and 75% of loans have records on both sides of an 80th-percentile cut, and the overlap gap persists there (+0.041 for drives, +0.043 for mortgages).

Contributions. 1. Controlled evaluation experiments. Fixed test rows and matched training counts isolate the effect of replacing other-unit training rows with test-unit rows. The experiments cover six datasets in five of the six domains, including both ICU datasets, and add multiple imputations and sepsis forecasting with chronological and clock-baseline controls (Sections 4–5). 2. A survey of seven datasets in six domains. Feature ablations locate identity and timing information in operational logs. Mortgage clocks account for most timing discrimination; ICU measurement counts carry both signals. Drawing the different unit from those most similar to the first shows that the identity signal belongs to individual units in drives, mortgages, vessels and ICU records, and mostly to the kind of student in clickstreams (Section 3). 3. Reusable software and practical guidance. A panel adapter and a declaration of units, timestamps, features and offsets are enough to run the audits. Section 6 explains how to use them to choose follow-up comparisons, and Appendix B provides a demonstration requiring no data download. A separate library, whowhen, runs the audits on any table from one call (Appendix I).

papers.title: Bigger Model or Bigger Table? How Much Backbone a Chorus N-gram Module Replaces
papers.abstract: We ask how much of a transformer's backbone the Chorus N-gram module replaces. Chorus adds hashed tables of token bigrams and trigrams to its input and attention. We train models of 16M to 349M parameters on 1.34 billion tokens of Polish printed before 1918 and find the size of a plain model with the same held-out loss. A separate learning-rate search for each kind of model cuts Chorus's gain at 47M by about a third. With tables about as large as the backbone, Chorus then matches a plain model 1.34 times its size at 16M and 1.16 to 1.20 times from 107M to 349M. With these tables, each added parameter replaces at most 0.31 backbone parameters. Chorus trains slower than a plain model of its size and faster than one of the same loss. On a fact quiz the two differ about as much as two seeds of one model. The results rest on one corpus, one 8,000-token vocabulary and a fifth of an epoch.
papers.intro:
Lookup memories give a language model more parameters with little added computation per token. Engram (Cheng et al., 2026) reads hashed N-gram embeddings into the residual stream, and Chorus (Chung and Du, 2026a) shares one set of N-gram tables between the input and the attention values of many layers. Chung and Du vary Chorus’s tables from 20M to 9.6B parameters on a backbone of 21M and train one table size each on backbones of 17M and 133M. Someone choosing a model needs to know how many backbone parameters a table of a given size replaces, and whether that number changes with the size of the backbone.

We call the transformer that Chorus is added to the backbone, and the same transformer trained without Chorus the plain model. For each Chorus model we read off the size a plain model needs for the same held-out loss, its equivalent size. A learning rate shared by both kinds of model can favour one of them, so we search the rate at every size for each kind separately. Section 4 reports the effect of the rate search, equivalent sizes at several token budgets, larger tables, the parts of the module, a fact quiz and training throughput.

papers.title: Recursive Word Conditioning for Higher-Dimensional Partitions: Exact Enumeration and Complexity
papers.abstract: Let $p_d(n)$ denote the number of $d$-dimensional partitions of weight $n$. We develop an exact enumeration method operating on recursively parsed partition words (which are shown to encode $d$-dimensional partitions), beginning with an elementary interior-part decomposition of ordinary partitions. Conditioning on an interior word block separates the preceding and succeeding nested blocks. For higher-dimensional partitions, transversely re-parsing the preceding words permits the same conditioning operation to be iterated. Recursive containment and joins carry effective floors across the cuts, while a nonnegative excess permits exact truncation and pruning. The resulting procedure is a complete row-conditioning algorithm. For every fixed $d\ge3$, we prove that it computes $p_d(0),\ldots,p_d(N)$ using at most $\exp\!\bigl(O_d(N^{(d-1)/(d+1)}\log(N+2))\bigr)$ arithmetic operations. A diagonal refinement replaces the final row-conditioning stages by coupled interlacing chains of ordinary-partition words and sharpens the bound to $\exp\!\bigl(O_d(N^{(d-1)/(d+1)})\bigr)$. The algorithms count constrained completions through reusable weight-indexed coefficients rather than enumerating finished partitions. Exact computations with these algorithms reach weights 100, 50, 45, 40 and 35 in dimensions 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7, respectively. On a single 2.1\,GHz core the program computes $p_3(0),\ldots,p_3(100)$ in under four hours and each of the tables in dimensions 4--7 in under 30 minutes.

The computational history of solid partitions illustrates this difficulty. Early methods include those of Atkin, Bratley, Macdonald and McKay, and Knuth [11, 12]. Mustonen and Rajesh extended exact enumeration through weight 50 [1]. Balakrishnan, Govindarajan and Prabhakar subsequently developed shape-equivalence methods and parallel computation, extending the sequence through weight 68; an IIT Madras computation reached weight 72 in January 2013 [16, 17]. Other approaches, including Govindarajan’s structural decompositions and the more recent socle-reduction method of Graffeo, Monavari, Moschetti and Ricolfi, advance enumeration through different reductions [18, 24]. The present work instead uses recursive conditioning of nested partition chains.

The organizing operation in this paper is interior word conditioning: instead of generating a partition word from its first block (Section 2 shows that these words recursively encode dd-dimensional partitions), fix a block in its unique recursive parse. The blocks preceding the cut must contain it and therefore carry compulsory weight; the succeeding blocks form a bounded continuation (Figure 1). The resulting exact enumeration is of residual freedom above a forced minimum, not of completed partitions one by one. Re-reading the preceding blocks transversely produces a decreasing chain of coupled lower-dimensional words on which the same conditioning operation can be repeated. The re-reading itself preserves all information; it is the next conditioning cut that bounds an additional index direction. Recursive joins encode inherited floors, and nonnegative excess weights make the remaining budget explicit. This yields a complete row-conditioning algorithm. A second reading uses diagonal blocks, again ordinary partition words, but with interlacing in place of containment. Its stronger compulsory completion weights lead to the improved operation bound. In both algorithms the states remain partition words: the row construction uses recursive containment between parsed blocks, while the diagonal construction uses interlacing between ordinary-partition words.

The method has several antecedents but differs in how its counting problems are organised. Classical Durfee decompositions use distinguished interior structures [2]; transfer-matrix and umbral methods maintain boundary data across configurations [9]; and diagonal interlacing is classical in plane partitions and the Schur process [15]. Related enumerations with prescribed shapes or boundaries appear in the work of Stanley, Gansner, Sagan and Morales–Pak–Panova, and in topological-vertex constructions [4, 5, 6, 7, 8]. Amanov and Yeliussizov give a MacMahon-type product for higher-dimensional partitions counted by a corner-hook statistic rather than by volume [21]. Earlier solid-partition computations exploited sophisticated shape grouping, while recent all-dimensional methods use embedding-dimension and socle reduction. The contribution here is the systematic combination of interior conditioning, effective floors, recursive dimension reduction and reusable constrained completion counts, together with uniform complexity bounds. In particular, the method addresses completion above arbitrary finite floors rather than relying on an unrestricted product formula.

papers.title: Focus Only on What's Important: Training-Free Focus Maps for Frozen Vision Transformers in Long-Video Object Segmentation
papers.abstract: Vision transformers are strong but costly image encoders for video object segmentation. Training-free token merging cuts compute uniformly across the frame, including on tracked objects. We give a frozen DINOv3 ViT inside a trained Cutie head a training-free focus map: full resolution where the segmenter expects its objects and coarser merging elsewhere. Protecting only the previous frame's mask works on short clips but fails on long videos, where fast motion pushes targets outside the margin and into background merging, locking in loss. Our policy instead takes the union of velocity-shifted and block-matched masks, runs a camera-compensated surprise check, delegates uncertain regions to the compared merger, and falls back to it when all objects are lost. On long videos (LVOS V2 valid, pre-specified protocol, three ViT-S seeds), it beats ALGM 0.98 by +2.76 J&F (95% object CI [+1.22,+4.44]; video-cluster [+0.99,+4.52]) at 16% fewer counted encoder FLOPs (0.385 vs. 0.459), sitting 1.0 J&F point below the dense-encoder baseline; at ViT-B the gain over ALGM 0.95 is +3.89 [+2.03,+5.87]. On DAVIS 2017 val it stays within -0.19 J&F of the dense encoder at ViT-S (-0.12 at ViT-B). Controls qualify the result: protecting only the previous mask under ALGM matches or exceeds accuracy at higher FLOPs (0.486), so expectation and surprise mainly reduce counted encoder compute. Practically, lower counted encoder compute did not reduce startup-inclusive mean Cutie step time on a 12-video LVOS sample (3%-8% lower in steady state; an equally engineered ALGM is faster at ViT-S and ViT-B). Section 5.2 separately examines a Cutie permanent-memory schedule and its latency and memory trade-offs. Code: https://github.com/boletoms/focused-cv
papers.intro:
Frozen self-supervised vision transformers such as DINOv3 [36] give strong dense features, which makes them attractive encoders for video object segmentation (VOS). Their cost grows with the number of patch tokens, and VOS processes every frame at high resolution. Training-free token reduction [2, 27, 21, 39, 22] lowers that cost by merging similar tokens, with one rule for the whole image.

Frozen self-supervised vision transformers such as DINOv3 [36] give strong dense features, which makes them attractive encoders for video object segmentation (VOS). Their cost grows with the number of patch tokens, and VOS processes every frame at high resolution. Training-free token reduction [2, 27, 21, 39, 22] lowers that cost by merging similar tokens, with one rule for the whole image.

VOS offers something these methods do not use: the segmenter’s prediction for the previous frame says where the objects are. A natural design keeps the predicted objects, plus a margin, at full resolution and merges the rest hard. We call the per-patch map that decides how much compute each patch gets a focus map, and its full-resolution patches the focus areas. On short DAVIS clips the closed-loop focus map works: it comes within 1 𝒥&ℱ\mathcal{J}\&\mathcal{F} of dense at 0.29 of dense FLOPs, half of what ALGM 0.98 uses (Section 5.6). On long videos it fails. Our diagnostics (Section 3.2) show why: when a target moves more than two patches between frames, part of it falls outside the margin and is merged with the background; the target is lost, and since the map follows the prediction, it stays lost. On such frames the closed-loop map loses targets nine times as often as dense; away from fast motion it loses them no more often than dense.

We propose to stop trusting the last mask: expect where each object will be, then check the frame against that expectation. The method has four parts, all training-free (Figure 1): 1. Expectation. For each tracked object, take the union of its velocity-shifted and block-matched masks (found on the current frame’s pooled pixels), grown by one patch (two at ViT-B). This region runs at full resolution. 2. Surprise check. A per-patch mismatch between the current frame and the previous frame shifted by the estimated camera motion, with a variance floor and a small spatial tolerance. Patches that fire are promoted, never demoted. 3. Three tiers. The expectation (high tier) is never merged. Speed-scaled rings, search regions around lost objects and surprise patches (middle tier) are merged by the compared merger’s own rules. Everything else (low tier) is merged by an aggressive budget with a floor of context tokens. 4. Fallback. When every object is lost, the frame runs the compared merger unchanged.

Our contributions are: • A diagnosis of why closed-loop focus maps fail on long videos: fast motion causes compression-induced losses that the loop locks in. • A training-free focus policy that runs at inference time in a trained Cutie head receiving stride-16 features from frozen DINOv3 (tested with one segmenter, Cutie, and one backbone family, DINOv3), conditioning compute on an expectation of object and camera motion, a surprise check, and a fallback to the compared merger. • A pre-specified evaluation: the rule for every adoption decision was written in dated plan files before the run that tested it, and the long-video test pools three heads (one base head fine-tuned with three seeds), at ViT-S and again at ViT-B. We report every run, including failures. • Ablations showing that full resolution in the expected region is necessary, and an exact attribution of where the long-video gain comes from. • A training-free permanent-memory schedule for Cutie (a finding about the segmenter, not the focus map) and, with it, operating points at which the encoder runs at about a third of dense FLOPs at or above dense accuracy on held-out long videos (Section 5.2). • A graph-compatible implementation that takes the same decisions as the reference implementation and turns the FLOPs saving into wall-clock speed-ups over dense, with the same engineering applied to the strongest baseline.

papers.title: Weakly Pointed Fusion $\Pi$-supercategories over fields of characteristic not two
papers.abstract: We study a class of weakly pointed fusion $\Pi$-supercategories over a field $k$ of characteristic not equal to $2$, with unit $\mathbf 1$ satisfying $\mathrm{End}(\mathbf 1) = k$. Assuming the existence of a Brauer--Wall reference category over $k$, we classify these categories up to monoidal equivalence. We show that Brauer--Wall reference categories exist for $k = \mathbb C, \mathbb R$ but not for $k = \mathbb F_5$. For each finite group $G$, we also study a product of these categories equipped with a $G$-grading and define a group $\mathcal T_k(G)$, giving an explicit formula for the multiplication in terms of group cochains for $k = \mathbb C$ and $\mathbb R$.

A physical motivation for studying this class comes from anomalies of finite group symmetries in 1+11+1-dimensional systems. Let GG be a finite group. In physics, bosonic anomalies in 1+11+1-dimensions are described by H3​(B​G,U​(1))H^{3}(BG;U(1)) [CGLW13, CGLW12]. On the mathematical side, this agrees with the classification of pointed fusion categories with Picard group GG. For fermionic anomalies in 1+11+1-dimensions, the approach initiated in [GW14] was followed by the development of a general connection with algebraic topology [Kap14, FH21]. Based on this connection, a general description was obtained in [BM18]. This motivates the study of weakly pointed fusion Π\Pi-supercategories over ℂ\mathbb{C}. Time-reversal symmetry also motivates considering the real case [GJF19].
